title: fix(sso): leave SCIM-managed groups out of SSO group sync
body:
## Problem

On every OIDC sign-in whose provider maps a groups field, `syncUserGroups` compared the groups claim with every workspace group, matching on title or email, and removed the user from each group the claim did not name. It never looked at the group's source.

SCIM stores an Entra group with its object ID as the group ID and its display name as the title. When Entra sends object IDs in the claim (the "Group ID" option our OIDC Entra guide offers), no SCIM group matches, so each SSO sign-in removes the user from all of their SCIM groups and they lose project access. `GroupService/UpdateGroup` refuses manual edits to groups with a source, so only a SCIM re-sync restored the memberships.

Linear: BYT-10342

## Change

- SSO group sync skips groups with a source (Entra ID or Okta SCIM), the same rule `UpdateGroup` enforces: SCIM owns their members. Groups without a source still follow the claim, as before.
- The add/remove decision moves into a pure function, `groupPatchesFromClaim`, which copies a group's payload instead of editing the listed group in place.

Behavior change: a groups claim no longer adds a user to, or removes a user from, a SCIM group. When SCIM and the claim disagree, SCIM wins, and SCIM-group changes arrive on the SCIM provisioning schedule rather than at the next sign-in.

Not in this PR: groups without a source are still treated as owned by the claim, so manually curated groups lose members the claim omits (SUP-275). Fixing that needs a way to record which groups SSO owns, which is a separate decision. The Entra OIDC and SCIM docs are a separate PR.

## Testing

- `TestGroupPatchesFromClaim`: manual groups by title and by email, removal when the claim omits a manual group, no-op when already a member, and three SCIM cases (object-ID claim, claim omitting the group, claim naming its title). Without the skip, exactly the three SCIM cases fail.
- End to end on dev builds of main and this branch, with Entra-shaped SCIM requests and a mock OIDC issuer whose ID token carries `groups: [<object ID>, "eng"]`. Alice starts in the SCIM group and the manual group `qa`, not in the manual group `eng`:

  | Group | main | this branch |
  |---|---|---|
  | SCIM `data-platform` (object ID) | removed | kept |
  | manual `eng` (in claim) | added | added |
  | manual `qa` (not in claim) | removed | removed |

- `go build` passes. `backend/api/v1` tests that need Docker could not run locally.

title: fix(review): head an AI review result with its title
body:
## Problem

#21896 moved a review result's priority onto a heading row of its own and named a rule result there, beside its codes. An AI result kept its title as the first line of its comment, so its heading row held the priority alone, and the title read as the first paragraph of its text.

## Change

- `ReviewMetadata.title`, in the store and in v1: the name of the problem an AI result reports, on one line. Empty for a rule result, which `rule_type` names.
- The AI reviewer writes the title there, and the comment holds the evidence, the rule, and the fix. A finding's title is collapsed to one line. A kept result keeps its title as it keeps its text, and `CompleteReviewRun` takes the title with the text, databases, and priority.
- The heading shows the title beside the priority, styled like a rule's name. The collapsed thread rows and the finding names in the Review section read it too.
- Migration `3.25/0002` moves the first line of every stored AI result into its title. AI results have kept the title in their text since 3.23.1.

This follows Claude Code's code review, which reports a finding's short label as its own field beside the statement of the problem, and flattens them into one comment only on GitHub, where a review comment has no title.

An API client that reads only `comment` no longer gets an AI result's title there; it is in `review_metadata.title`. The field is additive, and the migration converts stored results.

## Testing

- Go: `reviewrun`, `aireview`, `migrator` (a new migration test), the full `store` suite with the kept-result collision test extended to the title, and `backend/tests` collision and lifecycle tests.
- Frontend: `pnpm --dir frontend test`.
- Browser: a dev build with SQL review V2 on and a stub Gemini model. The AI card reads "P0 Do not drop a table that holds data" beside the priority, as a rule card reads "P1 Dropping objects D0101", and its text starts with the evidence. The collapsed row shows the title.

title: feat(mcp): administer_workspace changes the masking rules after a confirmation
body:
## Summary

MCP sessions could change the masking rules only in the console. This PR gives `administer_workspace` a second entry: it replaces the workspace's masking rules after the user confirms the change in their MCP client. This is part of admin changes over MCP (BYT-9292).

- The entry takes `OrgPolicyService/UpdatePolicy` for this workspace's masking rule policy, with the rule fields the console's rule editor writes: each rule's `id`, `condition.expression`, `condition.title` and `semanticType`. It also takes `policy.enforce` and `policy.resourceType` as GetPolicy returns them, since this write ignores both. It refuses every other field, and a stored rule that holds one, since the write would drop it. The tool sets the update mask.
- Before asking, it refuses a rule with no ID, an ID used twice, a kept rule whose ID changes, a rule with no condition, a condition the handler's CEL check rejects, two rules with one condition in the request or in the stored rules, another policy or workspace, and a first save without `allowMissing`.
- Rules are matched by their condition, as the approval entry matches its rules. A changed condition reads as a removed rule and an added one. A kept rule can change its type, its place or its title.
- Each line names the rule's semantic type and what masking does with it, as the masker applies it:
  - the algorithm, named as masking reasons name it: Full mask, Partial mask, Hash (MD5) or Inner/Outer mask;
  - "masks nothing", for a type whose algorithm returns every value unchanged;
  - "no such type, masks nothing", for an ID that names no type;
  - "no type (each column's own type)", for an empty type, the old None level.
- A change that can show data unmasked says so in the message: "This can unmask data, for you too." Masking gives a column the type of the first rule that matches it, so the line appears when a rule is removed or moved, or when a rule is added or given a type that is not a full mask. An added full mask and a rename never show it.
- A change too long for one form is refused. The refusal suggests smaller steps when each rule change fits a form alone, and the unmask line counts only toward the changes it is about. A step adds a rule under a new UUID before it removes the one it replaces, since two rules cannot share an ID.
- On a workspace with no rules stored, `allowMissing` makes the handler create the policy, which checks `bb.policies.createMaskingRulePolicy` and the same payload rules.
- The masker knowledge moves to `backend/component/masker`: the built-in types and how they join the workspace's types, the masker each type applies, its algorithm's name, and whether a masker can change a value or hides every value. `api/v1` calls the same functions, so the form and masking read a type the same way.
- The two entries share one form builder: the question, the fit, the too-long refusal and the place of the fixed sentence. The approval form reads as before.
- The gate's refusal, the exemption tool

title: fix(mcp): fit the approval form to the rules an agent writes
body:
## Summary

In a Claude Code test of #21876, an agent set up two approval rules: prod changes need the DBA, and test changes need no approval. The two rules did not fit one confirmation form. The prod rule's line took 71 of the form's 70 columns, so the tool refused the change as five lines, and the agent split it into two forms that applied separately. This PR makes the form fit and read closer to the console. This is part of admin changes over MCP (BYT-9292).

- Each change line states a proposal: `Add rule 1, …`, `Remove, …`, `Change, "Project owner" to "Workspace DBA"; move to rule 2: …`. An added rule's line always gives its place, since the first matching rule decides. The shorter verbs make the journey's two rules fit.
- A condition shows between backquotes, as typed, when it is one line of characters `strconv.IsPrint` accepts. For a condition that is not empty, the console's rule list shows the same text. Escaping costs a column for each quote inside a condition: with the new verbs, the prod line for `resource.environment_id == "production"` takes 72 columns escaped and 70 as typed. Any other condition stays escaped, as on main: one with a tab, a newline, a backquote, or a format character such as U+202E or U+200B. `strconv.CanBackquote` alone passes a tab and U+202E, so the check also requires `strconv.IsPrint`. The console writes a long condition on several lines, so such a condition shows escaped.
- A long change line continues on the next line after `> `, which takes 2 of the 70 columns. Every other line of the form starts with a letter, so no part of a value can pose as a line of its own. Without the mark, a string literal in a condition could wrap into a line that matched a real change line or the issue line exactly, once the condition's quotes showed as typed.
- The issue line says why it names the user's issues: `Plan edits recheck your "hr#12" under these rules.` A plan edit runs the approval check again under the rules in force. When no name fits, the line counts the issues, and it drops the count when that does not fit either.
- The refusal for a change too long for one form says that each smaller step is a form of its own and applies when the user accepts it. It tells the agent to say so to the user, to add a rule before removing the one it replaces, and to read the rules again before each step and build the step from them.

The journey's form now reads:

```
Change the approval rules for database changes, as jordan@example.com?
Add rule 1, "Workspace DBA": `resource.environment_id == "prod"`
Add rule 2, no approval: `resource.environment_id == "test"`
Plan edits recheck your "hr#101" under these rules.
```

## Notes for review

- The issue line covers issues whose approval is still being checked as well as pending ones. "Plan edits recheck" is true of both. The line does not say that an issue keeps its approvers, which would be false for an issue still being checked.
- "Plan edits recheck" holds for a plan edit that changes t

title: fix(review): post a review run's results in reading order
body:
## Summary

Resolves BYT-10401. The activity timeline shows a review run's findings in the order they posted, and that order was whatever the reviewer produced: for the AI review, database by database and then the model's own order. Two findings on line 28 could sit apart, with lines 16 and 19 between them.

A run posts its results in one batch, offset by one microsecond each to keep the batch order, so inside a run "by time" means "the order the executor returned". This PR sorts that list before it posts, so the timeline's time order becomes reading order with no frontend or API change.

- `sortReviewResults` (`backend/runner/reviewrun/result_order.go`) orders results by the plan's spec order, then the anchored start line, then priority (P0 first, unset last). The sort is stable, so remaining ties keep the reviewer's order. Results without an anchor on one of the plan's specs go last, as the plan page's finding walker already does.
- Both executors call it on their finished results. The rule executor sorts after its fingerprints are computed, so every existing thread keeps its identity.
- Every reader of the comments sees the same order: the plan page, the issue page, the API and MCP, and the in-console agent.

## Not in this PR

- Showing several findings on one line as one card with one code excerpt. With this order the frontend can do it by grouping adjacent cards, without reordering.
- The plan page's finding walker breaks ties on one line by comment name, a random UUID. It should use creation time so it agrees with the timeline.
- Runs posted before this change keep their order. A rule finding that a later run repeats keeps its thread and its place in the run that first posted it.

## Test plan

- [x] `TestSortReviewResults`: spec order, line order, priority on one line, stable ties, no anchor, a spec the plan no longer has
- [x] `TestRuleExecutorSortsItsResults` and `TestAIReviewExecutorSortsItsResults`: each fails with its executor's sort call removed
- [x] `go test ./backend/runner/reviewrun/`
- [x] `TestCollision_RunReviewLifecycle`, `TestCollision_ReviewRunProjectPurge`, `TestRuleReviewKeepsThreadsAcrossRuns`
- [x] golangci-lint v2.15.0: nothing on changed paths
- [x] Server build

+package reviewrun
+
+import (
+	"cmp"
+	"math"
+	"slices"
+
+	storepb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/store"
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/store"
+)
+
+// sortReviewResults puts a run's results in reading order: by the plan's spec
+// order, then by the line each result is anchored on, the highest priority
+// first on one line. A result without an anchor on one of the specs goes
+// last. The sort is stable, so results tied on all three keep the order the
+// reviewer gave. A run's results post in this order, and the activity
+// timeline shows them in the order they posted.
+func sortReviewResults(specs []*storepb.PlanConfig_Spec, results []*store.IssueCommentMessage) {
+	specIndex := make(map[string]int, len(specs))
+	for i, spec := range specs {
+		specIndex[spec.GetId()] = i
+	}
+	type place struct{ spec, line, priority int }
+	placeOf := func(result *store.IssueCommentMessage) place {
+		p := place{spec: len(specs), priority: priorityRank(result.Payload.GetReviewMetadata().GetPriority())}
+		anchor := result.Payload.GetStatementAnchor()
+		if i, ok := specIndex[anchor.GetSpecId()]; ok {
+			p.spec = i
+			p.line = int(anchor.GetStartPosition().GetLine())
+		}
+		return p
+	}
+	slices.SortStableFunc(results, func(x, y *store.IssueCommentMessage) int {
+		a, b := placeOf(x), placeOf(y)
+		return cmp.Or(cmp.Compare(a.spec, b.spec), cmp.Compare(a.line, b.line), cmp.Compare(a.priority, b.priority))
+	})
+}
+
+// priorityRank orders P0 first and a result with no priority last. The enum
+// numbers P0, P1, and P2 in that order.
+func priorityRank(priority storepb.IssueCommentPayload_ReviewMetadata_Priority) int {
+	if priority == storepb.IssueCommentPayload_ReviewMetadata_PRIORITY_UNSPECIFIED {
+		return math.MaxInt
+	}
+	return int(priority)
+}

title: feat(review): keep an AI review finding's thread across runs
body:
## Why

An AI review run resolved every earlier result of its reviewer and posted all of its findings again. Two problems followed (BYT-10372):

- A finding a person had resolved, such as a false positive or an accepted risk, came back as a new open thread and held the rollout again.
- A finding still under discussion moved to a new thread, and its replies stayed behind on the old one.

The standard rule review already keeps a finding's thread across runs (#21869, #21889) by matching fingerprints. AI results carried none, so nothing ever matched.

## What

AI results now follow the standard review's model.

- **Fingerprint.** `<statement segment>/<random>`. The segment is a hash of the spec, the statement's body, and its ordinal among equal bodies. The body is the one the rule review reads, from the first token to the last, taken from omni's `Review()` with no rules. An edit to a statement changes its segment, which makes its results outdated. An edit to the comments around it does not. An AI finding has no other stable part, so the rest is random.
- **Matching.** A run offers the merge each earlier result whose segment matches a statement of the sheet under review, as one more source beside the databases' findings on that statement. The merge prompt marks these as `earlier`, with title, rule, and fix but no evidence, because a multi-database comment names the databases there. A list holds at most one earlier finding, and the reply check enforces it.
- **Keeping.** A problem the merge groups with an earlier result keeps that result's fingerprint and text, so `CompleteReviewRun` keeps the thread with its state and replies, moves its anchor, and the problem skips summarize. Two guards hold in code:
  - A resolved result is not kept for a more severe problem: accepting a P2 does not accept a P0.
  - Nothing is kept when the merge fails.
- **Superseding.** As in the rule review, an earlier result whose statement changed, or that no finding of the run reports, is superseded.
- **Store.** A kept result now also takes the databases and priority of the result that repeats it. For the rule review these never differ.

What a user sees:

| | Statement unchanged | Statement changed |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved, found again | Stays resolved, not posted again | Superseded, posted as a new thread |
| Open, found again | Same thread, replies kept | Superseded, posted as a new thread |
| Not found again | Superseded | Superseded |

## Known limits

- **Older results.** AI results posted before this change have no fingerprint. They are superseded once on the next run, as today.
- **A missed run.** If the model misses a finding in one run, that result is superseded, and a later run posts it as a new thread. The rule review cannot hit this because it is deterministic.
- **Engines omni does not cover.** The body is the statement block's text, comments included.

## Test plan

- [x] `backend/plugin/aireview`: earlier candidates render without a database or evidence; a r

title: fix(sql-editor): migrate disable_export to disable_download and check it in the SQL Editor only
body:
Workspaces that had `disable_export = true` ("export requires approval") lost that setting in the 3.25 migration with nothing in its place. The migration now sets `disable_download = true` on their workspace query data policy, so the SQL Editor stops offering Download there. Exports from those workspaces go through an approved grant to a project's SharePoint folder. The new key is set whether or not the policy is enforced, matching how the migration already treats approval-only workspaces. Project-level `disable_export` is just dropped, because `disable_download` is a workspace-level setting.

`disable_download` becomes a SQL Editor setting only. `SQLService.Export` no longer reads the workspace policy, so API and MCP callers can still download when it is set. The SQL Editor still hides Download, as before. This removes `Store.GetWorkspaceQueryDataPolicy`, whose only caller was this check, along with the tests that asserted server-side rejection.

The **Allow download** setting description (all five locales), the `disable_download` proto comments with their generated API docs, `CONTEXT.md`, ADR 0006, ADR 0007 and `docs/design/sql-export-permission.md` now say the setting applies to the SQL Editor and that API and MCP clients can still download. The design doc also covers the new migration step, a release-note item, and the Terraform drift on `disable_download`.

Neither change is breaking for released versions: `disable_download` and the 3.25 migration are both newer than 3.24.0.

## Validation

- `go test ./backend/migrator/ -run '^TestMigration3_25_0'`: the approval-only and unenforced workspaces gain `disableDownload: true`, and every other payload is unchanged.
- `go test ./backend/api/v1/ -run 'Export|SharePoint|QueryData'` and `./backend/store/ -run 'TestGetExportSetting|QueryData'` pass.
- `golangci-lint` reports no issues in changed files, server build succeeds, and `useExportDestination.test.ts` passes.
- `buf format`, `buf lint` and `buf generate` run cleanly; the generated changes are the updated field comment.

title: feat(sql-editor): show elapsed time while exporting to SharePoint
body:
A SharePoint export can wait for minutes while the server retries throttled or unavailable Microsoft Graph requests. During that time the export sheet showed only "Exporting to SharePoint…" with an indeterminate bar, so a slow export looked the same as a stuck one.

The progress label now shows the elapsed time from the start, in whole seconds: "Exporting to SharePoint… 12s". Exports that cover several databases show it too: "Exported 3 of 10 databases 12s". After a minute, a line under the bar explains the wait: "Large results or a busy SharePoint can take a few minutes. Bytebase retries automatically." Downloads are unchanged.

The timer is the SQL Editor query panel's `useElapsed` hook, moved to `src/hooks/useElapsed.ts` so both use it. It now returns whole seconds, so the query panel shows "3s" instead of "3.2s". The hook updates once per second, so the decimal never changed while it ran.

The new message is translated in all five locales.

## Validation

- `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` pass.
- New `DataExportButton` tests use fake timers to cover the SharePoint timer at 0s, 10s and 75s, the slow-export message after a minute and its removal when the export finishes, and an unchanged download.

title: fix(cosmosdb): group and order cross-partition queries the way the service does
body:
Four fixes to how the pure-Go query engine answers a grouped or ordered
cross-partition query. Each one was measured against the service, with the
gateway given a partition key as the oracle — on that path the engine is
bypassed, so its answer is the one Cosmos itself gives.

### A grouped query came back in the wrong order

A grouped query the user also ordered reaches the engine as a plan with no
order fields at all: `orderBy` and `orderByExpressions` are empty and the
ORDER BY survives only inside `rewrittenQuery`. #21895 therefore read the
direction off the data, comparing adjacent documents inside one partition
response and taking the first pair that differed. A response that reports a
single group tells it nothing, so when no physical range holds two distinct
group keys the direction stayed unknown and the rows went out ascending — an
`ORDER BY … DESC` answered in the wrong order. That needs only a group key the
partition key determines, which is what grouping on the partition key does.
The same inference also read a direction out of whatever order an unordered
GROUP BY happened to come back in, so that query's output direction could
differ between runs.

The order now comes from the clause, one key at a time: each key is matched to
the group expression it names and compared in its own direction, so a
multi-key clause mixing ASC and DESC is answered as written, and a clause
naming only some of the keys orders by those first. Keys the clause leaves out
are appended ascending, since the clause does not constrain them and ordering
them is what makes repeated runs agree. The clause naming a subset was wrong
before this too: `GROUP BY c.bucket, c.seq ORDER BY c.seq` came back ordered by
bucket first.

### …and could not be read at all through a quoted property path

Locating the ORDER BY by plain substring, and refusing a key that holds a
quote, broke two grouped queries the service accepts: an order on a property
that needs bracket notation, and a property named `order by`, whose name was
read as the clause. The clause is now located and split outside quoted text.

### A grouped query failed outright on a column some documents lack

Ordinary in a schemaless store, and the gateway reports that group's key as a
`groupByItems` entry with no `"item"` at all. Canonicalizing it failed, so one
document missing one property failed the whole query with
`unexpected end of JSON input`. It is a group of its own now — the service
counts it apart from an explicit `null` — and its alias is left out of the row,
which is how the service spells it.

### An array or object in an ORDER BY column overtook every other row

The comparator refused those shapes and the merge then fell back to comparing
partition indexes, so instead of sorting last they appeared at the front:

| | order |
|---|---|
| service | undefined, null, false, 1, "a", [1,2], [2], [1,3], {"b":1}, {"a":2}, {"a":1} |
| engine before | undefined, **[1,2]**, **{"b":1}**, undefined, null, null, false,

title: feat(review): head a review result with its priority, rule, and codes
body:
## Why

Review result comments showed too much, some of it twice, and in a different order on each surface (BYT-10374). Following GitHub, a result now reads: who and when, the databases it applies to, its priority and rule, then the finding. omni's finding codes (omni #620) name the condition each finding reports, the same on every engine, but Bytebase only used them for a finding's identity across runs and never showed them.

## What

**Review result layout** (plan page threads, Review activity, issue detail):

- Row 1: reviewer and time. The priority badge and the Open badge are gone from it.
- Row 2: targets, unchanged except that the database chips now line up with the label.
- Row 3: the priority, then for a standard rule result the rule name (description on hover) and its finding codes.
- Then the finding's text. The separate "Rule" line at the bottom is gone.
- A resolved thread shows Resolved in its footer beside Reopen, also for a reader who can neither reply nor reopen. Its collapsed row keeps Resolved.

**Finding codes:**

- `codes` is added to `ReviewMetadata` in both the store and v1 protos (additive). The rule review fills it from omni's `Finding.Codes`, and AI results leave it empty.
- A code shows as a chip with omni's title on hover, such as `WT101` "Object doesn't exist". The chips don't link yet, because the per-code pages don't exist.

**Standard rule settings** (workspace and project SQL Review pages, dev builds):

- The rule list names the engines the rule review covers.
- Each rule lists its codes. A rule that fewer engines check lists its engines:
  - walk-through: every engine but Snowflake;
  - online migration: MySQL, MariaDB, and OceanBase;
  - prior backup: every engine but Snowflake and OceanBase.
- An engine counts for a rule only if it checks it. An engine that only reports it has no such feature (OM101 or PB101) is left out.
- The facts live in `frontend/src/components/sql-review/standardRuleCatalog.json`:
  - `TestFrontendStandardRuleCatalogInSync` (reviewrun) builds it from `reviewFuncs`, each engine's omni `Rules`, a probe for OM101 and PB101, and `review.Codes()`. It fails when the file drifts. Set `recordCatalog` to regenerate it. This follows the gh-ost `flags.json` check.
  - The plan page's hand-kept list of reviewed engines now reads the catalog.

**P0 hover text:** removed. It said the SQL must change, but omni has decided a P0 can be resolved without a change. P1 and P2 keep theirs.

AI results keep their `Rule:` and `Suggested fix:` text. Row 3 shows only their priority until there is a separate rule field.

## Screenshots

Standard rule results on the plan page (P1, P0):

![P1 card](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rebelice/4895fdfcff32371538631e35ec8618cb/raw/654ee6451cf329f5ffb65abccffbcef1209986d4/rule-card-p1.png)

![P0 card](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rebelice/4895fdfcff32371538631e35ec8618cb/raw/678b11822516daaf1702ec91d9d7e8887848e139/rule-card-p0.png)

Resolved, expanded and collapse

title: fix(cosmosdb): implement the query-plan operators the engine composed wrongly
body:
> Based on main so CI runs — `.github/workflows/ci.yml` only triggers for pull requests targeting `main`, so a PR stacked on another branch gets no checks at all. The branch carries #21893's commit first, so **review the second commit**; this diff narrows to it on its own once #21893 merges.

Part 2 of two for BYT-10397, stacked on https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/pull/21893. Part 1 made every plan field the chosen pipeline could not honour an error; this one implements the compositions, so the queries answer instead of failing.

Every number below is measured on the emulator fixture the issue names: two physical partitions, 2130 rows across 8 partition key values, every row carrying a distinct `seq`. Each row of the table has a case in `TestCrossPartition*` that fails on `main` and passes here — the "before" column is that run's output.

| query | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket` | 2130 rows (every row in the container) | the 8 buckets, sorted |
| `SELECT DISTINCT VALUE c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket` | `unsupported plan feature` | the 8 buckets, sorted |
| `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3` | `[big-1, big-1, big-1]` | `[small-1, small-2, small-3]` |
| `SELECT TOP 5 c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq DESC` | 10 rows: `2129…2125, 2114…2110` | `2129, 2128, 2127, 2126, 2125` |
| `SELECT TOP 1025 c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq ASC` | 2050 rows | 1025 rows, `0…1024` |
| `SELECT DISTINCT VALUE c.bucket FROM c OFFSET 0 LIMIT 3` | 6 rows | 3 rows |
| `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3` | 4 rows | 3 rows |
| `SELECT c.bucket, COUNT(1) AS n FROM c GROUP BY c.bucket ORDER BY c.bucket` | 8 groups, unordered and different every run | 8 groups, ascending by bucket |
| … `ORDER BY c.bucket DESC` | same unordered rows | 8 groups, descending |
| `SELECT c.bucket, COUNT(1) AS n FROM c GROUP BY c.bucket` | a different order on each of 3 runs | the same order on each |
| `SELECT VALUE MIN(c.seq) FROM c WHERE c.seq > 99999999` | `gonative/agg.min: unexpected end of JSON input` | no rows |
| `SELECT VALUE MAX(…)` / `AVG(…)` over the same empty set | the same error / one row of `null` | no rows |
| `SELECT MIN(c.seq) AS m FROM c WHERE c.seq > 99999999` | `{"m":null}` | `{}` |
| `SELECT MIN(c.seq) AS lo, MAX(c.seq) AS hi FROM …` | `{"lo":null,"hi":null}` | `{}` |
| `SELECT VALUE MIN(c.seq) FROM c` (rows do match) | `json: cannot unmarshal number into Go value of type gonative.minPartial` | `0` |
| `SELECT c.seq FROM c OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3` | `unsupported plan feature` | 3 rows |
| `SELECT VALUE COUNT(1) FROM c OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1` | one row, `2130` | no rows |

The gateway is the oracle for all of these: run the same query with a partition key supplied and the engine is bypassed, which is where every "after" comes from.

Unchanged on purpose: `COUNT` and `SUM` over an empty set really are one row of `0`, and both are controls in the new test.

## How each one works

**TOP, DISTIN
author: d-bytebase
diff:
--- backend/plugin/db/cosmosdb/cosmosdb_test.go (+277/-0)
@@ -998,3 +998,280 @@ func TestCrossPartitionQueryLimit(t *testing.T) {
 	assert.Len(t, results[0].Rows, 7)
 	assert.EqualValues(t, 7, results[0].RowsCount)
 }
+
+// ------------------------------------ composed operators, local emulator
+//
+// The query classes in BYT-10397: each composes two operators the gateway
+// reports in one plan, and the engine used to honour only one of them. Every
+// case here runs on the multi-page fixture, because two of them (TOP with
+// ORDER BY, and DISTINCT with a LIMIT) answer correctly on a single physical
+// partition however the engine is broken.
+
+// pagedQuery runs a query against the multi-page fixture and returns its rows
+// as raw JSON, in the order the engine emitted them.
+func pagedQuery(t *testing.T, container *azcosmos.ContainerClient, sql string) []string {
+	t.Helper()
+	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Minute)
+	defer cancel()
+	items, err := QueryEveryPartition(ctx, container, sql, nil, 0)
+	require.NoError(t, err, "QueryEveryPartition: %s", sql)
+	rows := make([]string, 0, len(items))
+	for _, item := range items {
+		rows = append(rows, string(item))
+	}
+	return rows
+}
+
+// pagedBucketValues reads the bucket out of every row, for both spellings of
+// a projection: `{"bucket":"big-1"}` and the VALUE form's bare `"big-1"`.
+func pagedBucketValues(t *testing.T, rows []string) []string {
+	t.Helper()
+	out := make([]string, 0, len(rows))
+	for _, row := range rows {
+		var object struct {
+			Bucket *string `json:"bucket"`
+		}
+		if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(row), &object); err == nil && object.Bucket != nil {
+			out = append(out, *object.Bucket)
+			continue
+		}
+		var scalar string
+		require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal([]byte(row), &scalar), "row: %s", row)
+		out = append(out, scalar)
+	}
+	return out
+}
+
+// sortedPagedBuckets is the fixture's partition key values in ascending order.
+func sortedPagedBuckets() []string {
+	buckets := append(append([]string(nil), pagedBigBuckets...), pagedSmallBuckets...)
+	slices.Sort(buckets)
+	return buckets
+}
+
+// pagedBucketRows is how many rows each partition key value holds.
+func pagedBucketRows(bucket string) int {
+	if slices.Contains(pagedBigBuckets, bucket) {
+		return pagedBigRows
+	}
+	return pagedSmallRows
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionDistinctComposed covers DISTINCT alongside an ORDER BY or
+// a page. The service reports distinctType "Unordered" for the object form
+// even under ORDER BY, so the engine dropped the DISTINCT and returned every
+// row in the container; a paged DISTINCT ran the user's own query per range,
+// so each range applied the LIMIT to itself before anything was deduplicated.
+func TestCrossPartitionDistinctComposed(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+	buckets := sortedPagedBuckets()
+
+	t.Run("order_by_object_form", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, buckets, pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket`)))
+	})
+
+	t.Run("order_by_value_form", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, buckets, pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT VALUE c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket`)))
+	})
+
+	t.Run("order_by_descending", func(t *testing.T) {
+		want := sortedPagedBuckets()
+		slices.Reverse(want)
+		assert.Equal(t, want, pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket DESC`)))
+	})
+
+	// An ordered DISTINCT pins the page against exact values; the unordered
+	// forms below can only be held to the count, since Cosmos defines no
+	// order for them.
+	t.Run("order_by_with_a_page", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, buckets[2:5], pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c ORDER BY c.bucket OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3`)))
+	})
+
+	t.Run("limit_value_form", func(t *testing.T) {
+		got := pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT VALUE c.bucket FROM c OFFSET 0 LIMIT 3`))
+		assert.Len(t, got, 3)
+		assert.Subset(t, buckets, got)
+		assert.Len(t, slices.Compact(slices.Sorted(slices.Values(got))), 3, "values must be distinct")
+	})
+
+	t.Run("offset_limit_object_form", func(t *testing.T) {
+		got := pagedBucketValues(t,
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT DISTINCT c.bucket FROM c OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3`))
+		assert.Len(t, got, 3)
+		assert.Subset(t, buckets, got)
+		assert.Len(t, slices.Compact(slices.Sorted(slices.Values(got))), 3, "values must be distinct")
+	})
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionTopWithOrderBy covers TOP alongside an ORDER BY. The
+// rewritten per-range query carries the TOP, so the merge saw n rows from
+// every range and emitted all of them: n x partitions rows, in order.
+func TestCrossPartitionTopWithOrderBy(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+	rows := pagedRows()
+
+	t.Run("ascending", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, ascendingSeqs(0, 5),
+			pagedSeqs(t, container, `SELECT TOP 5 c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq ASC`))
+	})
+
+	t.Run("descending", func(t *testing.T) {
+		want := ascendingSeqs(rows-5, rows)
+		slices.Reverse(want)
+		assert.Equal(t, want, pagedSeqs(t, container, `SELECT TOP 5 c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq DESC`))
+	})
+
+	// A TOP past the gateway's page cap has to keep reading the ranges after
+	// the cap, and still stop at n.
+	t.Run("above_the_page_cap", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, ascendingSeqs(0, pagedPageSize+25),
+			pagedSeqs(t, container, fmt.Sprintf(
+				`SELECT TOP %d c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq ASC`, pagedPageSize+25)))
+	})
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionGroupByOrder covers the order GROUP BY rows come back in.
+// The pipeline emitted them straight out of a Go map, so the same query
+// answered in a different order every run, and a GROUP BY the user ordered
+// reaches the engine as a plan with no order fields at all — the ORDER BY
+// survives only inside the rewritten query.
+func TestCrossPartitionGroupByOrder(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+
+	type group struct {
+		Bucket string `json:"bucket"`
+		N      int    `json:"n"`
+	}
+	groupsOf := func(t *testing.T, rows []string) []group {
+		t.Helper()
+		out := make([]group, 0, len(rows))
+		for _, row := range rows {
+			var g group
+			require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal([]byte(row), &g), "row: %s", row)
+			out = append(out, g)
+		}
+		return out
+	}
+	want := make([]group, 0, len(sortedPagedBuckets()))
+	for _, bucket := range sortedPagedBuckets() {
+		want = append(want, group{Bucket: bucket, N: pagedBucketRows(bucket)})
+	}
+
+	t.Run("order_by_the_group_key", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, want, groupsOf(t, pagedQuery(t, container,
+			`SELECT c.bucket, COUNT(1) AS n FROM c GROUP BY c.bucket ORDER BY c.bucket`)))
+	})
+
+	t.Run("order_by_descending", func(t *testing.T) {
+		reversed := slices.Clone(want)
+		slices.Reverse(reversed)
+		assert.Equal(t, reversed, groupsOf(t, pagedQuery(t, container,
+			`SELECT c.bucket, COUNT(1) AS n FROM c GROUP BY c.bucket ORDER BY c.bucket DESC`)))
+	})
+
+	// Without an ORDER BY the order is Cosmos's to choose, but it must be the
+	// same on every run.
+	t.Run("unordered_is_stable_across_runs", func(t *testing.T) {
+		const sql = `SELECT c.bucket, COUNT(1) AS n FROM c GROUP BY c.bucket`
+		first := groupsOf(t, pagedQuery(t, container, sql))
+		assert.ElementsMatch(t, want, first)
+		for range 2 {
+			assert.Equal(t, first, groupsOf(t, pagedQuery(t, container, sql)))
+		}
+	})
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionEmptyAggregates covers an aggregate whose filter matches
+// no row. MIN and MAX failed the query outright, because an empty partition's
+// partial is an absent one; the aliased form answered `{"m":null}` where the
+// gateway omits the alias. COUNT and SUM really are 0 over an empty set and
+// are here as controls.
+func TestCrossPartitionEmptyAggregates(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+	const noRows = `WHERE c.seq > 99999999`
+
+	for _, tc := range []struct {
+		name string
+		sql  string
+		want []string
+	}{
+		{"min_value", `SELECT VALUE MIN(c.seq) FROM c ` + noRows, nil},
+		{"max_value", `SELECT VALUE MAX(c.seq) FROM c ` + noRows, nil},
+		{"avg_value", `SELECT VALUE AVG(c.seq) FROM c ` + noRows, nil},
+		{"min_aliased", `SELECT MIN(c.seq) AS m FROM c ` + noRows, []string{`{}`}},
+		{"min_max_aliased", `SELECT MIN(c.seq) AS lo, MAX(c.seq) AS hi FROM c ` + noRows, []string{`{}`}},
+		{"count_value", `SELECT VALUE COUNT(1) FROM c ` + noRows, []string{`0`}},
+		{"count_aliased", `SELECT COUNT(1) AS n FROM c ` + noRows, []string{`{"n":0}`}},
+		{"sum_value", `SELECT VALUE SUM(c.seq) FROM c ` + noRows, []string{`0`}},
+	} {
+		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			got := pagedQuery(t, container, tc.sql)
+			require.Len(t, got, len(tc.want))
+			for i := range tc.want {
+				assert.JSONEq(t, tc.want[i], got[i])
+			}
+		})
+	}
+
+	// The same MIN and MAX over rows that do match: the VALUE form reads its
+	// partial from item2, which is where the count lives.
+	t.Run("min_max_over_rows_that_match", func(t *testing.T) {
+		assert.Equal(t, []string{`0`}, pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT VALUE MIN(c.seq) FROM c`))
+		assert.Equal(t, []string{fmt.Sprint(pagedRows() - 1)},
+			pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT VALUE MAX(c.seq) FROM c`))
+	})
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionOffsetLimitWithoutOrderBy covers ordinary result paging,
+// which the engine rejected although it advertises OffsetAndLimit. Cosmos
+// defines no order for it, so only the count and the rows' provenance hold.
+func TestCrossPartitionOffsetLimitWithoutOrderBy(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+
+	seqs := pagedSeqs(t, container, `SELECT c.seq FROM c OFFSET 2 LIMIT 3`)
+	require.Len(t, seqs, 3)
+	assert.Len(t, slices.Compact(slices.Sorted(slices.Values(seqs))), 3, "rows must not repeat")
+	for _, seq := range seqs {
+		assert.Less(t, seq, pagedRows())
+		assert.GreaterOrEqual(t, seq, 0)
+	}
+
+	// A window wider than the gateway's page cap reads several pages of a
+	// range before it is full.
+	wide := pagedSeqs(t, container, fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT c.seq FROM c OFFSET 0 LIMIT %d`, pagedPageSize+25))
+	assert.Len(t, wide, pagedPageSize+25)
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionAggregateWithOffsetLimit covers a page applied to an
+// aggregate. The query produces exactly one row, so OFFSET 1 skips past it and
+// the gateway answers with nothing; the engine returned the row regardless.
+func TestCrossPartitionAggregateWithOffsetLimit(t *testing.T) {
+	container := pagedFixture(t)
+
+	assert.Empty(t, pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT VALUE COUNT(1) FROM c OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1`))
+	assert.Equal(t, []string{fmt.Sprint(pagedRows())},
+		pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT VALUE COUNT(1) FROM c OFFSET 0 LIMIT 1`))
+	assert.Empty(t, pagedQuery(t, container, `SELECT COUNT(1) AS n FROM c OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1`))
+}
+
+// TestCrossPartitionDistinctWithOrderByThroughTheDriver runs the worst of
+// these through QueryConn, the entry point the SQL editor uses, so the SQL
+// validator is in the path too.
+func TestCrossPartitionDistinctWithOrderByThroughTheDriver(t *testing.T) {
+	driver := emulatorFixture(t)
+	rows := runQuery(t, driver, crossPartitionContainer, `SELECT DISTINCT c.country FROM c ORDER BY c.country`)
+	got := make([]string, 0, len(rows))
+	for _, row := range rows {
+		var object struct {
+			Country string `json:"country"`
+		}
+		require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal(row, &object))
+		got = append(got, object.Country)
+	}
+	assert.Equal(t, slices.Sorted(slices.Values(crossPartitionCountries)), got)
+}

title: fix(frontend): list project instances in the Create Database instance select
body:
Fixes BYT-10398.

The instance select in the Create Database sheet listed only workspace instances, so a project's own instances could not be chosen. `ListInstances` without a parent returns workspace instances only, and the select never asked for the project's.

The select now takes the sheet's project and lists that project's instances first, followed by workspace instances, in one paginated list. When the project's instances do not fill a page, the same page continues with workspace instances, so they are not hidden behind "load more". Each source is fetched only when the user can list it, so a user with only project access now sees their project's instances instead of an empty list.

On the workspace Databases page, project instances appear once a project is chosen; picking one still locks the Project field to its owner, as before.

Validation: added `InstanceSelect.test.tsx` (ordering, pagination across both sources, no project, missing permissions) and a sheet test that the project reaches the select. `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` pass.

title: feat(review): summarize a merged AI finding's evidence across databases
body:
## Why

#21890 merges the findings that several databases report into one thread, and the thread keeps every database's evidence, labeled by database. On a 10-database pilot a merged thread carries up to 3.5 KB of evidence, and the pieces say the same thing in different words: the same table comment quoted ten times, the same lock explained eight times. What sets the databases apart is usually one fact, such as a row count past the policy's limit or a column that only some tenants have. Showing one database's evidence instead hides that fact.

Other review tools show no evidence at all, since the reader can open the code. The reader of a SQL review cannot open the production database, so the evidence is the part to keep, but once, with the differences in plain sight.

## What

A step after the merge writes the comment of each problem that more than one database reports.

- `aireview.Reviewer.Summarize` makes one model call without tools per problem. The prompt shows the problem's statement and its findings as JSON lines. Each database appears as a random six-character id that occurs nowhere in the statement or the findings, so no database name reaches the model. The reply is a title, the evidence every database shares, the databases split into groups by the facts that change what the author does or how serious the problem is, and a fix.
- Code checks the reply: every database is in exactly one group, at most one group (the databases with nothing beyond the shared evidence) has no facts, and no text holds a database id, however the reference is worded. An invalid reply gets one correction round. A prompt over 256 KiB is not sent.
- `reviewrun` runs the summaries in parallel under the run's concurrency, each holding a server slot, and recovers a panic as that problem's failure. The executor reads the AI setting again before the comments post, since the merge and the summary fall back on a call that a switch-off refused.
- The comment, with names rendered by code, up to 10 per line:

  ```
  Build the orders.user_id index without blocking writes

  CREATE INDEX orders_user_id_idx ON orders (user_id) runs without CONCURRENTLY, so it takes a SHARE lock on orders for the whole build, blocking all inserts/updates/deletes to the table until it finishes.

  - **P1** on tenant_047: orders has 3,333,329 rows, over 1 million.
  - **P2** on tenant_039, tenant_046: orders has 29k to 300k rows.
  - Not flagged on tenant_001, tenant_002, tenant_003, tenant_006, tenant_036, tenant_038, tenant_044

  Rule: Flag a schema change that blocks writes on a table with more than 1 million rows, and say how to make it without blocking.

title: feat(review): merge the AI review findings that several databases report
body:
## Why

An AI review run reviews each database of the sample in its own model session. Findings merged only when the spec, the line, and the title were equal, and each session writes the title on its own, so the same problem came back as one thread per database. A dropped column on a 50-tenant group posted up to 50 threads.

A pilot on 20 sample tenants, two sheets, and the four floor models (`claude-sonnet-5`, `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gemini-3.5-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`) posted 424 threads for 594 findings, where a hand labeling counts 65 problems. Two deterministic keys were measured on the same findings and rejected:

- The cited rule: 102 threads with 8 wrong merges. Models cite different sentences for one problem, join two rules, or quote a sentence that is not a rule.
- The line alone: 43 threads with 17 wrong merges.

Both wrong-merge the finding that only one tenant has, such as a view that exists in one tenant's schema, into the problem every tenant shares. That is the finding a group review exists to show.

## What

Map-reduce, the shape of the Claude Code review plugin: independent reviews, then one call that decides which findings are the same.

- `aireview.Reviewer.MergeFindings` makes one model call without tools. The prompt shows each statement's numbered lines and the findings as JSON lines. A statement longer than 40 lines shows its first line and the lines around its findings. Databases appear as ordinals, so no database name reaches the model. The reply is only lists of finding ids.
- Every finding must be in exactly one list, and a list holds the findings of one statement. An invalid reply gets one correction round. Statements are packed into calls of at most 256 KiB, and a statement too large for one call is not merged.
- `reviewrun` takes the statements from the engine's splitter (`base.SplitMultiSQL`). Without one, or when the databases of a sheet run different engines, the whole sheet is one statement.
- Only statements that more than one database reported on go to the merge, so a single-database plan makes no extra call. The merge takes a server slot like a review.
- One thread per problem:
  - It is anchored to the line most of its findings start on, so a finding inside a long procedure keeps its own line.
  - It carries the highest priority and its lead finding's title, rule, and fix.
  - Every database's evidence is kept, labeled by database.
- When the merge fails for any reason, every finding posts on its own. The run still completes, and no finding is lost.

## Evaluation

The pilot's saved reviews were merged offline with this code, three times per model and sheet, 24 calls:

| Model | Threads per pass (labeled) | Passes with a wrong merge | Tokens per call | Seconds per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| claude-sonnet-5 | 15, 16, 15 (16) | 2 of 3 | about 30K | 28 to 113 |
| gpt-5.6-terra | 16, 16, 16 (16) | 3 of 3 | about 10K | 4 to 8 |
| gemini-3.5-flash | 14, 15, 14 (14) | 0 of 3 | about 15K | 17 to 36 |
| deepseek-v4-pro

title: fix(review): show a kept rule finding's current text
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #21869 (BYT-10385). When a rule review run reports a finding again, the earlier result keeps its thread, and until now it took only the new anchor. Its text stayed as first posted.

The fingerprint leaves the text out on purpose, so the kept text can be stale:

- **omni rewords a finding:** for example in bytebase/omni#626, which is already pinned. A thread opened before the bump keeps the old wording.
- **The finding names what it found differently, with the same code, statement, and position:** for example ``` `w` is a view, not a table.``` becomes ``` `w` is a sequence, not a table.``` after an earlier statement changes. The thread kept the old kind.

A kept root now takes the repeating result's `comment` together with its anchor, in the same `UPDATE` (`CompleteReviewRun`):

- A finding on the whole change has no anchor, and the kept one stays as it is. `jsonb_strip_nulls` drops the missing key.
- `updated_at` is unchanged, as for the anchor move. The thread UI shows "(edited)" when `updated_at` differs from `created_at`, and this is no person's edit.
- Predicates are unchanged: `project`, `issue_id`, run type, not superseded, equal fingerprint.

Not breaking: no API, proto, or schema change, and the rule review runs only on dev builds (`profile.SQLReviewV2`).

## Test plan

- [x] `backend/store`: `TestCompleteReviewRunKeepsResultsReportedAgain` now expects each kept root to carry the second run's text ("open again", "accepted again", "whole again"), and "new again" after the third. Each kept `updated_at` is unchanged, and the anchors move as before.

- [x] full `backend/store` and `backend/runner/reviewrun` suites

- [x] golangci-lint v2.15.0: no issues in changed files. The 44 `revive` findings it reports are in untouched files.

title: fix(cosmosdb): resume a partition whose query result spans several pages
body:
## What

`gonative`, the pure-Go query engine the CosmosDB driver falls back to when the gateway refuses a cross-partition query, treated a continuation token as an error. Every operator — `pipeline.go` (both aggregate forms), `distinct.go`, `merge.go`, `topskiptake.go`, `group.go` — returned `multi-page not supported in Stage N` the moment a range's response carried one. The gateway caps a page at 1000 items (or 4 MB), so an ordinary SQL Editor query such as `SELECT c.name FROM c ORDER BY c.population DESC` failed outright on any container holding more than a page of rows in one physical partition.

Each operator now carries that token back through `queryengine.QueryRequest.Continuation`, which the SDK already forwards as `x-ms-continuation`, and treats a range as drained only once a response for it carries no token. A new `rangeFanout` (`fanout.go`) owns the per-range paging state for all six pipelines and rejects a token that repeats itself, so a non-advancing range errors instead of paging forever.

The ORDER BY merge is incremental as a result: it pops the heap only while every range that still has pages has a row buffered, so the first range to run dry ends the turn and its next page is fetched before any row that might sort after it is emitted. It also asks only for the ranges it is actually waiting on — the merge consumes ranges unevenly, and a range whose rows all sort later would otherwise accumulate a page per turn for rows a `LIMIT` may never return. Rows already emitted are dropped from a range's buffer when its next page arrives. DISTINCT and TOP flush what they have before asking for the next page, so a long result still streams; aggregates and GROUP BY stay blocking, as they must.

`ErrUnsupportedPlanFeature` still covers the plan features the engine does not implement (multi-key ORDER BY, ordered DISTINCT, non-streaming ORDER BY, GROUP BY composed with other operators). This change is only about pagination.

## Measured before and after

New emulator fixture `paged`: 2,130 rows over 8 partition key values, two of them holding 1,050 rows each, spanning more than one physical partition. The gateway's page cap with no page size named measured 1,000 items — a 1,500-row range answers in pages of 0, 1,000 and 500.

| query against the fixture | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SELECT c.seq FROM c ORDER BY c.seq ASC` (2,130 rows) | `order-by partition returned a continuation token` | all 2,130 rows, 0…2129 in order |
| same, `DESC` | same failure | all 2,130 rows, reversed |
| `ORDER BY c.seq OFFSET 995 LIMIT 10` (spans the page boundary) | same failure | exactly seq 995…1004 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT c.seq FROM c` (2,130 values) | `distinct partition returned a continuation token` | 2,130 distinct values |
| `SELECT c.seq, COUNT(1) FROM c GROUP BY c.seq` (2,130 groups) | `group partition returned a continuation token` | 2,130 groups, each count 1 |
| `SELECT TOP 1025 c.seq FROM c` | `top partition returned a continuation token` | 1,0

title: refactor(cosmosdb): drop the azcosmos fork for upstream v1.6.0-beta.4
body:
## What

Drops the `azcosmos` fork. `go.mod` moves from
`github.com/bytebase/azure-sdk-for-go/sdk/data/azcosmos@eac0db373bca` (a fork of
upstream `v1.5.0-beta.5`) to upstream `v1.6.0-beta.4`, and the `replace` line is gone.

The fork was load-bearing for exactly one call site:
`container.NewCrossPartitionQueryItemsPager`, which did two things upstream could not
— run a query with no partition key, and, when the gateway refused that query, replay
it through a pure-Go distributed query engine. Upstream `v1.6.0-beta.2` restored the
`queryengine` extension point (`QueryOptions.QueryEngine`) and documents
`NewPartitionKey()` for cross-partition queries, so both halves now live here:

- `QueryEveryPartition` in the driver pages with an empty partition key, and engages
  the engine only on the gateway's cross-partition refusal — so queries the gateway
  can serve still never leave the gateway path, and pay no extra round-trip.
- The engine moves to `backend/plugin/db/cosmosdb/queryengine/gonative`
  (~2,030 lines, plus its ~2,430 lines of tests), unchanged in behavior.
- `scripts/cosmos-repro-go`, the BYT-9239 parity harness, calls the same helper, so
  the pivot has one implementation rather than two.

## Why now

- The pin was the fork's `main`, untouched since April. Because `replace` shadowed the
  `require` line, Renovate's bumps there were no-ops, so we sat on upstream
  `v1.5.0-beta.5` and missed GA's retry/failover and cache fixes.
- The only two things the fork added over upstream — `ClientOptions.QueryPlanCacheSize`
  and `queryengine.Disabled` — were never set anywhere in this repo. The engine's
  `BB_COSMOS_DISABLE_QUERY_ENGINE` kill switch, which a fork comment referenced, does
  not exist here either.

## Behavior

No functional change to the cross-partition path. Two things worth knowing:

- **Query plans are no longer cached.** The fork held a 256-entry per-container LRU of
  gateway query plans; nothing configured it, and each SQL Editor query is distinct, so
  it rarely hit. An engine-routed query now costs one plan fetch.
- **Still on the beta line.** GA `v1.5.0` has no `queryengine` package and no
  `QueryOptions.QueryEngine`, so cross-partition aggregates require `v1.6.0-beta.*`
  until that hook GAs. This moves us from a fork of a beta to upstream's beta.

## Housekeeping in the moved files

- Error construction moves to the repo's `errors` helpers, and the tests pick up the
  switch-default, type-assertion and table-test conventions `golangci-lint` enforces
  here. The engine was written under the Azure SDK's lint config and arrived with 64
  findings against ours.
- The per-file `Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation` / MIT notices are removed. They
  came from the SDK repo's file template, not from upstream code: every `gonative` file
  was authored in the fork by a Bytebase engineer, none of its identifiers appear
  anywhere in upstream `v1.6.0-beta.4`, and this repo carries no per-file notices.

title: test(cosmosdb): cover cross-partition queries against a local emulator
body:
## Why

The forked `azcosmos` SDK exists for one thing: the Cosmos gateway cannot serve an aggregate, `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY`, `TOP`, `OFFSET/LIMIT` or `GROUP BY` that spans partitions, so `NewCrossPartitionQueryItemsPager` pivots to a query engine that merges the per-partition streams itself. That pager is the only API we call that upstream does not have.

Its only coverage was the live-Azure `TestIntegration_BYT9239_*` suite, which can assert little more than non-emptiness and orderedness because it does not control the data it reads — and which needs a subscription to run at all.

## What

`SharedCosmosContainer` plus a `TestCrossPartition*` suite that drives `Driver.Open` → `Ping` → `QueryConn` over a fixture of known contents, so every aggregate, group and page has exactly one correct answer:

| Test | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `TestCrossPartitionAggregates` | `COUNT`=40, `SUM`=12,000,000, `AVG`=300,000, `MIN`/`MAX`, multi-aggregate — VALUE and aliased forms |
| `TestCrossPartitionDistinct` | the 8 partition key values exactly, VALUE and object form |
| `TestCrossPartitionOrderBy` | 40 rows, globally sorted, both directions |
| `TestCrossPartitionTop` / `GroupBy` | 3 rows; 8 groups of 5 with per-group sums and no duplicate group |
| `TestCrossPartitionOffsetLimit` | the page equals the globally ordered slice `[5:10]` |
| `TestCrossPartitionGatewayServable` | projection and single-partition filter, which must **not** reach the engine |
| `TestCrossPartitionQueryLimit` | `QueryConn`'s own row cap |

The `go.mod` line is `go mod tidy` promoting `github.com/moby/moby/api` out of the indirect block — the fixed port binding goes through `HostConfigModifier`, since testcontainers v0.44 rejects the `"8081:8081/tcp"` form in `ExposedPorts`. No new module, no `go.sum` change.

## Manual, and why

Behind `AZURE_COSMOS_EMULATOR=1`:

```bash
AZURE_COSMOS_EMULATOR=1 go test -count=1 -run "^TestCrossPartition" -timeout 600s ./backend/plugin/db/cosmosdb/
```

The emulator is a 4.9 GB image that needs most of a minute to boot and a fixed host port, so it is not something to put in every CI run. The gate sits in the fixture helper, where the container is first touched, so a default run neither pulls nor boots it — the package still finishes in about two seconds. Note the image prints a `[128] days left in the evaluation period` countdown, so the `2.14.28` pin will want refreshing periodically.

## Three emulator facts behind the setup

- **Only the classic image reproduces the gateway's refusal.** The `vnext-preview` emulator is PostgreSQL-backed: it answers all of these queries itself, reports one partition key range at any throughput, and returns a query plan the engine rejects as an unsupported feature. It would pass and fail for the wrong reasons in equal measure.
- **Throughput, not document count, spreads a container over physical partitions** — one per 10k RU (measured: 400→1 range, 12,000→2, 30,000→5). The fixture provisions 30k and refuses to run below tw

title: feat(sql-editor): cancel running exports
body:
Cancel in the SQL Editor export drawer only closed the drawer. The Export request kept running, a download still arrived later, and the server recorded the canceled query as `timeout reached: 0s`. With this change, Cancel stops the export and the server records a canceled export as canceled. `SQLService.Export` stays one unary call, with no API or proto change.

**Frontend**

- `DataExportButton` creates an `AbortController` per export and passes its signal through `onExport` to `exportData`, for single exports (`ResultView`) and batch exports (`BatchQuerySelect`). While an export runs, Cancel and the drawer's close button abort it and close the drawer. Escape and clicking outside do nothing until the export ends, so a stray dismissal can neither cancel a long export nor leave it running with no visible progress. The password dialog in DROPDOWN mode follows the same rule. Both read the close reason Base UI passes to `onOpenChange`.
- A canceled download ends quietly. Nothing is saved, including a multi-database ZIP canceled while it is being built, and no toast appears, because `exportData` ignores `Canceled` in the error middleware.
- A canceled batch starts no further databases. For SharePoint, the result dialog keeps the results of databases that finished. It marks a database canceled mid-flight as **Canceled** with "Some files may exist in SharePoint", because ADR 0007 does not let Bytebase claim nothing was created. Databases that never started are listed as **Not exported**.

**Backend**

- `executeWithTimeout` tells a canceled request apart from a deadline. A canceled run returns `CANCELED` with "the request was canceled before the query finished", and query history records that message. The query policy's timeout and a caller deadline still produce `timeout reached: …`. Query and AdminExecute share this function. For them the client has already gone, so only the history row and the status code change.
- SharePoint reconciliation runs on a context that keeps going for up to 30 s after the request is canceled. A file that arrived before the cancel is confirmed instead of being reported as unconfirmed, so the audit row and query history record the real outcome. Uploads not yet started are still skipped after a cancel. A cancel before any upload reports that nothing was uploaded. A canceled upload maps to `CANCELED`, unless a file remains unconfirmed, which stays `UNAVAILABLE`.

**Validation**

- Unit tests cover the abort path in `DataExportButton` (download quiet, nothing saved even when canceled while zipping several files, SharePoint outcome shown; Escape and outside clicks ignored while exporting, close button aborts), `BatchQuerySelect` (no new databases after cancel; Canceled, Exported, and Not exported per database; no failure toasts for a canceled download), `ResultView`, `SharePointExportResultDialog`, and `exportData`.
- Go tests cover cancel, query policy timeout, and caller deadline in `executeWithTimeout`, reconciliation after a

title: perf(sql-editor): export up to 4 databases at a time in batch export
body:
SQL Editor's batch export now runs up to 4 database exports at a time instead of one after another. On a 10-database SharePoint batch (measured on a prototype of this change against a real SharePoint tenant, with the server changes from #21868), the batch went from about 9.6 s one at a time to about 3.3 s with 4 at a time.

The limit is a fixed constant, `EXPORT_CONCURRENCY = 4`, not a setting. Browsers allow about 6 connections per origin over HTTP/1.1, so 4 leaves room for the SQL Editor's other requests, and each running export holds its whole result in server memory. 8 at a time was faster still in the prototype, but it would starve those other requests and double the peak server memory.

What stays the same:

- The SharePoint results dialog and the downloaded files keep the order in which the databases were selected, whatever order the exports finish in.
- One database failing doesn't stop the others. SharePoint exports still get a Delivered/Failed row each, and Download failures still raise a toast per database.
- Cancel or closing the drawer works as before: the batch keeps running in the background and delivers its results when it finishes.

Progress now counts completions, so "Exported N of M" advances as each export finishes, in any order, and reaches M of M. Before, it was reported before each export started and stopped at M-1.

The order-preserving concurrency helper `runWithConcurrency` already existed in the plan-detail route folder. It moves to `frontend/src/lib/concurrency.ts` because modules may not import from `src/routes/`. Its code is unchanged.

## Validation

- New `BatchQuerySelect` tests settle deferred exports out of order. A 6-database SharePoint batch checks that at most 4 exports are in flight, that the next export starts as each one finishes, that progress counts 0 through 6, and that results keep selection order with a failure first. A Download batch checks file order, skips the failed database, and checks its toast. Both tests fail against the previous sequential loop.
- `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` pass.

title: fix(snowflake)!: require an encrypted private key's passphrase
body:
## What

`decodeRSAPrivateKey` now rejects an `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` when no passphrase is
supplied, and `go.mod` resolves `github.com/youmark/pkcs8` upstream again — the
`=> github.com/bytebase/pkcs8` replace is gone.

## Why

The fork's entire diff against upstream was one commented-out block in
`ParsePrivateKey`:

```go
// No password provided, assume the private key is unencrypted
// if len(password) == 0 {
// 	privateKey, err := x509.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey(der)
// 	return privateKey, nil, err
// }
```

It was added in #12346 because `decodeRSAPrivateKey` hardcoded an empty passphrase,
and said so:

```go
// TODO(zp): Assume the passphrase is empty because we do not have input area in frontend.
pk, err := pkcs8.ParsePKCS8PrivateKeyRSA([]byte(block.Bytes), []byte(""))
```

Upstream reads an empty password as "the key is unencrypted" and misparses the
ciphertext, so against upstream that branch could never succeed for any key.
Removing the guard in a fork is what made it run at all — the fork was a workaround
for a missing form field, not a feature.

The passphrase field landed in #18309, which deleted the TODO but left the fork in
place. Since then the fork has covered exactly one input: a key encrypted under an
empty passphrase, which `openssl pkcs8 -topk8` produces if you press Enter at its
prompt, and which carries no protection at all. Snowflake's
[docs](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/key-pair-auth) list the Go driver as
supporting unencrypted keys only, so such a key is unusable with other Snowflake
clients regardless.

Rejecting a missing passphrase explicitly makes upstream sufficient, so the replace
can go. Both documented ways to generate a key are unaffected: `-nocrypt` produces a
`PRIVATE KEY` block handled by `crypto/x509`, and an encrypted key with its
passphrase works on upstream.

## Breaking Changes

A Snowflake data source holding an `ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY` whose passphrase is the
empty string, with the passphrase field left blank, connected before and now fails
at connection time with:

```
failed to decode rsa private key: private key is encrypted, but no passphrase was provided
```

Remedy: regenerate the key unencrypted (`openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -out
rsa_key.p8 -nocrypt`), or set a real passphrase and enter it in the **Private Key
Passphrase** field. A key encrypted under an empty passphrase is not protected, so
accepting it silently was itself the defect — the failure is now named instead of
implied.

## Verification

- Eight subtests in `TestDecodeRSAPrivateKey` covering unencrypted, unencrypted with
  a stray passphrase, encrypted with the right/wrong/absent passphrase, a non-RSA
  (ed25519) PKCS#8 key, a PKCS#1 block, and non-PEM input. Keys are generated in the
  test, so no PEM fixtures are checked in.
- Mutation-checked rather than trusted for passing first time: deleting the guard
  fails `encrypted key without a passphrase`, inverting it fails the three
  encrypted-key cases, and weakening the RS

title: fix(mssql): retire the go-mssqldb fork and stop sending credentials twice
body:
Drops `github.com/microsoft/go-mssqldb => github.com/bytebase/go-mssqldb`, so the
`require ... v1.11.2` already in `go.mod` finally takes effect.

## The fork held two patches, and upstream has outgrown both

| Patch | Status upstream |
|---|---|
| `case typeUdt` in four `types.go` functions, so a `geometry` column does not panic in each `default` | v1.11.2 handles `typeUdt` in all four, plus `makeDecl`. One gap remains — see *Accepted regression* below |
| `config.RootCAs = x509.SystemCertPool()` in `msdsn.SetupTLS` when no certificate is given | A no-op: `crypto/x509` sends a nil `Roots` and a `SystemCertPool()` `Roots` down the same path (`verify.go` checks `opts.Roots == nil \|\| opts.Roots.systemPool`) |

The replace was pinned at 2024-08-01, two commits past upstream v1.7.2, and it has
shadowed every Renovate bump since — 138 commits and 15 releases, including the
v1.11.0 fixes for three DoS panics (SQL Browser DAC response parsing, PRELOGIN
option offset overflow, NTLM challenge out-of-bounds).

Only two modules move: `go-mssqldb` to the real v1.11.2, and `azkeys` v1.0.1 →
v1.5.0, which the fork's 2024 `go.mod` was holding down. `azkeys` is not in the
server binary.

## Removing it surfaced a latent bug in our own DSN

`connectionDSN` builds a URL DSN and then also passed, in the query, values the URL
form already carries. `splitConnectionStringURL` derives exactly four keys from the
URL itself — `user id` and `password` from the userinfo, `server` and `port` from the
host — and v1.11.2 added a duplicate-key check that rejects a second value for any of
them:

```
key "user id" provided more than once (connection string keys are case-insensitive; remove the duplicate)
```

We were duplicating all four:

| Duplicated | Who hit it | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `user id` and `password`, in the userinfo *and* in the query, where the Azure IAM branch sets them | Any Azure IAM service principal, and anyone setting `User ID` or `Password` in Extra Parameters | Drop `url.URL.User` and keep the query copy, the one Azure IAM and Extra Parameters override |
| `server` and `port`, in the URL host *and* in the query whenever Extra Parameters set `Server` or `Port` | Anyone reaching a named instance — `Server=host\INSTANCE` is the only way, since the Host field has no room for a backslash | Build the URL's host from them instead of passing them in the query, with a named instance in the path, which is how the parser reads one back (`sqlserver://host/SQLEXPRESS`) |

The old parser let the later value win silently, so neither showed up until now, and
those four are every key the URL form pre-populates.

## Accepted regression: columns of a custom CLR user-defined type

Three of the four functions the fork patched take any UDT: `makeGoLangScanType`
returns `[]byte`, `makeGoLangTypeName` returns the type's own name, and
`makeGoLangTypePrecisionScale` returns no precision. `makeGoLangTypeLength` is the
exception — it switches on the type *name* and panics on anythi

title: chore(deps): drop three dead replace directives
body:
## What

Three `replace` directives in `go.mod` point at modules that are no longer in the build list, so they redirect nothing. This removes them.

| replace | added for | why it is dead |
|---|---|---|
| `antlr4-go/antlr/v4` → `bytebase/antlr/v4` | bytebase/bytebase#9104, when the SQL parsers here were ANTLR-generated | nothing in the repo imports antlr any more; the parsers moved to omni, which has no antlr dependency |
| `mattn/go-oci8` → `bytebase/go-obo` | bytebase/bytebase#8851, the OceanBase Oracle skeleton | that engine was removed in bytebase/bytebase#17084; no require line, no `go.sum` entry, absent from the module graph |
| `dgrijalva/jwt-go` → `form3tech-oss/jwt-go` | copied from pingcap/tidb to neutralize CVE-2020-26160 in a transitive dependency | no module in the graph declares `dgrijalva/jwt-go`; we and our dependencies use `golang-jwt/jwt` (v5 directly, v4 transitively) |

The only module still reaching antlr is `cel-go/parser`, via `backend/api/mcp`. The fork is upstream v4.13.1 plus two patches — exporting ATN internals (`getTarget` → `GetTarget`, `IntervalSet.Contains`, `ATN.GetRuleToStartState`, …) and a `SetContext` hook for cancelling a long parse. cel-go was written against upstream and uses neither, so it builds and runs unchanged on upstream v4.13.1, which is the version the `require` line already named. v4.13.1 is also still the newest upstream tag, so nothing is given up by dropping the fork.

`go.sum` moves by exactly one module: the fork's two hashes out, upstream v4.13.1's two in. Removing the other two directives changed no hashes at all, which is the clearest evidence they were inert.

Also drops the now-orphaned `// Other fixes.` divider, which only existed to separate the tidb-copied jwt-go block from the rest.

## Reviewer note

The jwt-go directive was inert but it was also the last trace of a CVE mitigation: had a future tidb bump reintroduced `dgrijalva/jwt-go` transitively, the replace would have silently redirected it to the patched fork. I dropped it because a replace nobody can observe firing is weak protection, and it would have pinned an archived `+incompatible` fork rather than fixing anything — `exclude` or the CVE scanner is the honest way to express that intent. Say so if you would rather keep it; it is a one-line restore.

## Breaking changes

None. No API, schema, proto, configuration, or behavior change — the only code swapped is a dependency whose public surface is identical for its one consumer.

## Verification

- `go mod tidy` — no further changes
- `go build -ldflags "-w -s" ./backend/bin/server/main.go` — clean
- `go test ./backend/common/... ./backend/component/iam/... ./backend/component/review/... ./backend/api/mcp/...` (the cel-go users) — pass
- `golangci-lint run -j 8` at the CI-pinned v2.15.0 — 0 issues

title: fix(pg,redshift,cockroachdb): read the session time zone once per statement
body:
## What

`timestamptz` results still render in the database session's time zone. The lookup that produces that zone moves out of Bytebase's pgx fork and into the three pgx drivers, where it runs **once per statement** instead of once per value.

## Why

The fork patch resolved `ParameterStatus("TimeZone")` through `time.LoadLocation` inside `(*Rows).initValueFuncs`, in the closure that decodes each value. Go does not cache named locations — it reparses the zoneinfo file on every call:

```
LoadLocation("Asia/Shanghai")   4341 ns/op   1376 B/op   10 allocs/op
LoadLocation("UTC")                2.7 ns/op      0 B/op    0 allocs/op   <- special-cased
```

Per cell. Same query, 20k rows x 5 `timestamptz`, only the session zone differing:

| session `TimeZone` | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UTC` | 19 ms / 2.3 MB | 17 ms / 2.3 MB |
| `Asia/Shanghai` | **484 ms / 133.5 MB** | **21 ms / 2.3 MB** |

The UTC default hid this, which is why it went unnoticed; every non-UTC instance paid it.

## Why once per statement is the right level, and enough

Too coarse would be wrong, and `SET` is reachable: [`query_antlr.go`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/backend/plugin/parser/pg/query_antlr.go) accepts `*ast.VariableSetStmt` on the read-only editor path, and `QueryConn` splits a batch and runs each statement on one pinned `*sql.Conn`. So `SET TimeZone TO 'Asia/Kolkata'; SELECT created_at FROM t;` changes the zone between two iterations of the same loop. A location resolved at connect time would label the second statement's rows with the first's zone. Measured — the server does resend the setting:

```
after SET UTC                 ParameterStatus="UTC"              decode=05:06:07+00 (UTC)
after SET Asia/Tokyo          ParameterStatus="Asia/Tokyo"       decode=14:06:07+09 (JST)
after SET America/New_York    ParameterStatus="America/New_York" decode=00:06:07-05 (EST)
```

Finer than per statement buys nothing, because PostgreSQL reports a `TimeZone` change at command completion, *after* the rows. Measured with the fork patch still in place, so this is what the per-value lookup actually did:

```
SELECT set_config('TimeZone','Asia/Tokyo',false), '...'::timestamptz
  -> decoded UTC+0.00h, while ParameterStatus afterwards reads "Asia/Tokyo"

SELECT CASE WHEN i = 3 THEN set_config('TimeZone','Asia/Tokyo',false)
            ELSE current_setting('TimeZone') END, '...'::timestamptz
       FROM generate_series(1,5)
  -> all five rows decoded UTC, rows 3-5 reporting tz=Asia/Tokyo
```

One result set resolves one setting. Reading it immediately before the statement therefore returns exactly what the per-value lookup returned, 100,000 times fewer.

## Behavior change: POSIX time zones no longer fail the query

PostgreSQL accepts `TimeZone` values `time.LoadLocation` rejects — `+08:00`, `GMT+8`, `EST5EDT,M3.2.0/2,M11.1.0/2`. The patch returned that error, so on such an instance **every** `timestamptz` read failed with a bare scan error and aborted the
