title: feat(sql-editor): draw Databricks plans, the last engine explaining without one
body:
## What

Databricks plans draw. With this, **every engine the SQL Editor can explain, it can also draw** — Databricks was the last one left showing its plan as text.

Spark's `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` answers in two parts: a tree of operators, each tagged with a number, then a block of detail per number. The parser puts them back together, so a node carries the filters pushed into a read, the partitions it skipped, the keys a join matched on, and the operator number Spark's own output prints beside it.

## What it looks like

The broadcast join from `broadcast-join.txt`, with the read selected: the detail
block becomes the node's panel, so the filters Spark pushed into the scan are
one click from the operator that did it. The header says what the plan cannot
do — rank, since Spark states no cost or rows here.

![A Databricks plan drawn as a graph, with a scan selected and its pushed filters in the panel](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bytebase/bytebase/be6a0acb1fa6f20fd7aedbd5f31380b557ee7efc/databricks-plan-node.png)

A read of a partitioned table, from `partition-filter.txt`: the partitions it
skipped, and the one directory it was left with.

![A partitioned read, with its partition filters and the single partition path](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bytebase/bytebase/be6a0acb1fa6f20fd7aedbd5f31380b557ee7efc/databricks-plan-partition.png)

## What the graph does and does not say

It ranks nothing, deliberately. `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` states neither cost nor rows; Spark reports those from `EXPLAIN COST`, and only for the *logical* plan, which is not the plan that ran. Mixing the two would attach numbers to operators they do not describe.

What is left is the shape and the detail, which is what a Spark plan is read for: whether a filter reached the scan, which partitions it skipped, whether a join broadcast or shuffled, and where the exchanges are.

## Verification

Checked against **Spark 3.5.3** in Docker, which is what Databricks SQL runs. Every fixture is a capture from it:

| Fixture | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `single-scan.txt` | a filter over a read, predicate pushed in |
| `broadcast-join.txt` | broadcast hash join under two aggregates and an exchange |
| `union-all.txt` | one tree, two branches |
| `sort-limit.txt` | `TakeOrderedAndProject` |
| `partition-filter.txt` | a partitioned read stating the partitions it skipped |
| `exists-subquery.txt` | an EXISTS turned into a left semi join |

Databricks itself is reachable from neither a dev box nor CI. The statement is identical and the layout is Spark's own, though a Databricks runtime may name operators these fixtures do not show — the fixture notes say exactly that rather than implying the plans came from Databricks.

Frontend gate green: 649 files, 7478 tests. No backend change needed — the driver already sends `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` and the capability table already declares TEXT, both from #21677.

## Notes for review

- **A line's depth comes from the branch markers before its operator, not

title: feat(sql-editor): draw the stages of a BigQuery job
body:
## What

BigQuery's query plan reaches the viewer. It is the one plan that arrives **with an ordinary run** rather than from an explain, so `QueryResult.QueryPlan` gains a `content` field for a plan the engine states beside the result's rows, and the Plan view draws it without explaining anything.

## Why it looks different from every other engine here

BigQuery has no `EXPLAIN` — its explain action is a dry run, which validates a statement and reports bytes. What it does have is the plan of a job that *ran*: the stages the query executed as, each naming the stages that fed it, with the records each really read and wrote. The driver already received that in `bigquery.QueryStatistics` and threw it away.

So this crosses a line the design doc drew ("attaching a measured plan to an ordinary run is deferred"), and the doc now says why BigQuery is the exception: Spanner's profiling mode and SQL Server's `SET STATISTICS XML` stay deferred because having the plan ready would mean profiling *every* run — overhead Spanner discourages, and a `SHOWPLAN` permission that would fail queries the user may run. BigQuery asks for none of that. Every job reports its stages anyway; the only cost is one `jobs.get` after the rows.

## Decisions worth a look

- **Nothing is ranked by time.** A stage reports what its average and slowest *shard* spent waiting, reading, computing and writing. That is a shard's time, not the stage's, and summing the phases of one shard would not produce a duration — so the milliseconds stay on the node and the graph shades by rows. Same judgement as Trino's `NaN` costs.
- **The ratio fields are dropped** from what the driver encodes: each is relative to the longest-running segment of the whole query, which a single node's card cannot explain, and the milliseconds beside them say it absolutely.
- **A carried plan leaves the data table alone.** A single-column result used to mean "these rows are the plan"; that is false once a plan can arrive beside them, and an end-to-end test caught it replacing a one-column BigQuery result's table with its plan.
- **A project-qualified table stays unresolved.** `dataset.table` resolves against the connected database; `project.dataset.table` names a table outside the connection, so it stays on the card as the subject rather than being answered with this project's table of the same name.
- **`content` is `audit_behavior = OMIT`**, as the rows are — the statement is what an audit reads.

## Verification, and its limit

- Go: the stage encoding is tested against a stage list in the shape a job reports, including nil stages and steps, and the audit-redaction inventory accepts the new field. `golangci-lint` 0 issues, server build, `buf format`/`lint`/`generate` clean.
- Frontend: a parser test per shape — the DAG, the measured records, the tree root, a stage two others read, a cycle, the depth cap — plus the plumbing (`inlineQueryPlan`, `planAvailability`, and the result view drawing a carried plan with no fetc

+				// it goes; BigQuery has no EXPLAIN to ask for them instead.
+				result.QueryPlan = queryPlan(ctx, it.SourceJob())
 				return result, nil
 			}
 
--- backend/plugin/db/bigquery/query_plan.go (+140/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,140 @@
+package bigquery
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"log/slog"
+	"time"
+
+	"cloud.google.com/go/bigquery"
+
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/common/log"
+	v1pb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/v1"
+)
+
+// BigQuery has no EXPLAIN. What it has is the plan of a job that ran: the
+// stages the query was executed as, each naming the stages that fed it, the
+// records it read and wrote, and how long its shards spent waiting, reading,
+// computing and writing. That makes it a record of the run rather than an
+// estimate of the next one, and it arrives with the job rather than in the
+// result's rows — which is why the result carries it in QueryPlan.content.
+
+// queryStage is one stage of a query plan, named as BigQuery's own REST API
+// names it (ExplainQueryStage) rather than as the Go client's fields, so the
+// viewer reads the shape Google documents. Durations are milliseconds, as that
+// API states them; the ids are numbers here, where it quotes them.
+//
+// Its four ratio fields are left out. Each is relative to the longest-running
+// segment of the whole query, which a single node's card cannot explain, and
+// the milliseconds beside them say the same thing absolutely.
+//
+// The record counts carry a zero, where everything else here drops one. A stage
+// that wrote no records measured that — a filter left nothing for the aggregate
+// above it — and the viewer reads these two as the rows a node really moved, so
+// dropping the zero would leave it showing an unknown count instead. A stage
+// that spent no time writing has nothing to say about writing, so those fields
+// stay out.
+type queryStage struct {
+	ID                        int64       `json:"id"`
+	Name                      string      `json:"name"`
+	Status                    string      `json:"status,omitempty"`
+	InputStages               []int64     `json:"inputStages,omitempty"`
+	Steps                     []queryStep `json:"steps,omitempty"`
+	RecordsRead               int64       `json:"recordsRead"`
+	RecordsWritten            int64       `json:"recordsWritten"`
+	ParallelInputs            int64       `json:"parallelInputs,omitempty"`
+	CompletedParallelInputs   int64       `json:"completedParallelInputs,omitempty"`
+	ShuffleOutputBytes        int64       `json:"shuffleOutputBytes,omitempty"`
+	ShuffleOutputBytesSpilled int64       `json:"shuffleOutputBytesSpilled,omitempty"`
+	WaitMsAvg                 int64       `json:"waitMsAvg,omitempty"`
+	WaitMsMax                 int64       `json:"waitMsMax,omitempty"`
+	ReadMsAvg                 int64       `json:"readMsAvg,omitempty"`
+	ReadMsMax                 int64       `json:"readMsMax,omitempty"`
+	ComputeMsAvg              int64       `json:"computeMsAvg,omitempty"`
+	ComputeMsMax              int64       `json:"computeMsMax,omitempty"`
+	WriteMsAvg                int64       `json:"writeMsAvg,omitempty"`
+	WriteMsMax                int64       `json:"writeMsMax,omitempty"`
+}
+
+// queryStep is one operation within a stage, in dependency order.
+type queryStep struct {
+	Kind     string   `json:"kind"`
+	Substeps []string `json:"substeps,omitempty"`
+}
+
+func milliseconds(d time.Duration) int64 {
+	return int64(d / time.Millisecond)
+}
+
+func toQueryStages(stages []*bigquery.ExplainQueryStage) []queryStage {
+	encoded := make([]queryStage, 0, len(stages))
+	for _, stage := range stages {
+		if stage == nil {
+			continue
+		}
+		steps := make([]queryStep, 0, len(stage.Steps))
+		for _, step := range stage.Steps {
+			if step == nil {
+				continue
+			}
+			steps = append(steps, queryStep{Kind: step.Kind, Substeps: step.Substeps})
+		}
+		encoded = append(encoded, queryStage{
+			ID:                        stage.ID,
+			Name:                      stage.Name,
+			Status:                    stage.Status,
+			InputStages:               stage.InputStages,
+			Steps:                     steps,
+			RecordsRead:               stage.RecordsRead,
+			RecordsWritten:            stage.RecordsWritten,
+			ParallelInputs:            stage.ParallelInputs,
+			CompletedParallelInputs:   stage.CompletedParallelInputs,
+			ShuffleOutputBytes:        stage.ShuffleOutputBytes,
+			ShuffleOutputBytesSpilled: stage.ShuffleOutputBytesSpilled,
+			WaitMsAvg:                 milliseconds(stage.WaitAvg),
+			WaitMsMax:                 milliseconds(stage.WaitMax),
+			ReadMsAvg:                 milliseconds(stage.ReadAvg),
+			ReadMsMax:                 milliseconds(stage.ReadMax),
+			ComputeMsAvg:              milliseconds(stage.ComputeAvg),
+			ComputeMsMax:              milliseconds(stage.ComputeMax),
+			WriteMsAvg:                milliseconds(stage.WriteAvg),
+			WriteMsMax:                milliseconds(stage.WriteMax),
+		})
+	}
+	return encoded
+}
+
+// queryPlan returns the plan of the job a finished read came from, or nil where
+// there is none to report.
+//
+// Reading it costs one jobs.get after the rows, since the responses the row
+// iterator fetches on its way through them do not carry the plan. A read that
+// came from no job of its own has none; neither does a job still without
+// statistics, nor a failure to fetch them, which leaves the rows the caller
+// asked for exactly as they were.
+func queryPlan(ctx context.Context, job *bigquery.Job) *v1pb.QueryResult_QueryPlan {
+	if job == nil {
+		return nil
+	}
+	status, err := job.Status(ctx)
+	if err != nil {
+		slog.Debug("failed to read the job status for its query plan", log.BBError(err))
+		return nil
+	}
+	stats, ok := statisticsOf(status)
+	if !ok || len(stats.QueryPlan) == 0 {
+		return nil
+	}
+	content, err := json.Marshal(toQueryStages(stats.QueryPlan))
+	if err != nil {
+		slog.Debug("failed to encode the query plan", log.BBError(err))
+		return nil
+	}
+	return &v1pb.QueryResult_QueryPlan{
+		Format: v1pb.QueryOption_JSON,
+		// The plan records the run that returned these rows rather than
+		// planning another, which is what the viewer's measured badge says.
+		Executed: true,
+		Content:  string(content),
+	}
+}

title: feat(sql-editor): explain on Databricks, and draw Snowflake and Hive plans
body:
## What

Three more engines reach the query plan viewer:

- **Databricks** explains at all. It was refused outright, because its driver runs whatever SQL it is handed and an explain request skips the read-only validation an ordinary query gets. It now plans the statement through the parser, so what the driver runs always begins with EXPLAIN — Spark's `EXPLAIN FORMATTED`, which compiles without executing. No parser yet, so the plan is text.
- **Snowflake** is drawn from `EXPLAIN USING JSON`, which its own explain builder already named as the plan nothing downstream read.
- **Hive** is drawn from `EXPLAIN FORMATTED`.

## Why these three, and what their plans carry

| Engine | Plan | Ranks by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Databricks | `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` (text) | — | numbered tree + a detail block per operator, the shape the Redshift/StarRocks parsers already read |
| Snowflake | `EXPLAIN USING JSON` | nothing | states each operation's *parents*, so the parser inverts the edges; carries pruning (micro-partitions assigned out of total, bytes) instead of cost or rows |
| Hive | `EXPLAIN FORMATTED` → `CBOPlan` | nothing | Calcite's flat rel list; an operator naming no `inputs` reads the one declared before it; row counts and average row widths |

Neither new graph ranks anything, deliberately: Snowflake estimates no cost at all, and Hive states one on its joins alone, which reads `"not available"` even on an analyzed table. Ranking on the one number the plan is least sure of is the trap this viewer already avoided for Trino.

A scan Snowflake assigned every partition of a table with more than one carries the existing full-scan warning — pruning is what a Snowflake plan is read for.

## Verification

- **Hive 4.0.0** in Docker: every fixture captured through HiveServer2, including `analyzed-join.json` taken after `LOAD DATA` + `ANALYZE TABLE … COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS`, so the row counts are real (a scan at 5.0 rows, 1.67 after the filter's selectivity) rather than a table of 1.0s. `no-cbo-plan.json` is `hive.cbo.enable=false`, which returns stages and no `CBOPlan` — the case the viewer shows as text.
- **Spark 3.5.3** in Docker for the statement Databricks is sent, Databricks SQL being Spark SQL. Databricks itself is not reachable from CI or a dev box.
- **Snowflake** runs nowhere but Snowflake, so its fixture is the output [Snowflake publishes](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/sql-reference/sql/explain) — the one fixture here not captured through a driver, which `test-data/README.md` records. The cases a published plan cannot show (a scan assigned every partition, a statement compiled into several steps) are written inline in the test.
- Go: `gofmt`, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, changed-package tests, server build.
- Frontend: `pnpm fix` then `pnpm test` — 640 files, 7372 tests, green.

## Notes for review

- Adding two parsers broke the test that asserts *every* parser's failure messages are localized, which is what it is for: the new message

title: docs(sql-editor): record the TiDB version that prints tidb_json
body:
## What

Records the TiDB version floor for the query plan the SQL Editor draws, beside the format name it builds (`backend/plugin/parser/tidb/explain.go`), in the design doc's "when the plan cannot be drawn or fetched" section, and in the fixture README. No behavior changes.

## Why

`EXPLAIN FORMAT=tidb_json` is new as of #21670 and unreleased, so it was worth knowing which servers answer it. Measured against twelve TiDB versions in Docker, each probed for the unquoted, double-quoted and single-quoted spellings and for `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`:

| TiDB | Released | `FORMAT=tidb_json` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| v4.0.16, v5.4.3, v6.1.7, v6.2.0, v6.3.0, v6.4.0 | to 2022-11-17 | `ERROR 1791 Unknown EXPLAIN format name` quoted, `ERROR 1064` syntax error unquoted |
| v6.5.0, v6.5.12, v7.1.6, v7.5.6, v8.1.2, v8.5.5 | from 2022-12-29 | returns the plan |

Two facts came out of it:

- The format name does not exist before **v6.5.0**, so no spelling reaches an older server, and the MySQL compatibility version cannot stand in for the TiDB one — v6.1 and v6.5 both report `5.7.25`.
- From v6.5.0 through v8.5.5 the plan carries the same keys (`id`, `estRows`, `taskType`, `accessObject`, `operatorInfo`, `subOperators`, plus `actRows`, `executeInfo`, `memoryInfo`, `diskInfo` when measured), so one set of fixtures stands for every release that answers at all.

Every release without the format predates December 2022, so this adds no version gate: the editor asks for the format unconditionally, and a server older than that answers an explain request with its own error rather than a plan. The doc says so, and says the floors of the other structured formats are unmeasured — `json = 1, indexes = 1` makes ClickHouse the one worth measuring next.

## Verification

Comments and docs only. `gofmt` clean and `golangci-lint` reports 0 issues; local links and referenced paths check out.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(oracle): sync object tables, invisible and virtual columns
body:
## Summary

Oracle's schema sync left out objects that exist in the schema, so the metadata reported names as absent that Oracle finds. omni's SQL review WALK_THROUGH for Oracle needs the synced schema to list everything `DROP TABLE` and `DROP`/`RENAME COLUMN` can reach. The sync now lists:

- **Object and XMLType tables** (`CREATE TABLE … OF`), from `ALL_OBJECT_TABLES`, which `ALL_TABLES` omits. They are marked `SkipDump`; the dump and single-table DDL skip them, and the differ already did.
- **Invisible columns**, without the `COLUMN_ID IS NOT NULL` filter. They carry `IsInvisible`, sort after the visible columns, and take the positions that follow. Hidden system columns stay out (`USER_GENERATED = 'YES'`, which is how `ALL_TAB_COLUMNS` is defined).
- **Virtual columns** in `Generation` rather than `Default`. The dump used to write them as `DEFAULT expr`, which recreates an ordinary column.
- **Materialized view indexes and triggers**, attached to the materialized view instead of being dropped.

It also stops attaching a trigger the schema owns on another schema's table to a same-named table of its own.

Consumers:

- The dump and migration generator write `INVISIBLE` and `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) VIRTUAL`.
  - A visibility change becomes `MODIFY (c VISIBLE|INVISIBLE)`.
  - An expression change becomes `MODIFY (c AS (…))`.
  - A switch between stored and virtual becomes a drop and re-add, since Oracle rejects both conversions (ORA-54026, ORA-54025).
- The DDL parser reads `INVISIBLE` and keeps virtual expressions in `Generation`.
- The migration generator rebuilds a column Oracle cannot alter in place: one switched between stored and virtual, or a virtual column given a new type or expression.
  - The table's indexes and constraints on rebuilt columns are dropped once, before the table's first column change, and added back once after its last. Oracle otherwise rejects the change (ORA-12991, ORA-54022, ORA-54023).
  - Other tables' foreign keys on a rebuilt key are dropped and added back too (ORA-02273). For that, `MetadataDiff` now carries the old and new metadata it was taken between; other engines ignore it.
  - A virtual column's type and expression change in one `MODIFY` (ORA-54027).
  - A named NOT NULL is restored by name, because a CHECK would leave the column nullable.
- Query span resolves invisible columns by name but leaves them out of `SELECT *`, so result columns and masking stay aligned.
- Prior-backup restore leaves out invisible columns, since the backup copies `t.*`, and virtual columns, now that they carry `Generation`.

## Behavior changes

- Schema dumps change for tables with invisible or virtual columns. They also change for JSON collection tables: their `RESID` and `ETAG` are user-generated invisible columns, and `RENAME COLUMN etag` succeeds, so they are listed.
- Object and XMLType tables appear in the schema tree and the SQL editor.
- A schema diff against text dumped before this change shows virtual columns as changed,

title: feat(api): add SearchDatabases and resolve MCP databases through it
body:
Replaces #21551. Part of BYT-10347.

`query_database`, `get_schema` and `propose_database_change` find a database by name. On main they list databases under the workspace, which needs `bb.databases.list` at the workspace. Project roles grant it only inside their project, so a Project Developer or a SQL Editor user gets PERMISSION_DENIED from all three tools, even for a database in their own project.

## What changed since the first review

The first version of this PR added the wildcard parent `projects/-` to `ListDatabases`, as ecmadao suggested on #21551, and checked `bb.projects.get` in each project. ecmadao then asked here:

> I'm thinking that do we need to also check the "bb.databases.list" permission? If so, we may need to implement the getProjectIDsSearchFilter to make it be able to check multiple permissions

We discussed it on 2026-10-27 and decided to follow Google Cloud's pattern. A list method checks its own list permission on its parent, and reading across parents is a separate search method. So the change is now two PRs:

- #21692, merged: `ListDatabases` with `projects/{project}` checks `bb.databases.list` instead of `bb.projects.get`.
- This PR: `projects/-` is gone, and a new `SearchDatabases` returns the databases of each project where the caller holds `bb.databases.get`. Each method checks one permission, so the helper stays as it is.

The first push of this rework had the search check `bb.databases.list`, so its result equaled the union of the per-project listings. d-bytebase asked in review for `bb.databases.get`, the permission Google's search methods use, and this version checks it.

## `SearchDatabases`

`POST /v1/databases:search` returns the databases of every active project where the caller holds `bb.databases.get`. A caller who holds it at the workspace gets every active project's databases.

- **The get permission, as other searches use.** Google's `projects.search` returns projects the caller can get, and Bytebase's `SearchProjects` and `SearchIssues` filter by their get permissions. `ListDatabases` keeps checking `bb.databases.list` on its parent, as Google's list methods do. Every built-in role holds both permissions or neither, so the two methods agree for built-in roles. A custom role with only one of them gets different results: with only `bb.databases.get`, the search finds the project's databases and `ListDatabases` refuses; with only `bb.databases.list`, it is the other way around.
- **No parent.** The workspace comes from the request, as for `SearchProjects` and Google's `projects.search`. The filter takes the `ListDatabases` syntax, so `project == "projects/x"` narrows to one project.
- **No `order_by`.** AIP-159 says cross-parent requests should not support it. Pages use the default order, which ends on the `(instance, name)` primary key, so it is total.
- **Full pages.** The project set is applied in SQL, before `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`. The store's `FindDatabaseMessage.ProjectIDs` applies `db.project = ANY(

title: fix(oracle): set the current schema on every session the driver opens
body:
## Summary

`Open` ran `ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA` with `d.db.ExecContext`, which runs on the connection pool, so only the session it borrowed switched schema. `Execute` and the SQL editor (`QueryConn`) take a connection with `db.Conn`, and they got the right schema only because `database/sql` handed back that one idle session. Whenever the pool opened a new one (none idle, or the idle one went bad), statements ran in the login user's schema. Nothing reported an error: unqualified DDL and DML landed in the login user's schema, and queries resolved names there.

- The driver's `connector` now runs `ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA` on each session it opens. If that fails, it closes the session and returns the error, so the pool never hands out a session in the wrong schema.
- go-ora's `AddSessionParam` doesn't fit: it stores the parameter on go-ora's default driver, which every Bytebase Oracle connection shares.
- `Open` pings when a schema is set, so a schema that doesn't exist still fails `Open` with `failed to set current schema to "..."`.

## Test plan

- [x] New `TestCurrentSchemaOnNewSessions` runs against a new shared Oracle Free container (`gvenzl/oracle-free:23.26.3-slim-faststart`, about 20 s to start). With `SetMaxIdleConns(0)`, every connection is a new session. It checks `SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CURRENT_SCHEMA')` through `QueryConn`, checks that `Execute`'s `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT SYS_CONTEXT(...)` lands in the target schema, and checks that `Open` fails on a schema that doesn't exist.
- [x] On the old driver, the test fails: the query returns `SYSTEM`, and the table lands in `SYSTEM` instead of the target schema.
- [x] `go test ./backend/plugin/db/oracle/` passes.
- [x] golangci-lint reports nothing new in the changed code.
- [x] Server build passes.

## Notes

- The Oracle image is about 6.5 GB on disk. A runner that hasn't cached it pulls it the first time this package's tests run.
- Not covered: if a user's own statement runs `ALTER SESSION SET CURRENT_SCHEMA`, that session returns to the pool with the other schema, and later checkouts from the same driver keep it.

title: feat(review): lay out the plan page around the automated reviewers
body:
## Summary

Under SQL Review V2 (dev builds), the plan page now lays out a database change as one review loop and then a rollout, with the machine reviewers in Review instead of a Checks footer in Changes. This implements the frontend part (build steps 1–6) of the plan page review layout proposal.

**Sections**
- Until the rollout exists, Changes and Review stay open together, and Deploy lists what the automatic rollout waits on, each line with a Show link. Deploy opens by default only once the rollout exists. Before this change, a plan held only by open findings opened on an empty Deploy step.
- Review is active from draft, because the rule review already runs on drafts. Drafts take comments and replies.
- Deploy's waiting list replaces the review readiness footer. "Bypass and deploy" moves with it.

**Automated review** (in Review, between Approval and Activity)
- One line per reviewer: Standard rules, AI review, the review policy for engines the rules don't cover, and the gh-ost dry run. Each line has one conclusion: passed, resolved, open, couldn't run, running, out of date, or not run. On a narrow screen, the conclusion moves under the reviewer's name.
- Open findings show as P0/P1/P2 counts, colored like the priority badge on each finding. Each count opens the statement editor on the first finding of that priority and narrows the walker to it. Its hover says what the priority means and where the click goes.
- "N resolved" counts the latest run's findings that people resolved; its hover names them by rule. A P0 resolved without a change is called out on the same line and counts as needing attention, but it does not hold the rollout.
- An ⓘ hover says what the reviewer covered: databases and engines, the effective rule set, and the AI review's sample.
- The statement summary report is no longer counted as a passed check. It now describes the SQL beside the statement title. When the report has ERROR or WARNING results, it gets its own **Statement report** row, and its errors hold the rollout.
- Plan check errors show as "N errors". A plan check run that is queued, running, or stopped before producing results gets a **Plan check** row. The row holds the rollout and shows the error, with a Retry.
- Every reviewer with a result can rerun, because rule settings and the synced schema change what the reviewers find:
  - Standard rules reruns through RunReview, without rerunning the plan checks.
  - A rerun that would reopen findings people resolved asks first. Re-run all and the plan check rerun ask too, since they restart the rule review.
  - The AI review always asks, because each run costs model calls.

**Shared**
- One gate model (`utils/planGates.ts`) feeds the Review rows, the Deploy waiting list, the header status popover, and the collapsed summaries. All of them use the same P0/P1/P2 and "resolved" wording.
- The editor walker can filter to one reviewer's findings of one priority, its resolved findings, or all of its open findings, and step

title: feat(sql-editor): draw query plans for twelve more engines
body: The SQL Editor's query plan viewer drew a picture for 3 of the engines the editor explains. It now draws 15 of 17, and the editor offers Explain on Trino, OceanBase, MongoDB and Doris for the first time. Hive and Snowflake are the two left: both have a machine-readable plan, and neither can be captured from this repository. Each engine states a plan its own way, so each gets its own reading. The engine-neutral `PlanNode` model and the viewer itself are unchanged except where an engine states something no earlier one did. | Engine | How the plan is asked for | What it carries | | --- | --- | --- | | MySQL, MariaDB | `EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON` | named objects nested under `query_block`; one parser reads both dialects | | TiDB | `EXPLAIN FORMAT=tidb_json` | an operator tree, with no cost in any format the editor can ask for | | Oracle | plan-table rows, rendered as JSON by the driver | the tree rebuilt from each step's parent link | | ClickHouse | `EXPLAIN json = 1, indexes = 1` | PostgreSQL's spelling, no cost, and the granules each read skips | | Trino | `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` | the fragments it would distribute, spliced at each `RemoteSource` | | OceanBase | `EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON` | an operator tree under `CHILD_n`, costed in estimated microseconds | | MongoDB | `.explain("queryPlanner")`, appended to the statement | one document, and no estimate at all | | CockroachDB | the plan encoded in the link `EXPLAIN (DISTSQL)` prints | the physical flow: processors and the streams between them | | Redshift | `EXPLAIN` | a text plan, and the distribution strategy on each join | | StarRocks, Doris | `EXPLAIN` | a text plan: fragments joined at their exchanges, each a tree | Two of the twelve, drawn from the fixtures this PR adds — Doris, whose plan is text, and CockroachDB, whose plan is decoded from the diagram link its EXPLAIN prints: | Doris | CockroachDB | | --- | --- | | | | Three details worth a reviewer's attention: - **Two parsers read text plans**, which §4 of the design says not to do. Redshift, StarRocks and Doris publish nothing else at all. Two things hold off the hazard §4 names — a literal holding a newline putting a line that looks like an operator into the output: all three return the plan one row per line, so a newline inside a value stays inside its row, and an operator is recognized only by a whole heading (a complete cost tuple on Redshift, a number and a name on the other two). §6 of the design records the departure. - **MongoDB did not explain at all** — the driver refused outright. +// diagramLink is the line EXPLAIN (DISTSQL) prints after the text plan. What
+// follows the fragment marker is the plan itself, deflated and base64'd.
+var diagramLink = regexp.MustCompile(`https?://\S*#([A-Za-z0-9+/_=-]+)`)
+
+// planDiagram returns the physical plan EXPLAIN (DISTSQL) encodes in the link
+// it prints, as the JSON document the query-plan viewer parses.
+//
+// CockroachDB publishes no plan as a document: every EXPLAIN option of its own
+// returns text, and the one machine-readable form it has is the payload behind
+// this link, which its own diagram page decodes in the browser. Decoding it
+// here is what lets the viewer draw the plan without the browser fetching
+// anything, and it is the same move the Oracle driver makes in rendering the
+// plan table.
+func planDiagram(result *v1pb.QueryResult) (*v1pb.QueryResult, error) {
+	var payload string
+	for _, row := range result.GetRows() {
+		for _, value := range row.GetValues() {
+			if match := diagramLink.FindStringSubmatch(value.GetStringValue()); match != nil {
+				payload = match[1]
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	if payload == "" {
+		return nil, errors.New("the plan carried no diagram to read")
+	}
+	// CockroachDB encodes with the standard alphabet, but the payload rides in
+	// a URL fragment, so accept either spelling of the two bytes that differ.
+	normalized := strings.NewReplacer("-", "+", "_", "/").Replace(strings.TrimRight(payload, "="))
+	deflated, err := base64.RawStdEncoding.DecodeString(normalized)
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, errors.Wrap(err, "failed to decode the query plan")
+	}
+	reader, err := zlib.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(deflated))
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, errors.Wrap(err, "failed to read the query plan")
+	}
+	defer reader.Close()
+	// A plan is small; the bound keeps a corrupt payload from inflating
+	// without end.
+	plan, err := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(reader, maxPlanBytes))
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, errors.Wrap(err, "failed to read the query plan")
+	}
+
+	return &v1pb.QueryResult{
+		ColumnNames:     []string{"plan"},
+		ColumnTypeNames: []string{"TEXT"},
+		Rows: []*v1pb.QueryRow{{Values: []*v1pb.RowValue{
+			{Kind: &v1pb.RowValue_StringValue{StringValue: string(plan)}},
+		}}},
+	}, nil
+}
+
+// maxPlanBytes bounds the inflated plan. CockroachDB's diagrams run to a few
+// tens of kilobytes; this is far above that and far below anything that would
+// trouble the editor.
+const maxPlanBytes = 8 << 20

title: fix(sql): record the statement each result ran, and close the query plan design
body:
`docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md` was all that was left of the query plan
work. Three of its passages had gone stale, and §3.4's requirement that every
driver record the statement it ran was still unmet in three drivers and on the
timeout path. This closes both, so the design has nothing open but the §1
usability question, which needs evidence rather than code.

## The doc

- The header said **partly implemented**. Every section is implemented, so it
  says so, and the SHA its code references are pinned to is labelled as the
  commit the design was written against — most of those line numbers have moved.
- §3.5's body still called SQL Server's `SET STATISTICS XML ON` "the one
  permission item still open here", which #21648 closed and §6 already recorded.
  The section contradicted itself; now it doesn't.
- §6 opened with "plus the §3.1 and §3.3 work on the branch below". There is no
  branch below, and those two were its only bullets without a PR link.

## Every driver records the statement it ran

A result's statement is what the Plan view explains, what the status bar shows
and what *Show in Editor* looks for, so a result holding the wrong one explains
a query the user never ran. I swept all 24 `QueryConn` implementations; three
held the wrong one.

- **Redis** indexed results by command but statements by text line, so a single
  blank line gave every result after it the previous command's text. `Execute`
  and `QueryConn` split identically, so the split moves into one
  `splitCommands` that returns each command's arguments beside the line it came
  from — keeping those aligned is the point, so they are built together.
- **DynamoDB** gave every result in a multi-statement request the whole request.
- **Databricks** recorded nothing at all.
- **A run cut off at the query timeout** returned an error and no result, so the
  editor had an error and nothing to point at. The timeout is its own error type
  now, and the two paths that run a whole script in one call — SQL Server, and
  engines with no splitter — answer it with the statement, as the per-statement
  loop already did.

### Behavior note

On those two paths a timeout now reaches the client as a 200 with
`results[0].error` and `results[0].statement`, where it used to be an RPC error.
Not labelled breaking: a result-level `error` is how every ordinary SQL failure
already arrives on this API, including from the per-statement path in the same
function, so a client that reads it is unaffected and one that doesn't was
already missing SQL errors. Worth a second opinion.

## Two fixes in the result pane

- ***Show in Editor*** searched the editor for the recorded statement after
  stripping a trailing `LIMIT n`. Where the parsers cannot fit a `LIMIT` they
  wrap the whole statement in `WITH result AS (…) SELECT * FROM result LIMIT n`
  instead — Redshift, BigQuery, TiDB, ClickHouse, SQL Server and the PostgreSQL
  fallback all do — and that text is nowhere in the editor, so the button did

title: feat(sql-editor): Explain action, measured plans, and the table a node reads
body:
Closes §3.1 and §3.3 of [the query plan visualizer design](docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md), which leaves nothing in its "Not yet" list but a usability question.

Three changes, one per commit.

## 1. Explain in Run's dropdown

Explaining was reachable only by `Ctrl/Cmd+E` or right-click, so it was invisible unless you already knew it was there. Run's dropdown now starts with **Explain**, which plans the statement Run would run — as written, with no row limit appended, since `LIMIT` changes plan shape and we would be showing the plan of a query nobody ran. Without `bb.sql.explain` it is disabled with that reason rather than hidden, as the Plan option already is.

There is deliberately no "Explain analyze" action: measuring works too differently per engine (a statement prefix on PostgreSQL, text-only on MySQL 8.0.18+, a session setting on SQL Server, an API on Spanner, a hint on Oracle, automatic on the warehouses) to be one control, and typing `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)` already draws a measured plan.

## 2. A measured plan is read by what it measured

A plan produced by running — a typed `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` — carries what each operator really did, and the viewer now reads it. Planner costs are arbitrary units and are wrong in exactly the cases worth investigating, so ranking a measured plan by estimate points at the wrong operator precisely when it matters.

The screenshots below are the same plan of the same statement. The estimate says the root scan is 89% of the work; the measurement says the inner `Index Scan` is 69% of it.

The metric is exclusive and per execution: a node's own time is its measured time less its children's, and PostgreSQL's per-loop averages are multiplied back out. Without the subtraction the ranking only ever finds the root; without the multiplication a node that ran nine times reads nine times cheaper than it was.

Planned and actual rows now sit together on a node, with the misestimate stated as a multiple once it is worth a line — the comparison that explains a bad plan when cost alone does not.

SQL Server's actual plan is read for rows only. Its `ActualElapsedms` is cumulative on a row-mode operator but per operator on a batch-mode one, so one plan can mean both and a ranking built on it would be wrong for half of it; those plans keep ranking by the estimated cost they always carry.

**Before**

![measured plan before](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bytebase/bytebase/061ebd0fea399de7634698d86dc7da8d729f11bb/before-measured.png)

**After**

![measured plan after](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bytebase/bytebase/061ebd0fea399de7634698d86dc7da8d729f11bb/after-measured.png)

## 3. Warnings by relevance, and the table a node reads

Warnings reach the side panel now, grouped by warning. One of Bytebase's own scan heuristics has to own a tenth of the plan to get there — warning about every full scan teaches readers to ignore the colour, since a full scan of a small lookup table is the correct plan. A diagnost

title: fix(masking)!: refuse SQL Server queries whose joins and row limits read masked columns
body:
## Summary

SQL Server has refused queries whose conditions read a masked column for a while, but its query span recorded predicate columns only from `WHERE` and `HAVING`. A masked column read anywhere else that decides which or how many rows come back ran without refusal. This brings SQL Server's extraction up to the coverage #21651 gave PostgreSQL. Refs [BYT-9455](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-9455).

Now recorded as predicate columns:

- `JOIN ... ON` conditions, including subqueries in them and nested or parenthesized joins
- arguments of `APPLY` and table-valued functions (`STRING_SPLIT`, `OPENJSON`), which decide how many rows the function returns
- `TOP`, `OFFSET`, and `FETCH` expressions
- the output columns of both arms of `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`, including in derived tables and CTEs
- the conditions of subqueries in `ORDER BY`

As for PostgreSQL, `UNION`, `GROUP BY`, and `ORDER BY` keys stay out of scope.

Also:

- A `JOIN ... ON` condition now resolves its columns as `WHERE` does, so an unknown column fails the span and the query is refused.
- Removes `query_span_predicate.go`, an unused helper whose comment said `JOIN ON` is deliberately not collected.
- Bumps omni for nested and parenthesized joins (bytebase/omni#499), `PIVOT` after a join (bytebase/omni#500), and the `OPENJSON`/`OPENXML` `WITH` schema (bytebase/omni#504). The span still refuses `PIVOT` and `OPENJSON ... WITH` as unsupported table sources.

## Breaking Changes

On SQL Server, users subject to masking are now refused queries that read a masked column in the clauses above. Before, those queries ran. `JOIN ... ON` conditions that name a column missing from the last metadata sync now fail, as `WHERE` conditions already did.

## Testing

- `backend/plugin/parser/tsql`: a table test covers each clause, plus valid shapes that must still pass, such as `ORDER BY` on an alias, `UNION`, and `GROUP BY`. Two golden fixtures gain their `JOIN ON` predicate columns. Two fixtures joined on a column their metadata lacks, so they now name a real one.
- Ran every test statement on SQL Server 2022. Each compiles under `SET NOEXEC ON`. The three that also execute fail only on fixture data, because the strings are not JSON or numbers.
- `go test` for the parser, advisor, schema, `runner/reviewrun`, and `api/v1` packages; the e2e server builds.
- `golangci-lint` v2.14.0 reports nothing in the changed files.
- Ran a temporary Playwright spec, not committed, against a SQL Server 2022 container added to the e2e server:
  - 11 statements that read a masked column in the clauses above were refused.
  - 5 statements were allowed and returned masked output: a join on unmasked columns, a nested join, `UNION`, `ORDER BY` a masked column, and `TOP` with a constant.
  - The SQL Editor shows the refusal:

![Refused join](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rebelice/96b9ded1ceed8d52bdff2919bd63a179/raw/mssql-refused.png)

![Allowed join with masked output](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/rebe

title: fix(sql-editor): explain in the format the viewer draws, and translate its label
body:
Two fixes to the SQL editor's explain entry points, split out of a larger query-plan branch so they can land on their own.

## `Ctrl/Cmd+E` and right-click → Explain planned the statement twice

The action sent `explain: true` with no explain format, so the engine answered in its own default — text, on PostgreSQL — and reaching a diagram meant pressing **Visualize**, which explained the same statement a second time. An explain is a planner run on the user's database, so that is two of them for one picture, on every engine the viewer can draw.

Both the editor and the admin terminal now ask for the format the viewer reads, so the plan comes back in one call.

The choice of format moves into `explainQueryOption`, beside the table the viewer already keys its parsers on, replacing the copy the result pane spelled out inline. The two can no longer drift.

## The editor's context-menu entry was hard-coded English

`label: isBigQuery ? "Dry Run Query" : "Explain Query"` in both the standard editor and the admin terminal, so it read "Explain Query" in the other four locales whatever the user had chosen. It and BigQuery's Dry run are translated now.

## Test plan

- New `frontend/src/utils/queryPlanEngines.test.ts`: the format each engine is asked for, and that an engine the viewer cannot draw is left on its own default.
- The label change is covered by `scripts/check-i18n.mjs`, which requires the key in all five locales and the same placeholders.
- `pnpm fix` and `pnpm test` green on this tree: 614 files, 7011 tests.

No API, schema, proto or configuration change; frontend only.

title: feat(mariadb): sync sequences and system-versioned tables
body:
## Summary

MariaDB sequences and system-versioned tables share the table namespace with base tables (with sequence `s1` present, `CREATE TABLE s1` fails with 1050, and `DROP TABLE s1` drops the sequence). The MySQL driver's `SyncDBSchema` kept only `BASE TABLE` and `VIEW` rows from `information_schema.TABLES`, so both kinds were missing from the metadata. As a result, nothing downstream could conclude that a table name is free on MariaDB.

On **MariaDB instances** (`Engine_MARIADB`), sync now records:

- **System-versioned tables** as ordinary `TableMetadata`, with the same columns, indexes, foreign keys, checks and triggers as a base table. `information_schema` reports versioning only as `TABLE_TYPE = 'SYSTEM VERSIONED'`, and `TableMetadata` has no field for that (it lives in omni). So sync appends the `WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING` table option to `CreateOptions`, which holds the table options. Hidden `row_start`/`row_end` stay absent. Explicit `GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START/END` columns keep the form `information_schema` reports: a stored generated column with expression `ROW START`/`ROW END`. MariaDB also treats writes to them like writes to generated columns (error 1906).
- **Sequences** in `SchemaMetadata.Sequences`: name, comment, data type, start, min, max, increment, cache size, and cycle. The attributes come from each sequence's own row (`SELECT start_value, … FROM db.seq`). `information_schema.SEQUENCES` exists only from 11.5 and has no cache size. The data type is the `start_value` column type without its display width, which matches `information_schema.SEQUENCES.DATA_TYPE` (for example `int unsigned`). If the user lacks SELECT on a sequence, the sequence keeps its name and a warning is logged, so its name still counts as taken.

The new behavior is keyed on the registered engine. Instances registered as MySQL keep their sync result even when the server is MariaDB, and so do OceanBase and TiDB. A test pins the MySQL-registered case against a real MariaDB server.

### DDL writers

Once versioned tables reach the metadata, the MySQL-family writers would emit a `CREATE TABLE` without versioning. For explicit period columns they would emit invalid DDL instead (`GENERATED ALWAYS AS (ROW START) STORED` is a syntax error, and MariaDB requires both `PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME` and `WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING`, otherwise error 4125). `writeTable` (dump / `GetTableDefinition`), `writeTableSDL`, and the legacy migration generator now emit:

- `GENERATED ALWAYS AS ROW START|ROW END`
- `PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME (start, end)`
- `WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING`

That path has no UI caller for MariaDB (the Sync Schema page excludes MariaDB), and it alr

title: fix(masking): show the masked-condition refusal without a code prefix
body: ## Summary Follow-up to #21651 (BYT-9455). A query whose conditions read a masked column is refused with `Using sensitive columns in query conditions is not allowed: `. The refusal was a connect `InvalidArgument` error, so the SQL editor showed it with a code prefix: - **PostgreSQL**: `invalid_argument: …`, because each statement's error becomes its result through `err.Error()`. - **SQL Server**: `[invalid_argument] …`, because the whole request failed and connect-es prefixed the code. The refusal is now the refused statement's result error on both engines, so the message has no prefix. On SQL Server the request no longer fails; the result carries the error, as it did before #21651 moved the check ahead of execution, so the editor also offers **Show in Editor** for it. Unchanged: the check still runs before execution, and on PostgreSQL the statements before the refused one still run while the ones after it do not. The query history entry no longer records the refusal in its error field, which the history pane does not show. ## Screenshots | | Before | After | |---|---|---| | PostgreSQL | | | | SQL Server | | | ## Test plan - `TestSensitiveData` now requires the refusal to start with the bare message, and the batch case to equal `Using sensitive columns in query conditions is not allowed: .public.tech_book.author`. - `go test ./backend/api/v1/`, `go test ./backend/store/`, and `go test ./backend/tests/ -run '^(TestClaim|TestCollision|TestSensitiveData)'` pass. - The screenshots come from the Playwright E2E harness, run against builds of `main` and this branch on the sample PostgreSQL instance and a SQL Server 2022 container. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
author: rebelice

title: fix(helm-charts): probe /healthz for readiness, not liveness [BYT-10353]
body:
## Summary

Bytebase runs metadata migrations in `server.NewServer` before `Server.Run` opens the HTTP listener, so `/healthz` is unreachable for the whole migration. The chart probed `/healthz` for liveness (300 s initial delay, 300 s period, 3 failures), so any migration longer than about 15 minutes got SIGTERM and a restart. An interrupted SQL migration rolls back as a whole, so a large upgrade can loop without ever finishing. BYT-10353 is a customer upgrade cut off this way mid-migration.

A failing readiness probe only removes the pod from the Service, so the migration runs to the end and the pod becomes ready once Bytebase starts serving.

## Changes

- Replace the `livenessProbe` on `/healthz` with a `readinessProbe`.
- Add `bytebase.readinessProbe` for the probe timing. Defaults: `periodSeconds: 10`, `timeoutSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 3`. Any other probe timing field passes through.
- Bump the chart to 1.1.7 and package it into `docs/` with `scripts/package_helm.sh`. Chart 1.1.6 (`bytebase.podAnnotations`, #21228) was never packaged, so 1.1.7 also publishes that value.
- Chart README and `docs/operations/upgrade.md`: the pod stays unready during migration, `helm upgrade --timeout` guidance, and which health checks stop a migrating server versus only draining it.

## Breaking Changes

- `helm upgrade --wait` now waits until migrations finish. Before, the pod had no readiness probe and counted as ready as soon as the container started. Helm's default `--timeout` is 5m, and `--atomic` rolls back to the previous Bytebase version when it expires. Set `--timeout` above the expected migration time.
- There is no liveness probe. A running but hung server is no longer restarted automatically. `/healthz` returns a static `OK`, so the old probe only caught a hung HTTP server. Crashes and fatal errors still exit the process, and the StatefulSet restarts it.

## Test plan

- [x] `helm lint helm-charts/bytebase`
- [x] `helm template` with defaults renders the readiness probe with the default timing and no `livenessProbe`

title: fix(frontend): keep the selected expiration chip readable on hover
body:
## Problem

In the Grant Access sheet, hovering over the **selected** expiration chip hid its label: the background turned light gray but the text stayed white.

`ExpirationChip` renders as `<Button appearance="secondary">`, whose `hover:bg-control-bg` also applied to the selected chip. The selected classes set `bg-accent text-accent-text` but no hover background.

## Fix

Give the selected chip `hover:bg-accent-hover`, the primary button's hover color. `cn()` drops the secondary variant's conflicting hover class. Unselected chips keep their gray hover.

## Screenshots

Pointer resting on the selected "1 week" chip (Playwright doesn't draw the cursor).

**Before**

![Before: selected 1 week chip hovered, label unreadable](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b473d1e0-8c5d-4d21-a4cf-7e340eab378c)

**After**

![After: selected 1 week chip hovered, label readable on darker accent](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/11f813f2-db65-4b27-b80b-8cd6f6a94cb9)

The before shot comes from the fixed build with the chip's hover class swapped back to `hover:bg-control-bg` in the DOM, which is the only difference this PR makes.

## Testing

- `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` pass.
- `node frontend/scripts/check-ui-guideline.mjs` passes.
- A local Playwright check against the embedded build (not committed) confirmed that hovering the selected chip computes `rgb(55, 48, 163)` with white text, and that an unselected chip still hovers to `rgb(243, 244, 246)`.

title: test(e2e): build the e2e server with SQL review V1, as release builds ship
body:
## Summary

The e2e suite has to boot a **non-release** build, because the dev license in `frontend/.env.dev` validates only against the dev key (a `release` build checks `keys/prod.pub.pem`). Since #21630, every non-release build turns on SQL review V2 (`profile_dev.go` sets `SQLReviewV2 = true`), while release builds keep V1. So the suite stopped testing what ships: 8 specs that check V1's review rules, the plan-check gate and the bypass flow failed, and 13 more did not run behind them.

We decided the e2e suite covers **V1** for now; V2 is under active development.

## Changes

1. **`frontend/tests/e2e/build-server.sh` (new)** builds the server the suite boots: `-tags embed_frontend`, no `release` tag, plus a Go `-overlay` that swaps `profile_dev.go` for a generated copy with `SQLReviewV2 = false`. The source tree is not modified, and no product code changes. If the `p.SQLReviewV2 = true` line moves, the script fails instead of silently testing V2.
   - The e2e README prerequisites, the missing-binary hint in `mode-start-new-bytebase.ts`, the e2e routine's `build.sh` and its SKILL.md use it.
   - `build.sh`'s cache stamp now includes the script's hash, so a binary built the old way (V2 on) is never reused.
2. **`sql-editor-admin-mode.spec.ts`** follows #21646: the result toolbar's "Vertical display" switch became a Table / Vertical display / Plan view switch, so the test picks the "Vertical display" option of the "Result view mode" radio group.
3. **`.claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md`** builds with the same script. Its plain dev build gave a V2 backend under the embedded frontend's V1 UI (`sqlReviewV2Enabled()` is `import.meta.env.DEV`, false in any embedded bundle), a mix no release build has.

## Notes for reviewers

- @rebelice: this keeps the e2e suite on V1 without touching #21630's switch. Testing V2 later needs both halves of the switch (backend `Profile.SQLReviewV2`, frontend `sqlReviewV2Enabled()`) to read one runtime value; today they diverge in an embedded dev binary (backend V2, UI V1).
- @d-bytebase: change 2 follows #21646's view switch.
- Only test, script and skill files change.

## Test plan

- Full suite with the new build on main `ef31ba2`: 233/234 passed. The one failure was the #21646 spec fixed in change 2, and its file then passed 19/19 (`--retries=0 --repeat-each=2`).
- Following the updated verify skill: `plan-detail-checks`, `-lifecycle`, `-review` and `-rollout` specs passed 59/59 (`--retries=0`).
- After rebasing onto `3bfc536`: rebuilt, then `sql-editor-admin-mode` + `plan-detail-checks` passed 15/15.
- `build-server.sh` fails with a clear message when `profile_dev.go` has no `p.SQLReviewV2 = true` line (checked against a copy without it).
- The changed TypeScript files type-check with `tsc --strict`; the frontend gate's `tsc` projects and Biome do not cover `tests/e2e`.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Build the Bytebase server binary the e2e suite boots.
+#
+#   frontend/tests/e2e/build-server.sh [output]   # default ./bytebase-build/bytebase
+#
+# The suite tests what release builds ship, but a release build only accepts
+# a license signed with the production key, and the suite uses the dev
+# license. So this builds a dev binary (no `release` tag) and, through Go's
+# -overlay, sets each dev-only product switch in profile_dev.go back to its
+# release value. The source tree is not modified. Embed the frontend first:
+# `(cd frontend && pnpm release)`.
+set -euo pipefail
+
+repo="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.." && pwd)"
+out="${1:-$repo/bytebase-build/bytebase}"
+profile="$repo/backend/bin/server/cmd/profile_dev.go"
+
+overlay_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
+trap 'rm -rf "$overlay_dir"' EXIT
+
+# SQL review V2 is under development and on only in dev builds; release
+# builds run V1. A missing line means the switch moved: fail rather than
+# silently testing V2.
+if [ "$(grep -c '^[[:space:]]*p\.SQLReviewV2 = true$' "$profile")" != 1 ]; then
+  echo "build-server.sh: expected one 'p.SQLReviewV2 = true' line in $profile; update this script" >&2
+  exit 1
+fi
+sed 's/^\([[:space:]]*\)p\.SQLReviewV2 = true$/\1p.SQLReviewV2 = false/' "$profile" >"$overlay_dir/profile_dev.go"
+node -e 'require("fs").writeFileSync(process.argv[3], JSON.stringify({ Replace: { [process.argv[1]]: process.argv[2] } }))' \
+  "$profile" "$overlay_dir/profile_dev.go" "$overlay_dir/overlay.json"
+
+cpus="$(nproc 2>/dev/null || sysctl -n hw.ncpu)"
+mkdir -p "$(dirname "$out")"
+cd "$repo"
+go build -overlay="$overlay_dir/overlay.json" -tags embed_frontend -ldflags "-w -s" -p="$cpus" \
+  -o "$out" ./backend/bin/server/main.go

title: fix(tsql)!: resolve UPDATE/DELETE targets through the FROM clause
body:
On SQL Server, an UPDATE or DELETE target can name a table in the statement's FROM
clause. `UPDATE o ... FROM dbo.Orders AS o` writes `dbo.Orders`. So does
`UPDATE Orders ... FROM otherdb.dbo.Orders`, where the FROM table has no alias, even when
the request database has its own `Orders`. The changed-resource extractor recorded the
target as written: the alias `o`, or `Orders` in the request database.

Three readers use the recorded table:
- approval rules on `resource.table_name`;
- approval rules on `statement.table_rows`, the synced row count of the recorded tables;
- the SQL Editor's per-table check for table-scoped `bb.sql.dml` grants.

This resolves an unqualified UPDATE/DELETE target the way SQL Server binds it. The
extractor looks through the FROM clause, including join and APPLY operands, for the table
with that exposed name: its alias, or its own name when it has none. It records that table
with its own schema and database. So `UPDATE T ... FROM sales.T` now matches a grant scoped
to `sales.T`; before, its schema was unknown and no schema-scoped grant matched it. A
qualified target names its own table and is unchanged. Names match exactly, because synced
metadata reports every SQL Server database as case-insensitive, even one with a
case-sensitive collation.

Prior backup keeps its own lookup (`findPhysicalTableForAlias`), unchanged. That lookup
matches aliases only, and it also runs for a qualified target. Changing it changes which
table prior backup saves, so BOT-162 tracks it.

## Breaking Changes

The SQL Editor now checks a FROM-bound target against the database it writes.
`UPDATE o ... FROM otherdb.dbo.T AS o` and `UPDATE T ... FROM otherdb.dbo.T` used to be
checked as a table in the request database, so a grant there could authorize them. They are
now checked against `otherdb`'s project and grants, as a qualified cross-database write
already is. If `otherdb` is not in Bytebase, or sits in another project, the statement is
refused.

Approval routing can change too. An aliased UPDATE/DELETE now matches table-name rules for
its real table. For aliased and unaliased targets alike, `statement.table_rows` now uses the
bound table's synced row count. It is 0 when that table is in another database, as it
already is for a qualified cross-database target.

## Out of scope

- **Case-folded matching (BOT-158).** A differently cased name, such as
  `UPDATE O ... FROM dbo.Orders AS o`, stays as written and is still checked against the
  request database. On a case-sensitive database that statement writes a real table `O`, and
  synced metadata cannot tell the two databases apart.
- **CTE and derived-table targets (BOT-160).** They stay as written and are still checked
  against the request database. BOT-160 also covers failing closed for unresolved targets.
- **Linked-server FROM tables (BYT-10235).** `FROM SRV.otherdb.dbo.T AS o` is recorded as
  the local `otherdb.dbo.T`, the same as a direct four-part target today.
- **`OUTPUT ... INTO` targ

title: feat(sql-editor): open query plans on the costliest operator
body:
## Why

The query plan viewer kept the pop-up page's layout after moving into the SQL Editor's result pane: five tabs, opening on the raw text, the diagram starting at the root, and the summary of where the cost goes hidden behind a tab. The design doc's main journey, fixing a slow query, starts from the expensive step, and the result pane is short on height. The pop-up page itself had no remaining link.

This is the first slice of `docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md` §3.3, with the §3.4 deletion of the pop-up page.

## What

- The viewer opens on the **Diagram** tab, centered on the operator that adds the most estimated cost, which starts selected. `planOpeningViewport` takes the focus node; with none it still opens on the root.
- Three tabs remain: **Diagram**, **Table** (was Grid) and **Text**.
- The three costliest operators are ranked at the top of the side panel, beside both the diagram and the table. Choosing one selects it and, on the diagram, brings it into view.
- What the diagram's bars and edges encode moves from its own line into a tooltip on the totals line.
- Removed: the **Query** tab, since the result pane's status bar already shows the statement that ran, limit included, with a copy control; and the Summary tab's cost timeline and per-operation table, along with their model helpers and text.
- The pop-up page is deleted: `explain-visualizer.html`, its app, stylesheet and Vite input, the sessionStorage token hand-off, and the selection-in-URL support only it used. The engine table it shared with the result pane moves to `src/utils/queryPlanEngines.ts`. `frontend/AGENTS.md` describes the viewer as part of the app instead of a separate entry.
- The Table tab indents every level by one step shared by all rows, narrowed for a plan deeper than twelve levels so the indent stays within 144px. It used to cap the indent at six levels and draw each row's deepest six tree lines, so a seventh-level row lost its indent and its lines shifted a column left, leaving a stray vertical line (a bug since #21443).
- From review: the legend opens from a focusable button; the table scrolls the selected row into view when it is chosen beside the table; collapsing the subtree that holds the costliest operator keeps the opening view on the collapsed card; the ranking's heading says it ranks by estimated cost; the UI guideline scanner no longer exempts the viewer, which passes it.
- The design doc's §3.3, §3.4 and §6 are updated.

## Before and after

The result pane maximized on the sample PostgreSQL, for a four-table join that plans as 11 operators. Captured from the embedded-frontend binary of `main` and of this branch, driven with Playwright.

### Opening the Plan view

**Before:** the viewer opens on the raw JSON, with five tabs.

**After:** it opens on the diagram, centered on t

title: fix(masking)!: refuse PostgreSQL queries whose conditions read masked columns
author: rebelice

title: fix(masking): refuse a result whose columns do not match its query span
body:
## Summary

SQL Editor masking applies one masker per query-span result to each result column **by position** (`doMaskResult`). When span extraction falls back and cannot know a relation's columns, the span lists a different number of results than the database returns. Earlier columns then shift onto the wrong maskers, and every column past the last masker comes back **in plaintext**.

`MaskResults` now refuses a result with rows whose column count differs from `len(span.Results)` when the span touches a masked column, in the style of the existing unresolved-columns refusal:

> masking cannot be applied: the query returned 5 columns but Bytebase resolved 4 from the synced schema, so the query was not returned

This covers Query, Export, and the MCP query tool, which all reach `doMaskResult` through `MaskResults`.

### Reproduction (PostgreSQL, on main today)

`tech_book(id, name, author)` with `id` and `author` masked, plus a set-returning function created on the target after the last schema sync:

```sql
CREATE FUNCTION unsynced_rows() RETURNS TABLE(a int, b int) LANGUAGE sql AS 'SELECT 1, 2';
SELECT * FROM unsynced_rows() f CROSS JOIN tech_book;
```

The parse-tree fallback lists one placeholder column for `f`, so the span has 4 results and the database returns 5. Before this change the Query API returned:

| a | b | id | name | author |
|---|---|----|------|--------|
| 1 | `******` | 1 | `******` | **bber** |
| 1 | `******` | 2 | `******` | **Egor Rogov** |

`author` came back in plaintext, `id` was unmasked, and the unrelated columns `b` and `name` were masked instead.

### Decisions

- **A mismatch with no masked column still passes.** Every masker is None, so position cannot change what is returned. Refusing would block queries over unsynced objects that masking could never have covered anyway (`SELECT * FROM unsynced_rows()` still returns `a, b`; the e2e test asserts this).
- **A result without rows passes.** It has no values to misplace, and BigQuery returns no column names for an empty result, so the check would otherwise refuse every empty BigQuery query on a masked table.
- **DML and DDL results are not checked.** Their `Affected Rows` column doesn't project `span.Results`. Cassandra UPDATE/DELETE and Redshift UNLOAD spans carry predicate columns, so without this exclusion a write that filters on a masked column would be refused.
- No re-sync is triggered on a mismatch. A function created after the last sync would resolve after the next sync, but a permanent mismatch (an extension function, or an extractor gap) would re-sync on every query, which is the throttling problem BYT-10074 tracks.

### Other masking paths

- The document maskers (CosmosDB, MongoDB, Elasticsearch) don't map maskers to columns by span position. They mask a JSON document by field path against the collection's object schema (CosmosDB, MongoDB) or by result column name (Elasticsearch), so this check doesn't apply to them.
- Every other masking engine (MySQL, MariaD

title: feat(mcp): say when no other person can approve an access request, and stop pointing agents at dead ends
body:
# feat(mcp): say when no other person can approve an access request, and stop pointing agents at dead ends

Part of BYT-9292 user journey 1, and of BYT-10347. This is PR 2 of 2 for the access-request tool design in `plans/2026-10-22-mcp-access-request-tool-design.md`, after #21643. It also carries the small fixes #21643 listed as a follow-up.

Two dead ends were left after #21643:

1. **A request no other person can approve.** In the journey 1 rerun, the requester was the project's only owner, and the project refused self-approval. The request could never be approved, yet the agent told the user to approve it themselves.
2. **A role request MCP always refuses (BYT-10347, 3.24.0).** A user with no query role asked an agent to read a table. `query_database`'s refusal advised "request the SQL Editor role on the project", so the agent filed a role request. MCP refuses every role request, but the refusal read as if an approval rule would lift it ("completes on creation whenever the workspace approval rule produces no template"). The tester added approval rules for both request types, and the request still failed.

What changes:

- **`request_access_grant` says when no other person can approve.** After it files the request, the tool reads the request's approval flow. Take a remaining step whose role no person holds, or only the requester holds while the project refuses self-approval. The result then says so in place of "a person approves it", and names the ways around: an approver can be added only in the console, since MCP excludes `SetIamPolicy`, and for an unmask request whose statement already runs with masked values, a project owner can grant a masking exemption with `grant_masking_exemption`. An exemption does not help a requester who cannot run the statement at all, since the SQL access check runs before masking. It never suggests turning on self-approval, and it says whether another person can approve, not who. The request stays filed, as the console files it.
- **The self-approval rule is one function** in the review package. The approval check and the new check both call it, the new one for each person who holds the step's role. People are found the way approval notifications find them: from the project and workspace IAM policies, with groups expanded and service accounts left out. Deactivated accounts are skipped; the skip sits in the shared lookup, so approval notifications stop naming them too. A holder with no workspace binding still counts, since sign-in can add one: self-hosted login adds it, and so does workspace SSO on SaaS. A binding counts a person only under their own principal type, the way the permission check matches it, so a `serviceAccounts/` binding on a person's email does not make that person an approver. That check sits in the shared lookup, so approval notifications and the workspace-admin checks that use it now agree with the permission check too. If any lookup fails, the check gives up and the tool keeps its normal resu

title: fix(sql)!: require bb.sql.explain for SQL Server's STATISTICS XML and PROFILE
body:
## Why

`SET STATISTICS XML ON` and `SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON` make every later statement of a SQL Server batch run and return its plan as well. They were not recognized, so a user holding `bb.sql.select` but not `bb.sql.explain` could read plans:

```sql
SET STATISTICS XML ON;
SELECT * FROM orders;
```

The `SHOWPLAN_*` settings were recognized by a regex over the statement text in `parser/base`, which a trailing comment (`SET SHOWPLAN_XML ON -- x`) or an option list got past.

This is the last open item of `docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md` §3.5.

## What

- The T-SQL span extractor reads these settings from the parsed `SET` statement (`ast.SetOptionStmt`), so comments and option lists such as `SET STATISTICS IO, XML ON` are handled, and carries them through the batch in the span context, next to the temporary tables it already carries. Each option is tracked by name, since SQL Server keeps each on until its own `OFF`.
- Under `SHOWPLAN_*` a read is an Explain, as before. Under `STATISTICS XML` or `PROFILE` a statement is marked as an executed plan (`QuerySpan.ExplainAnalyze`), so it needs its own permission, write-target checks included, and `bb.sql.explain`, exactly like a typed `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (#21642). A `SET` that names either option is marked the same way.
- The regex pass `tsqlRecognizeExplainType` and its test are removed from `parser/base`.
- The design doc's §3.5 and §6 mark the section closed.

## Breaking Changes

Permission logic changes on SQL Server:

- Running statements after `SET STATISTICS XML ON` or `SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON` now requires `bb.sql.explain` in addition to the statement's own permission. So does the `SET` itself.
- `SET SHOWPLAN_*` written with a comment or in an unusual layout is now recognized, so the reads after it need `bb.sql.explain`, as the plain form already did.

`SET STATISTICS IO` and `TIME` are unaffected.

## Tests

- `TestGetQuerySpanMarksPlanOutput` runs a SQL Server batch through `base.GetQuerySpan` and checks every span: on and off for `STATISTICS XML` and `PROFILE`, an option list, comments around the setting, a DML statement under `STATISTICS XML`, `STATISTICS IO` alone, `SHOWPLAN_TEXT` on and off with a trailing comment, unrelated `SET` statements under each setting, and one option's `OFF` leaving another that is still on in force.
- That an executed-plan span needs both permissions is already covered by `TestExplainRequiresEachReferencedDatabase` in `backend/api/v1`.
- Gates: gofmt, golangci-lint (clean), `backend/plugin/parser/...`, `backend/plugin/schema/mssql`, `backend/plugin/db/mssql`, `backend/api/v1`, and the server build.
- Not run: an end-to-end run against a live SQL Server.

title: feat(auth): center the sign-in form and drop the login illustration
body:
## What

Every auth page (sign-in, sign-up, password forgot/reset, MFA) now renders in one centered column. The sign-in and sign-up illustrations are deleted, along with the Enterprise-plan gate in `SplashLayout` that hid them.

## Why

The gate came from BYT-5355 (2024): a white-label Enterprise customer asked for the illustration to go, and the cheapest fix was to hide it for paid, non-trialing Enterprise workspaces only. So the people who saw the rocket scene were exactly the ones still evaluating Bytebase: prospects, trials, free self-hosted, and cloud users. Of 11 comparable tools (Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, MongoDB Atlas, Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Snowflake, Databricks, Retool, dbt Cloud, Vercel), none uses a scene illustration on login and nine use a plain centered form.

Paid Enterprise workspaces see no change: this is the layout they already had, and the custom logo still renders in the logo slot. The auth chrome now reads no plan or subscription state at all.

## Details

- `SplashLayout`: single centered column (`items-center`); the setup route alone keeps its two-column split, and below `lg` it no longer mounts the wizard panel into the hidden column (via `useMediaQuery`). Dead `mx-auto`, `relative`, and root `overflow-hidden` removed. The comment now states that `relative` and `pb-24` anchor the sign-in/sign-up `AuthFooter`, and that pages fill the column up to their own cap.
- `SplashLayout.test.tsx`: asserts the `lg:` column classes are absent on a single-column route and present on setup, plus the below-`lg` case.
- `OAuth2ConsentPage.tsx`: the comment for staying outside the layout now names the real reasons (the `pb-24` footer reserve, the 16px gutter the e2e spec pins) instead of the half-width column that no longer exists.
- `docs/design/onboarding-flow.md`: no longer records the rocket on sign-in and sign-up.

## Verification

- `pnpm --dir frontend fix`, `node frontend/scripts/check-ui-guideline.mjs`, and `pnpm --dir frontend test` (6881 tests) pass.
- `/verify`: built with `embed_frontend` and ran `workspace-setup` e2e, whose setup step signs in through the real sign-in page and whose spec drives the setup route's split column. 2 passed.
- Rendered sign-in and sign-up on the dev server at 1280px and phone width.

## Follow-ups (from review, out of scope here)

- The `SplashPanel` portal API now serves only `/auth/setup`; that route could own its two-column layout outside `SplashLayout`, which also lets it fix the pre-existing squeeze of the setup form (352–479px) between 1024 and 1407px.

body:
## Why

The SQL Editor draws query plans, but a picture appeared only when the result already was a plan: a typed `EXPLAIN`, or Ctrl/Cmd+E. The design doc's main journey, fixing a slow query after an ordinary run, needs the plan of the statement that just ran without re-running it. The doc asked for a Plan tab beside every result; this PR changes that to one option in the result pane's existing view switch, since the warehouses' tabs exist because the plan came back with the job, ours is fetched on demand, the journey's frequency is unmeasured, and the toolbar is already full.

## What

- The result toolbar's Vertical switch becomes a three-segment view switch on the SQL engines: Table, Vertical, Plan. Document and search engines keep their own controls and get no Plan. The segment icons share one small component, which also removes the arbitrary `h-[26px]` from the document control.
- Plan is offered when the engine can explain, the result is not already a plan, the run recorded an executed statement, and every earlier statement of the run was a plan that did not execute: any other statement may have changed session state the plan request would miss, and a result cannot show it (`SELECT set_config('search_path', …)` returns a row like any read). It is disabled with the reason in its tooltip when the user lacks `bb.sql.explain`; the backend stays the source of truth and a refusal shows as the view's error.
- Choosing Plan sends one explain request for `result.statement`, the executed statement with its limit wrapper, in the visualizer's format on PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Spanner and the engine's default elsewhere, and shows the plan in place of the grid: graph on the three, text on the others. The plan is cached on the result, so switching back and forth sends nothing. A re-run gets a fresh view keyed by its result.
- A one-word Estimated badge sits at the end of the viewer's tab row; its tooltip carries the §3.4 wording, "A new plan, made just now. It may differ from the plan that ran." The viewer's Query tab shows the executed statement, limit and all.
- The view switch's choice is remembered per editor tab (`SQLEditorTab.resultLayout`), so the next run in that tab opens the same way; a remembered Plan falls back to the table where the result offers none.
- §3.5 on the view: loading shows a spinner with Cancel, which aborts the request and returns to the table; a failed load shows the engine's message; past 1000 operators the viewer shows the plan as text instead of the graph.
- `docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md`: §3.1 to §3.5 describe Plan as a view-switch option, §4 records the rejected tab, and §6 moves this item to Landed, adds the #21642 link, and keeps SQL Server's `SET STATISTICS XML ON` as the one open §3.5 permission item.

## Before and after

Result pane on the sample PostgreSQL, same query. Captured from the embedded-frontend binary of `main` and of this branch, driven with Playwright.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
