title: feat(review): show a review result as its reviewer
body:
Built on #21621 (the AI review Run button), now merged: click Run on the plan page and the findings render as described below.

## Why

A review result is an issue comment with review metadata and no creator. The plan page rendered it as a comment by an unknown user, without its priority or the databases it applies to. The text of an AI result comes from a model that read SQL and schema text, so a markdown image in it could make every reader's browser request a URL built from that text.

## What

- A review result shows its reviewer instead of a person: an icon and "AI review" for AI results, "Standard rules" for RULE results. This applies in the expanded card, the collapsed resolved thread in the review timeline, and the collapsed row in the editor stack.
- A priority badge beside the reviewer: P0 red, P1 amber, P2 gray, nothing when unspecified. Its title says what resolving the thread means, in the wording of the proto comments.
- An "Applies to" row lists the target databases with the plan's target display. More than four fold to three and "+N more". The row is left out when the targets equal the databases of the spec the result is anchored to, as `IssueCommentPayload.ReviewMetadata.targets` describes. It stays whenever that cannot be proven: an unknown spec, a database group, a release-backed spec, or any other target form.
- `MarkdownEditor` gains an `untrusted` prop, set only for review results, in the view and in the edit box's Preview tab. Untrusted text renders without raw HTML and without images: a markdown image becomes a link to its source, labeled with its alt text, which loads nothing unless clicked. The output then passes DOMPurify with an explicit allowlist of tags and attributes, with no `src`, `style`, or `class`.
- Ordinary comments keep the old renderer, images and HTML included, since people already embed screenshots in comments.

## Checked in a browser

On a throwaway backend and dev frontend, with RULE and AI results on a plan:

- The reviewer, badges, targets, fold, and both collapsed rows render as described, also at 375 px.
- The AI result's image URL pointed at a local logging server and was requested 0 times. A user comment's image on the same server, the control, was requested 58 times.
- The check found two layout faults, fixed here: a stray "!" before an image link, and the "Applies to" label left alone on its line when the chips wrapped.

## Not in this PR

- Hiding the edit pencil on review results. Whether a finding's text can be edited is an open decision.
- A dark theme. The plan page has none.

## Tests

- `ThreadComment.test.tsx` (new): reviewer, badge, and targets for AI and RULE results with the real markdown renderer; a user comment renders as before; a remote image in a result renders as a link, never an image; the spec targets apply only to a result anchored to that spec.
- `ReviewResult.test.tsx` (new): priority labels, the fold, and when the targets row hides.
- `MarkdownEditor.test.tsx`: untrusted t

title: fix(oracle): apply the TLS settings to Oracle connections
body:
Design doc and implementation: [`docs/design/oracle-tls.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/cc/byt-10315-persistence-aa4ec7/docs/design/oracle-tls.md) ([BYT-10315](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10315)).

**The TLS section decides the connection: TLS mode TLS and Mutual TLS connect over TCPS with the section's certificates, Verify server certificate checks the certificate chain and the name of the server Bytebase connects to, and go-ora's own TLS keys in Extra Parameters give way to the section, with a notice under each.** The upgrade turns TLS mode off and removes the certificates on existing Oracle data sources, where they never applied, so they keep connecting.

## Why

The Oracle driver has never applied the instance form's TLS section. `Driver.Open` gives go-ora only the Extra Parameters, the SID and a dial timeout:

- A data source with TLS mode TLS and a pasted CA saves successfully and connects without TLS. Against a TCPS port it fails with `EOF` or `connection reset by peer`.
- Trusting a private CA or sending a client certificate takes an Oracle wallet in Extra Parameters, a directory on the Bytebase host. Bytebase Cloud has none, and making one from a PEM CA takes Oracle's `orapki`.
- Oracle was the only engine in the form's TLS list whose driver read none of the section.

## What the doc decides

- **D1.** Build the TLS configuration from the section with `util.GetTLSConfig` and give go-ora a copy per connection through `WithTLSConfig`. go-ora writes `ServerName` on the configuration it is given, so a shared one races when the pool opens connections in parallel.
- **D2.** TLS mode TLS and Mutual TLS set `SSL=TRUE`. Mutual TLS sends the section's client certificate, which `AUTH TYPE=TCPS` signs in with.
- **D3.** Verify checks the chain against the CA (pasted or file path) or the system roots, and the name against the server go-ora dials, as go-ora's own `SSL VERIFY` does. A `SERVER` failover address is checked against its own name, not Hostname.
- **D4.** TLS mode Disabled keeps today's connection, including the documented wallet setup with `SSL=TRUE` in Extra Parameters.
- **D5.** Under TLS mode TLS, the section replaces go-ora's TLS keys: an `SSL` key in any spelling becomes `TRUE`, and `SSL VERIFY` and a wallet's certificates aren't used. A password stored in the wallet still signs in when Password is empty.
- **D6.** On an Oracle data source with TLS mode on, a warning line appears under each `SSL`, `SSL VERIFY` and `WALLET` Extra Parameters row, in any spelling and whatever its value. Saving isn't blocked.
- **D7.** Migration `3.24.2` turns TLS mode off and removes the stored CA and client certificate on every Oracle data source. TLS mode never applied, so they keep connecting; a kept CA would be trusted once TLS is turned back on while the form showed System trust.

## What

| TLS mode | Verify server certificate | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disabled | any | No TLS, unless Extra Parameters set `SSL=TR

title: feat(recovery): non-interactive recovery beside a running Bytebase
body:
Implements the design in #21586 (`docs/design/non-interactive-recovery.md`).

## Summary

- **Two subcommands that need no terminal.** `bytebase recovery enable-password-signin` and `bytebase recovery reset-password --email <email> --password <password>` each run one action and exit, so a Kubernetes Job or `docker exec` can recover a locked-out workspace. `bytebase recovery` without a subcommand still opens the interactive menu.
- **Recovery runs beside the running servers.** `userEmailCache`, `settingCache` and `policyCache` become `expirable.LRU` with a one-minute lifetime (`store.OutOfBandCacheLifetime`), so a recovery change is live on every server within a minute, with no stop or restart. Servers started with `--ha` already read these from the database on every request.
- **Safe beside a server.**
  - The menu's role grant is computed inside the IAM policy lock and does not count an expired conditional binding as the role.
  - A setting fill that waited for the publish lock looks at the cache again.
  - With embedded PostgreSQL, recovery refuses to start a second postmaster on a data directory that may be in use, and reports the connection error it got.
- **No error repeats the password.**
  - The flag parser's and cobra's errors, which quote what was typed, are replaced.
  - The service names an email only after it matched an account, so a password passed as `--email` by mistake is not printed even when it looks like an email address.
  - `reset-password` refuses an unexpanded variable reference (`$NAME`, `${NAME}`, `$(NAME)`) and characters that cannot be typed at sign-in.
- **Result contract.**
  - The result line is printed whenever the change is stored, before the error of any later step (the audit record, clearing the lockout).
  - The exit status is 0 only when every step succeeded.
  - `reset-password` reads the email as sign-in does, so it clears the lockout sign-in counted.
- **Docs.**
  - The runbook drops the stop and restart steps, adds the Job for each way a deployment supplies `PG_URL` (literal, file path, IAM authentication, the chart's `escapePassword` start script), and states the limits below.
  - The HA guide matches.

## Limits (documented, not changed)

- The menu offers a role only to a user with no workspace role, as it has since #21182. With no usable administrator left, recovery cannot promote a user who already holds another role, for example Member after directory sync deactivated the only administrator.
- A sign-in attempt by a user with no role adds the member role, even when the attempt is refused, so `reset-password` says to add the role before the user tries to sign in.
- Each server reloads the user list about once a minute on a cache miss (D7). A one-row read on a miss is a possible follow-up.

## Breaking changes

None. The subcommands are additive, the menu still works as before, and no flag, API or schema changes.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./backend/bin/server/cmd/ ./backend/component/recovery/ ./bac

title: feat: onboarding flow, the first four screens
body:
Implements the onboarding flow designed in #21578 ([`docs/design/onboarding-flow.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/onboarding-flow.md)), and amends that doc with what building it settled. Frontend only.

**The rule:** a new workspace opens on four screens (workspace, goal, project and database, team). Continue only records answers in a local draft; Finish on screen 4 is the one commit, and it lands on the project home, whose next steps are ordered by the goal.

## What changed

- **The wizard** (`routes/auth/WorkspaceSetupPage.tsx`, `routes/auth/workspace-setup/`): four screens on the shared step indicator and form primitives, each validation message under its field. The left panel shows what each answer is for: a live preview of the workspace being named, then the chosen goal (the homepage hero for "Plan, review and roll out a database change", a statement above its result for the query goal, people and agents reaching the databases through Bytebase for "just exploring"), then the workspace holding the project as it is named with lines to its instances (the one the database choice brings, two more dimmed), and on screen 4 the workspace window again with the team: each address listed as a Workspace Member, dimmed rows while the team is bigger than "Just me". Every picture takes 70% of the panel column, from 512 to 800px, and never grows taller than the window; the drawn ones scale as one picture.
- **Finish, the one commit:** names → project → sample → project roles → workspace members. Every step but the create is safe to repeat, so a failed step is reported beside the button with Try again, and a retry, a reload or a second tab resumes from the draft. A create whose answer was lost is recognized from the server on the retry. The wizard takes back only the project roles it gave: each role's additions are recorded before the write, and every roles write carries the policy's etag.
- **One tab at a time:** the tab that saved the draft last holds setup. Another tab shows "This setup continued in another tab" with Continue here, or "This setup ended in another tab". Work a tab had started stops writing once it loses setup, the wizard is left, or setup ends.
- **Cloud and self-hosted:** Cloud invites teammates ("Send N invites and finish"); self-hosted asks the team size only, since a member added there would have no password, and keeps "I'll do this later". On self-hosted the project name is optional, as in the earlier wizard: left empty, no database is offered and Finish saves the answers, creates nothing, and lands on the projects page.
- **Project home and guide:** the goal and team size are stored for the guide; "Not sure yet, just exploring" uses the query journey; the project home and databases page put the goal's step first.
- **Shared code:** `StepIndicator` gains an opt-in `fitOneRow`: when the titles do not fit one row (a phone, or Spanish and Vietnamese at any width), only the current step keeps its title in s

title: test(review): cover the AI review on Azure OpenAI
body:
## What

Tests that pin the AI SQL review on Azure OpenAI to Microsoft's current documentation, and a live test for when a resource is at hand. The Azure path already matched the documentation, so `openai.go` is unchanged.

Part of BYT-9846.

## Checked against the documentation

From learn.microsoft.com (Foundry OpenAI how-to pages and the v1 REST reference) and the v1 OpenAPI spec:

- URL: `https://{resource}.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/responses` and `/openai/v1/chat/completions`, the settings page defaults. The adapter posts to the saved endpoint as typed and picks the API by the `/responses` path.
- Auth: the key goes in the `api-key` header on both endpoints.
- `api-version`: optional on v1 paths. The adapter adds none and keeps one the user typed.
- Deployment name: the `model` body field on both APIs.
- Tool calls: `function_call` and `function_call_output` on Responses, `tool_calls` and `role: tool` on chat completions.
- Reasoning items: with `store: false` every output item goes back before the function output, with `encrypted_content`. The adapter resends the output as received.
- Errors: a blocked prompt is a 400 with code `content_filter`. A 429 carries `retry-after-ms`, which the retry from #21590 reads first.

## Tests

- `backend/plugin/ai/openai_azure_test.go`: the documented request (path, query, headers, body) and reply on both endpoints, a full tool round trip on each, the documented 429 and `content_filter` errors.
- `backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_azure_openai_test.go`: the review loop through the real adapter on both endpoints, a retry that waits `retry-after-ms`, no retry on a `content_filter` 400, and a reply that was cut short fails the review.
- `backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_live_azure_openai_test.go`: `TestReviewLiveAzureOpenAI`, one case per endpoint, skipped unless all three variables are set.
- Each of these broke the tests on purpose: a Bearer header on Responses, an empty `api-key` on chat completions, the reasoning item dropped from the resent output, the incomplete status check removed.

```bash
AIREVIEW_LIVE_AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://YOUR-RESOURCE-NAME.openai.azure.com \
AIREVIEW_LIVE_AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY=... \
AIREVIEW_LIVE_AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT=... \
go test ./backend/plugin/aireview/ -run '^TestReviewLiveAzureOpenAI$' -v -count=1
```

## Not verified

No Azure resource was available, so nothing ran live. Open until someone runs the live test:

- whether Azure accepts the resent reasoning items exactly as returned,
- whether its error body is wrapped in `error` or flat (the adapter works with both for what it reads),
- how a real deployment behaves in the review.

- A gpt-5.6 deployment rejects tools on chat completions unless `reasoning_effort` is `none`. The settings page sends gpt-5.6 to Responses, so only a custom model on a chat completions endpoint meets this. The live test comment says to run the chat case with a deployment such as gpt-4o.

title: fix(review): run the AI review on Claude with room for its answer
body:
## What

The AI SQL review runs on Claude with room for its answer, and a live test proves it.

The Claude adapter fixed `max_tokens` at 4096. Claude counts its thinking against that limit, and `claude-sonnet-5` thinks by default, so a review with a long findings list could be cut short.

Part of BYT-9846.

## How

- `ai.Chat` takes `ChatOption` values. `ai.WithMaxOutputTokens(n)` sets the output limit of an adapter whose API requires one. Only Claude does, so only the Claude adapter reads it. A call with no option keeps 4096, so the SQL editor and release lint are unchanged.
- The review asks for 16000. `claude-sonnet-5` allows 128K, but Anthropic advises streaming above about 16K and `ai.Chat` does not stream. 16000 is also under Claude Haiku 4.5's 64K maximum.
- The Claude adapter lowers the limit to the model's documented maximum, since Anthropic rejects a larger `max_tokens` with a 400: 8192 for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku, 4096 for Claude 3 and Claude 2.x and Instant. Dated, aliased, Bedrock, and Vertex ids match. A newer or unknown model keeps the request.
- The Claude adapter sends the results of parallel tool calls in one user message, as Anthropic documents. Separate messages were accepted, but they teach Claude to stop calling tools in parallel.

## Tests

- `backend/plugin/ai/claude_test.go`: the 4096 default, 16000 when asked, the merge of parallel tool results using a real Claude reply, and `TestClaudeMaxTokens` for the cap of every older family across id forms, the newer models that keep 16000, and a request below the cap. It failed with the cap removed.
- `backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_claude_test.go`: the review through the real Claude adapter sends 16000 and the merged turn shape. It failed with the option removed.
- `backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_live_claude_test.go`: `TestReviewLiveClaude`, skipped unless `AIREVIEW_LIVE_CLAUDE_API_KEY` is set.

```bash
AIREVIEW_LIVE_CLAUDE_API_KEY=... go test ./backend/plugin/aireview/ -run '^TestReviewLiveClaude$' -v -count=1
```

## Live results

Three runs on `claude-sonnet-5`, all passed: 3 to 4 model calls, about 8K to 11K tokens, 3 tool calls (`read(orders)`, `search(legacy_status)`, `read(orders_summary)`), 2 findings each, one of them the view that depends on the dropped column. Thinking blocks and the `caller` field on `tool_use` blocks replay unchanged and are accepted.

## Notes for the reviewer

- Only `claude-sonnet-5` ran live. The older families' maximums come from Anthropic's model overview and release notes. No current Anthropic page lists Claude 3 Sonnet or Claude 2.x and Instant, so they take 4096, the adapter's old default that they already accepted.
- A proxy alias that does not contain the family name keeps 16000.
- `model_ai.go` also changes in #21589 and `claude.go` in #21591. Whichever lands later needs a small rebase.
- The live test uses `catalogTools`, which #21546 replaces.

title: feat(review): read a review run back
body:
## What

`IssueService.GetReviewRun` reads one reviewer's run on an issue back, so the issue page can tell a review that passed, one that failed, and one that never started apart. Until now `RunReview` was the only RPC, and the status it returned went stale the moment the run moved on.

Part of BYT-9846.

## How

- Proto: `rpc GetReviewRun(GetReviewRunRequest) returns (ReviewRun)` at `GET /v1/{name=projects/*/issues/*/reviewRuns/*}`, shaped like `PlanService.GetPlanCheckRun`. `RunReview`'s comment now says the results are issue comments and points to the new read.
- Handler: parses the name with the helper `RunReview` uses. An unknown reviewer id is `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. A missing issue or a slot never created is `NOT_FOUND`. The row goes through the converter `RunReview` uses.
- Store: `GetReviewRun(ctx, projectID, issueUID, reviewType)` reads by the full primary key `(project, issue_id, type)` and returns nil when there is no row.
- Permission: new `bb.reviewRuns.get`, granted to the five predefined roles that hold `bb.planCheckRuns.get`. No migration: a new RPC takes nothing away from custom roles.
- MCP: `READ`, like `GetPlanCheckRun`. The "Read the change workflow" row already covers it under "Issues and comments", so no locale changes. The ladder counts in `docs/design/mcp-capability-ladder.md` move by one.

## Tests

- `backend/store/review_run_test.go`: `TestGetReviewRunCollidingIssues`, two projects that share issue 201 with different slots.
- `backend/api/v1/issue_service_review_run_test.go`:
  - `TestGetReviewRun`: never started, Get after Run, a FAILED run read back, a slot never created, a missing issue, an unknown id, a malformed name.
  - `TestGetReviewRunCollidingIssues`: the same issue id in two projects, each read back as its own row.
- Each test failed when the code was broken on purpose: `project` or `type` dropped from the predicate, or the error copied on the wrong status.

## Notes for the reviewer

If the ladder should name reviews outright, "Issues, comments and reviews" would mirror the write row's "Run plan checks and reviews". That touches all five locale files, so it is left out.

title: test(review): prove the AI review on OpenAI
body:
## What

A live test that proves the AI SQL review works on OpenAI, on both endpoints the AI setting accepts. No adapter or review loop change was needed.

Part of BYT-9846.

## How

`TestReviewLiveOpenAI` in `backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_live_openai_test.go`, shaped like `TestReviewLiveGemini`. It runs one review of a risky PostgreSQL change on each endpoint and asserts that the model looked up an object with a tool and returned findings:

- Responses API, `gpt-5.6-terra` by default, or `AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_MODEL`.
- Chat completions, `gpt-4o`.

It is skipped unless `AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_API_KEY` is set, so CI skips it.

```bash
AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_API_KEY=... go test ./backend/plugin/aireview/ -run '^TestReviewLiveOpenAI$' -v -count=1
```

## Live results

- Responses: 3 model calls, 2 P1 findings, one of them the view that depends on the dropped column.
- Chat completions: 2 model calls, 1 P1 finding.

Reasoning items, parallel tool calls, the system message and the correction round all round-trip as OpenAI expects.

## Notes for the reviewer

The test uses `catalogTools`, which #21546 replaces. Whichever lands later adapts this one test.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

--- backend/plugin/aireview/model_ai_live_openai_test.go (+77/-0)

+package aireview
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"os"
+	"strings"
+	"testing"
+
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+
+	storepb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/store"
+)
+
+// TestReviewLiveOpenAI reviews a risky change with real OpenAI models, once on
+// each endpoint. It needs a key and network access that CI does not have:
+//
+//	AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_API_KEY=... go test ./backend/plugin/aireview/ -run '^TestReviewLiveOpenAI$' -v -count=1
+//
+// AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_MODEL replaces the model of the Responses case.
+func TestReviewLiveOpenAI(t *testing.T) {
+	apiKey := os.Getenv("AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_API_KEY")
+	if apiKey == "" {
+		t.Skip("AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_API_KEY is not set")
+	}
+	responsesModel := os.Getenv("AIREVIEW_LIVE_OPENAI_MODEL")
+	if responsesModel == "" {
+		responsesModel = "gpt-5.6-terra"
+	}
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name     string
+		endpoint string
+		model    string
+	}{
+		{name: "responses", endpoint: "https://api.openai.com/v1/responses", model: responsesModel},
+		{name: "chat completions", endpoint: "https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions", model: "gpt-4o"},
+	}
+	for _, tc := range tests {
+		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			statement := strings.Join([]string{
+				"-- Speed up the order history page.",
+				"CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders (created_at);",
+				"",
+				"ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN legacy_status;",
+			}, "\n")
+			request := &Request{
+				WorkspacePolicy: "An index on a table with more than 1 million rows must be created with CONCURRENTLY.",
+				Target: Target{
+					Engine:      "POSTGRES",
+					Version:     "16.2",
+					Environment: "prod",
+					Schemas:     []SchemaSummary{{Name: "public", ObjectCount: 2}},
+				},
+				Statement: statement,
+			}
+			model := NewModel(&storepb.AISetting{
+				Provider: storepb.AISetting_OPEN_AI,
+				Endpoint: tc.endpoint,
+				Model:    tc.model,
+				ApiKey:   apiKey,
+			})
+			tools := &catalogTools{}
+
+			result, err := NewReviewer(model).Review(context.Background(), request, tools)
+			require.NoError(t, err)
+			t.Logf("model: %s, model calls: %d, tokens: %d, tool calls: %v", tc.model, result.Calls, result.TotalTokens, tools.calls)
+			for _, finding := range result.Findings {
+				t.Logf("%s line %d: %s\n  rule: %s\n  evidence: %s\n  fix: %s", finding.Severity, finding.Line, finding.Title, finding.Rule, finding.Evidence, finding.Fix)
+			}
+			for _, note := range result.Notes {
+				t.Logf("note: %s", note)
+			}
+			require.NotEmpty(t, tools.calls, "the model should look up the objects before it judges")
+			require.NotEmpty(t, result.Findings)
+		})
+	}
+}

title: feat(mcp): let MCP sessions approve and reject issues after the user confirms
body:
# feat(mcp): let MCP sessions approve and reject issues after the user confirms

Part of BYT-9292 user journey 1 (the second of three PRs in `plans/2026-10-13-mcp-decision-matrix.md`). The first, #21588, is merged.

Today an agent can prepare a change or file an access request, but every approval waits for someone to open the console: `ApproveIssue` and `RejectIssue` are refused to MCP in every mode. A refusal does not stop a user who wants their agent to approve, because they can hand it a browser with their own session. So the guard becomes asking the user. The question is asked by the client, not by the model in chat, so an instruction planted in something the agent reads cannot approve anything.

What changes:

- **A new tool, `decide_issue(issue, decision, comment?)`,** approves or rejects a database-change issue or an access request. First it asks the user through MCP elicitation, the MCP specification's way for a server to ask the user something. The form shows the issue's name and title, what it changes, the current approval step, the requester and the comment the decision records, with one checkbox. For an access request, what it changes is the targets, schema and container, the query, whether results are unmasked or exportable, and when the grant expires. For a new database, it is the instance and, when set, the cluster, owner, table, character set and collation. The tool acts only when the user ticks the box and accepts. Declining, cancelling or leaving the box unticked changes nothing.
- **The form fits Claude Code's dialog.** Read from the Claude Code 2.1.300 binary and confirmed live on 2.1.302: its dialog shows four lines of a form's message, or the first three and "… (+N more lines)", and cuts each line six columns short of the terminal width. So each line does one job, with its bounded part first: the decision and the issue; the targets, counted before they are named; the statement or query; then the approval step, the requester and the comment. An access request's terms (unmasked, export, expiry) open the last line. Its schema and container stay on the targets line: the requester can set them to any length, so only a fixed label comes before the query. They follow a single database's name, so on an 80-column terminal a long name can cut them, and the dialog's "…" shows the cut. With several databases they come after the count and before the names. A form for one change or for an access request fits in four lines. A plan with several changes shows its first change, numbered with the total ("Change 1 of 3"), then Claude Code's "… (+N more lines)", so what the first change does (its statement, its release or its new database's settings) is always within the first three lines. A long list of targets or a long comment is cut at the end of its own line, not the statement: on an 80-column terminal the statement line shows at least 55 characters of SQL.
- **An answer counts only for a form this server sent, about the issue as it still i

title: fix(pg): cancel queries over an SSH tunnel when their context ends
body:
Fixes BYT-10314: a query on a PostgreSQL, Redshift or CockroachDB instance that connects through an SSH tunnel kept running on the database after it was canceled or timed out ([issue](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10314/canceled-and-timed-out-queries-keep-running-on-ssh-tunneled-postgresql)).

## What changes for a user

- **A query on an SSH-tunneled instance stops when its request ends.** Dropping the request, clicking Cancel in SQL Editor, and reaching the workspace maximum query time now stop the query on the database. Before, the query ran to completion and the request handler stayed blocked until it did.
- Other database calls that are stopped through their context, such as a canceled rollout task, are released the same way. Only the SQL Editor query path was tested end to end.
- Direct connections are unchanged. They already canceled correctly.

## Old behavior, measured

OpenSSH 8.0p1 in front of a PostgreSQL 16 that is reachable only through it. `SELECT pg_sleep(n)` sent through `POST /v1/instances/*/databases/*:query` on a running Bytebase server, and the request dropped after 5 s:

| Build | 2 s after the request ended | PostgreSQL log |
|---|---|---|
| main | the query is still active and runs its full 22 s | no cancel |
| this PR | the query is gone | `ERROR: canceling statement due to user request` at the drop |

## Root cause

pgx stops a query in two steps. It sets a deadline on the connection so the blocked read returns, then it dials the connection's `RemoteAddr` and sends a PostgreSQL cancel request. A connection made through `ssh.Client.Dial` supports neither step:

1. **It rejects deadlines.** `util.NoDeadlineConn` turned that into a silent no-op, so the blocked read was never released and pgx never got to the cancel request.
2. **It reports `0.0.0.0:0` as its remote address.** With the first defect fixed alone, the caller returns promptly but the cancel request is dialed to `0.0.0.0:0` and the query keeps running. Confirmed by running the new pg test with only the address left wrong.

Nothing stated what a tunneled connection has to provide for a driver to cancel a query.

## The contract now

`util.DialSSHTunnel` is the one place that states it: the connection it returns honors deadlines and reports the dialed address.

- It relays the ssh channel through a `net.Pipe`. The driver holds the near end, so a deadline interrupts a blocked read or write with a timeout error, and the connection stays usable once the deadline is cleared.
- `Close` lets the bytes `Write` already accepted reach the channel before closing it, so pgx's Terminate message is not lost. The wait is bounded to 1 s for a peer that stopped reading.
- The dial uses `ssh.Client.DialContext`, so it honors its context.

pgx's own cancel path is unchanged, so a tunneled connection is canceled exactly as a direct one is: the caller gets the context error, the server gets the cancel request, the connection is discarded and the pool reconnects.

@@ -0,0 +1,157 @@
+package testcontainer
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"crypto/ed25519"
+	"crypto/rand"
+	"encoding/pem"
+	"io"
+	"net"
+	"strconv"
+	"sync"
+	"testing"
+
+	"github.com/pkg/errors"
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+	"golang.org/x/crypto/ssh"
+)
+
+// SSHServer is an in-process SSH bastion for tests that reach a database
+// through an SSH tunnel. It runs in the test binary rather than in a container,
+// so the addresses it forwards to are the ones the test itself can dial.
+type SSHServer struct {
+	host       string
+	port       string
+	privateKey string
+}
+
+func (*SSHServer) GetUser() string { return "bytebase" }
+
+func (s *SSHServer) GetHost() string { return s.host }
+func (s *SSHServer) GetPort() string { return s.port }
+
+// GetPrivateKey is the PEM-encoded key the server accepts, for any user.
+func (s *SSHServer) GetPrivateKey() string { return s.privateKey }
+
+// NewSSHServer starts an SSH server that forwards TCP connections and stops it
+// when the test ends.
+func NewSSHServer(t testing.TB) *SSHServer {
+	t.Helper()
+
+	_, hostKey, err := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	hostSigner, err := ssh.NewSignerFromKey(hostKey)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	clientPublicKey, clientKey, err := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	authorizedKey, err := ssh.NewPublicKey(clientPublicKey)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	clientKeyPEM, err := ssh.MarshalPrivateKey(clientKey, "")
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	config := &ssh.ServerConfig{
+		PublicKeyCallback: func(_ ssh.ConnMetadata, key ssh.PublicKey) (*ssh.Permissions, error) {
+			if !bytes.Equal(key.Marshal(), authorizedKey.Marshal()) {
+				return nil, errors.New("unknown public key")
+			}
+			return nil, nil
+		},
+	}
+	config.AddHostKey(hostSigner)
+
+	host, port := NewTCPServer(t, func(conn net.Conn) { serveSSHConn(conn, config) })
+	return &SSHServer{host: host, port: port, privateKey: string(pem.EncodeToMemory(clientKeyPEM))}
+}
+
+// NewTCPServer listens on a loopback port and runs handle on each connection it
+// accepts. A connection stays open after handle returns, until the test ends,
+// so a handle that does nothing is a server that never answers.
+func NewTCPServer(t testing.TB, handle func(net.Conn)) (host, port string) {
+	t.Helper()
+
+	listener, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	host, port, err = net.SplitHostPort(listener.Addr().String())
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	var mu sync.Mutex
+	var conns []net.Conn
+	t.Cleanup(func() {
+		_ = listener.Close()
+		mu.Lock()
+		defer mu.Unlock()
+		for _, conn := range conns {
+			_ = conn.Close()
+		}
+	})
+
+	go func() {
+		for {
+			conn, err := listener.Accept()
+			if err != nil {
+				return
+			}
+			mu.Lock()
+			conns = append(conns, conn)
+			mu.Unlock()
+			go handle(conn)
+		}
+	}()
+	return host, port
+}
+
+func serveSSHConn(conn net.Conn, config *ssh.ServerConfig) {
+	_, channels, requests, err := ssh.NewServerConn(conn, config)
+	if err != nil {
+		return
+	}
+	go ssh.DiscardRequests(requests)
+	for newChannel := range channels {
+		if newChannel.ChannelType() != "direct-tcpip" {
+			_ = newChannel.Reject(ssh.UnknownChannelType, "only direct-tcpip is supported")
+			continue
+		}
+		go forwardSSHChannel(newChannel)
+	}
+}
+
+// forwardSSHChannel serves one direct-tcpip channel as sshd does: it dials the
+// requested address and closes both sides once either one ends.
+func forwardSSHChannel(newChannel ssh.NewChannel) {
+	// RFC 4254 section 7.2.
+	var request struct {
+		DestAddr   string
+		DestPort   uint32
+		OriginAddr string
+		OriginPort uint32
+	}
+	if err := ssh.Unmarshal(newChannel.ExtraData(), &request); err != nil {
+		_ = newChannel.Reject(ssh.ConnectionFailed, err.Error())
+		return
+	}
+	target, err := net.Dial("tcp", net.JoinHostPort(request.DestAddr, strconv.FormatUint(uint64(request.DestPort), 10)))
+	if err != nil {
+		_ = newChannel.Reject(ssh.ConnectionFailed, err.Error())
+		return
+	}
+	defer target.Close()
+
+	channel, requests, err := newChannel.Accept()
+	if err != nil {
+		return
+	}
+	defer channel.Close()
+	go ssh.DiscardRequests(requests)
+
+	done := make(chan struct{}, 2)
+	go func() {
+		_, _ = io.Copy(channel, target)
+		done <- struct{}{}
+	}()
+	go func() {
+		_, _ = io.Copy(target, channel)
+		done <- struct{}{}
+	}()
+	<-done
+}

+		{name: "ssh tunnel, deadline exceeded", sshTunnel: true, timeout: 2 * time.Second, wantErr: "context deadline exceeded"},
+		{name: "ssh tunnel with TLS, canceled", sshTunnel: true, tls: true, wantErr: "context canceled"},

+		t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {

+			var rawDB *sql.DB
+			if tc.tls {

+				Port:     pgContainer.GetPort(),

+				UseSsl:   tc.tls,
+			}
+			if tc.sshTunnel {
+				sshServer := testcontainer.NewSSHServer(t)
+				dataSource.SshHost = sshServer.GetHost()
+				dataSource.SshPort = sshServer.GetPort()
+				dataSource.SshUser = sshServer.GetUser()
+				dataSource.SshPrivateKey = sshServer.GetPrivateKey()

+			t.Cleanup(func() { _ = driver.Close(background) })

+			done := make(chan []*v1pb.QueryResult, 1)
+			go func() {

+				if err != nil {

+				}

+			const runningQueries = `state = 'active' AND query LIKE '%pg_sleep%'`
+			require.Eventually(t, func() bool { return countSessions(t, rawDB, dbName, runningQueries) == 1 }, 10*time.Second, 20*time.Millisecond,
+				"the query never started on the server")
+			if tc.timeout == 0 {
+				cancel()
+			}
+
+			select {
+			case results := <-done:
+				require.Len(t, results, 1)
+				require.Contains(t, results[0].Error, tc.wantErr)
+			case <-time.After(10 * time.Second):

+			}
+			require.Eventually(t, func() bool { return countSessions(t, rawDB, dbName, runningQueries) == 0 }, 10*time.Second, 20*time.Millisecond,
+				"the query kept running on the server after its context ended")
+			require.Eventually(t, func() bool { return countSessions(t, rawDB, dbName, `application_name = 'bytebase'`) == 0 }, 10*time.Second, 20*time.Millisecond,
+				"the canceled connection stayed open on the server")
+
+			require.NoError(t, driver.Ping(background), "the driver must reconnect once the canceled connection is discarded")
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+// countSessions counts the sessions in the database, other than the one asking, that match the pg_stat_activity condition.
+func countSessions(t *testing.T, rawDB *sql.DB, dbName, condition string) int {
+	t.Helper()
+	var count int
+	err := rawDB.QueryRow(`SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = $1 AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() AND `+condition, dbName).Scan(&count)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	return count

title: feat(review): fail a review whose reply was truncated or blocked
body:
## What

The AI chat response says why the model stopped, and the AI SQL review uses it.

The review loop could not tell why a reply ended:

- A reply cut at the output limit was parsed as if it were whole. When its first complete JSON object held findings, the rest were lost without notice. Every model has an output limit, 16000 tokens for a Claude review call since #21597, so this stays reachable.
- A refusal that arrived as text got a correction round, as if the model had only formatted its answer wrong. A second try could pass a change the provider refused to judge.
- Every empty reply failed the review, also the one Gemini returns when it garbled a tool call, which deserves a second try.

Part of BYT-9846.

## How

- Proto, additive: `AIChatResponse.stop_reason`, of the nested enum `AIChatResponse.StopReason`: `TURN_COMPLETED`, `TOKEN_LIMIT`, `BLOCKED`, `MALFORMED_TOOL_CALL`, `OTHER`.
- Each adapter in `backend/plugin/ai` fills it from what its provider reports. The mappings are in `stop_reason.go`, one function per API, each checked against the provider's API reference:
  - OpenAI and Azure OpenAI chat completions: `finish_reason` and `message.refusal`.
  - OpenAI Responses: `status` and a `refusal` content part. An incomplete response stays an adapter error, as before.
  - Claude: `stop_reason`.
  - Gemini: the candidate's `finishReason`, and `promptFeedback.blockReason` when there is no candidate.
- A value the reference does not list maps to `OTHER`, never to `TURN_COMPLETED`.
- The review loop:
  - `TOKEN_LIMIT` fails with `ErrTruncatedReply`. Nothing is parsed and no tool runs, also when the turn carries tool calls, since their arguments may be cut.
  - `BLOCKED` fails with `ErrBlockedReply`, with or without text.
  - `MALFORMED_TOOL_CALL` is never final, whatever text or tool calls came with it. Nothing from that turn runs or enters the history. It gets one correction round, from the budget an invalid final reply already has, and fails with `ErrInvalidReply` when that round or the call limit is spent.
  - `OTHER`, and any value added later, fails with `ErrUnfinishedReply`: nothing is parsed, no tool runs, no correction round. Gemini's `OTHER`, `UNEXPECTED_TOOL_CALL`, `TOO_MANY_TOOL_CALLS`, `MISSING_THOUGHT_SIGNATURE`, and `MALFORMED_RESPONSE`, a failed or cancelled Responses reply, and Claude's `pause_turn` all land there.
  - `TURN_COMPLETED`, and no stop reason at all (a compatible server without `finish_reason`), behave as before, `ErrEmptyReply` for an empty reply included.
- `AIService.Chat` returns the field as the adapters set it. The frontend does not use it yet, only the generated types change.

## Tests

- `backend/plugin/ai/stop_reason_test.go`: every documented value of every provider through the real adapter and a scripted HTTP server, plus an unknown value each.
- `backend/plugin/aireview/reviewer_test.go`: the loop for every stop reason, with and without text and tool calls.
- One line of `model_ai_test.go`: a Gemini sa

title: fix(review): retry a transient provider failure inside the AI review
body:
## What

A transient failure of the AI provider no longer fails an AI SQL review.

One failed HTTP call failed the whole review. One run sends up to 8 reviews to the provider at once, each with up to 20 model calls, so a rate limit is likely on a plan with several databases.

Part of BYT-9846. Go only: no proto change, no frontend change.

## How

- `backend/plugin/ai` returns a typed error for a failed call. `HTTPError` carries the provider, the status, the wait the provider asked for, the provider's `x-should-retry` answer, and whether the quota is used up. `TransportError` is a call that got no complete reply. The text of both is what callers saw before.
- What each vendor says in its own format is read in that package, one small reader per adapter: the `insufficient_quota` code of OpenAI, the `enforced_spend_limit_reached` code of Anthropic, and the `RetryInfo` delay in the body of a Gemini error.
- `settingModel.Chat` in `backend/plugin/aireview` retries what the official OpenAI and Anthropic Go SDKs retry, at most 3 times: the provider's `x-should-retry` header decides when it is sent, and otherwise 408, 409, 429, every status of 500 and above, and transport failures. A 429 for a used-up quota fails at once.
- It waits as long as the provider asked, `Retry-After-Ms` before `Retry-After` as in those SDKs, or else backs off from about one second with jitter, so the concurrent reviews of one run do not retry at the same moment.
- It never starts a wait that would end after the review deadline: the provider's error comes back at once. When the context ends, the context's error comes back.
- A retry is not a model call of the review loop. The limit of 20 calls counts turns, as before.
- The SQL editor assistant and the release lint call the same adapters. They do not retry, and their error text and code are unchanged.

## Tests

- `backend/plugin/ai`: the `Retry-After` parser, and each adapter's typed error through a scripted HTTP server, including the three vendor markers.
- `backend/plugin/aireview`: retry through the real Gemini, OpenAI, and Claude adapters with a clock that does not sleep. A 429 with a wait then success, 503 on every attempt, 400 and 401 once, the unrecoverable 429 cases, a transport failure then success, a dial timeout, a canceled context during the wait, a wait past the deadline, the call count of the review loop, and the retry log line.

## Known limits

- `TestCollision_RunReviewLifecycle` is about 8 seconds slower. Its stub model answers 503, which is now retried with real waits. The test is untouched here because two other open PRs edit it. A status that is not retried, such as 401, restores its speed.
- The provider's wait has no cap of its own, only the review deadline of 10 minutes.
- A Gemini daily quota is not told apart from a rate limit, so it gets the 3 retries.

title: feat(review): add a workspace switch for the AI SQL review
body:
## What

A workspace switch for the AI SQL review, off by default, beside the standard SQL review rules.

Until now the AI review ran whenever AI was on in the workspace setting. That one flag also turns on the SQL editor assistant. A review sends more than the assistant does: the statements of a change as written, and it can send the schema of the target databases and their table statistics. A company can accept the one and not the other.

Part of BYT-9846.

## How

Backend:

- `AISetting.sql_review_enabled`, in the store and the v1 proto. A stored setting without the field reads as off, so a workspace that already has AI on stays without the review until an admin turns it on.
- `aireview.CheckSetting` is the one place that says whether the setting allows a review: AI on and the switch on.
- `RunReview` refuses an AI run with `FAILED_PRECONDITION` while the switch is off, and creates no run.
- The executor reads the setting again before every provider request, the retries of a failed call included, through the model option `CheckBeforeEachCall`. Switching the review off stops a run in flight at its next request, and the run fails with the reason.
- Every one of these gates, `RunReview` included, reads the setting through the new `GetAISettingUncached`. The setting cache has no TTL and only in-process writes refresh it, so a switch-off written anywhere else still stops the review.
- `UpdateSetting` accepts the mask path `value.ai.sql_review_enabled`.
- `UpdateSetting` merges the AI setting under the row lock, as APP_IM and the workspace profile do, so two admins saving at once cannot restore each other's change, a switch turned off included. Workspace creation seeds no AI row, so the new store function `UpsertSettingAtomic` inserts an empty one with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and locks it in the same transaction. `UpdateSettingAtomic` still refuses a missing row.
- `ActuatorInfo.ai_sql_review_enabled`, output only, beside `ai_enabled`. A user who cannot read the AI setting still sees whether the review is on.

Frontend, on the SQL Review pages that are dark launched behind `sqlReviewV2Enabled()`:

- Workspace SQL Review page: an "AI review" section under the standard rules, with one switch and a line that says what a review sends. It saves from the page's one footer, together with the standard rules. While AI itself is off the section says so.
- Project SQL Review page: the same section, read only, since the switch is workspace wide.
- A user without `bb.settings.set`, and every user in SaaS mode, sees the state as text.
- Strings in all five locales, under `sql-review.ai-review`.

## Not in this PR

- A release build shows no control for the switch until SQL Review V2 is no longer dark launched. The API works either way.
- SaaS mode. There the whole AI setting is read only, so the review stays off. Letting an admin flip this one switch on Cloud puts the token cost on the platform key, which is a decision of its own.
- A rolling upgrade from 3.23.1

title: feat(mcp): let MCP sessions read who can approve and the policies that apply
body:
Part of BYT-9292 user journey 1 (the first of three PRs in `plans/2026-10-13-mcp-decision-matrix.md`).

In a live run of journey 1 on 2026-10-13, an agent helping a workspace admin could not confirm that the admin owned the project, and could not see the masking exemptions: MCP refused both reads as "administers the workspace", although everyone who holds the permission reads them in the console. It also could not say who would approve a request, because the project and workspace members behind an approval role were unreadable too.

This moves 11 read RPCs from EXCLUDED to READ:

- `ProjectService/GetIamPolicy` and `WorkspaceService/GetIamPolicy`
- `GroupService/GetGroup`, `ListGroups` and `BatchGetGroups`
- `RoleService/GetRole` and `ListRoles`
- `OrgPolicyService/GetPolicy` and `ListPolicies`
- `AccessGrantService/GetAccessGrant` and `ListAccessGrants`

RBAC still runs after the MCP gate, so each read reaches only whom the API already serves: holders of its permission, a group's own members, and, for the two masking policy types read one at a time, holders of the type-specific permission. Once a request exists, an agent can tell which people its approval step waits on: the issue names the approver roles (already readable), and these reads map roles to members and groups. Before a request is filed, the workspace approval setting that picks the rule stays refused.

The Access policy page and the consent screen gain a Read-only row, "Read members, roles and policies" (exact copy in the diff). The section's shared line already says every session is limited by the user's own Bytebase permissions. Both mode summaries now mention members, roles and policies. The `ADMINISTERS_THE_WORKSPACE` reason's comment loses its second sentence, a hand-written read rule that no code reads and that did not hold for every method keeping the reason; each method's annotation and the generated inventory already record which reads carry it.

## Why these reads are safe to serve

- **No response carries a credential.** IAM policies return bindings and an etag; groups return members and an email; roles return permissions. Policies return only their type's payload: masking rules (a condition and a semantic type), masking exemptions (members and a condition), rollout (a flag and roles), tag (a review-config reference), data query (limits and flags), review rules (rule names) and AI review (admin-written text; the AI key lives in the AI setting, which stays refused).
- **They show what these users already see.** Access-grant reads need project owner, workspace admin or DBA, the people who approve those requests.

## Not in this change

- `ListPolicies` checks only `bb.policies.list` and returns every policy type. `GetPolicy`, which the console uses, asks for `bb.policies.getMaskingExemptionPolicy` or `bb.policies.getMaskingRulePolicy` in place of `bb.policies.get` on those two types. Every built-in role that holds `bb.policies.list` holds both, so the difference reaches cust

title: fix(api)!: refuse an access grant where just-in-time access is off
body:
An access grant applies only in a project that allows just-in-time access: at query time, `SQLService.preCheckAccess` ignores every grant in a project where it is off. `CreateAccessGrant` never checked the setting. So a request through the API or MCP in such a project was accepted, sent to its approvers, could be approved, and then did nothing.

After this change, `CreateAccessGrant` refuses that request with FAILED_PRECONDITION, before the grant or its issue is written. The message names the project and the setting a project owner can turn on ("Allow access grants").

## Breaking Changes

- API and MCP callers who file an access grant in a project with just-in-time access off now get FAILED_PRECONDITION, and no grant or issue is written. Before, the request was accepted as PENDING, could be approved, and did not take effect. A script that files a request and turns the setting on later must turn it on first.
- Console users see no change. The console files requests only from the SQL Editor's request drawer, and every way to open it already requires the setting.

Found in a live run of MCP journey 1 on 2026-10-13 (a build of main `32ef4e4019`): a request filed over MCP with the setting off was approved by a second project owner, and the rerun stayed masked with no message.

## Not in this change

- The check runs only when a request is filed; activation and the setting toggle never read the setting. So a request filed while the setting is on and approved after an owner turns it off becomes an active grant that does not apply, and it goes live if an owner turns the setting back on (the same run saw a grant go live that way). Grants filed before this change behave the same.
- The proto comment on `CreateAccessGrant` does not list the new error. Adding it means a regeneration and the frontend gates.

## Tests and verification

- `TestRefuseAccessGrantWithoutJIT` (`backend/api/v1`): with the setting off, FAILED_PRECONDITION naming the project and the setting; with it on, no error.
- `TestMCPGateRefusesGrantIssues` (`backend/tests`, on the live MCP session it already starts): with the setting off, the MCP request returns 400 with code `failed_precondition`, the API request returns FAILED_PRECONDITION, and neither leaves an access grant or an issue. After the setting is turned on, the same request files exactly one grant and one issue.
- Four existing backend tests filed requests in projects without the setting; each now turns it on with a new `allowJustInTimeAccess` helper. `mcp_masking_test.go` replaces its inline update with the same helper and drops a comment the fix made false.
- Mutations: removing the check fails `mcp_gate_test.go` (expected 400, got 200); making the helper a no-op fails all five tests that use it, with the new message.
- Local gates on `b743bb4e5c`: `gofmt`, `go vet`, repo-root golangci-lint (no findings on changed lines), the server build, comment share 16%, and CI's test command (`go test -p=8 -timeout 30m ./backend/tests ./ba

title: docs(design): non-interactive recovery beside a running Bytebase
body: Design doc for running `bytebase recovery` without a terminal and without stopping Bytebase: `docs/design/non-interactive-recovery.md`. `bytebase recovery` runs only as an interactive menu today, and its runbook stops every Bytebase server first and restarts them after. Teams that operate only through Kubernetes jobs cannot use it. The doc lands on one rule: **recovery runs as one command with arguments beside a running Bytebase, and its change is live within one minute, with no stop and no restart.** ### What the doc decides - **Each recovery action is also a subcommand.** `bytebase recovery enable-password-signin` and `bytebase recovery reset-password --email --password ` run one action and exit. The interactive menu stays as it is. - **The password is a flag,** as in `redis-cli`, `docker login` and the Grafana and Gitea admin commands. A Kubernetes Job fills it from a Secret. There is no password file in this version. - **The subcommands do not add a workspace role.** That case stays with the menu, which shows the roles as a list. - **Recovery runs beside the running server.** The runbook and the command stop telling the operator to stop and restart Bytebase. Recovery reaches the metadata database exactly as the server does. On Kubernetes that is a Job built from the server's pod template: the same image by digest, service account, environment and mounts. With the embedded database, recovery runs inside the server's container. - **The user, setting and policy caches expire after one minute.** These caches are what kept a running server from seeing a recovery change. A change is now live within about a minute on every server. The minute runs from when a server stored its copy, so a read in progress when recovery commits makes that server late by the length of that read. Rejected: a message to running servers (it can be missed, silently), a counter in the database (a schema change), and `--ha` (it reloads the user list on every request). - **Recovery states the limit and does not wait.** It prints `Live within one minute.` and exits 0. Any failure exits 1. - **No shared reload yet.** The user list reloads about once a minute. Sharing that reload between simultaneous requests is the first thing to add if a large workspace shows a spike. ### Figures Captured from the design page. Nothing here is built yet. **A · The flow.** A recovery pod runs one action beside the running Bytebase pod and exits. Within one minute the running pod reads the database again by itself. Nothing is stopped or restarted. **B · The two subcommands.** Each runs one action, prints the result and exits. The password is a flag, and the exit status is 0 only when the change is saved.

title: feat(mcp): let Read-write sessions request access grants
body:
Part of BYT-10292 (problem 2) and BYT-9292 user journey 1.

An agent that meets masked data, or a table it cannot read, has no way to ask for access today. MCP refuses `AccessGrantService/CreateAccessGrant` (EXCLUDED) and refuses an ACCESS_GRANT issue through `CreateIssue`. After this change a Read-write session can file an access request, but only one that a person has to approve.

What changes:

- **Read-write sessions can call `CreateAccessGrant`.** It moves from EXCLUDED to WRITE. Read-only sessions are still refused.
- **A request that no person would approve is refused.** An approved access grant takes effect at once. So when no approval rule sends the request to a person, because no rule matches or the matching rule names no approver, an MCP session's request is refused before any row is written. The refusal tells the user what an admin has to change.
- **The approval decision is made once, when the request is created.** The server evaluates the approval rules against the request itself, before it writes the grant or its issue, and saves the finding on the issue. A rule edit afterwards cannot change whether the request waits for a person. Before, the finding was computed after both rows existed. Because a finding saved at creation emits no approval event, `CreateAccessGrant` notifies the approvers itself.
- **A console request is decided the same way as before, with one change.** If evaluating the approval rules fails, for example on a rule that does not compile, the request now fails before any row exists. Before, the grant and its issue were created, and the issue waited in CHECKING until someone ran `RetryIssueApproval` after fixing the rule.
- **The session still cannot approve its own request.** `ActivateAccessGrant` moves from EXCLUDED to FORBIDDEN, refused as an approval decision. `ApproveIssue` and `RetryIssueApproval` were already FORBIDDEN. The reason the four approval methods give now covers access requests as well as changes: "it decides whether a change or an access request passes its human approval, and an agent does not decide that for its own work".
- **An ACCESS_GRANT issue through `CreateIssue` now points to `CreateAccessGrant`.** `CreateIssue` has no ACCESS_GRANT arm for any caller, so the old refusal, which said the issue "completes on creation" and to use the console, sent the agent nowhere. The gate and the `UpdateIssue` allow_missing guard share one allow-list, so their wording cannot drift. ROLE_GRANT keeps its refusal. To let one entry name a different way out, the gate's request-shape table now returns a way out with each reason; the masked-write refusals keep the console.
- **The Access policy page and the consent screen gain a Read-write row, "Request access grants".** Its details: "Ask for a time-boxed grant to run a specific statement, optionally with results unmasked or exported; the statement must be a read as far as the engine can check it · The grant starts only after a person approves it, and a request th

title: fix(frontend): show one error toast when the sample instance fails
body:
## What the user saw

On Bytebase Cloud, clicking **Use sample instance (Available for 7 days)** on a project's create-instance page, while the server's sample target was misconfigured, showed two error toasts for one failure:

1. `Code 9: FailedPrecondition` with body `[failed_precondition] Sample Project Instance is not configured`
2. `Failed to prepare Sample Project Instance.` with the same body

The workspace setup wizard reports a failed sample step the same way.

## Root cause

- `errorNotificationInterceptor` (`frontend/src/api/middlewares/errorNotificationMiddleware.ts`) is a global Connect interceptor. It pushes an error toast for every failed request unless the request is marked `silent`.
- The store action `prepareSampleProjectInstance` (`frontend/src/stores/app/instance.ts`) sent a plain request, so the interceptor toasted the failure.
- Both callers of the action also catch the error and push their own toast: `CreateInstanceView.tsx` (create-instance page) and `WorkspaceSetupPage.tsx` (setup wizard).

So every failure was reported twice. There are no other callers.

## Fix

The existing `silentContextKey` would remove the duplicate, but it answers two questions at once: who shows the error toast, and whether the app reacts to permission and session failures. It is meant for background requests and turns both off. "Use sample instance" is a user click, so a permission failure should still lead to the Missing required permissions page, as on other pages.

This PR adds a request context value for the missing case, `skipErrorNotificationContextKey`, read only by the error toast interceptor, and sets it on the sample request.

| Request marked as | Global error toast | Missing-permissions redirect | Token-expired notice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nothing (default) | shown | yes | yes |
| `skipErrorNotificationContextKey` (new) | skipped | yes | yes |
| `silentContextKey` | skipped | no | no |

The callers' toast stays: it has the localized title, and the wizard needs its own handler anyway because it finishes setup when the sample step fails.

## Not changed: the `[failed_precondition]` prefix in the toast body

The body comes from `extractGrpcErrorMessage` (`frontend/src/utils/connect.ts`), which returns `ConnectError.message` (prefixed with the code) rather than `rawMessage`. I left it alone:

- It has 8 call sites, including SQL editor query results, the web terminal, the schema editor and the Roles page. Changing it changes the text on all of them.
- Existing tests pin the prefixed text, for this toast (`CreateInstanceView.test.tsx`) and for the global toast (`errorNotificationMiddleware.test.ts`).
- Call sites that want the unprefixed text already read `rawMessage` directly (`InstanceFormContext.tsx`, `CreateWorkloadIdentitySheet.tsx`).

## Tests

- `stores/app/instance.test.ts`: a rejected sample request reaches the caller and carries the new value; the request is not sent `silent`.

title: fix(pg): reject prior backup for data-modifying WITH queries
body:
## Summary

With prior backup enabled, PostgreSQL copies the statement's `WITH` clause verbatim into the backup `CREATE TABLE … AS`, which runs in autocommit before the change. A data-modifying CTE therefore executed twice:

```sql
WITH d AS (DELETE FROM u WHERE id > 1 RETURNING *)
UPDATE t SET c = 1 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM d);
```

The backup deleted `u`'s rows (which were never backed up), then the real `DELETE` found nothing and the `UPDATE` matched 0 rows — with no error. INSERT CTEs inserted twice, UPDATE CTEs applied twice, and MERGE CTEs (PG 17) ran too.

- **Executor:** the PG backup (`TransformDMLToSelect`) now refuses an `UPDATE`/`DELETE` whose `WITH` clause contains `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE`, before executing anything. The task fails with a message pointing at disabling or skipping prior backup.
- **Plan check:** the PG `BUILTIN_PRIOR_BACKUP_CHECK` advisor warns on these statements. It also warns on other statements with a data-modifying CTE (e.g. `WITH d AS (DELETE …) INSERT …`), whose CTE changes run but are not covered by prior backup.
- Other engines are not affected: MySQL/MariaDB/TiDB/SQL Server/Oracle only allow `SELECT` in CTEs (MySQL 8.0 rejects `WITH d AS (DELETE …)` with error 1064).

## Behavior change

With prior backup enabled, an `UPDATE`/`DELETE` with a data-modifying CTE used to "succeed" while corrupting data; it now fails at the prior-backup step. Users can disable prior backup for the change or skip it for the run. Not labeled breaking: it replaces silent data loss with an explicit failure.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./backend/plugin/parser/pg/ ./backend/plugin/advisor/pg/ ./backend/plugin/advisor/`
- [x] New `TestBackupRejectsDataModifyingCTE` (DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE/MERGE CTEs, mixed with a read-only CTE, after an earlier valid statement) and `TestBackupAllowsReadOnlyCTE` (VALUES/TABLE/set-op CTEs still back up); new advisor fixtures for UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT/SELECT with data-modifying CTEs. Both fail with the check disabled.
- [x] Ad-hoc server-backed rollout against PostgreSQL (not committed). With the fix: plan check shows the warning, the task fails at prior backup, `u` keeps 3/3 rows. With the check disabled: the rollout succeeds, `u` drops to 1 row, `t` updates 0 rows.
- [x] `go build` of the server binary
- [x] golangci-lint v2.13.2: no findings in changed files
- [ ] Playwright `/verify` not run: no E2E license in this environment

Not covered here: side-effecting functions in `WHERE`/`FROM` (e.g. MySQL stored functions that write, PG volatile functions) also execute during the backup `SELECT`; that needs a separate design.

title: feat(mcp): name masked columns and their reasons in query_database
body:
Part of BYT-10292.

When an agent reads a masked column with `query_database`, it gets `"******"` or a partial mask such as `**rn**`. Nothing in the result says the value is masked, why, or how the user can see it. The Query API already returns a masking reason for each column, in `QueryResult.masked`, but the tool threw it away.

After this change, when a result has masked columns:

- A new `maskedColumns` field lists each one: its name, its position, the semantic type's title, the algorithm, and the context, such as `Global masking rule: PII`. The position tells apart two columns with the same name, which a `SELECT *` over a join can return. Unmasked columns are left out, and the field is omitted when nothing is masked.
- The text result gets one line that names the masked columns, such as `Masked columns: ssn, email.`

On every result, `appliedAccessGrant` from the Query response passes through. An Unmask grant skips masking, so a granted result looks like one that no masking rule touched. This field is the only one that tells the two apart.

The tool description now says how the user can see masked values. They can ask a project owner for a masking exemption. Or, if the project allows just-in-time access, they can request an access grant with Unmask for this exact statement, schema and container. In a Read-write session the agent files the request itself with `AccessGrantService/CreateAccessGrant`; otherwise the user requests it in the SQL Editor. After a person approves it, the agent finds the grant among the user's access grants, then reruns the granted statement unchanged with the grant's schema and container. This text is the same for every masked result, so it goes in the description, not in each result.

#21585 serves `CreateAccessGrant` to Read-write sessions, so the how-to names it for that mode. In a Read-only session the MCP ceiling refuses the call, and its refusal points to the console, so the description sends the user to the SQL Editor there. `search_api` lists `CreateAccessGrant` in every workspace, because it hides only methods that no ceiling serves. MCP serves `SearchMyAccessGrants` to every session, so `search_api` finds the user's grants. The filing clause names the schema and the container because a grant applies only when both match the query's (next section). The grant path also needs a project that allows just-in-time access: the server applies grants only there, and the SQL Editor offers "Request unmask" only there.

What the agent reads for two masked columns:

```
Result: 1 rows, 3 columns (id, ssn, email) | 0ms

```

title: docs(design): onboarding flow, the first four screens
body:
Design doc for the first-run setup wizard: `docs/design/onboarding-flow.md`.

**Builds on the project home (#21572, merged Oct 13).** Finish lands there on both paths, and the project home puts the goal's step first.

The Cloud wizard asks for six things and explains none of them. Mandatory setup fixed the instance step (24% to 70% of signups end with a database) but not what follows: only 24% do first work, and 73 of 100 finishers idled for under two minutes on the databases page it ended on until Oct 13. The doc lands on one rule: **a screen asks only for what a later step uses and explains it where it asks, and setup always ends with a project, a decision about its database, and one next step.** Four screens: workspace, goal, project with its database, team. Frontend only.

**Revised 2026-10-13 after review.** The instance form is out of the wizard: connecting your own instance is now a choice on screen 3 that defers the connection until after setup. Everything is created in one step at Finish, so Back works on every screen, the team screen included. The goal screen gains a quieter third answer for people who are just exploring. Finish lands on the project home (#21572) whichever database choice was made, and the project home's two steps are ordered by the goal; the wizard builds no landing of its own.

### What the doc decides

- **Three contracts are taken as given.** The sample is ADR-0004's Sample Project Instance: one database, seven days, single-use, prepared by a synchronous request (self-hosted prepares its own on the server's embedded PostgreSQL, with no expiry). Invitation emails are sent only where the workspace has a mail setting, which Cloud workspaces do. A new workspace is on the free plan, so nothing the wizard promises depends on masking or custom approval.
- **Four screens in this order: workspace, goal, project with its database, team.** Screen 1 is a confirmation (name and workspace name prefilled, Continue enabled on arrival). The goal comes before the database because it is what the user came for, and it decides which step the project home and the guide put first. Team is last and always offered, because invitees should find something when they click the invite.
- **Two goals, and a quieter third answer.** Under the two cards sits a lighter "Not sure yet, just exploring", which commits to neither; the project home and the guide then put a query first. Every product in the study that asks an intent question lets the user decline it (PostHog, Metabase, n8n, Greptile); here 3 of 20 left the goal blank while it was optional, and 2 leavers stalled on it once it was required. "Mark sensitive data" is removed as a goal: masking guards querying rather than being a destination, and as an Enterprise feature it led its choosers into a gate (1 of 9 acted). Every finish line is reachable on the free plan.

title: fix(review): list and name service accounts and workload identities on approval steps
body:
Design doc and implementation: `docs/design/approval-step-non-human-approvers.md`. Fixes [BYT-10304](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10304/plan-page-shows-no-reviewers-for-an-approval-step-whose-role-is-held).

QVC's ServiceNow integration ends every change's approval flow with a custom role "ServiceNow Approver" held only by service accounts. The plan page showed that step as "No reviewers", and the code comment beside the string said the step could never be approved (BYT-9711). Both were wrong: `canReview` resolves roles through `GetUserFormattedRolesMap`, which matches `serviceAccounts/` and `workloadIdentities/` members, so a service account holding the role approves through the API, which is what QVC does and what Bytebase recommended when external approval was removed. The review UI applied a display filter the authorization model does not have, and once the service account had approved, the step showed its email's local part with no title and no account-type mark. The rule: **a principal that holds a step's role is an approver whatever its type; the review surfaces list it, name it, and attribute its decision the same way they do for a person. Notifications stay human-only.**

### What the doc decides

- **The reviewer list is every principal holding the step's role**, project IAM plus workspace IAM, with service accounts and workload identities kept instead of dropped. "No reviewers" then means no principal holds the role. A listed holder can still be barred by the self-approval or last-plan-editor rule, as a person is today. Rejected: keep the human filter and reword to "No human reviewers".
- **Non-human principals resolve through their own services, never the user service.** `BatchGetUsers` and `GetUser` reject their emails, and one such name fails the whole batch. `usePrincipal` (already routing by email domain on the issue page) becomes a shared hook for "Approved by", the chip avatars, the activity header, the header status and the rejection banner.
- **The account-type mark is the existing `AccountTypeBadge`**, with a `compact` form for dense rows. It reads the email domain the server reserves for these accounts, so a person cannot carry it. The name identifies the principal and the mark only qualifies it, so the mark is drawn in neutral colors on every surface, as the Users and Service Accounts pages already draw the account type, and never in accent.
- **A candidate of any type carries the attribution name `users/<email>`**, the name `issue.creator` and `plan.lastPlanEditor` already use for every actor, so the self-approval and last-plan-editor checks hold unchanged for a service account that created the plan.
- **The stored approver principal stays `users/<email>`.** Every consumer was inventoried; none needs the type in the string, and a new format would need a backfill of every stored approval and dual-format readers forever.
- **Notifications are unchanged.** A machine has no IM identity to mention.

title: fix(oracle): bound the dial timeout and honor extra parameters in any spelling
body:
Fixes two defects in the options Bytebase passes to the Oracle driver. Together they made failover to a second address take about two minutes, and made the workaround unreliable ([BYT-10309](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10309/oracle-connections-have-no-dial-timeout-and-a-connection-timeout-set)).

## What changes for a user

- **An Oracle address that doesn't answer is given up on after 10 seconds.** Before, Bytebase set no limit and waited for the operating system's TCP timeout, 133 to 135 s in the lab below. With a standby database listed in the `SERVER` extra parameter (Oracle Data Guard), Test Connection, schema sync and queries now reach the standby after 10 s.
- **`CONNECTION TIMEOUT` in Extra Parameters applies in any spelling.** `connection timeout` and the driver's alias `CONNECT TIMEOUT` now always replace the default. Before, only the exact uppercase key did. Any other spelling applied on some connections and not on others.
- **`SID` in Extra Parameters replaces the SID field in any spelling.** Before, a lowercase `sid` won only some of the time.
- Every other extra parameter reaches the driver exactly as typed, as before. That includes `SERVER` for Data Guard, and `SSL`, `SSL VERIFY`, `WALLET`, `WALLET PASSWORD` and `AUTH TYPE` for TCPS wallet connections.

## Old behavior, measured

Bytebase 3.23.0 on 2026-10-10, two Oracle 26ai Free databases, the first address silently dropping packets and the second address in `SERVER`:

| Extra Parameters | Time to reach the second address |
|---|---|
| none | 133 to 135 s, for Test Connection, schema sync and a query each |
| `CONNECTION TIMEOUT=5` | 5.0 s |
| `CONNECT TIMEOUT=5` | 5.0 s on one run, 132.8 s on another, same settings |

With `CONNECTION TIMEOUT=5`, a 12-second statement still completed: the key limits connecting, not how long a statement runs.

## Root cause

`Driver.Open` built the options like this:

```go
options["CONNECTION TIMEOUT"] = "0"
if sid != "" { options["SID"] = sid }
for key, value := range extraConnectionParameters { options[key] = value }
```

**No dial timeout.** When the first line was added (2bb7ffe312, February 2024, go-ora 2.8.7), `CONNECTION TIMEOUT` was the driver's timeout for every network read and write, 120 s by default. Setting it to `0` let statements run longer than two minutes, and removed the dial timeout as a side effect. go-ora 2.9.0 split the option. `TIMEOUT` and `READ TIMEOUT` now set the read timeout, which is off by default. `CONNECTION TIMEOUT` and `CONNECT TIMEOUT` set only the TCP dial timeout, 60 s by default. Since Bytebase moved to 2.9.0 (#17563, October 2025), the line has had one effect left: turning the dial timeout off.

**Unreliable override.** The loop merges keys by exact spelling. go-ora upper-cases each key before reading it, and treats the alias as the same option. A user key in another spelling therefore went into the connection URL next to Bytebase's `CONNECTION TIMEOUT=0`. go-ora read both back in Go map order, wh

+const (
+	sidOption              = "SID"
+	dialTimeoutOption      = "CONNECTION TIMEOUT"
+	dialTimeoutOptionAlias = "CONNECT TIMEOUT"
+	// defaultDialTimeoutSeconds bounds the wait for one address to accept a connection, DNS
+	// lookup included, so an unreachable address fails over in seconds. It does not limit
+	// how long a statement runs.
+	defaultDialTimeoutSeconds = "10"

+
+// connectionOptions returns the go-ora URL options for a data source: the extra connection
+// parameters as typed, plus the SID field and the default dial timeout unless an extra
+// parameter sets the same option.
+//
+// go-ora upper-cases option keys and reads CONNECT TIMEOUT as CONNECTION TIMEOUT. A Bytebase
+// key sent next to a user key for the same option would leave the winner to go-ora's map
+// iteration order, so the user's key replaces it in any spelling.
+func connectionOptions(sid string, extraParameters map[string]string) map[string]string {
+	options := make(map[string]string, len(extraParameters)+2)
+	userOptions := make(map[string]bool, len(extraParameters))
+	for key, value := range extraParameters {
+		options[key] = value
+		userOptions[strings.ToUpper(key)] = true
+	}
+	if sid != "" && !userOptions[sidOption] {
+		options[sidOption] = sid
+	}
+	if !userOptions[dialTimeoutOption] && !userOptions[dialTimeoutOptionAlias] {
+		options[dialTimeoutOption] = defaultDialTimeoutSeconds
+	}
+	return options
+}
+

 	return d.db.Close()

title: fix(frontend): make the instance form's user examples run on Oracle and MySQL 8.4
body: Fixes [BYT-10307](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10307). The instance form gives users SQL to create Bytebase's database user, and two of those statements failed when copied: - **Oracle**: `CREATE USER bytebase IDENTIFIED BY 'YOUR_DB_PWD';` fails with `ORA-00988: missing or invalid passwords` on every Oracle version, because Oracle passwords take double quotes. - **MySQL 8.4 and later**: the GRANT ended with `/*!80000 , SET_USER_ID */`. A version comment runs on that version and every later one, and 8.4 removed `SET_USER_ID`, so the whole GRANT fails with `ERROR 1149 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax`. The statement sat in two places: the create flow's Authentication info panel, which TiDB, MariaDB, and OceanBase share (MariaDB reports 10.x, so it ran the comment too), and "Show how to create" on an existing instance, for password, AWS RDS IAM, and Google Cloud SQL IAM authentication. ### What changes Following the rule that the product shows the most generic statement and the docs hold the per-version and per-provider details: - **MySQL**: the example grants only what every MySQL version and cloud provider accepts, and leaves out the definer privilege, which has no portable name. `SET_USER_ID` exists only on 8.0, `SET_ANY_DEFINER` only from 8.2, 5.7 needs `SUPER`, and Amazon RDS for MySQL 8.4 refuses to grant `ALLOW_NONEXISTENT_DEFINER`. A warning under the example names the 8.0 and 8.4 privileges and links to the MySQL connection docs. TiDB, MariaDB, and OceanBase get the corrected statement without the warning, since it names MySQL versions. - **Oracle**: the password is double-quoted, a comment says to run the statement in the database Bytebase connects to, which in a container database is the pluggable database, and a warning says `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES` doesn't work on Amazon RDS for Oracle, linking to the Oracle connection docs. RDS exempts the master user's DBA role from `GRANT ANY PRIVILEGE`. The warning replaces the line "If you use Cloud RDS, you need to checkout their documentation…". On MySQL 8.0, the copied statement no longer grants `SET_USER_ID`. Changes that set `DEFINER` to another account fail until someone grants it; MySQL's error names the missing privilege, and so does the warning. Bytebase's own schema sync strips `DEFINER`, so only user-written statements need it. ### Screenshots Captured from this branch on a disposable server. **Create flow, MySQL Authentication info panel.** **Existing MySQL instance, "Show how to create".** **Existing Oracle instance, "Show how to create".**
