body:
Design doc and implementation: [`docs/design/sql-server-tls.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/cc/byt-10305-sql-server-tls/docs/design/sql-server-tls.md) ([BYT-10305](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10305)).

**The TLS section decides the connection: TLS mode TLS encrypts the whole session, Verify server certificate checks the certificate chain and the host name, and Extra Parameters can make that stricter, never weaker.** The upgrade turns Verify server certificate off on existing SQL Server data sources that use TLS, where it was on but never applied, so they keep connecting.

## Why

The SQL Server driver has never applied the instance form's TLS section. Reproduced on 2026-10-09 against SQL Server 2022 CU24 from Bytebase 3.23.0:

- With Verify server certificate on, Bytebase connects without a CA, and through an IP address that isn't in the certificate. Nothing is verified.
- TLS mode TLS doesn't encrypt the session. Only the login packet is encrypted.
- `TrustServerCertificate=false` in Extra Parameters fails with `key TrustServerCertificate provided more than once`.

## What the doc decides

- **D1.** Map the TLS section onto go-mssqldb's own `encrypt`, `TrustServerCertificate` and `certificate` options, not a Bytebase-built `tls.Config`. The Azure AD connector accepts only a DSN, and go-mssqldb re-checks the host name when SQL Server routes the login.
- **D2.** TLS mode TLS sets `encrypt=true`, which encrypts the whole session. `strict` stays an Extra Parameter.
- **D3.** Verify on sets `TrustServerCertificate=false`. The chain is checked against the CA (pasted or file path) or the system roots, and the host name against Host.
- **D4.** TLS mode Disabled keeps today's connection.
- **D5.** Extra Parameters can raise the TLS section's floor (`encrypt=strict`, `TrustServerCertificate=false`) but not lower it. This matches MySQL and PostgreSQL, where the TLS settings override Extra Parameters when TLS is on.
- **D6.** Every key Bytebase sets merges case-insensitively, so a repeated key no longer fails with `provided more than once`. `app name` and `tlsmin` can be overridden; the database and the Azure credential can't.
- **D7.** A migration turns Verify off on SQL Server data sources that have TLS and Verify on. Since 3.18.0 the form turns Verify on whenever TLS is enabled, so honoring the stored value would break every data source whose server presents SQL Server's self-signed certificate.
- **D8.** Mutual TLS stays hidden for SQL Server, because go-mssqldb has no client-certificate option.

## What

SQL Server connections now follow the instance form's TLS section:

| TLS mode | Verify server certificate | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disabled | any | Login packet encrypted, any certificate accepted | Unchanged |
| TLS | Off | Same as Disabled | Whole session encrypted, any certificate accepted |
| TLS | On, CA pasted or file path | Same as Disabled | Whole session encrypted; chain checked against the CA, host name

+-- Before 3.24, SQL Server connections never verified the server certificate,
+-- even with verifyTlsCertificate on. The driver now verifies, so turn it off
+-- where TLS is on: those data sources keep connecting as they did, and the
+-- instance form shows that the certificate is not verified. Deleting the key

+UPDATE instance
+SET metadata = jsonb_set(
+    metadata,
+    '{dataSources}',
+    (
+        SELECT jsonb_agg(
+            CASE

+                ELSE ds
+            END
+            ORDER BY ord

+        FROM jsonb_array_elements(metadata->'dataSources') WITH ORDINALITY AS t(ds, ord)

+)

title: fix: return "database not synced" instead of panicking before a schema sync
body:
Fixes SQL Editor answering `internal error` when someone queries a SQL Server database that Bytebase has not synced yet ([BYT-10306](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10306/sql-editor-sql-server-querying-a-database-before-its-first-schema-sync)).

## What changes for a user

- A SQL Editor query against a SQL Server database whose schema Bytebase has not synced now fails with `database metadata for database "appdb" not found (database not synced)`. Before, it failed with `internal error`, and the server logged a recovered nil-pointer panic in `ListSchemaNames`. PostgreSQL already returns this error in the same situation. Once the sync finishes, the query runs as before.
- The window is easy to hit: `CreateInstance` returns as soon as it has saved the instance's database list, and each database's schema sync runs in the background.
- The same situation no longer panics for a Snowflake or Redshift query, a PostgreSQL prior backup, or an Oracle rollback preview. Each now fails with the same error.

## Why it panicked

When a database has no synced schema, `parsercontext.BuildGetDatabaseMetadataFunc` and the task runner's getter both return no metadata and no error. Nothing stated that: the `GetDatabaseMetadataFunc` type had no contract, and every test fake returned an error for a database it did not hold, so no test ever ran a caller's nil branch. Most callers check anyway. These six did not:

| Call site | Reached from | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tsql` query span, table lookup | SQL Editor query and export, and access-grant approval rules, on SQL Server | panic | not-synced error |
| `snowflake` query span, table lookup | SQL Editor query on Snowflake | panic | not-synced error |
| `redshift` query span entry | SQL Editor query on Redshift | panic | not-synced error |
| `pg` prior backup | a PostgreSQL task run with prior backup | panic | not-synced error |
| `plsql` rollback SQL | `PreviewTaskRunRollback` on Oracle | panic | not-synced error |
| `tsql` completion, two sites | nothing today: the LSP getter returns an error instead of nil | — | no candidates |

## Why an error rather than "table not found"

MySQL, TiDB and Oracle treat a database with no metadata as one where the table was not found. For a query, that path runs the statement first, re-syncs, and only then works out which columns it read. An unsynced database would therefore run every statement before Bytebase can trace its columns for masking. Failing first, as PostgreSQL does, keeps the statement from running until that is possible. A table missing from a synced SQL Server database still takes the not-found path.

## How it is kept true

- The contract is now on the type: `GetDatabaseMetadataFunc` may return nil metadata with a nil error, and callers must check before use.
- `TestBuildGetDatabaseMetadataFunc` pins the real getter against PostgreSQL. A synced database returns metadata. An unsynced or untracked one returns nil and no error, which is what the new test

title: perf: persist access grant query hashes
body:
Access-grant discovery recomputes hashes from stored SQL, and runtime authorization compares full statements. Persist the normalized SHA-256 as `AccessGrantPayload.queryHash` and use the indexed hash for both CEL discovery and `SQLService.preCheckAccess`.

The store derives the hash on creation and every payload replacement using one shared helper. Migration `3.24.0` backfills existing grants and adds an expression index on project, creator, and query hash. Caller/workspace/project scope, execution context, expiry, export capability, and read-only validation remain enforced. No public API or frontend changes.

Follow-up to #21563 and [BYT-10272](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10272).

## Breaking Changes

Coordinate the server upgrade: stop older writers before running the migration. Older servers can omit or discard `queryHash`, and grants without it no longer match discovery or runtime authorization. The backfill and index creation run in the normal migration transaction; upgrade duration depends on stored SQL volume.

## Validation

- Full `backend/api/v1`, `backend/store`, and `backend/migrator` suites passed against PostgreSQL, including shared normalization vectors, payload updates, backfill preservation, isolation, missing hashes, and read-only enforcement.
- Proto formatting, lint, generation, and server build passed. Change-scoped Go lint passed; full-repository lint reports 45 pre-existing findings in unchanged files.
- Synthetic PostgreSQL lookup with 1,000 grants containing 110-KB SQL and 100 caller-eligible grants used the new index: 47.7 ms before, 0.15 ms after. Backfill plus index creation took 0.8 seconds. These are not production latency estimates.
author: RainbowDashy

title: fix(frontend): fill project pages after permission filtering
body:
Fixes https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10303/projects-list-returns-short-pages-for-users-with-project-level-access

Users with project-level access can receive short project pages because SearchProjects checks permissions after pagination. The frontend now accumulates short and empty responses until the requested row count is reached or the backend runs out of results.

Refill requests keep the original batch size to avoid scanning one project per request near the target. All returned rows are retained, so a displayed batch may exceed the requested count; the last continuation token resumes without discarding overflow.

Project-list callers pass cancellation through the store to Connect. Replaced searches and component cleanup stop obsolete refill chains, including project selectors, advanced filters, expression editors, and initial project loads. StrictMode effect replay restarts canceled initial searches, and canceled responses are not cached or displayed.

Sparse access can still require multiple requests per UI batch. Backend API behavior is unchanged.

Validation: `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` passed: 6,058 tests, typecheck, build, and guards. Regression coverage exercises page filling, overflow continuation, request failures, cancellation, and StrictMode replay.
author: RainbowDashy

title: fix: support long SQL in export grant discovery
body:
Long SQL exceeded the CEL filter limit during export-grant discovery, leaving approved exports unavailable. Use a client-computed SHA-256 `query_hash` predicate in the existing CEL filter, with identical ASCII boundary trimming in the browser and PostgreSQL. Hashes are computed during lookup in this version; database persistence is deferred.

Include exact schema/container context, fix PostgreSQL vertical-tab trimming, and distinguish failed lookups from missing grants with retry controls for single and batch exports. Actual export authorization retains full-SQL matching. Record the contract and exercise shared normalization vectors, long SQL, isolation, partial failures, and stale responses.

Addresses [BYT-10272](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10272).

Validation:
- PostgreSQL-backed store and API regressions passed; server build passed.
- Full frontend gate passed: 551 files, 6,058 tests, typechecking, formatting, guards, and bundling.
- Proto formatting, lint, and generation passed; change-scoped Go lint passed.
- Full-repository Go lint reports 45 existing findings in 23 unchanged files. Browser E2E was unavailable without an enterprise test license.
- Synthetic lookup with 100 eligible 110-KB queries among 1,000 grants used the existing index and took 43–44 ms; this is not a production latency estimate.

title: fix(tidb): retain access tables for EXPLAIN ANALYZE
body:
TiDB `EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT` lost its referenced tables during query-span extraction, causing authorization to require database-wide SELECT access even when a user had a grant for the referenced table. Extract access tables from the inner statement so table-scoped SELECT grants can match.

Use a full AST walk when extracting original table names so derived joins and nested expressions retain every referenced table. Correct the existing fixture and cover joins, nested derived queries, predicate/expression subqueries, qualified/cross-database tables, plain EXPLAIN, and analyzed-write classification. Analyzed spans retain uncached physical targets for authorization and resolve CTE scope without requiring grants on CTE names. Plain EXPLAIN skips source extraction and mixed-table validation, preserving its existing behavior. Permission selection remains based on the statement type.

Fixes https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10244

title: fix(store)!: refuse a create-database upsert that rebinds an existing database
body:
A create-database change can no longer take over a database that is already live in another project. Before this fix, a create-database plan that named such a database rebound it to the plan's project, changed its environment, and dropped its labels before the engine create ran, so the caller's own project roles (SQL select, DDL and DML) then applied to its data. The rebind committed in its own transaction, so it stayed whatever happened next: on PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, Redshift and MongoDB the engine create was skipped or wrote into the moved database and the task completed, so the move was silent; on the other engines the task failed at the create, but the database had already moved. The caller needed only the rights to drive a plan and a rollout in their own project (running the task through task-run permission, or an automatic rollout policy), and no access to the project the database belonged to. The path is the same for the console, the public API and MCP.

## The fix

`Store.UpsertDatabase` overwrites project, environment and metadata on an `(instance, name)` conflict, and the create-database task is its only caller. The refusal now lives in that write:

```
ON CONFLICT (instance, name) DO UPDATE SET … WHERE db.project = EXCLUDED.project
```

and the call refuses when the statement returns no row. Because the guard is part of the write, not a prior read, two concurrent first-creates of one name from different projects cannot both win: one inserts, the other meets the conflict and its `WHERE` fails. A project-scoped instance forces its own project in `projectForUpsert`, so the clause always holds there and its behavior is unchanged. A genuine move between projects still goes through `DatabaseService/UpdateDatabase`, which checks both projects.

The guard does not exempt a soft-deleted row. A `deleted` row is either a genuinely dropped database or a live one the instance's sync allowlist excluded, and the store cannot tell them apart (`backend/runner/schemasync/syncer.go`), so exempting it would re-open the takeover for the excluded-but-live case. The cost is narrow and stated below.

`UpsertDatabase` has one caller, so the guard sits safely in the statement with no new parameter and no split of a shared-looking primitive; a short comment on the clause says so.

## Who was affected

- Present in every supported release, including 3.4.0 and through 3.23.0: `UpsertDatabase`'s overwriting `ON CONFLICT` clause is there in each (`git show <tag>:backend/store/database.go`). The exact first release is older still and not pinned here.
- Workspace-level instances (instances not bound to a project). Project-bound instances were already guarded.
- Callers who can drive a plan and a rollout on any project — Project Owner, Workspace DBA, Workspace Admin, the GitOps Service Agent, or a Project Developer with a Project Releaser — and can run the task (task-run permission, or an automatic rollout policy).

## The narrow cost

Reusing a genuinely-dropped da

title: fix(mcp)!: refuse database and database-group writes to MCP sessions
body:
Five methods are no longer served to MCP sessions: `DatabaseService/UpdateDatabase`, `DatabaseService/BatchUpdateDatabases`, `DatabaseGroupService/CreateDatabaseGroup`, `DatabaseGroupService/UpdateDatabaseGroup` and `DatabaseGroupService/DeleteDatabaseGroup`. Through them a session could move a database to another project or environment, relabel it, or create, change or delete a database group. They move from WRITE to EXCLUDED and carry a new denial reason, `REDRAWS_GOVERNANCE_BOUNDARY`. A person still makes these changes in the console, and API callers outside MCP are unaffected.

Why: these writes change which checks apply to a change.

- A database's project and environment decide which approval, SQL review and access rules a change to it must pass. Masking rules key on them too, and decide what a query against the database returns.
- A database group selects databases by an expression over their environment and labels. A change that targets a group runs on whatever the group selects when the rollout's tasks are created, not on what it selected when the change was approved.

So an agent that can make these writes can choose the checks on its own change. On 2026-09-28 a live run on main showed two cases. Moving a database into a project that does not require approval let a change run while its approval was still pending. Under approval rules that required a DBA only for production, with no fallback rule, moving a database out of production let a change skip approval. Both need nothing past the user's own permissions. A local run, whose test is not part of this PR, showed the group case: after approval, a database relabeled into the group got the change, and a later rollout call added a database that joined after the rollout existed.

Who can make these writes today: anyone whose role grants `bb.databases.update` or the database-group writes. Of the predefined roles, that is Project Owner, Workspace DBA and Workspace Admin. Project Developer and SQL Editor User hold neither, so nothing changes for them.

The methods are EXCLUDED rather than FORBIDDEN because they do not break the MCP boundary. A reviewed request form or a handoff to a person could serve them later. The reason is new rather than `ADMINISTERS_THE_WORKSPACE`: labels and group expressions are not workspace administration, and agents relay the reason to users, so it has to name what the method does.

Settings page: the Read-write row "Manage database housekeeping" drops "Database settings and labels", "Move databases between projects" and "Database groups" in all five locales. It now lists syncing instances and databases, and saved queries. `docs/design/mcp-capability-ladder.md` gets the new counts and explains the change in the paragraph that used to defend the moving item. The floor line ("Never, in any mode: …") is unchanged. The doc's note on it now names the two denial reasons the floor has no verb for.

No built-in MCP tool calls these methods, so only `call_api` reached them.

title: fix(mcp)!: replace the stale skills with server instructions
body:
This removes the MCP server's two embedded skills, `query` and `database-change`, and the `get_skill` tool that served them. Static server instructions take over the routing. In a client that cannot show Bytebase's confirmation form, they also tell the agent to ask the user before it runs DML or DDL directly.

The skills taught the wrong path:

- The `query` skill sends reads through `call_api` to `SQLService/Query` instead of `query_database`, and says `dataSourceId` is required. `SQLService/Query` picks a data source when the request has none.
- The `database-change` skill tells the agent to create the rollout itself, right after it creates the issue.
- It also tells the agent to add an `engine` field to the sheet. `Sheet` has only `name`, `content` and `content_size`.

`get_skill` served only these two skills, so it goes too. The package's `AGENTS.md` documented only how to write skills, so it goes with its `CLAUDE.md` import. Main edited the `query` skill twice since this PR opened: #21673 added `SearchDatabases` and the canonical-name rule, and #21709 added that a write goes through `query_database`. The merge drops those edits with the file. `call_api`'s description already carries the canonical-name rule, and the instructions now carry the other two.

## Server instructions

Since #21649, `initialize` returns one line that names the session's Bytebase account. This PR adds a short, static text after it. The text says:

- which tool to use: `SearchDatabases` through `call_api` to find a database, `query_database` for reads, `get_schema` for schemas, `propose_database_change` for changes, and for anything else, a tool whose description covers the task before `search_api` and `call_api`;
- that `propose_database_change` changes one database per call;
- that under a Read-write policy, `query_database` can also run DML and DDL, which take effect at once, without an issue or approval, and that `call_api` refuses them;
- that `propose_database_change` is the tool for a change that should be reviewed, or for a write that fails on a read-only data source;
- that a refused call states its reason and may name a next step, such as a tool to use.

One server serves every workspace, and an admin can change a workspace's policy at any time. So the text names no workspace and assumes no mode. The account line already says whose permissions the calls use, so the text does not repeat it.

### Asking before a write

Peter's review asked the agent to ask the user before it runs DML or DDL directly. #21709 made that a form the server shows from `query_database`, in clients that can show one. This PR covers the clients that cannot: a session whose client declared no form gets one more paragraph after the text. It says that `query_database` runs any statement that may write there without asking, not only DML and DDL but also, for example, a `GRANT` or a procedure call. It tells the agent to show the user the exact statement, say it runs at once with no issue or

-
-This directory contains the Bytebase MCP server implementation with embedded skills that provide step-by-step guides for common tasks.

-## Writing Skills

-
-### File Structure
-
-```

-### Skill Format
-
-Each skill file must have YAML frontmatter followed by markdown content:
-
-```markdown
----
-name: skill-name

-# Skill Title
-
-## Overview
-

-
-## Prerequisites
-

-

-
-1. **Description starts with "Use when..."** - Include triggering conditions and keywords for discoverability

-2. **Always include `search_api` before `call_api`** - Claude needs to fetch the schema to know exact field names

-3. **Use placeholders consistently**:
-   - `{project-id}` - project identifier
-   - `{instance-id}` - instance identifier
-   - `{database-name}` - database name
-   - `{sheet-id}` - sheet identifier
-   - `{plan-id}` - plan identifier
-
-4. **Prefer discovery over hardcoding** - Use `search_api(schema="EnumName")` instead of listing enum values
-
-5. **Note encoding requirements** - e.g., sheet content is base64 encoded
-
-6. **List required permissions** in Prerequisites
-
-7. **Include common errors** to help with troubleshooting
-
-### Adding a New Skill
-
-1. Create `skills/new-skill.md` with frontmatter and content

-# Run all skill tests

-
-# Verify skill loads correctly

-```
-

-```go

-

title: fix(plan): keep the reading position when editing a statement
body:
## Summary

- Clicking **Edit** on a statement keeps the lines the reviewer was reading in view and keeps their cursor, so they can change the line they were reviewing without finding it again.

Fixes BYT-10287.

## Key Changes

- Add `captureEditorViewAnchor` and `focusEditorAtAnchor` in `components/monaco/viewAnchor.ts`. They record a place by line number instead of scroll pixels, because the read-only editor has thread view zones that the edit editor lacks.
- On Edit, keep the top visible line at the top. Keep the cursor or selection when it is visible; otherwise place it on the top visible line. Then focus the editor.
- Clamp restored lines to the editor's line count.
- Apply the same behavior to the issue-detail statement section, which swaps editors the same way.

## Motivation

- Edit mode mounts a new Monaco editor. Its view-state cache is keyed by a per-mount model URI, so it never matched and the editor opened at line 1.

## Test plan

- `pnpm --dir frontend test`
- Unit tests for capturing and restoring a place; a component test for keeping the reading position and cursor when entering edit mode.

title: feat(review): let the AI review read and search the synced schema
body:
## What

The AI review judged a change from the prompt alone: the target facts and the statements. This PR gives the model two tools over the synced schema of the database under review, so a finding can rest on a row count or on a view that reads the column.

- `search({text, schema, from})` finds the objects whose name or definition contains the text, without regard to case. It answers "what depends on this table".
- `read({objects: [{schema, name}], from})` returns the definition and statistics of the objects of up to 20 names. A table comes with its columns, indexes, constraints, and triggers, and with its row count, data size, and index size.

Part of BYT-9846. Follows #21523, where the executor ran without tools.

## How

- `catalog.go` holds the two tools. They take the schema proto the executor already loads for the target facts. They read nothing live and they make no store reads.
- `catalog_definition.go` builds the definitions. A definition is what the renderer in `backend/plugin/schema` writes, the same text the product shows a user. A renderer writes a schema dump, so it leaves parts out: the MySQL one writes no triggers, and the PostgreSQL one skips a trigger an extension owns and writes a bare table when the sync holds no columns. The tools add such a part. The test is a second rendering without the part, and an equal result means the part was left out. An engine with no renderer gets a plain listing with every part.
- Event triggers and extensions belong to the database, not to a schema, and are objects too.
- A table with no statistics synced comes without statistics. Zeros would say the table is empty.
- A result is one JSON object, so text from the database stays inside string values.
- A result over 32 KiB is cut and carries `next_from`. The model repeats the call with `from` set to it. For `read` the cursor is a position in the definitions laid end to end, so every overload of a function can be reached. A cut falls behind a line break and never inside a character.
- A name returns every object of that name. An exact schema and name win over ones that differ in case.
- A definition is rendered on its first use. A read renders only what it returns, and a search keeps its matches for the next page.
- Arguments the model got wrong come back as text it can correct. Only a failure of the tool itself fails the review.
- `AIReviewExecutor` passes the tools in place of `NoTools`, which is removed.

## Tests

- `catalog_test.go` covers PostgreSQL, MySQL, and an engine with no renderer. It covers search by column, trigger, foreign key, and enum value, name lookup, schemas that differ in case, overloads, every comment the sync stores, the parts a dump leaves out, and bad arguments. The paging tests follow `next_from` to the end and compare the joined text with the source.
- `model_ai_test.go` uses the real tools in place of the canned catalog.
- `review_run_lifecycle_test.go` creates a table in the target database and syncs it. The stub m

title: fix(frontend): find every actor kind in the audit log actor filter
body:
Fixes the Actor filter on the audit log page (BYT-10291). In 3.23.0 it could not find a service account or a workload identity, and it could not find a user by the `users/<email>` name its own dropdown shows.

Why: #21505 searched service accounts and workload identities only when the keyword started with `serviceAccounts/` or `workloadIdentities/`, compared case-sensitively. AdvancedSearch lowercases the keyword before it calls `onSearch`, so the keyword arrived as `serviceaccounts/…` and every search fell back to `ListUsers`. Service accounts are not users, so the dropdown said "No matching result found". A typed `users/admin@example.com` missed too: the list filters match the display name and the email, and neither contains `users/`. The #21505 test mocked AdvancedSearch and called `onSearch("serviceAccounts/deploy")` directly, so CI never saw a lowercased keyword.

What changes:

- The actor search asks for users, service accounts and workload identities together, the way AccountMultiSelect does, after reducing the keyword to its email part. An empty keyword lists all three kinds, which is what the customer expected, so the hint drops the prefix instructions in all five locales, and the trailing period that rendered as "actors.. Type to search".
- A full service account or workload identity email is offered as its account even when no list returns it. The lists reach only the page's own parents. On the workspace page that is the workspace alone, so a project-level account (every account on Cloud) or a deleted one only shows up this way.
- One helper reads the actor value for both the search and the filter, so a lowercased prefix or a bare account email committed with Enter still builds the right filter. Picking `serviceAccounts/x` still sends `(actor == "serviceAccounts/x" || actor == "users/x")`.
- The two account lists are now requested with a silent context, and the four client-side permission checks from #21505 are gone. A client copy of the server's list permissions can only drift toward hiding accounts or sending the viewer to /403. With `silent`, the server refuses and the page drops that kind quietly. `listUsers` keeps its own check inside the store; I left that alone.
- The column-resize handle has no z-index now. It and the AdvancedSearch menu were both `z-10` in the page's stacking context, and the table comes later in the DOM, so the handles painted over the menu: the bars through the hint in the ticket. The handle got `z-10` in #20334, when it overhung the next column by 6px. #20936 moved it back inside its own cell and left `z-10` behind. The fix applies wherever an AdvancedSearch menu opens over a resizable table header. Its tests move beside it.

Tests: the new AuditLogTable cases type full names into the real AdvancedSearch (the old test mocked it): the three kinds, plus a project-level service account on the workspace page. Other cases check the parents listed on a project page, `silent` on every account list, the prefix in

title: feat(frontend): fold retried attempts into one row in the task-run log
body: Implements the task-run log design in `docs/design/task-run-log-previous-attempts.md` (#21427), and amends that doc where implementation settled what it had left open. Frontend-only; every surface that embeds the log viewer inherits the change. ### What changed for the reader - **A run that retried reads like the run it was.** When the PostgreSQL driver retries a statement after a lock timeout, the superseded attempts fold into one gray **Previous attempts** row above the final attempt's sections, with their count and total time. Before, each failed attempt showed as red sections beside the final one, so a run that passed looked failed. Only the final attempt's failure is state. - **The history is one click away, unchanged.** Opening the row lists each attempt with the error that ended it; opening an attempt shows its sections, the failed one already open with its error entry untouched. With a single previous attempt, the row opens straight onto its sections. - **A live retry says so, and only while it is live.** While the run is running and its final attempt is still going, the row reads "N attempts · retrying". This is the one mark that reads the run status, so a run whose server stopped mid-attempt is not called retrying forever. - **Nothing opens on its own when a marker lands.** Section ids are positional and a retry marker regroups them, so before, the id of a section the reader had open could land on an unrelated section, which then opened in its place. Expansion and load-more now reset in the same render as the regrouping. A reader's statement folds from #21530 are keyed by entry and survive the marker. - One-time sections (prior backup, database sync) stay outside the attempts, in place. The unused "Retry" section and its `retry-attempt` detail are removed from the model and all five locales. ### Screenshots Real product, built from this branch and captured by the e2e spec below. **After a retried run: one closed gray row above the final attempt's green sections.** **While the final attempt waits on the lock, the row says it is retrying.** **Opened: a row per attempt with the error that ended it. An opened attempt shows its failed section, already open, with the error entry untouched.** ### Rebased over #21530 (statement unfold) #21530 landed while this was in review, and two of its rules had to hold through the fold. Each now has a test that fails when it is broken: - **The failure mark is picked per context, before the cut** (its D4). An attempt on its own has lost the marker tha

## Summary

- Keep inline comments on visible lines usable after a large statement is saved and reloaded.

Fixes BYT-10278.

## Key Changes

- Show existing threads whose complete anchor range is inside a truncated preview, while keeping new comment creation disabled there.
- Restore “View in Statement” for visible anchors. Show older visible anchors as Outdated when comparison cannot place them, with a tooltip for the size limit.
- Match comparison eligibility to GetSheet’s 2,097,152-character preview limit.
- Show the large-sheet preview warning while editing, before the statement is saved.

## Motivation

- A sheet-wide truncation check hid inline comments, and the previous byte-based comparison cap and delayed warning made large-sheet review confusing.

title: feat(review): switch every standard rule on for a new workspace
body:
## Summary

Every new workspace now starts with its own `REVIEW_RULE` policy row: every standard SQL review rule on, enforced. `CreateWorkspace` inserts it in the same transaction as the workspace IAM policy and the default project.

The workspace SQL Review page (dev builds, #21529) saves through `UpdatePolicy(allow_missing=true)` and gates editing on `bb.policies.update` alone, on the premise that the row exists. Without it the first save went through `CreatePolicy`, so a role with update but not create failed to save. Follow-up to the Codex finding on #21529.

## Scope

- New workspaces only. Existing workspaces keep the `GetPolicy` stand-in, which returns the same every-rule policy, and `GetEffectiveReviewRulePolicy` still defaults to every rule when neither level has a row; a data migration for existing workspaces is deliberately left out.
- Nothing in production reads the row: v1 SQL review reads `ReviewConfig` and `TAG` policies only, the release frontend lists no policies generically, and review runs are dark-launched. The only observable change is that `ListPolicies` on a new workspace includes one more entry.

## Verification

- `gofmt`, `go vet`; `go test ./backend/store/` (full suite), `go test ./backend/tests/ -run '^(TestClaim|TestCollision)'`, and the policy tests in `backend/api/v1`; `go build`.
- `golangci-lint` v2.13.2 (the version CI pins, run through `go run` because the local binary predates go 1.27.1) reports only pre-existing `revive` findings in files this PR does not touch.
- The insert names every column of the `policy` composite key and touches no existing row, so the `CreateWorkspace` transaction acquires no new locks on existing rows. `TestCreateWorkspaceSwitchesEveryReviewRuleOn` creates two workspaces and checks that each gets exactly one row with every rule.

body: Fixes the MCP consent page being too narrow and too long ([BYT-10284](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10284/mcp-auth-page-seems-too-long)). ## What a reader sees - The consent card is 672px wide on any screen 704px or wider, centered on the whole viewport. It narrows only on a screen that cannot hold it, to the screen width less a 16px margin on each side. Every capability row fits on one line with its tier badge. - At 1440×900 the card was 264px wide and the page 1706px tall. It is now 672px wide and the page 1086px tall. - The consent page no longer shows the sign-in illustration. Consent is an interstitial, so it follows Supabase's `InterstitialLayout`: one centered card of a fixed width, no side art. - The header's title and description wrap into balanced lines instead of leaving one word alone on the last line. ## Why it was narrow #21517 sized the page as a fraction of its parent (`md:w-3/5 lg:w-1/2`) and added its own `px-4`. The parent is SplashLayout's right column, which is already the whole viewport below `lg` and half of it from `lg`, with 80–96px of side padding. So the fractions compounded: the card was 176px wide at 1024px, 264px at 1440px and 384px at 1920px. ## How it is kept true - The consent route renders outside SplashLayout. The page centers itself on the viewport and caps the card with `max-w-2xl`. - SplashLayout now states the rule for the pages that stay in it: the column owns the gutter and its share of the viewport, and a page fills the column up to its own cap, adding no width fraction or side padding. - `frontend/tests/e2e/oauth2-consent/oauth2-consent.spec.ts` registers an OAuth client and measures the card at seven widths from 390px to 1920px. The card must be `min(672, viewport − 32)` wide and centered. - The unit test that asserted the fraction classes is removed. jsdom has no layout, so that test passed for the broken page. ## Verification - The frontend gate is green: biome, the guard scripts, `tsc`, the release bundle, and 531 files / 5789 tests. - Against a build of the pre-change code, the e2e spec failed at all seven widths, with the card at 326, 620, 479, 176, 224, 264 and 384px. That run used an earlier 512px cap; none of those widths meets the 672px cap either. On this branch it passes at all seven. - The spec ran on a free-plan server, since it uses no licensed feature. The licensed suite was not run. ## Not included - The MCP denial messages that the consent page's capability list describes are being reworded in a separate PR. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat(frontend): make the role grant's environment field a direct-execution switch
body:
Design doc and implementation: `docs/design/role-grant-direct-ddl-dml.md`.

When a project owner grants a role that carries `bb.sql.ddl` or `bb.sql.dml`, the grant form showed a field titled **Environments** between *Databases* and *Expiration*. Its neighbors narrow the grant, so owners read this one the same way and ticked every environment to make the grant complete, and each tick actually let the member run DDL/DML in SQL Editor there without approval, while the empty field was the strict choice. The amber warning between the title and the picker said so and was not read, because people act on the control. The role did not help: SQL Editor User was described as *"Permissions for querying database data"*. The same field sat on the self-service request sheet, and the approver's page showed raw permission ids and comma-joined environment titles, hid the empty list as "degenerate", and never showed the grantee. Until 3.15.0 this was an environment-level policy set by admins; #19239 moved the decision into every grant. The rule this lands on: **the field is a permission you switch on, never a scope you fill in.** The stored binding is byte-for-byte what the forms produced before.

- The field is a `Switch`, off by default, titled *Direct DDL/DML execution*, labeled *Allow running DDL/DML in SQL Editor without approval*. Off shows the label's negation, *DDL/DML cannot run in SQL Editor without approval*, and submits exactly what the empty picker submitted.
- On reveals the picker; on with nothing picked shows *At least one environment is required* beside it and blocks submit. The switch is form state beside the list, reset together on a role change, so the field can never be left on with an empty list.

title: feat(frontend): unfold and copy a statement in the task-run log
body:
Implements the task-run log design in `docs/design/task-run-log-statement-unfold.md` (#21428), and amends that doc where implementation review changed a decision. Frontend-only; the four surfaces that embed the viewer (changelog detail, revision panel, deploy history sheet, latest task-run card) inherit the change.

### What changed for the reader

- **The statement is no longer cut.** The 80-character `substring` in `model.ts` is gone. A row shows one line — the error when the command failed, otherwise the statement collapsed to one line — and the line is clamped by CSS `truncate` to the width it is given, so a wide screen shows more and the deploy sheet shows less.
- **Every row that ran a statement can unfold it and copy it.** A fold control (shared `Button`, `xs`, `aria-expanded`) and a `CopyButton` sit on rows whose statement differs from the line, is clamped by its width, or sits behind an error. Copy always takes the verbatim statement: from the row's right-hand cluster while the statement is the line, from the block once it is a block. The error never gets a copy button and is never copied.
- **A failed command keeps its SQL.** The row shows the error as its line and carries the statement it ran; unfolding shows both. Previously the failed row was the error and nothing else.
- **The failure that explains the outcome is surfaced but not opened.** `buildSectionsFromEntries` marks the last failed command in an execution context, and only when nothing after it succeeded or was retried (a lock-timeout retry re-logs every command; a `DONE` run marks nothing). The marked row is rendered even past the 50-row *Load more* window, keeps its real index, and the section scrolls to it. It starts folded like every other row.
- **Clicking a line toggles it.** Any part of a foldable row's line — index, times, glyph, empty space, the clamped statement, the error — toggles the row; the unfolded block does not, so an identifier in the SQL can be double-clicked. A drag across the text never toggles.
- **The list keeps its height.** The section's box stays at ten rows (280px) whether or not a block is open; a block scrolls inside it, its copy button sticky to the box's top so a statement taller than the box stays copyable. Unfolding the bottom row scrolls the section by the least that shows the block; folding lets the browser's clamp put the line back where it was clicked from, and the page never moves.
- **The columns before the statement line up.** The index and relative-time columns are sized once per section from their widest value, so the chevrons form a straight column (the old log started statements at three different x positions in one section).
- Row keys are the entry's identity (replica · full-precision log time · type · tie ordinal), assigned once over the run's whole entry list, so the reader's folds survive a second replica appearing or a retry marker splitting a section.

### Decisions revised from the merged doc

title: feat(review): switch the standard review rules on and off
body:
## Summary

SQL Review V2 keeps eleven standard rules behind one `REVIEW_RULE` policy, but nothing in the product could switch them. This adds the switches at both levels with two rules:

- **Nearest policy wins.** A project follows the workspace until it customizes its own list.
- **SYNTAX is the master switch.** The other rules only judge SQL that parses, so switching it off saves an empty list and nothing runs.

## Backend

- `GetPolicy` on a project without its own `REVIEW_RULE` policy returns `NOT_FOUND` instead of the every-rule stand-in, so a client can tell "follows the workspace" from "customized to every rule". The workspace keeps the stand-in.
- `GetEffectiveReviewRulePolicy` returns an empty list when the nearest policy lacks `SYNTAX`. A RULE run with nothing on still runs: `RuleExecutor.RunOnce` returns no findings for an empty policy instead of asking omni, which evaluates `SYNTAX` whether or not it is listed, so the run completes with no findings and resolves the findings of earlier runs.

## Frontend (dev builds only)

Everything is behind `sqlReviewV2Enabled()`, a build-time gate on `isDev()`, so release bundles are unchanged.

- **CI/CD › SQL Review** (workspace) shows the standard rules as one centered card. A status line at the top always holds its place: "11 of 11 rules running", or the Syntax-off warning, so switching Syntax does not move the list.
- **CI/CD › SQL Review** (project, new page) follows the workspace by default and shows the rules in force as On/Off text. "Customize for this project" turns them into switches starting from the workspace's list; switching it back off deletes the project policy.
- Switching Syntax off turns every rule off and saves `[]`; switching it back on restores the session's previous set, else every rule.
- The v1 review policy surfaces are hidden in dev builds: the workspace create/detail routes, the project settings attach and "Enforce SQL review" toggle, and the environment attach.
- The policy store gains the `REVIEW_RULE` update mask it was missing; saving threw without it.
- A policy switched off through the API (`enforce=false`) counts as absent, as the backend reads it: the workspace shows every rule, and a project row that is not in force is updated rather than created. Each save needs only the permission for the RPC it makes: the workspace page needs `bb.policies.update`, since every workspace gets a review rule policy row by default (a follow-up PR creates that row; until then the workspace `GetPolicy` stand-in covers reads and an update on a missing row goes through the create path), and the project page needs create, update or delete for the save it makes. The link to the workspace rules needs only the workspace policy read, like the V2 route.
- A failed policy read shows an error with a retry instead of the switches, so it cannot pass for "follows the workspace" and be saved over. The policy store gains a fetch that tells an absent policy from a failed read, so a failed retry d

title: fix(masking): enable masking for Snowflake
body:
## Summary

Adds `SNOWFLAKE` to `common.EngineSupportMasking`, so semantic types and classifications set on Snowflake columns now mask Snowflake query results in SQL Editor, export, and MCP.

## Why

Snowflake has had a query span since #10982 (2024-03), and at first its results went through the masker with no engine check. #13775 (2024-09) added an engine allowlist that left Snowflake out, and #15776 later renamed it to `EngineSupportMasking` without changing it. Since then, `getMaskerForColumnResource` has returned `NoneMasker` for every Snowflake column. The UI still lets admins set semantic types on Snowflake columns, and those settings did nothing.

## Behavior change

Snowflake workspaces that already have masking rules, semantic types, or classifications on Snowflake columns will see those columns masked after upgrading. That is what those settings were meant to do.

## Verification

- Ran the Snowflake query span extractor (with store-backed metadata) and `MaskResults` against a real metadata PostgreSQL, in a local test that isn't part of this PR. It masked a plain column, an aliased column, `SELECT *`, `UPPER(col)`, a CTE, and a quoted lowercase identifier, and left an unmasked neighbor column alone. It fails when the flag is reverted. I didn't run it against a live Snowflake instance.
- `TestMaskersAreDisjoint` still passes: MongoDB, CosmosDB, and Elasticsearch keep using the document masker.
- `go test ./backend/api/v1 -run 'Mask|Masking|Predicate'`, `./backend/common`, build, and golangci-lint on the changed packages all pass.

## Known gaps (follow-ups)

These Snowflake span extractor gaps let masked data through, and this PR doesn't fix them:

- `OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*)` and other `*` inside expressions get no lineage (`query_span_extractor.go:634`).
- Table functions in `FROM`, such as `TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID()))`, expose no columns and don't fail closed (`query_span_extractor.go:990`).
- The extractor never sets `UnresolvedColumnsError`, so a table synced with no columns returns raw rows from `SELECT *` (the #21402 case, which today only PostgreSQL handles).

These gaps also affect engines that already mask:

- Snowflake isn't in `EngineSupportQuerySpanPlainField`, so an expression over one masked column reuses that column's masker instead of a full mask. PostgreSQL behaves the same way.
- Snowflake spans don't set `PredicateColumns`, which only error-message redaction uses for this engine. Oracle and TiDB don't set it either.
- Export calls `MaskResults` after `queryRetry` has already masked, so masking algorithms that change on a second pass (for example MD5) are applied twice. This affects every SQL engine.

title: refactor(mcp)!: retire the ignore-masking-exemptions policy field
body:
Removes the "Ignore masking exemptions" toggle from the MCP access policy, end to end: `MCPSetting.ignore_masking_exemptions` (field 2), the backend check that read it, the settings UI, the consent page badge, and eight locale keys.

Why: the toggle came from the MCP design (#21216), not from a customer, and no customer has asked for it. Peter and I decided on 2026-09-23 to remove it before 3.23.0. 3.23.0 is the first release that shows the MCP settings page, so removing it now costs nothing, while removing it later would be a deprecation with unknown self-hosted usage.

After this change an MCP session applies the caller's own masking provisioning exactly as the console does: their masking exemptions, and the unmask carried by an access grant, on both Query and Export. There is no setting to force masking for MCP sessions. The three call sites (`exemptionsForPrincipal` and the two `SkipMasking` terms in `sql_service.go`) are back to what they were before #21216.

The removed helper also answered "ignore" when an MCP request had no stamped settings. That fallback goes with it, since the caller's provisioning is now the only behavior and there is nothing stricter to fall back to. A request without stamped settings is a wiring bug the gate does not produce, and Query already fails closed on it (`mcpReadOnlyClampApplies`).

Stored rows need no migration. Every setting read goes through `common.ProtojsonUnmarshaler` (`DiscardUnknown: true`), so a row still carrying `"ignoreMaskingExemptions": true` reads with the key dropped, and the next save rewrites the row without it. `TestMCPRepairIgnoresARetiredKey` pins both halves. #21216 retired `mcp_capability` (field 26) from this setting family the same way.

With capability the only field left, the MCP arm of `UpdateSetting` now builds the row from the request instead of merging onto the stored one. An update whose mask does not name `value.mcp.capability` is refused. No writer sends one (the settings page always names the path).

What stays: the masked-write guard. It shipped in the same PR as the toggle but never depended on it, and it still refuses the `******` placeholder on every MCP session.

Frontend: the Access policy section loses the toggle, the "Masking exemptions ignored" chip and the pending-save footer line; `isDirty` is now just the mode change. The consent page loses the masking badge and the subscription read that #21347 added only to decide whether to show it (`refreshSubscription` on load and retry, and its test). The design doc drops D8 and gets a dated decision entry (D12).

## Breaking Changes

- `ignore_masking_exemptions = 2` is removed from `bytebase.v1.MCPSetting` and `bytebase.store.MCPSetting`, with no `reserved` entry since nothing is expected to take the number. It shipped in 3.22.0 and 3.22.1 and was settable through the settings API; the settings UI for it was behind `isDev()` in both.
- A client still sending the field gets INVALID_ARGUMENT. Over the REST API the gateway'

title: feat(frontend): date a record by what its surface is for
body:
Implements the timestamp design merged in #21257 (BYT-10140): a surface is either a work queue or a history view, and that decides how it dates a record.

## What a reader sees

- **Work queues and feeds** keep a relative age and switch to a date at 30 days, as before.
- **History views** — changelog, revisions, task-run history, audit log — now always date a record absolutely. A history row orients the reader, so it carries the date and the time to the minute; a record whose time is the evidence carries full precision inline.
- **Operational times** a reader acts on — a scheduled rollout, an expiration — name their timezone in the visible string rather than leaving it to a hover, which is the near-miss BYT-10023 reported.
- **Every reduced form** reveals the full date-time on hover, and the full form reveals the age.

## How it is kept true

- `HumanizeTs` takes an instant in milliseconds and a mode, and is the one way a record timestamp reaches the screen.
- A value that changes with time is a `TimeReading` — its value and the instant it next changes, defined together — and `useTimeReading` is the only way a display reads one, so a label cannot go stale on screen. A GritQL plugin (`frontend/biome-plugins/time-reading-through-hook.grit`) enforces that by member name.
- `displayableInstantMs` is the single domain check for what is an instant; `Intl` throws on the rest.

## Column widths

Moving a column off relative wording lengthens its value, so each timestamp column opens at the width its form needs — measured across every time zone and shipped locale — and the table decides what gives way when it cannot hold every column:

- **Access grants** shows its creation and expiration in the same explicit form, and gives way in a ruled order: the dates first, then the statement, the creator and the databases, with the status last, since the status turns Expired on its own.
- **A narrowed date keeps its day.** The label splits around the date as the locale writes a date alone, and only the time and zone ellipsize — after the date in most locales, before it in Vietnamese, which writes the time first. Cutting the label from its end, as `truncate` does, drops the day for a Vietnamese reader.
- **A fitted table measures its scroller**, inside the border and any scrollbar, floored: `clientWidth` rounds to a whole pixel, and a table half a pixel too wide still scrolls. Checked in a browser at Windows 125% and 150% scaling, where Chrome snaps a 1px border to 0.8 and 0.67px.

## Verification

- The frontend gate is green: biome, the guard scripts, `tsc --build`, the release bundle, and 531 files / 5804 tests.
- Rendering decisions that jsdom cannot measure — column widths, what a narrowed cell keeps, the fit — were measured in a browser and the numbers are recorded in the commits that set them.
- Eight rounds of correctness and simplification review on this branch, each finding fixed or recorded as an option not taken.

## Not included

- The audit log still l

title: feat(review): run the AI review and post its findings
body:
## Summary

Runs the AI review and posts its findings. Builds on #21518, merged, which stores the `REVIEW_AI` policy the review judges against.

`AIReviewExecutor` replaces the placeholder behind `reviewRuns/ai`.

- Loads the plan, the AI setting, and the workspace and project policy, derives every database of the plan (no sampling, like the rule review), and reviews each spec's sheet once per database with that database's engine, version, environment, and schema summary in the prompt.
- Posts every finding as an open thread anchored on the finding's line of the sheet, named as the AI reviewer's result, with the priority of its severity and every database it applies to. The same title on the same line across databases is one thread with the highest priority among them.
- Bounds: 8 reviews of one run at the model at once, a sheet over 256 KiB is reported as not reviewed rather than truncated, a database a spec names twice is reviewed once, and a failed or panicking review fails its database and the run with the same collect-all message the rule review uses. A panic in a review goroutine is recorded as that database's error, because the scheduler's recovery covers only the goroutine that called `RunOnce`.
- The model's notes, the facts it could not check, are logged for the operator and never posted.
- The reviewer runs without tools until the read and search tools land. The prompt says so and asks the model to list what it could not check.
- `loadReviewPlan` is shared with the rule executor.

## Tests

- `backend/runner/reviewrun`: the target facts, the finding-to-thread conversion with the cross-database merge, the concurrent review step (its cap, collect-all, and a panicking review recorded as that database's error rather than crashing the process), the sheet bound, and the dedupe of a database a spec names twice.
- `backend/plugin/aireview`: the prompt states when the review has no tools.
- `backend/tests`: the lifecycle test now runs the AI review for real: a model that answers 503 fails the run with the model error, and a stub model that answers completes the run and posts the thread with its priority, line, database, and open state.

## Next

PR 4 adds the read and search tools over the synced schema, where `NoTools` sits today. The frontend has no run button yet; the run starts through the API.

title: refactor(review): rename the GUIDELINE review run type to AI
body:
## Summary

Renames the review run type `GUIDELINE` to `AI` before it ships. The type landed on 2026-08-31 and is not in any release (latest tag 3.22.1, its migration sits under 3.23), so the enum value, the stored type string, and the resource id can still change without a compatibility path.

- Proto: `ReviewRun.Type.AI` in the store and the API, resource id `reviewRuns/ai` beside `reviewRuns/rule`.
- Store: `ReviewRunTypeAI = "AI"`, the value written to `review_run.type`.
- Runner: `GuidelineExecutor` becomes `AIReviewExecutor` in `backend/runner/reviewrun/ai_review_executor.go`. It still fails honestly until the AI review lands.
- Comments in the 3.23 migration and `LATEST.sql`. No schema change.

## Why

A guideline is advice, while an open finding from this review blocks the change, so the name undersold what the run does. The feature is called AI review in the design, and the policy that feeds it is `AI_REVIEW` (#21518), so the run type, the executor, and the policy now share one vocabulary. Inside `ReviewRun.Type` the bare `AI` reads as "the AI kind of review run". The executor carries the noun, because `AIExecutor` would not say what it executes.

## Tests

No behavior change. The existing review run tests were updated for the new value and pass at every layer: store, api/v1, runner, and the server-backed lifecycle and collision tests.

title: fix(mcp): mark the two MCP-origin refusals so their audit rows read WARNING
body:
Two MCP-origin refusals, `rejectMCPOriginatedGrantIssue` (issue_service.go) and `rejectMCPOriginatedIssuelessRollout` (rollout_service.go), returned a bare `connect.NewError`, so their audit rows were stored at INFO. Every sibling policy refusal is marked, so it reads WARNING wherever it lands: the read-only SQL clamp's row is stored at WARNING, the ceiling gate's refusal streams at WARNING. WARNING is what a compliance reader filters on (docs/design/audit-what-produces-a-row.md, section 3), and the gate's own comment files both guards as its class of refusal.

Fix: build the two refusals with `permissionDeniedError(ctx, ...)` instead. Messages are byte-identical, since `mcp.IsPolicyRefusal` matches on them.

Label only. Both guards run inside audited handlers (UpdateIssue, CreateIssue, CreateRollout, BatchRunTasks), so the row was already stored and streamed either way. Only the severity changes.

Over MCP the grant-issue guard is reached through UpdateIssue with allow_missing on a missing issue, and through CreateIssue with no issue type set, the one type the gate's allow-list lets through to the handler. That second path was refusing a malformed request as a policy verdict, and the mark would have filed it as a WARNING row. The guard now leaves an unset type to the handler, which rejects it as an invalid argument, the same call the gate already makes. That is the one behavior change here: an untyped MCP CreateIssue now gets INVALID_ARGUMENT instead of PERMISSION_DENIED, and its row stays INFO.

Tests: two probes in `TestAuditSinksOnBothChains` drive each guard over the MCP chain on a booted server and assert the stored row and the streamed line read WARNING. The first commit is the test alone and fails on main (INFO where WARNING was expected). The unit table for the guard and `TestMCPGateRefusesGrantIssues` pin the unset-type case.

Doc rider, same PR: section 3's implementation list names the two guards, and section 4 no longer calls the MCP chain "pre-release". The enforcement chain shipped in 3.22.0 and stored these rows; only the access-policy section of the settings page was behind a dev gate until 3.23.0.

Not in this PR: `rejectMCPOriginatedTokenMint`, a backstop behind three FORBIDDEN methods.

title: feat(policy): add the REVIEW_AI policy
body:
## Summary

Adds the `REVIEW_AI` policy type: the natural-language policy the AI SQL review judges a change against. It follows the `REVIEW_RULE` wiring from 30daddecef, with one difference in how the effective policy is resolved.

- Proto: `Policy.Type.REVIEW_AI` in the store, `PolicyType.REVIEW_AI` in the API, payload `ReviewAIPolicy { string content }`, oneof member `review_ai_policy`. Allowed on WORKSPACE and PROJECT.
- Service: create, get, list, update through the `review_ai_policy` and `enforce` mask paths, delete. Blank content or content over 64 KiB is refused. A missing row is NotFound: there is no default, unlike the rule policy.
- `UpdatePolicy` now refuses a request whose declared type differs from the stored policy's type. The payload is serialized by the declared type, so a mismatch stored the other type's empty payload under the policy; for this policy that would have bypassed the blank-content check. The check applies to every policy type.
- Store: `GetEffectiveReviewAIPolicy` returns the workspace policy text and the project policy text side by side. A policy that is not enforced counts as absent.
- `LATEST.sql`: comment lines only, no migration. The audit row keeps the content, it is policy text, not a credential.

## Why the lookup returns both levels

The workspace policy holds the company's standards and the project policy holds the team's conventions. With nearest-wins resolution, the company's standards would vanish the moment a team writes its own. The review prompt already states the conflict rule (the project policy wins), so the store returns both texts and the reviewer merges them.

## Naming

The policy type reads area first like its neighbors (`MASKING_RULE`, `REVIEW_RULE`), so `REVIEW_RULE` and `REVIEW_AI` sit side by side and mirror the run type pair `RULE` and `AI`. The feature keeps its prose name, AI review. The field is `content`, the name this API gives a resource body (`Sheet`, `SavedQuery`, `PlanCheckRun`, `Advice`). The text is called the policy everywhere, as the reviewer package already did. The market word "instructions" was dropped for the same reason as "guideline": the object is a policy the review enforces, not advice to an assistant. The five comments from #21521 that still said instructions are reworded here too. "Guideline" was rejected because a guideline is advice, while an open finding from this review blocks the change. The run type was renamed to `AI` in #21521, so the run, the executor, and the policy share one vocabulary.

## Tests

- `backend/api/v1`: type mapping both ways, resource types, mask path, payload validation, converter round trip, and the policy driven through `OrgPolicyService` against a real metadata store at both levels: NotFound on a missing row, create, get, list, update, validation, enforce, delete, and the refused type mismatch.
- `backend/store`: the effective lookup across the two levels, enforce off at each level, and another workspace's rows under the same resource

title: feat(review): call omni's SQL Review V2 contract from the rule review run
body:
## Summary

The RULE review run executor evaluated the v1 advisor and discarded the result. It now calls omni's SQL Review V2 contract (`review.ReviewFunc`, omni #428), one `Review` per (spec, engine), and posts the findings as issue comments. **SQL review v1 (`plugin/advisor`, the plan check statement advise executor) is untouched and keeps running beside it.**

- **reviewrun**: an engine registry (`reviewers.go`, empty until omni ships `pg/review`, `mysql/review`, ...), the executor that resolves every input the engine cannot derive from the SQL from the store (synced schema, backup database presence, session user, `lower_case_table_names`; no database connection), and the pure conversion of findings into comments carrying `review_metadata` and a statement anchor. An engine with no reviewer fails its units, so a run reports `FAILED` with `engine X has no standard rule reviewer` rather than a vacuous `DONE`.
- **store.CompleteReviewRun** takes the results: on `DONE` it resolves the same reviewer's `OPEN` roots on the issue and inserts the new results in the transaction fenced on the claim's attempt, so a superseded execution posts nothing. Lock order (`issue_comment`, then `review_run`) matches the project purge.
- **`issue_comment.creator` becomes nullable** (migration 3.23.5): a review result is posted by a reviewer, not a person, as `task_run.creator` is `NULL` for system runs. The v1 converter omits `creator` for such rows and exposes `review_metadata`.
- `plancheck.CheckTarget` carries `SpecID` for the anchor; `resolveDatabaseTarget` is exported for the executor (implementation unchanged).
- omni bumped `96fc86c5` → `3165d7e5`: the only commit in between adds the `review` contract package, no parser or catalog changes.

Still dark: nothing in the product triggers review runs; the frontend does not call `RunReview`. Follow-ups: register omni engine packages as they land (and flip the e2e expectation back to `DONE`); render the reviewer name on a creatorless comment (the frontend currently falls back to "Unknown").

## Tests

- `TestCompleteReviewRunPostsResults` (store, colliding issue ids across two projects): results post as creatorless `OPEN` roots, only the same reviewer's earlier results on the same issue are resolved, superseded and `FAILED` completions write nothing, the other project is untouched.
- `TestCompleteReviewRunLockOrder` (store, barrier-driven): a re-run landing mid-completion leaves the completion with zero writes; a purge racing the completion waits on it without deadlock, fails on the foreign key (the documented best-effort outcome) and succeeds on retry.
- `reviewrun`: grouping, options, priority coverage of every rule, finding → comment conversion (code-point columns, whole-line anchors, unknown rule dropped), session user, error aggregation.
- v1 converter and enum mirror tests; `TestLatestVersion`; e2e `TestCollision_RunReviewLifecycle` updated to the honest `FAILED`.

## Pre-PR checklist

- Breaking change: none. T

title: feat(ai-review): add the review agent loop
body:
## Summary

First piece of AI SQL review (BYT-9846): the agent loop that reviews one sheet against one target database. It has no store import, so it lands before policy storage, the review run wiring, and finding posting.

- `backend/plugin/aireview`
  - `Reviewer.Review` runs until the model replies without a tool call, then validates the findings. Bounds are 20 model calls and 10 minutes. Any error, bound, or invalid reply fails the review, so a failure never reads as a pass.
  - Two narrow interfaces: `Model` (one model turn) and `Tools` (tool calls for one database). Both speak the `AIService.Chat` proto types, the conversation vocabulary `backend/plugin/ai` and the frontend agent loop already share, so the package adds no message types of its own. `Tools.Call` returns text for the model and an error that fails the review, because a model that cannot get a fact raises no finding.
  - The final reply must be the bare JSON object or the object in a code fence, with only the keys of the answer format. It is decoded with `encoding/json/v2`, which rejects duplicate keys, unknown keys, trailing text, and case mismatches, so a second `findings` key cannot erase the first. An object inside prose (first `{` to last `}`) counts only when it holds findings, so prose that mentions `{"findings": []}` never passes a change. One invalid finding invalidates the whole reply. The model gets one correction round that carries the exact problems and offers a tool call as well as the JSON.
  - The answer format has a `notes` list for facts the model needed and could not get. The loop returns them in `Result.Notes` for the backend's telemetry. They are never findings and never shown to the user, so a model that cannot check something has a place to say so instead of inventing a key that a lenient parser would drop.
  - The tools of the last permitted model call do not run. An empty reply fails the review: a safety block, a refusal, and a garbled tool call all arrive as empty, `ai.Chat` carries no stop reason yet, and asking again could let a blocked review pass on the second try.
  - The prompt puts the stable part first for the vendor's prefix cache and numbers the physical sheet lines (one based, same as `Position.line`). Every text that comes from the database side is data, not instructions: the statements and the target facts each sit in a tag with a random nonce, and the base prompt states the same rule for tool results.
  - `NewModel` binds the workspace AI setting to `ai.Chat`, so every configured provider works on paper. Gemini is the one verified live.
- `backend/plugin/ai/gemini.go`
  - System messages go to `systemInstruction` instead of a first user turn. A request that holds only system messages still falls back to a user turn, because Gemini rejects empty `contents`. This also applies to the SQL editor assistant.
  - A tool result that is a JSON array or scalar is wrapped in an object. Gemini returns 400 otherwise, and a `search` result is a list.

N

title: feat(policy): wire the REVIEW_RULE policy through the service and store
body:
Follow-up to #21498, which added the `REVIEW_RULE` policy proto with no Go behind it: a client naming the type got `invalid policy type` from every RPC. This makes the policy usable end to end. Design: [SQL Review V2: Standard Review](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J4pBAS4rsgV6GDmSgYAJ-IBJVJYupAtZwdtI_v8JrW4/edit).

## What

Copies the `QUERY_DATA` shape, the other workspace-plus-project policy.

- **Service**: `allowedResourceTypes` admits WORKSPACE and PROJECT; the v1/store type maps, payload marshal and unmarshal, `pathMatchType`, and the update-mask allowlist gain the `review_rule_policy` case. `validatePolicyPayload` rejects unspecified, unknown, and repeated rules. `GetPolicy` on a missing row returns every rule on, as it already does for ROLLOUT, instead of NotFound.
- **Store**: `GetDefaultReviewRulePolicy` (every rule, declaration order) and `GetEffectiveReviewRulePolicy`, nearest wins: the project's policy as is, else the workspace's, else every rule. A policy that is not enforced counts as absent, as `getReviewConfigByResource` treats the tag policy.
- **Converters** cast between the two `ReviewRuleType` enums; `TestReviewRuleTypeEnumsMirror` holds their numbering together.
- `LATEST.sql` comment only; no migration, the column has no CHECK.

No license gate (`FEATURE_PRE_DEPLOYMENT_SQL_REVIEW` exists but nothing reads it) and no dedicated permission: `bb.policies.*` already lets a project owner set the project policy and not the workspace one.

## Tests

- Unit: converters, type maps, resource types, path, payload validation, the default.
- Store (real Postgres): no policy, workspace only, project overrides, empty list means everything off, unenforced falls through, another workspace never leaks.
- Integration: default on a missing row, create, get, list, update, invalid inputs, environment refused, workspace level, effective set follows delete.

## Not in this PR

The executor that reads `GetEffectiveReviewRulePolicy`; nothing calls it yet. Frontend.

title: feat(proto): add the review rule policy and review metadata for SQL Review V2
body:
Proto for the standard review design, [SQL Review V2: Standard Review](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1J4pBAS4rsgV6GDmSgYAJ-IBJVJYupAtZwdtI_v8JrW4/edit). Draft to look at the shape; nothing behind it is wired yet.

## What

- **`ReviewRuleType`** (`v1/review_rule.proto`, mirrored in store): the eleven standard rules as one top-level enum, shared by the policy and the comment payload. An execution check is named for what it checks (`SYNTAX`, `WALK_THROUGH`, `ONLINE_MIGRATION`, `PRIOR_BACKUP`); a rule about the SQL itself carries `REQUIRE` or `DISALLOW`. Store values are never removed, only deprecated, because the payload is jsonb and the unmarshaler discards an unknown enum name into `REVIEW_RULE_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED`.
- **`REVIEW_RULE` policy** on workspace and project, one field: `repeated ReviewRuleType rules`. The nearest policy wins: a project's own policy applies as is, a project without one uses the workspace policy, and with neither every rule is on. A rule added later is appended to saved policies by a data migration in that release.
- **`ReviewRun.Type`** added to the store proto, following how `issue.type`, `task.type`, and `policy.type` store a store enum by name in an un-CHECKed column. Moving the Go store and scheduler from string constants to it is a separate change.
- **`IssueCommentPayload.review_metadata = 10`** (9 is `statement_anchor`): `run_type` (`ReviewRun.Type`), `rule_type` (`ReviewRuleType`, set iff `run_type` is RULE), `priority` (P0, P1, P2; says what resolving means and has no bearing on blocking, which `thread_state` alone decides), and `targets`, always the complete list. v1 mirrors it on `IssueComment` at field 17 as `OUTPUT_ONLY`.

## Not in this PR

- `allowedResourceTypes`, `validatePolicyPayload`, and the store conversion for the new policy type, so the policy compiles but cannot be created through the API yet.
- `CreateIssueComment` rejecting `review_metadata`, and the store check that `rule_type` is set iff `run_type` is RULE.
- The review_run Go store and scheduler on `ReviewRun.Type` instead of strings.
- Frontend.

## Checks

`buf lint`, `buf format -d`, and `buf breaking --against main` pass. `buf generate` output is included. `go build` of `generated-go`, `api/v1`, and `store` passes. `TestLintAuditPayloadInventory` needed one line for the new `targets` field. Both tracked `openapi.yaml` outputs are regenerated and carry the new schemas.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
