title: fix(tidb): resolve _tidb_rowid reads in query span
body:
BYT-10230. Stacked on #21494, which has to merge first.

TiDB gives every table without a clustered index a hidden row handle, `_tidb_rowid`. A SELECT can read it, but no catalog lists it, so the metadata Bytebase syncs from `information_schema.COLUMNS` never has it. The TiDB query span extractor resolves select-list columns against that metadata only, so a select list naming `_tidb_rowid` missed and came back as `span.NotFoundError`. Since #20387 (3.18.1) the SQL service reads that as possibly stale metadata: it runs the query, resyncs the database, extracts again, misses again, and discards the rows with `failed to mask data: ... column: _tidb_rowid, err: cannot find the column ref`. That check sits outside the masking gate, so it fails on a FREE plan with no masking policy, and every attempt costs a full schema sync. A customer on 3.19.0 with TiDB 8.5.4 hit it with a pagination query that returns `MIN(_tidb_rowid)` and `MAX(_tidb_rowid)`. It reproduces on 3.19.0, 3.22.1 and `main`. The same query worked up to 2.13.2, before a column miss became an error.

On a lookup miss, the extractor now treats the name as the row handle when every table source the reference can bind to is built from base tables (a base table, an alias of one, or a join of them), and gives it empty lineage. TiDB rejects this name for a base-table column (`ERROR 1166`), so on a base table it can only be the handle, which holds a row number and no column data. A view, subquery or CTE column that really carries this name resolves through the normal lookup and keeps its lineage. `base.PseudoTable` drops whether an alias or join came from base tables, and `base.TableSource` is sealed, so the extractor keeps those marks in a small set of its own.

I went with empty lineage over the union of the table's columns, which is what the T-SQL extractor does for graph pseudo-columns. The union would mask the handle on any table with one masked column, so the customer's query on a message-log table would return `******`. Table access is still checked from the FROM tables either way.

There is no clustered-index check. TiDB answers `ERROR 1054` for a clustered table and that error already reaches the user, so the check would refuse nothing new.

One limit is deliberate. With a view, CTE or subquery anywhere in scope, including an enclosing query, an unqualified `_tidb_rowid` still reports not-found and the user has to write `tbl._tidb_rowid`. On TiDB 8.5.4, `SELECT _tidb_rowid FROM clustered_tbl, some_view` reads the view's real column when the view has one. If the cached view definition is stale, accepting that reference would return the real column unmasked and skip the resync that finds it today.

`getFieldColumnSource` now iterates a new `candidateTableSources`, so the row-handle rule and the column lookup share one qualifier match.

Codex reviewed this PR twice. Its P1 caught a masking leak in a first attempt at the qualified case. TiDB resolves a qualified `x._tidb_rowid` outward when
author: vsai12

title: fix(tidb): match names case-insensitively and resolve the nearest scope first in query span
body:
TiDB fixes `lower_case_table_names` at 2, so table, database and CTE names match without regard to case. `FROM c` reads CTE `C` even when a base table `c` exists. The TiDB query span extractor compared CTE names case-sensitively, skipped the CTE, and resolved `c` from metadata instead. It then traced the CTE's columns to the base table:

```sql
WITH C AS (SELECT secret AS s FROM sec) SELECT s FROM c
```

Bytebase traced `s` to `c.s`. TiDB 8.5.4 returns `sec.secret`. A masked column read through such a CTE was masked by the base table's policy, so with no policy on `c.s` it came back unmasked. The caller still needs query access to the table the CTE reads. What breaks is the masking.

The column path and the table and view lookup already fold case. This PR folds it at the remaining name matchers, so they agree once `FROM c` binds to the CTE: the CTE lookup, the two qualified-wildcard matchers (`c.*`), the check for an inner CTE that shadows a recursive one, and the detection of a recursive CTE's reference to itself. Fixing the CTE lookup alone makes `SELECT c.* FROM c` fail, because `c.*` no longer finds a source named `C`. Pre-review caught that before this was opened.

### Scope order (second commit)

Codex's P1 on this PR was right. Both lookup helpers searched the enclosing queries' table sources before the subquery's own FROM, which is the reverse of SQL scoping. Folding case in the wildcard matcher made an outer alias `T` match a local alias `t` first, so `SELECT (SELECT t.* FROM sec AS t JOIN d AS x ON TRUE) FROM pub AS T` went from the right lineage to `pub`. That was a regression from the first commit.

The order itself is older than this PR and also affects plain columns. `SELECT (SELECT v FROM sec LIMIT 1) FROM pub` traced to `pub.v` while TiDB returns `sec.v`, so the result was masked by `pub.v`'s policy instead of `sec.v`'s. Both helpers now search the statement's own FROM first, then the enclosing scopes from the nearest out. A reference the subquery cannot satisfy still binds outward.

The MySQL extractor has the same order (MariaDB and OceanBase share it). That is not changed here and is tracked separately. PostgreSQL resolves the same query correctly.

I found the CTE issue while probing the BYT-10230 fix against TiDB. That change is stacked on this one, because its rule would open a second way through the same comparison.

## Validation

- `TestGetQuerySpanNamesAreCaseInsensitive`, 8 statements. 7 fail on `origin/main`. The eighth is a column reference with an upper-case qualifier. It already passed, and it is there to show the column path folds case today.
- I ran each shape on TiDB 8.5.4 first. It accepts all of them, including a recursive CTE that names itself in another case and a database name in another case, and returns the CTE's data.
- `TestGetQuerySpanResolvesNearestScopeFirst`, 7 statements. 4 fail on `origin/main`. A fifth, Codex's example, passes on `origin/main` and fails on the first commit, which is the regression

body:
## Summary

- render query plans inline in the SQL Editor result pane instead of opening a pop-up
- use one compact tab row with Text first and selected by default
- automatically load and cache a structured plan when safely replaying a plain EXPLAIN
- keep text-only and failed structured plans readable inline
- retain the standalone visualizer as a legacy entry while the inline viewer reaches full parity

## Breaking Changes

The SQL Editor no longer exposes the Visualize Explain pop-up action. Query plans now open inline, and safe plain EXPLAIN results automatically make one structured-plan request for the visual tabs.

title: refactor(sql): build LIMIT statements in the parsers
body:
## What changed

Same move as #21485, for the other statement rewrite `plugin/db` owned: capping a query's row count in SQL text. Each engine's `getStatementWithResultLimit` (or `addResultLimit` for Oracle) moves from its `plugin/db` package to a `limit.go` beside that dialect's AST in `plugin/parser`, registered through `base.RegisterResultLimitFunc` / `base.StatementWithResultLimit`, mirroring the EXPLAIN registry that PR added. The drivers keep only the call site.

Oracle's clause depends on the connected server's version (`ROWNUM` before 12c, `FETCH NEXT` from 12c on), so the registered function signature carries an `engineVersion` string every other engine ignores — the same pattern `ExplainFormat` used for the format every non-PostgreSQL engine ignores.

## Three engines get more than a relocation

- **CockroachDB** always wrapped the statement in a CTE regardless of shape, where PostgreSQL — whose parser it already shares for EXPLAIN and the read-only gate — rewrites a `SELECT` in place and leaves anything else untouched. It now reuses PostgreSQL's rewrite directly, so a plain write like `DELETE FROM t` is no longer turned into a `SELECT` over a data-modifying CTE before the read-only classifier ever sees it.
- **Redshift** had the same unconditional-wrap gap and its own omni AST, whose `SelectStmt` carries the same `LimitCount`/`LockingClause`/`SortClause` shape PostgreSQL's does, so it gets its own precise rewriter built the same way.
- The **StarRocks** driver applied its one LIMIT function to **Doris** SQL too (`d.dbType` selects the engine, but there was only one function, built on the StarRocks-flavored parser) — the same gap EXPLAIN had before #21485, which gave Doris its own AST-based EXPLAIN function. Doris gets the same treatment here. Its `SetOpStmt.Limit` turned out to be unusable — the omni Doris grammar leaves it `nil` whether or not the text has a trailing `LIMIT` (confirmed directly against the parser: `UNION ... LIMIT 5` parses with `Limit == nil`, the text still inside the node's own span) — so a set operation takes the CTE-wrap fallback rather than risk a doubled `LIMIT`. A plain `SELECT`, including one wrapped in any number of parens (Doris has no distinct wrapper node; the grammar strips them transparently), still gets the precise in-place edit.

This was a scope call, not a silent expansion — asked and confirmed before writing the code.

## Left alone

**ClickHouse** and **BigQuery** keep their existing blind CTE-wrap, relocated unchanged: neither has a real AST here to place the clause precisely. **Spanner**'s rewriter — the one the immediately preceding commit on `main` ([13228ad](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/commit/13228ad54f7cface739d3526c0df01799e8028e)) had just fixed to handle a `WITH` query — moves unchanged too, along with the driver-level regression test that exercises it against a real Spanner connection (skips without `SPANNER_EMULATOR_HOST`, same as before); only its pure unit test moved to the pa

title: refactor(sql): build EXPLAIN statements in the parsers
body:
## What changed

The statement an explain request runs was built in `plugin/db` by prefixing `EXPLAIN` to whatever text arrived (`backend/plugin/db/explain.go`, a switch over engines). That file is gone. The rewrite now lives behind a parser registry — `base.ExplainStatement` in `backend/plugin/parser/base/explain.go` — with a per-engine implementation beside each dialect's AST: `pg` (also CockroachDB), `mysql` (also MariaDB/OceanBase), `tidb`, `redshift`, `snowflake`, `doris`, `starrocks`, `trino`, and `standard` (ClickHouse/Hive). The 10 drivers and the Query handler's gate call it. `plugin/db` keeps only `ExplainFormat`, the adapter from the API's format enum, so no parser package imports the v1 protos.

## Why

Prefixing blindly is wrong whenever the statement already asks for a plan: `EXPLAIN SELECT 1` became `EXPLAIN EXPLAIN SELECT 1`, a syntax error on every prefix engine. The plan visualizer hit this on every typed `EXPLAIN`, because it re-runs the statement as an explain request to get the JSON format it draws from.

Parsing first also makes the smuggle defense structural rather than incidental. `ANALYZE DELETE FROM t` is not a statement any dialect can plan, so it now fails before anything is built, instead of being caught after being wrapped into `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE` and validated as non-read-only.

`docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md` already specified both rules — never wrap a statement that already starts with `EXPLAIN`, and substitute the format rather than prefixing. This implements them; the doc's stale `db.ExplainStatement` reference and line citations are updated, and the one gap it now has is written down.

## Behavior

- A statement that already asks for a plan is rebuilt around the statement it plans, so the request's format replaces the caller's options. `EXPLAIN (FORMAT TEXT) SELECT …` asked for as JSON returns a JSON plan instead of a syntax error.
- An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` the caller wrote is **refused with a message saying why**, because it plans by executing what it plans. Before, it was refused too, as a confusing syntax error. Engines whose grammar has no `ANALYZE` (Snowflake, Doris, StarRocks) refuse it as a parse error; ClickHouse and Hive run it as written and their read-only gate refuses it. `TestExplainGateNeverAnalyzes` asserts that invariant across all 13 engines.
- The caller's other options (`VERBOSE`, `COSTS OFF`) are dropped with the format they came with. Keeping them needs per-engine option rendering; noted in the design doc as the remaining gap.
- ClickHouse and Hive have no AST, so they check the leading keyword only: never a second `EXPLAIN`, never a rebuild.

## Legacy cleaned up alongside

- **Result masker** (`backend/api/v1/query_result_masker.go`): skipping masking on a case-sensitive `"EXPLAIN"` prefix meant a typed lowercase `explain select …` took the masking path its uppercase twin skipped. It now asks `parserbase.StartsWithExplain`, which ignores case and leading comments. A plan carries

title: test(audit): pin the store and stream rule on a booted server
body:
## Summary

Part of BYT-10124, 4 of 4. Stacked on #21483 — **review #21482 and #21483 first; this diff is one new test file.**

`TestAuditSinksOnBothChains` holds the store and stream rule against a booted server, on the public chain and through `/mcp`, with stdout audit on and then off:

```
store  = the method has audit = true and the call reached its handler
stream = stdout is on and (stored or refused by a permission check)
```

18 probes × 2 stdout settings = 36 subtests. Each probe declares two facts — whether the call is stored, and whether a permission check refused it — and the test holds the rule against them: the row's severity and parent, one stream line or none, and, when both exist, that the line carries the row's request.

## What each chain covers

| Row of the design's table | Public chain | MCP chain |
|---|---|---|
| audited, reached the handler, ok | `UpdateProject` | `CreateSheet` |
| audited, refused inside the handler | `UpdateSetting` (stored, `WARNING`) | the read-only clamp inside `Query` (stored, `WARNING`) |
| audited, refused by the SQL Editor's access check | `Query` on a database the caller cannot read (stored, `WARNING`, RPC answers OK) | — |
| audited, refused at an interceptor | ACL on `UpdateProject` | the gate on `CreateUser`; ACL on `CreatePlan` |
| unaudited, refused inside the handler | `SearchIssues` | `SearchIssues` |
| unaudited, refused at an interceptor | ACL on `GetProject` | the gate on `ListUsers` |
| unaudited, reached the handler, ok | `GetProject` | `ListWorkspaces` |
| audited, validate-only, ok | `CreateDatabaseGroup` | `CreateDatabaseGroup` |
| audited, validate-only, refused | ACL on `CreateDatabaseGroup` | the gate on `UpdateDataSource` |
| reading the audit log | `SearchAuditLogs`, stored without its results | — |

## Why it can fail

The row search is unscoped, so a row filed under the wrong parent fails the assertion that names it instead of vanishing from the search. Mutations run before commit, each failing named subtests:

| Mutation | Fails |
|---|---|
| Public chain back to ACL-outside-audit | every public-chain probe that stores or streams |
| `SearchIssues`' handler verdict unmarked | both `unaudited refused in handler` probes |
| The omit on `SearchAuditLogsResponse.audit_logs` ignored | `audit_log_search` |
| A public-chain row filed under the workspace instead of the project | `audited_ok`, by name |
| The three marks in `accessCheckWithGrantedTargets` dropped | `refused by the SQL Editor access check`, alone |

The test is not parallel: it captures `slog.Default` to read the stream, and that is process-wide.

The SQL Editor probe is the one that pins a refusal the RPC itself hides: `Query` reports the denial inside its response, so the call answers OK and the row's status stays empty. The probe asserts both — `WARNING` severity and a nil status — because severity is the only field carrying the refusal.

## Not in this change

- Failed-login rows: `backend/tests/login_audit_test.

title: fix(audit): mark the IAM verdicts handlers make for themselves
body:
## Summary

Part of BYT-10124, 3 of 4. Stacked on #21482 — **review that one first; this diff is the last commit only.**

A method with `auth_method = CUSTOM` passes the ACL interceptor, because `doIAMPermissionCheck` returns true for every non-IAM method, and makes its own IAM check inside the handler. Some IAM methods make a stricter check there too. Those verdicts were unmarked: on an unaudited method the refusal was recorded nowhere, and on an audited one the row said `INFO`.

The design ([`audit-what-produces-a-row.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/feat/audit-sinks/docs/design/audit-what-produces-a-row.md), section 3) puts the mark at "the custom-auth handler sites that make the check themselves".

## How

`common.PermissionDeniedError(ctx, err)` builds the refusal and marks it in one call, so a handler's IAM verdict cannot answer `PermissionDenied` without the audit interceptor seeing it. Twenty-six verdicts move to it.

Two more refuse by answering `NotFound`, to keep a resource's existence from the caller — `BatchGetDatabases`, and the permission helper the saved-query reads and writes go through. They mark without changing what the caller is told, which also makes `BatchGetGroups`' mark through `GetGroup` deliberate rather than accidental.

A license gate, a workflow state and an ownership rule answer the same code without an IAM check. They keep `connect.NewError`, so the choice of constructor is the decision to mark, recorded at the verdict.

## Effect

| Method | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Unaudited, refused by its own IAM check | nothing anywhere | one `WARNING` line on the stdout stream; still never stored |
| Audited, refused by its own IAM check | stored, `INFO` | stored, `WARNING`, and streamed |

## Tests

`backend/common/context_test.go` pins that the constructor marks, and that it is safe when no setter is registered (a handler called outside the chain). PR 4 drives two of these sites — `UpdateSetting` and `SearchIssues` — through a booted server on both chains.

No lint stands over future handlers. The first version of this PR had a text scanner; it could not see three of the verdicts it was meant to cover (the rollout ones, whose check sits behind a helper), so the constructor replaced it: the mark is part of building the error now, rather than a second statement a scanner has to police.

## The second sweep

Codex asked on #21482 for the handler-side permission checks. A sweep of all 131 `CodePermissionDenied` sites in `backend/api` found six verdicts the first pass missed, in `8e856d2f62`:

| Verdict | Was | Why it was missed |
|---|---|---|
| The SQL Editor's three access checks in `accessCheckWithGrantedTargets` | stored `INFO` | they build a `queryError`, not a connect error |
| The approver-role check behind `ApproveIssue` and `RejectIssue` | stored `INFO` | the verdict is produced in `backend/component/review`, under the package's own error code |
| `SwitchWorkspace`'s membership check | nowhere at

title: feat(audit): stream refused calls to stdout; store what reached a handler
body:
## Summary

Part of BYT-10124, 2 of 4. The spec is [`docs/design/audit-what-produces-a-row.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/feat/audit-sinks/docs/design/audit-what-produces-a-row.md), committed here and approved by Danny, Edward and Xzavier ([draft 4 doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1z-Y10y7UP43zQFKGwzMH0CchBIPPLjwXPYp8He4VucI), [comparables research](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/579af5ff-ff73-41ad-b446-9c94e9da7b46)).

Two readers open the audit log. An administrator reads the database in the console to learn what an admitted caller changed. A compliance reader reads the stdout stream in a SIEM, and needs the refused attempts most of all. The database keeps exactly what it keeps today; the stream gains every refused call:

```
store  = the method has audit = true and the call reached its handler
stream = stdout is on and (stored or refused by a permission check)
```

Release note: Refused API calls are now streamed to the stdout audit log when it is enabled, with severity WARNING; the database audit log is unchanged. Reading the audit log is itself audited.

## Behavior changes

| # | Call | Before | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Public chain, refused at ACL | nothing | streamed, `WARNING`; never stored |
| 2 | Internal chain, refused at the ceiling gate (any method), or at ACL (audited method) | stored | streamed only |
| 2b | Internal chain, unaudited method refused at ACL | nothing | streamed, `WARNING` |
| 2c | Internal chain, audited call the gate or ACL failed for another reason (NOT_FOUND, an outage) | stored | nothing, as on the public chain |
| 3 | Read-only clamp refusal inside `Query` | stored, `INFO` | stored, `WARNING`, streamed |
| 4 | `SearchAuditLogs` | not audited | stored and streamed, without its result list |
| 5 | Everything else | — | unchanged |

One measured exception to 5: a public-chain row's `latency` now includes the ACL check, because audit times what it wraps. Internal-chain rows already did.

## How

- The public chain becomes validate, auth, audit, ACL, handler, matching the internal chain minus the gate. Auth stays outside audit: it populates the identity and workspace every row needs.
- ACL reports admission (`common.SetHandlerReached`) just before the handler. It is the last interceptor on both chains, so a call it refused, or failed to resolve, is never stored.
- `common.SetMCPPolicyDenied` becomes `common.SetPermissionDenied`. ACL sets it once, where it answers `PermissionDenied`; the MCP ceiling gate and the read-only clamp set it as before. It makes a call stream-eligible and stamps it `WARNING`, and never makes a row stored — so the `needAudit(ctx) || mcpPolicyDenied` override is deleted.
- Both sinks are fed from one built row, so redaction applies to the stream exactly as to the row. Every line is written before any insert, and a failed insert does not affect it.
- The insert goes through `common.AuditLogWriter` instead of the `createAuditLogFunc` seam, so a test can watch the t

title: fix(mssql): match each query result to its statement
body:
## What

SQL Server returns a batch's results as one stream and doesn't say which statement produced each one. `queryBatch` (`backend/plugin/db/mssql/mssql.go`) guessed the owner from each statement's type, and the API pairs result *i* with statement *i*, masking included. The guesses went wrong in three ways:

- **Crash.** `EXEC` of a procedure that returns rows or row counts, and `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE … OUTPUT`, panicked (`index out of range`, `makeslice`), and the Query API returned an internal error. This was a follow-up listed in #21476.
- **Masked data in clear text.** A statement that returns nothing where rows were expected (`SELECT @x = …`), statements that `SET NOEXEC ON` skips, or a statement that returns nothing at the end of a batch before `GO`, shifted later results onto other statements, and masking applied those statements' rules. For example, `DECLARE @x INT`, `GO`, then `SELECT <masked column> FROM t` returned the column unmasked.
- **Hang.** A result set larger than the result size limit stalled the request until the query timeout, or indefinitely without one.

## Changes

- `queryBatch` reads the whole batch first. Then `matchResults` gives each statement exactly one result, in statement order, including statements at the end of a batch.
  - `SELECT` and DML with an `OUTPUT` clause (no `INTO`) return one result set each. `SELECT … INTO` and `SELECT @v = …` return none (`stmt_type.go`).
  - `EXEC` may return any number of result sets. They are matched only when no other statement in its batch returns rows. Its result sets after the first come after every statement's result, so positions stay aligned across `GO` batches.
  - A batch that still doesn't add up fails with an error that suggests `GO`, instead of crashing or mislabeling results. Examples: two procedure calls that return rows, `SET STATISTICS XML`, or a trigger that returns rows.
  - Row counts are shown only when each belongs to one statement. Mixed `SET NOCOUNT` and procedure calls change how many arrive.
- `SET NOEXEC` and `SET PARSEONLY` are refused. They skip statements without an error, so the result sets that do arrive can't be matched safely.
- **Procedure and `OUTPUT` rows while masking applies.** Masking finds the columns to mask from the statement, and a procedure call or an `OUTPUT` clause doesn't reveal them. `queryRetry` now passes its `maskingEnabled` to the driver as `db.QueryContext.MaskingEnabled`, and the driver empties those result sets with an explanation. Users with an unmask grant still see the rows.
  - The check lives in the driver because only the driver knows which results came from an `OUTPUT` clause: `OUTPUT inserted.salary AS [Affected Rows]` looks like an affected-rows count.
- A result set cut at the size limit is read to its end, so the rest of the batch still runs. Procedure and `OUTPUT` rows are also cut to the row limit, which the `SELECT` rewrite doesn't cover.

## Breaking Changes

- On SQL Server, a query containing `SET NO

title: fix(acl): look up the project named by an instance lifecycle method
body:
## Summary

Part of BYT-10124, 1 of 3. The next PR moves the public chain's audit interceptor outside ACL, so every resource ACL publishes becomes the parent of a refused call's audit line. This PR removes the one path that published a project name without checking it.

`DeleteInstance`, `UndeleteInstance` and `PrepareSampleProjectInstance` resolved a bare project name through a shortcut that skipped the store read. Today, on the public chain, a caller holding the permission on the workspace passed the IAM check before any project lookup. The audit interceptor, which still runs inside ACL, then filed the handler's error under a project the store never confirmed, including one that does not exist. A caller without a workspace grant got `INTERNAL` ("project not found") from the IAM check. The MCP chain never reached the shortcut: its gate refuses these EXCLUDED methods before ACL runs.

The shortcut existed so an archived project still resolves. The resolver table already does that, because `store.GetProject` always returns deleted projects. So the shortcut is deleted, and `PrepareSampleProjectInstance` leaves the archived-project list, which it was on only for the shortcut.

## Behavior change

A lifecycle call naming a project the workspace does not have now answers `NOT_FOUND` at ACL. A deleted project still resolves, so a sample request against one still reaches the handler's "entitlement consumed" answer. The console only sends existing projects.

## Tests

`TestPopulateRawResourcesResolvesLifecycleProject` (real store): a deleted sample parent resolves, and an unknown project is `NOT_FOUND` for all three methods. It fails on main, and fails again if the shortcut is restored.

## Not in this change

The store read confirms the project exists in the caller's workspace, not that the caller holds a role on it. Every project-scoped method resolves this way today.

title: fix(spanner): run queries that start with WITH when a row limit applies
body:
## Summary

On Spanner, any query that starts with `WITH` failed whenever a row limit applied (the SQL editor's maximum result rows):

```
WITH is not supported on subqueries in this language version
```

The driver limited every query by nesting it in `WITH result AS (<query>) SELECT * FROM result LIMIT n`, and Spanner [doesn't allow a `WITH` clause in a subquery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/subqueries).

## Changes

- **`getStatementWithResultLimit`** no longer wraps the query. It parses the query with omni's GoogleSQL parser and sets the `LIMIT` of the outermost query in place:
  - With no `LIMIT`, it appends `LIMIT n` after the query, following any `ORDER BY`.
  - It lowers an existing literal `LIMIT` that is higher than `n` and keeps any `OFFSET`. A lower one is kept.
  - Anything it can't rewrite runs as written: parse failures (omni can't parse pipe syntax `|>` yet), a `LIMIT` that isn't a plain number (e.g. `CAST(5000 AS INT64)`), and `FOR UPDATE` queries.
- **`queryStatement`** stops reading rows at the limit, so the limit still holds for statements that ran unchanged.
- **Tests:**
  - Unit test for the rewrite.
  - Env-gated end-to-end test `TestQueryConnLimitsQueryStartingWithWith`, sharing the existing Spanner Omni test's `SPANNER_EMULATOR_HOST` / `SPANNER_TEST_DATABASE` gate. CI has no Spanner, so it skips there.

## Reviewer notes

- **Trade-off:** queries the rewrite can't handle no longer send Spanner a `LIMIT`. Before, queries starting with `SELECT` were wrapped. The row count is still capped, but Spanner may do more work; for example, `SELECT … |> ORDER BY x` sorts the whole result instead of only the top rows.
- **`FOR UPDATE`** is left unchanged. The `LIMIT` would have to go before it, but Spanner only allows `FOR UPDATE` [in read-write transactions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/use-select-for-update). This query runs in a read-only one, so it fails either way, and leaving it unchanged keeps Spanner's own error.
- **Not in scope:** `util.IsSelect` only recognizes statements that start with `SELECT` or `WITH`. Parenthesized, hinted (`@{…}`), graph, and `FROM`-first pipe queries still go down the DML path and fail with `query passed to Update`.

## Testing

- `go test ./backend/plugin/db/spanner/` passes; golangci-lint reports 0 issues; the server builds.
- Checked against the Cloud Spanner emulator:
  - On `main`, `TestQueryConnLimitsQueryStartingWithWith` fails with the error above; with this change it passes.
  - The emulator accepted every rewritten statement from the unit test wherever it accepted the original.
- With the emulator variables set, `TestExplainDMLWithoutRunningIt` still fails with `query plan unavailable`. That's expected: the emulator doesn't produce query plans, and that test is meant for Spanner Omni.

title: fix(sql): record the statement SQL Server and Spanner ran
body:
## What

SQL Server and Spanner now record on `QueryResult.statement` the text they ran, result limit included, as the other limit-rewriting drivers already do.

- **SQL Server** (`mssql.go`, `queryBatch`): each statement enters the batch through `getStatementWithResultLimit`, but its result recorded the statement as typed. It now records the rewritten text, still index-aligned with the results, including the empty ones padded in for statements that return nothing.
- **Spanner** (`spanner.go`, `QueryConn`): a SELECT ran as `WITH result AS (…) SELECT * FROM result LIMIT n;` but recorded the bare SELECT. It now records the wrapper.

## Why

The [query plan visualizer design, §3.4](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md#34-engine-differences), has a result's Plan tab explain the statement that ran, limits included, and names these two drivers as the ones recording something else. The limit changes the plan: on SQL Server 2022, `SHOWPLAN_XML` of the recorded text now has a `Top` operator; on Spanner Omni, it now has `Limit` nodes.

Readers of `statement`, checked:

- Masking skips results whose statement starts with `EXPLAIN`. Neither rewrite changes how a statement starts, apart from Spanner's wrapper, which starts with `WITH`.
- The SQL editor hides results whose statement starts with `SET`. `SET` statements keep their text.
- Export writes the executed text to `statement-N.sql`, as it already does on the other engines. The export request still sends the typed statement.
- **Show in editor** on a failed result finds its statement in the editor by text, stripping only a trailing `LIMIT n`, so it cannot find Spanner's wrapper. The same is already true for ClickHouse, CockroachDB, Redshift and BigQuery. Not changed here.

## Testing

- `TestQueryConnRecordsLimitedStatement` (shared SQL Server container): with limit 2, `SET NOCOUNT OFF; SELECT TOP 3 …` records `SET NOCOUNT OFF;` and `SELECT TOP 2 …` and returns two rows. On `main` it fails, recording `TOP 3`.
- Real engines, before and after, through the driver and through `SQLService.Query` (throwaway probes, not committed):
  - SQL Server 2022: for single and multi-statement batches (`SET`, `DECLARE`, `UPDATE`, `GO`), the recorded statements joined equal the batch the server ran (`sys.dm_exec_connections.most_recent_sql_handle`). On `main` they differ whenever a limit applies. Rows are the limited ones, in order.
  - Spanner emulator and Spanner Omni 2026.r2.1-beta: SELECTs record the wrapper, and DML and DDL record the text as typed. On Omni the rows are right, and explaining the recorded text returns a plan with `Limit`. The emulator has no plans, and it returned the limited rows out of the inner `ORDER BY` order, on `main` too.

title: chore: bump omni to 96fc86c5 and preserve CTEs in MSSQL prior backup
body:
## Summary

Bumps `github.com/bytebase/omni` from `848b1ffe` (2026-09-15) to `96fc86c5` (2026-09-17, current main), and fixes a pre-existing MSSQL prior-backup bug that Codex flagged on the bump.

### omni bump

Upstream commits picked up, both MSSQL parser fixes:

- **#426**: a leading `WITH` clause is now attached to the `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`/`MERGE` node that follows it, and the top-level node starts at the `WITH` keyword.
- **#427**: a CTE list in nested `SELECT` positions (derived tables, subqueries, set-operation operands, `INSERT` sources) is rejected.

The only consumer of MSSQL `WithClause` outside prior backup is the `disallow functions and calculations in WHERE` advisor rule, which already checks CTEs on `InsertStmt`/`UpdateStmt`/`DeleteStmt`/`MergeStmt`.

### MSSQL prior backup keeps CTEs

`WITH c AS (...) UPDATE t ... WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c)` produced a backup `SELECT INTO` that referenced `c` without defining it, so the backup failed before the DML ran. This was already the behavior on `848b1ffe`; the bump only moves the statement's start position to the `WITH` keyword.

`backend/plugin/parser/tsql/backup.go` now:

- emits the statement's `WITH` clause verbatim ahead of the `SELECT INTO`, the same approach `pg/backup.go` uses. T-SQL only allows a CTE list at the top of a statement, so a CTE referenced inside a `UNION` branch must be hoisted. Because the hoisted clause becomes the name scope of every branch, statements grouped on the same table must carry identical `WITH` clause text (including all having none); any other mix is rejected with an explicit error rather than risking a base table name binding to a sibling's CTE. `WITH XMLNAMESPACES` is rejected.
- rejects a DML whose unqualified target is one of its own CTEs. The executor treats an empty backup result as a no-op, so skipping such a statement would let the migration modify the base table without backup data. A schema-qualified target is still backed up even when a CTE shares its name. Name matching honors `TransformContext.IsCaseSensitive`, so `c` and `C` stay distinct under a case-sensitive collation.

## Verification

- `go build -ldflags "-w -s" -p=16 -o ./bytebase-build/bytebase ./backend/bin/server/main.go` passes.
- `go test -count=1 ./backend/plugin/parser/tsql/` passes with new cases in `TestBackupOmniBoundaryCases` (CTE on UPDATE, DELETE, aliased JOIN, identical clause hoisted once, differing clauses rejected, missing clause on a sibling rejected, separate scope per table, XMLNAMESPACES) and `TestBackupRejectsCTETarget`.
- `go test -count=1` also passes for `advisor/mssql`, `db/mssql`, `schema/mssql`, `parser/mysql`, `parser/mariadb`, `parser/tidb`.
- golangci-lint v2.13.2 reports no issues in the changed files. Its remaining findings are pre-existing `revive` unhandled-error hits in untouched files.

title: fix(oracle): resolve database links by exact connect endpoint
body:
## Summary

Fixes BYT-10226. (This PR now also carries the access check that was #21469.) In SQL Editor on Oracle, a table reached through a database link was never an authorization resource. The Oracle query-span extractor dropped every `schema.table@link` reference before building `span.SourceColumns`, so the access check only ever saw local tables.

Reproduced on a live Oracle 23ai rig with a loopback link. With a grant scoped to one table (`resource.table_name == "ALLOWED_T"`):

| Statement | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `SELECT * FROM SECRET_SCHEMA.SECRET_T` | denied | denied |
| `SELECT * FROM ALLOWED_T, SECRET_SCHEMA.SECRET_T@REMOTE` | **rows returned, including the SSN** | denied, names `.../databases/SECRET_SCHEMA/tables/SECRET_T` |
| same table in a JOIN, scalar subquery, EXISTS, UNION ALL | **rows returned** | denied, same resource |
| `... SECRET_T@REMOTE2` (link Bytebase cannot resolve) | executed on Oracle, rows withheld afterwards | refused before execution, message names the link |

With a database-level grant on the connected database, every link target was readable; the same table read directly was denied. Export and the MCP query tool share the path. Once the grant names the resolved database (`resource.database == ".../SECRET_SCHEMA"` or the table), the link reads work again.

## The rule

A table written `S.T@LINK` is authorized as the Bytebase database the link resolves to, with the same resource name the table carries on a direct connection. When Bytebase cannot name that database, no grant can authorize it, so the statement is refused before it runs. No new CEL attribute, no new grant vocabulary: the admin writes the same condition they write for a direct connection, and the denial names the resource to grant.

## What changes

- `parserbase.ColumnResource` gains `Instance`: the Bytebase instance that owns `Database` when the column was reached through a link (empty means the connected instance). `Server` keeps its meaning, the reference as written. `Server` set with `Instance` empty marks a remote reference Bytebase could not resolve.
- `collectOmniAccessTables` returns linked tables separately from local ones. Only local tables feed the system-schema classifier and the missing-table gate: both read connected-instance metadata, which says nothing about a remote schema, and a link into `SYS` fed to the classifier turned the statement into an info-schema read that skipped every table-level check. The system-schema classifier counts a linked table as a user table: a link-only statement is a Select, never an info-schema read (which returns no source columns and skips every table-level check), and a local system table next to a link is a mixed query and refused, as before. A linked table is authorized by the name written and resolved once through the same resolver the column pass uses. It bypasses `existsTableMetadata`, which would drop a remote table or keep a same-named local one as the wrong resource; that local-namesak

title: fix(doris): drop MySQL routine and event probes from the schema dump
body:
BYT-10211.

The StarRocks/Doris driver was copied from the MySQL driver, and its `Dump` still runs `SHOW FUNCTION STATUS`, `SHOW PROCEDURE STATUS` and `SHOW EVENTS` on every schema dump. The first error aborts the dump, and the syncer never stores the table and view metadata it had already collected. A customer on ApsaraDB for SelectDB kernel 4.1.9 (Alibaba Cloud's Doris kernel, built on Apache Doris 3.1.4) hits exactly that. SelectDB's [kernel release notes](https://help.aliyun.com/zh/selectdb/product-overview/kernel-release-record) for 4.1.9 say "移除 PL/SQL 存储过程和 package 能力" (PL/SQL stored procedures and packages removed), and 4.1.8, 4.0.12 and 5.0.5 carry the same bullet. `SHOW (PROCEDURE | FUNCTION) STATUS` is a rule of that grammar in Doris, so the server answers `Error 1105: errCode = 2, detailMessage = no viable alternative at input 'SHOW FUNCTION'(line 1, pos 5)`. Every database on the instance then fails to sync, and the SQL Editor object browser stays empty with "Code 13: Internal". Apache Doris master made the same removal in apache/doris#58700 and restored an always-empty stub in apache/doris#66659 because it blocked Bytebase. No Apache Doris release lacks the rule (every 3.1, 4.0, 4.1 and 4.2 tag has it, and 2.1/3.0 accept the statement through the legacy parser); the vendor kernel does.

The probes never produced anything on these engines. StarRocks has no stored procedures or events and answers with an empty MySQL-shaped set. Doris returns PL/SQL procedure rows as `ProcedureName, CatalogId, DbId, ...`, which the MySQL-shaped scan misreads: a stock Doris 4.1.3 with one procedure fails the dump with `failed to call getRoutineStmt("prod_tg", "0", "1789585700466"): ... no viable alternative at input 'SHOW CREATE 1789585700466'`, and `SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE` returns two columns where the scan expects six. Neither engine has `CREATE EVENT`. The routine and event steps could only ever succeed when they found nothing, so this PR removes them and their helpers, plus the unused `sequenceStmtFmt` and the `mysqldump` flag-list comment that no longer described the dump.

Error tolerance around the probes was rejected. It would keep sending a statement the vendor declared unsupported and would mask real failures on a driver two engines share. `information_schema.routines` is not a substitute either; the same upstream removal deleted its scanner.

## Validation

- `TestDumpSendsNoRoutineOrEventProbe` runs `Dump` for Doris and StarRocks against a scripted `database/sql` driver that answers the catalog queries with the column shapes a live Doris 4.1.3 returns and rejects the routine probes with the vendor's error. It fails on `origin/main` with the customer's exact error chain and passes here, including under `go test -count=2`.
- End to end on a local rig: a server built from this branch syncs `prod_tg` through a MySQL-wire proxy in front of Apache Doris 4.1.3 (FE and BE alive) that rejects only `SHOW (FUNCTION|PROCEDURE) STATUS`. The sync returns `

title: docs: design for the query plan visualizer
body:
Design doc for moving the query plan out of a pop-up browser tab and into the
SQL Editor result pane. `docs/design/query-plan-visualizer.md`.

## Why

The editor explains on 12 engines and draws a picture for 3, but reaching the
picture takes five steps, and a typed `EXPLAIN` never reaches it at all — the
Visualize link is gated on the request flag, which only Ctrl/Cmd+E sets. Type
`EXPLAIN SELECT …`, press Run, and you get rows and nothing else, even on
PostgreSQL.

## What the doc decides

- **Four triggers** — the Plan tab on a result, a typed `EXPLAIN`, Explain only
  in Run's dropdown, and Explain now on a History row.
- **One drawing rule** — draw whenever the engine returned a machine-readable
  plan, otherwise show text. We read the result, never the user's SQL.
- **A cost rule** — a picture never costs more than one extra `Query()` call and
  never re-executes a statement that already ran.
- **Engine differences are part of the UI** — Spanner and SQL Server can return a
  *measured* plan with no extra run; PostgreSQL and the rest get an estimate,
  badged as such, because an estimated plan shown against a slow run is easy to
  mistake for the plan that ran.

## Two findings worth highlighting

A typed `EXPLAIN` is **already** classified as an explain server-side and already
requires `bb.sql.explain` (`backend/api/v1/sql_service.go:1480`). None of that
reaches the browser, so problem 1 is a plumbing gap, not a parsing gap.

Of the SQL editors surveyed, **none rewrites a typed `EXPLAIN`**. The four that
draw one — SSMS, Azure Data Studio, VS Code MSSQL, pgAdmin — all recognize the
shape of the result instead. Supabase shipped the alternative (parsing the text
plan) in Dec 2025 and deleted it seven months later for non-use.

## Open decisions, called out in the doc

1. Whether to ask for `FORMAT JSON` on the first call for a typed
   `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. A second call would execute the statement twice; this is
   the one place the design would depart from every product surveyed.
2. Whether to auto-fetch the picture for a plain typed `EXPLAIN` rather than
   offering a Visualize button. The doc ships the button and names the
   instrumentation that would settle it.

## Verification

Docs-only, so the code gates do not apply. Per the pre-PR checklist's
documentation rule, every cited path, symbol and line number was checked against
`main` at `7664688752`: nine line citations and five symbols, all current. None
of the cited files changed in the three commits that landed while this was
written.

title: feat(sql-editor): maximize the query result pane
body: ## Why The result pane opens at 40% of the editor height. On a 900px window with the sidebar showing, that is about **four data rows** — too few to read a wide result, and far too few for the query plan visualizer we want to move into this pane next. There was no way to give the pane more room beyond dragging the splitter, and nothing remembered the drag. ## Screenshots Docked (4 rows, pane 1079px) vs maximized (16 rows, pane 1440px), at 1440x900: The control, at the right end of the result pane's tab row: ## What changed - **A maximize toggle** beside the query tabs, so rows, errors and (later) plans all get the same control. `Escape` restores, unless an overlay owns the key. - **Maximizing collapses the editor pane rather than unmounting it**, so Monaco keeps its cursor, scroll and undo history. The sidebar collapses in place for the same reason: the tree keeps its scroll position and its dragged width. - **A dragged height persists** per browser under `bb.sql-editor.result-panel-size`, debounced so a drag doesn't write to storage once per frame. Two invariants worth calling out, because both were bugs first: - **Maximizing is momentary, not remembered.** It lasts exactly as long as the pane it belongs to: `StandardPanel` clears it when the result pane goes away and on unmount, so a tab switch, a metadata view or a lost connection all hand back an editor and a sidebar. Only the dragged *height* is remembered. - **The separator is locked while maximized.** Dragging it otherwise produced a half-state — the editor visible again under a sidebar that was still hidden — reachable by drag but by no control. Restore first, then drag. - Whether the pane is maximized is the reader's decision, taken through the toggle — never derived from the layout. The panel group reports its default size once on mount, and reading that back cancelled a maximized pane immediately. ## Testing - `pnpm --dir frontend test` — green on the rebased tree (511 files, 4007 tests). - New: `StandardPanel.test.tsx` (collapse/expand, the resize mapping, the clearing rules and the locked separator), `ResultPanel.test.tsx` (when the pane hands the editor back), a sidebar block in `SQLEditorHomePage.test.tsx` pinning the desktop/narrow distinction, and `MaximizeToggle.test.tsx`. - Driven in a real browser against a local build at 1440x900 and at 600x800: 4 → 16 rows, Escape and the toggle both return the exact prior geometry, Monaco text and undo survive a cycle, the height persists across a reload, and the narrow-window drawer still behaves. ## Notes Not a breaking change: the control is additive and the default split is unchanged (40%) until the reader drags or maximizes. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix(sql-editor): restore the database label when the result bar widens
body:
## What changed

`ResultStatusBar` hides the instance/database label to give a long statement room, but it never brought the label back. Once hidden it stayed hidden at every width until the page was reloaded.

The overflow check measured the statement as the larger of the row wrapper's `scrollWidth` and the text span's:

```ts
const statementWidth = Math.max(statementLabel.scrollWidth, statementText?.scrollWidth ?? 0);
```

The wrapper is `flex-1`, so its `scrollWidth` is the *stretched* row width, and hiding the label let it grow to fill the whole row. `statementWidth + databaseWidth > rowWidth` was then true at every width — the state the predicate produced was an input to the decision that produced it, so it could never flip back.

The fix measures only the text span. It is a content-sized flex item (`flex: 0 1 auto`), so it is sized to `min(content, available)` and never stretches — its `scrollWidth` is the statement's intrinsic width in every layout state. Measured in Chromium:

| state | wrapper.scrollWidth | text.scrollWidth |
|---|---|---|
| 1440, label shown | 1078 | 994 |
| 600, label shown | 256 | 994 |
| 600, label hidden | 479 | 994 |
| 1440, label hidden | **1319** | 994 |

The check is now a pure function of three values that do not change when the label toggles — intrinsic text width, the remembered natural label width, and the container width — so the latch is removed rather than masked with hysteresis.

## Why

Reported repro: open the SQL Editor at 1440x900, run a query, resize to 600x800 (label hides, correct), resize back to 1440x900 — the label stays hidden permanently, losing the record of which database the result came from.

## Verification

Mounted the real component in Chromium via a throwaway probe page (deleted; not part of this diff) and drove it with Playwright:

- **Before the fix:** reproduces the report exactly — hides at 600, still hidden at 1440, and at every width after.
- **After the fix:** hides at 600 and returns at 1440 across repeated cycles.
- **Sweep 1600 -> 520 -> 1600:** the transition sits at 1300px in *both* directions (no hysteresis gap, no direction-dependent state), with one class change at the boundary and zero flips while idle there — no oscillation or flicker.

New test `shows the database label again when the container widens back` in `ResultStatusBar.test.tsx` uses the Chromium-measured widths. It was run against the unfixed component first and fails precisely at the widen-back assertion.

## Notes for reviewers

- The two existing overflow tests set `scrollWidth` on the row wrapper, which is no longer the measured element, so their fixtures moved onto the text span. They would otherwise have passed vacuously.
- Extracted the duplicated resize-flush `act` block into a `flushResize()` helper now that three tests use it.
- Out of scope, pre-existing: `databaseWidthRef` only refreshes while the label is visible, so switching database without changing the statement can leave it stale (the effec

title: perf(store): cache the auth secret for the life of the Store
body:
## Summary

- `GetAuthSecret` keeps the first successful read of `server_config` for the life of the `Store`, independent of `enableCache` (so HA deployments benefit too). A failed read is not cached.
- `ListAllInstances` deobfuscates all instances in one pass instead of once per workspace.
- Removes the unused exported `Store.Secret` field.

## Why

Cloud SQL Query Insights for `bytebase-metadb-01` (7 days) shows `SELECT payload FROM server_config LIMIT 1` as the most-called query: ~9.5M calls (~14/s). Cloud Monitoring attributes them to the schema syncer's pod at ~150 reads per `ListAllInstances` call. `syncQueuedDatabases` calls it every 10 seconds, and the per-workspace grouping re-read the secret for every workspace, so the count grows with signups (129 → 150 per call over the week).

The secret is safe to hold forever: only migrations write `server_config` (`LATEST.sql` generates it; `3.17/0009` copies the old value), nothing writes it at runtime, and `server.go` already keeps its startup copy for token signing, OAuth2, MCP, and LSP. Stored instance credentials are XOR-obfuscated with it and never re-obfuscated, so changing it would already break every saved data source credential.

This PR doesn't cover the 10-second `ListAllInstances` poll itself (~85% of query time on that database); that's a separate change.

## Test plan

- [x] `TestGetAuthSecretKeepsFirstSuccessfulRead`: error while the row is missing, then the first value is kept after the row changes (store cache disabled, as in HA)
- [x] `TestListAllInstancesDeobfuscatesAcrossWorkspaces`: plaintext passwords come back for instances in two workspaces
- [x] Both new tests fail with the fix removed
- [x] `go test ./backend/store/ ./backend/runner/schemasync/`
- [x] `go test ./backend/tests/ -run '^(TestClaim|TestCollision)'`, plus `TestDataSource`, `TestListQueryHistories`, `TestChangePasswordProofAndRevocation`
- [x] `golangci-lint run` clean; server binary builds

title: chore: deploy api.bytebase.com to Cloudflare Pages
body:
## Summary

Moves api.bytebase.com from Vercel to Cloudflare Pages, following the same wrangler-based workflow used by pgplex.

- Add `.github/workflows/deploy-api-docs.yml`: on pushes to `main` that touch the OpenAPI spec, `docs/api/`, or the workflow, it assembles the Scalar page, favicon, and `proto/gen/grpc-doc/openapi.yaml` into `out/`, creates the `bytebase-api` Pages project on first run, and deploys with `cloudflare/wrangler-action`.
- `docs/api/index.html` now loads the bundled `./openapi.yaml` instead of fetching it from raw.githubusercontent.com on every page load, and uses Scalar's current `createApiReference` entry point.
- The assemble step replaces the buf plugin's placeholder `info.title` ("API") with "Bytebase API Reference" so the in-page heading matches the tab title. The remote plugin rejects a `title=` option and cannot read a local base file, so this is done at deploy time.

## Rollout

1. Add `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` (Account / Cloudflare Pages / Edit) and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` repository secrets before merging.
2. After the first successful run, attach the `api.bytebase.com` custom domain to the `bytebase-api` project and remove the Vercel project. The Vercel deployment is already stale (it serves a pre-July-30 `index.html`), so it will not pick up this change.

## Test plan

- Served the assembled `out/` directory locally and loaded it in a browser: heading, description, favicon, and spec fetch all render with no console errors.
- Workflow YAML parses.

title: chore: bump omni to pick up a MySQL/MariaDB/TiDB comment-parsing fix
body:
## What

`github.com/bytebase/omni`'s MySQL, MariaDB, and TiDB lexers and splitters counted `/* */` nesting depth instead of stopping at the first closing `*/`, so a `/* /* */ ... */`-shaped comment could read through to the LAST `*/` and absorb a trailing statement or predicate as comment content instead of tokenizing it. Fixed upstream in [bytebase/omni#425](https://github.com/bytebase/omni/pull/425), oracle-verified there against real MySQL, MariaDB, and TiDB containers.

## Fix

Bump the `github.com/bytebase/omni` dependency. That's the entire change.

Every Bytebase consumer of MySQL/MariaDB/TiDB statement splitting and parsing — `base.SplitMultiSQL`, `base.ParseStatements`, `CountAffectedRows`, the SQL review advisors, the SQL editor — calls straight into omni's `Split`/`Parse`, so no other source change is needed here. Per this repo's own test-placement convention ("Engine dialect and DDL fidelity tests belong in omni"), the regression coverage lives entirely in the omni PR rather than duplicated here.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go mod tidy` (no-op), gofmt clean, `golangci-lint run` 0 issues, final server binary build, and every affected package tested (`plugin/db/{mysql,tidb}`, `plugin/parser/{mysql,tidb}`, `plugin/advisor/*`, `runner/plancheck`, `api/v1`, `common/testcontainer`) — all green.

title: feat(frontend): standardize instance secret inputs
body:
Instance secrets are write-only, so a blank input cannot express both “keep the stored value” and “clear it.” Add a shared `SecretInput` with direct editing and an explicit clear control, inspired by Directus.

Untouched fields show “Unchanged.” Typing replaces the secret; the eye icon reveals only the new input. Clicking × explicitly clears supported fields without first typing a character. Changes are applied with the form’s Update action, and the form’s Cancel discards them. Required secrets cannot be submitted empty, including drafts on inactive data-source tabs. Whitespace is preserved, and explicit update masks distinguish clearing from leaving a secret unchanged.

Trial scope: database and Redis Sentinel passwords, SSH password/private key, Snowflake private key/passphrase, and Databricks token. TLS and cloud/Vault credential groups remain unchanged because their API updates require coordinated handling of sibling secrets.

## Breaking Changes

Instance secret fields use direct replacement and an inline clear control. Clearing a password uses × followed by Update instead of the separate empty-password checkbox. API and storage schemas are unchanged.

## Validation

- `pnpm --dir frontend fix` passed.
- `pnpm --dir frontend test` passed, including guards, TypeScript, production bundle, and 3,650 tests across 493 files.
- Browser-checked the actual Bytebase instance page against the production frontend build and a local Bytebase server: untouched placeholder, clearing without typing, form Cancel, replacement input, and reveal control. The full E2E suite was not run.
- Regression coverage includes unchanged versus explicit empty values, required secrets, whitespace, multiline input, visibility, form resets, disabled controls, and secret update masks.

title: feat(sql-editor): one query plan visualizer for PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Spanner
body:
## What

PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Spanner plans now open in the same query plan visualizer, the React viewer #21443 built for PostgreSQL.

**Why now: the SQL Server view is about to stop working.** It was drawn by `html-query-plan`, which renders showplan XML through the browser's `XSLTProcessor`. Chrome turns XSLT off on Stable in [Chrome 158 (Nov 17, 2026)](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/deprecating-xslt), it is already off by default in Canary/Dev/Beta, and Firefox and WebKit plan to follow. With XSLT off, `main`'s SQL Server view throws `ReferenceError: XSLTProcessor is not defined` inside `qp.min.js`, and the tab stays blank with only a console error to show for it. Spanner had a separate tree view with hard-coded colors.

**One model, a parser per engine**

- **SQL Server** reads `SHOWPLAN_XML` with `DOMParser`, so no XSLT.
  - Statements become nodes above their operators. IF/ELSE branches, procedure calls, cursors, called functions and multi-statement batches keep their structure, with each branch, cursor query and function body labeled. That includes SQL Server 2016's form, which puts each statement of a batch in its own `<Statements>` block.
  - Operators are named as SSMS names them, e.g. "Key Lookup", "Hash Match (Inner Join)". Every showplan attribute is listed under SQL Server's name, with flags as True/False and memory and compile figures in KB or ms.
  - SQL Server's own warnings (no join predicate, plan-affecting conversions, unmatched filtered indexes) become node warnings. A missing-index suggestion appears as a ready `CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX [idx_orders_total] …`, named in Bytebase's `idx_<table>_<columns>` convention.
- **Spanner** keeps the relational operators, named as Spanner tooling names them ("Local Distributed Union", "Global Stream Aggregate"). The conditions each operator names become properties, subqueries hang under their subquery node, and Spanner's own `Full scan` flag becomes a warning. The emulator's placeholder plan gets a message saying the emulator doesn't plan queries.
- **PostgreSQL** is unchanged apart from full-scan detection moving from the model into its parser.

**The viewer shows only what a plan carries**

Estimates are optional per node. Spanner's PLAN mode reports none, so its cards show operators and conditions, with no Summary tab or highlight control. SQL Server has no startup cost, so its summary leaves out cost ranges. Costs under 1 keep three significant digits, because SQL Server's small cost units printed most operators as `0`, and row estimates keep two decimals.

**One path in the SQL editor**

A single table in `src/utils/explainToken.ts` lists the engines the visualizer draws and the explain format each needs. The editor offers Visualize from it and the visualizer keys its parsers on it, so the two cannot drift. PostgreSQL and SQL Server re-run their explain in that format; Spanner explains only as JSON, so it reuses the plan already in the result.

title: fix(sql): reject a smuggled write in an EXPLAIN request
body:
## What

`QueryRequest.explain=true` skipped the query-span access check in
`SQLService.Query`, so a caller holding only `bb.databases.get` could reach real
statement execution. The driver prepends `EXPLAIN`: `ANALYZE DELETE FROM t` is
not valid SQL on its own, but the wrapped `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM t` is —
and it deletes the rows on PostgreSQL (and other engines whose `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
executes).

## Fix

- **`backend/plugin/db/explain.go`** (new): `db.ExplainStatement(engine,
  statement, format)` is the single source of the `EXPLAIN` wrapping. Each
  prefix driver calls it to build the statement it runs, and the Query handler
  calls it to validate the exact statement that will run. Engines whose `EXPLAIN`
  is not a prefix (Oracle `EXPLAIN PLAN`, SQL Server `SET SHOWPLAN`,
  Spanner/BigQuery plan APIs) return `ok=false` and build their plan on their own.
- **`backend/api/v1/sql_service.go`**: for an explain request, validate that the
  `db.ExplainStatement` form is read-only and refuse otherwise — a smuggled write
  (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a write) is rejected before it runs, for any role. The
  access check also runs for explain requests now (previously guarded by
  `!Explain`), requiring `bb.sql.explain`.
- **`backend/plugin/parser/pg/query_type.go`**: `classifyExplainedQuery` fails
  closed for an inner node type it does not recognize.

This also centralizes what used to be per-driver `fmt.Sprintf(\"EXPLAIN %s\", …)`
and PostgreSQL's `explainStatement`, so EXPLAIN generation lives in one shared
place used by the API and the drivers — no per-engine capability list.

## Why validate the wrapped form (not just "is the raw statement valid SQL")

The smuggle `ANALYZE DELETE FROM t` is invalid SQL, so most engines' parsers
reject it — but **ClickHouse and Hive** use a keyword-based validator that does
*not* error on it. Those same validators do flag the *wrapped* `EXPLAIN ANALYZE
DELETE` as non-read-only, so validating the wrapped form closes the gap on every
engine; validating only the raw statement would not.

## Behavior

- **Plain `EXPLAIN` of DML still works**, returning a plan and changing nothing.
- **An explain request needs `bb.sql.explain`**.
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a write via the flag is refused** for everyone. Typing
  `EXPLAIN ANALYZE …` as a query still runs it, authorized by its inner statement.

## Testing

- `backend/tests/sql_explain_access_test.go`: smuggle refused for every role
  (no rows changed), `bb.sql.explain` required, plain `EXPLAIN` of a write
  returns a plan without executing, typed `EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE` runs.
- `db.ExplainStatement` unit test, pg `query_type` classification test.
- `gofmt`, `golangci-lint` (0 issues), and the release build pass.

title: feat(sql-editor): React query plan visualizer, replacing pev2
body:
## What

Replaces the PostgreSQL plan view — the last Vue in the codebase — with a React viewer built on PostgreSQL's own `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` output.

The old view mounted `pev2`, a Vue component, inside a React island. Because the new viewer reads structured JSON, there is no plan text to parse, and nothing in it derives from pev2: it was written against PostgreSQL's documented JSON fields and real captured plans.

**Backend**

- `QueryOption.explain_format` (`TEXT` / `JSON` / `XML`) replaces the SQL Server-only `mssql_explain_format`. One field serves every engine.
- The PostgreSQL driver emits `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON|XML)`; SQL Server keeps mapping `XML` to `SHOWPLAN_XML`.
- `validateExplainFormat` refuses a format an engine cannot produce, rather than silently returning a plan the caller cannot parse.

**Viewer**

- **Diagram** — node cards carrying each node's share of the plan's cost, edges weighted by estimated rows, a warning on sequential scans of large tables, subtree collapse, a mini-map, and deep links to a node.
- **Grid** — every node as a table with tree guides, for plans too large to read as a diagram.
- **Summary** — a cost timeline plotting each node from its startup cost to its total cost, which is the closest an estimate-only plan comes to showing *when* work happens, plus the costliest operators and cost by operation.

**Removed** — `pev2`, `vue` and `bootstrap`, their Biome and AGENTS.md exceptions, and the Font Awesome workaround pev2 needed.

**Also** — the visualizer entry stopped pulling Monaco and the i18n bundle through `utils/util` for a 16-byte random token: **2,627 KB → 208 KB gzip**.

## Breaking Changes

`QueryOption.mssql_explain_format` (field 2) is **removed** from `bytebase.v1`; its number and name are reserved. Callers that set it must send `explain_format: XML` instead.

A client still sending the old field has it dropped as an unknown field, and SQL Server falls back to `SHOWPLAN_ALL` — a text plan where the caller expected XML. The only in-tree caller is the SQL editor, which is updated here.

## Verification

- End to end against a running server and a real PostgreSQL instance: Explain in the SQL editor, Visualize, plan renders from the JSON the backend returned.
- 20 plan shapes from `SELECT 1` to a 27-node eight-join plan, including recursive CTEs, `INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT`, parallel plans, partitioned scans, `LATERAL` with Memoize, and `UPDATE`/`INSERT` plans. Node counts match PostgreSQL's own JSON in every case.
- Full gates green: `buf lint`, `gofmt`, `golangci-lint`, server build, and the frontend gate (biome, tsc, guards, release bundle, tests).
- The viewer was driven in a browser in light and dark at 1280px and 400px.

title: fix(plancheck): estimate affected rows correctly across engines
body:
## Summary

TiDB's `CountAffectedRows` always returned 0: it was copied from MySQL and looked for a `rows` column that TiDB's EXPLAIN does not have. That silently disabled `statement.affected_rows` approval rules on TiDB. Auditing every engine's estimate turned up the same class of problem elsewhere: the wrong plan node read, WHERE filters ignored, an engine that was never estimated, and failures that quietly counted as 0. This fixes them in one change.

## What changed

**Per engine**
- **TiDB:** reads `estRows` of the node below the DML root.
- **PostgreSQL:** uses `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` and sums the ModifyTable inputs, including data-modifying CTEs. The extractor now records INSERT … SELECT, MERGE, DEFAULT VALUES and CTE targets.
- **Redshift:** reads the first `rows=` estimate. The extractor counts VALUES rows from the AST, records TRUNCATE and MERGE targets, and replays a changed search path for the EXPLAIN, as PostgreSQL and CockroachDB do.
- **MySQL, MariaDB, OceanBase:**
  - Plans are read as JSON, with `explain_json_format_version` pinned to 1 for the EXPLAIN and reset afterwards.
  - The estimate follows the target table through joins, semi-joins, `insert_from` and set operations, including MySQL 8.0.31+ nested UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT plans.
  - When the JSON plan has no estimate to read, as MySQL 8.0 prints none for an INSERT … SELECT with window functions, the estimate of the first query block of `EXPLAIN FORMAT=TRADITIONAL` is used instead.
  - Single-table UPDATE and DELETE are explained as `SELECT 1 FROM <table> <WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT>`. For single-table DML, MySQL and MariaDB estimate the rows scanned, not the rows the filter keeps.
  - An INSERT whose SELECT reads no table, which MySQL's plan does not describe, counts at most one row per SELECT branch, combined by its UNION, INTERSECT, or EXCEPT.
- **Oracle:**
  - Runs EXPLAIN PLAN and reads PLAN_TABLE on one pinned connection.
  - Plans with `OPT_PARAM('optimizer_dynamic_sampling' 11)`.
  - A MERGE reads the rows below its MERGE operation, because the statement row is unreliable under sampling.
  - An INSERT ALL counts its rows once for each INTO target, as an upper bound for conditional inserts; an INSERT FIRST counts them once.
- **CockroachDB:** never had an estimate; the old `stats.go` was an unused copy of the PostgreSQL code.
  - New EXPLAIN tree reader. It handles limits and falls back when a delete-range plan has no estimate.
  - Foreign-key cascades are excluded, matching the `DELETE n` count CockroachDB reports.
  - Adds a changed-resources extractor and statement types.
  - COCKROACHDB joins `EngineSupportStatementReport`.
- **SQL Server:** no estimator change; more live test coverage.

**Statement report (`backend/runner/plancheck`)**
- DML statements are grouped by shape: the same text apart from literal values, spacing, and comments other than hints and executable comments. The existing 10-EXPLAIN limit is spread across shapes and extrapolated within each one,

title: fix(plancheck): classify OceanBase statements so sql_type approval rules match (BYT-10136)
body:
Fixes [BYT-10136](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10136). Same capability as [BYT-9621](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-9621).

## What was wrong

An OceanBase database-change plan produced a SQL summary report whose `StatementTypes` list was empty. The approval evaluator populates `statement.sql_type` only from that list, so the variable was absent from the CEL activation, cel-go resolved it to an unknown, and every rule naming `statement.sql_type` was dropped as a non-match in either polarity. `risk_level` derives from the same list, so it was always `LOW` for OceanBase. The parser fallback from #21245 does not apply: it fires only when a target has no report at all, and OceanBase has one.

## Root cause

Statement types worked for OceanBase until #13270 (2024-08-10). That refactor merged the per-engine report functions into one switch. OceanBase needed `EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON` for affected rows where MySQL used `EXPLAIN`, so the MySQL arm got an if/else on the explain calculator, and the classifier call landed in the MySQL-only branch. #13278 rewrote that placement as an explicit `engine != OCEANBASE` guard the next day. The calculator split has since moved into `mysql.Driver.CountAffectedRows`, so the guard outlived the only reason it was written for. No PR body, comment, or issue recorded a reason.

The executor kept its own per-engine table of six classifier calls beside `base.RegisterGetStatementTypes`, which is how OceanBase could be registered for classification (#19833) yet skipped in the report.

## What this changes

`GetSQLSummaryReport` resolves statement types through the parser registry via a new `plancheck.SummaryStatementTypes`. The engine switch keeps only what is genuinely per-engine: driver cast, explain calculator, default schema. Six classifier call sites, six parser imports, and the guard are gone. The report and the evaluator's parser fallback now share one classifier per engine.

Two deliberate side effects:

- TiDB and MSSQL logged a classifier error and continued with an empty list. Registered classifiers error on an AST-type mismatch, and TiDB's also when its lazy PingCAP re-parse fails; both already fail changed-resource extraction on the same report, so propagating the error changes no outcome and removes the log-and-continue branches.
- An engine with no registered classifier is an error, never an empty list, because an empty list is the silent state that hid this bug.

Unclassified MySQL-family statements (`SET SESSION` and the like) surface as `STATEMENT_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED`, so a DDL rule written as the negation of a DML list fails closed. OceanBase-only grammar that omni rejects (index `LOCAL`/`GLOBAL`, `TABLEGROUP`, `REPLICA_NUM` table options) fails at syntax check before the report runs, with or without this change; that is [BYT-10013](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10013).

## Behavior change on upgrade

Not breaking; same class as #21245. A workspace with a `statement.sql_type` rule and OceanB

title: test(plan): pin the thread walker to one editor scroll per step
body:
The walker had no coverage for what a step does to the editor's scroll position. Stepping onto a thread taller than the editor scrolled twice: the walker revealed the range start, then the thread's zone re-aligned the card two frames later, so the editor jumped and jumped back.

Coverage added:
- `MonacoViewZone` unit tests drive the reveal through Monaco's layout getters instead of DOM rectangles, and cover the cases the old tests could not: a zone outside the rendered viewport (Monaco parks its widget off screen), a range anchored above the card, a range taller than the viewport, sibling zones stacked on the same line, and content revealing a part of itself.
- `StatementThreadsLayer` tests assert one `setScrollTop` per walker step and per "View in Statement", and none when the target is already in view.
- A new E2E suite (CUJ N) records Monaco's per-render scroll offsets and asserts a single scroll per step, including the single-thread case. It is skipped with the other thread suites under the dev-build gate; it passed against a build with the gate forced on and failed against the previous behavior.
- Both fake editors share `src/test-utils/monacoLayout.ts`, and the editor scrolling helpers live in the plan-detail page object.

To make these pass, the view zone computes its reveal once, synchronously, from the editor layout, with a `revealFromLine` prop that keeps the anchored range above the card. The walker and thread-focus paths no longer scroll the editor themselves, and the zone's reveal is keyed on an explicit open nonce, as the composers already were.

Also: the walker strip no longer forces a height that clipped its buttons, and the shared editor defaults use an 8px vertical scrollbar.

title: chore(frontend): remove Vue migration leftovers, consolidate tests and checks
body:
## Why

The Vue→React migration is done, but the frontend still carried its scaffolding: guard tests that only block re-creating deleted code, comments narrating Vue origins, dead shim files and Vue/React-prefixed names. The guard tests were also the slowest files in the suite (two `import.meta.glob(?raw)` scans at 16–20s each). Tests and code checks were spread across three mechanisms (vitest files grepping source, `scripts/check-*.mjs`, Biome) with no rule for which goes where.

## What changed

**Migration leftovers**
- Deleted the migration guard tests (`src/architecture`, `components/header/no-vue-deps.test.ts`, the migration parts of the locale tests). Every legacy store and path they banned no longer exists, and tsc rejects imports of deleted modules.
- Comments that narrate the Vue origin (≈270 files) are removed or reworded; real constraints are kept.
- Removed dead code: `*Page.tsx` mount wrappers, `ProjectRouteShell`/`IssuesRouteShell`, mocks of removed Pinia stores, Naive UI selectors in the agent DOM tooling, unused `KEY`, `savedQueryList`, route `meta`, `utils/types.ts`.
- Renamed Vue/React-disambiguation names: `pushReactNotification` → `pushNotification`, `useSQLEditorReactStore` → `useSQLEditorStore`, `VueSearchParams` aliases dropped, `ReactAIContext` → `AIContextValue`, schema-diagram `composables/` → `hooks/`.

**Tests** (rules now in `frontend/AGENTS.md` → "Tests and checks")
- One test file per source file, named after it: suffixed (`Foo.i18n.test.ts`, `FooLayout.test.ts`), concept-named and `__tests__/` files were merged, split or renamed.
- Tests never read source files as text. The ~150 cases that only string-matched component source were deleted rather than rewritten.

**Checks**
- Import boundaries → Biome `noRestrictedImports`: Vue only in `src/apps/explain-visualizer`, shared code must not import `src/routes`.
- CEL filter literal escaping and the `crypto.randomUUID` ban → Biome GritQL plugins in `frontend/biome-plugins/`, so editors show them. The CEL rule matches whole template literals, so it also catches multi-line ones the line-based script missed.
- Locale rules consolidated into `scripts/check-i18n.mjs` (renamed from `check-react-i18n.mjs`): placeholder parity with en-US, SQL Review section layout, and the two linked-wording rules. This replaces per-component locale tests and the test-only `lib/i18n/messages.ts`. Three dead locale keys that only tests kept "used" are removed.
- `run-gate.mjs` runs every `scripts/check-*.mjs`; scripts use kebab-case names (`sort-i18n-keys.mjs`, `copy-config-files.sh`, …). `check-frontend-structure.mjs` is gone (its import rule moved to Biome, the rest guarded retired Vue-era directories).

## Reviewer notes

- **Test count 4454 → 3562.** 719 of the removed cases were `messages.test.ts` generating one test per SQL Review rule/locale pair; the same checks now run as one test in `types/sqlReview.test.ts` plus `check-i18n`. Most other removals are source-text assertions and migratio
