title: chore(ci): consolidate pull request checks into one workflow
body:
## What changed

Replaces the five real/stub workflow pairs (`backend-tests`, `frontend-tests`, `golangci-lint`, `proto-linter`, `test_link`, each with a `*-default` / `*_default` stub) with a single `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

- **`detect-changed-files`:** runs on a GitHub-hosted runner, diffs the PR merge commit against its base (`git diff --name-only HEAD^1 HEAD`), and outputs `go`, `frontend`, and `proto` flags. It also prints those flags to its log and the run summary.
- **`go-tests`, `golangci-lint`, `frontend-tests`, `lint-protos`:** keep their steps and run only when their flag is `'true'`.
- **Link test:** `go test ./scripts/...` is now the last step of `frontend-tests` instead of its own self-hosted job.
- **`all-checks-passed`:** needs every job above, runs with `if: always()`, and fails if any of them failed or was cancelled. Jobs skipped because their paths are untouched count as passing. It lists every job's result and adds an error annotation naming each job that did not pass.
- **Ruleset:** the `main` ruleset now requires only `all-checks-passed`. It previously required `go-tests`, `golangci-lint`, `frontend-tests`, and `lint-protos`. This was switched before merge.
- **Link fix:** bytebase.com moved `/terms` to `/legal/terms` (the old URL now 301-redirects), and its sitemap lists only the new path. That made link validation fail on this PR's first run, so the three Terms of Service links now point to `/legal/terms`.

## Why

A workflow skipped by `paths:` never reports its checks, so they stay pending forever. That is why each stub workflow existed. Gating at the job level and requiring one aggregate check removes the stubs and takes job layout out of the ruleset:

- **Fewer runs:** 1 workflow run per PR instead of 5, and no runner time on "Not required" stubs.
- **Fewer self-hosted jobs:** a PR touching backend and frontend schedules 3 jobs on the 2 shared self-hosted slots instead of 4.
- **No ruleset edits for CI changes:** adding, removing, or merging jobs means editing `needs` in `ci.yml`, and that gets reviewed like any other code change.
- **Path-filter bugs fixed:**
  - The `test_link_default.yml` stub job was named `go-tests`, so backend PRs carried two required `go-tests` checks. #21220 has one failing and one passing "Not required", and both are marked required.
  - Changing `.golangci.yaml` ran both the real lint and its stub.
  - A change to only `go.sum`, or to the backend files the frontend `prepare` script reads (`plan.yaml`, `permission.yaml`, `openapi.yaml`), triggered nothing.
  - Edits to `ci.yml` now run every job.

## Reviewer notes

- **Open PRs are blocked until they get the new check.** Until this merges, only this PR can produce `all-checks-passed`. After it merges, other open PRs need "Update branch" or a push to pick up `ci.yml`.
- **Fail-closed:**
  - If `detect-changed-files` fails, the gated jobs are skipped and `all-checks-passed` fails.
  - If a run is cancelled, `all-checks-passed` still runs be

title: perf(tests): direct database fixtures, read-first rollout waits, leaner webhook test
body:
Four changes to `backend/tests`, each measured on its own.

## 1. Test databases are created directly, not by rollout

Of 209 databases a run creates, 204 went through the full create-database plan → issue → rollout → task: **338 ms each**, against **58 ms** to create the database on the test Postgres, sync the instance and move it into the project. `createDatabase` does the latter now and leaves the database as the task did — schema synced, environment set when given, project opted into last-plan-editor approval. It finds the container from the instance's admin data source, so **no call sites change**.

`createDatabaseByRollout` keeps the old path for the gh-ost MySQL tests and for `TestDatabaseEnvironment`, which covers the workflow itself.

Two things surfaced and are fixed here:
- Tests that approve their own plans relied, unstated, on the old fixture opting the project into last-plan-editor approval. The direct fixture does the same, through one shared helper.
- A race the slow fixture hid: parallel subtests share an instance, and a sync that reads its `sync_databases` list before another subtest's update marks that subtest's database deleted. `registerDatabase` serializes the list update and sync per instance.

## 2. Rollout waits read before they wait

`waitRollout` ticked before its first read, twice — approval, then completion — so every caller paid 600 ms whatever the state already was. It now reads, acts, then waits at 100 ms. `createDatabase` went 0.92 s → 0.33 s before change 1 made it direct.

## 3. The completion predicate is tested where it lives

Ten webhook rollouts covered one predicate. `planTasksComplete` comes out of `checkPlanCompletion` with a table over task statuses, and `plan_webhook_delivery.go` — which had no test — gets one pinning the claim/reset state machine and the cross-project UID collision. Four end-to-end cases stay, one per trigger.

## 4. Webhook pipeline cases run in parallel

With no creation rollouts there are no creation `PIPELINE_COMPLETED` events to flush, so `createDatabasesFlushingCompletion` goes and the four pipeline cases run in parallel. Serial cases that assert on every collected request keep their resets.

## Measured

The command CI runs, `-count=1 -p=8`:

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `backend/tests` summed test time | 1179 s | **1051 s** |
| `TestWebhookIntegration` | 60.2 s | **13.4 s** |

Standalone `backend/tests`: 46–47 s over three runs. The whole run stays ~1 m 38 s — it is bound by the sum across all packages now, not by this one.

Gates: `gofmt`, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, full suite green, collision gate (`./backend/store/`, `^(TestClaim|TestCollision)`), and three consecutive clean `backend/tests` runs.

+package store_test
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"testing"
+
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/common/testcontainer"
+	storepb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/store"
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/store"
+)
+
+// TestPlanWebhookDeliveryClaims pins the state machine behind PIPELINE_COMPLETED
+// and PIPELINE_FAILED: one row per plan, so the first claim wins and the second
+// event of either kind stays silent until a retry resets the row.
+func TestPlanWebhookDeliveryClaims(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+	ctx := context.Background()
+	db, stores, _ := testcontainer.NewMetadataDB(t)
+	_, err := db.ExecContext(ctx, `
+		INSERT INTO workspace (resource_id) VALUES ('default');
+		INSERT INTO principal (name, email, password_hash) VALUES ('c', 'c@example.com', 'x');
+		INSERT INTO project (resource_id, workspace, name) VALUES ('p1', 'default', 'P1'), ('p2', 'default', 'P2');
+	`)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	newPlan := func(projectID string) int64 {
+		plan, err := stores.CreatePlan(ctx, &store.PlanMessage{
+			ProjectID: projectID, Name: "plan", Config: &storepb.PlanConfig{},
+		}, "c@example.com")
+		require.NoError(t, err)
+		return plan.UID
+	}
+	planA, planB := newPlan("p1"), newPlan("p2")
+
+	claimed, err := stores.ClaimPipelineCompletionNotification(ctx, "p1", planA)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.True(t, claimed, "the first completion claims the plan")
+
+	claimed, err = stores.ClaimPipelineCompletionNotification(ctx, "p1", planA)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.False(t, claimed, "a second completion for the same plan sends nothing")
+
+	// Both events share the row, so a completed plan cannot then report failure.
+	claimed, err = stores.ClaimPipelineFailureNotification(ctx, "p1", planA)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.False(t, claimed)
+
+	// A retry resets the row, which is what re-arms both events.
+	require.NoError(t, stores.ResetPlanWebhookDelivery(ctx, "p1", planA))
+	claimed, err = stores.ClaimPipelineFailureNotification(ctx, "p1", planA)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.True(t, claimed, "the reset re-arms the plan")
+
+	// Plan UIDs restart per project, so a neighbor's claim must not be read as
+	// this plan's.
+	require.Equal(t, planA, planB, "plan UIDs must collide across projects for this to prove anything")
+	claimed, err = stores.ClaimPipelineCompletionNotification(ctx, "p2", planB)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	require.True(t, claimed, "project p2 claims its own plan")
+
+	var rows int
+	require.NoError(t, db.QueryRowContext(ctx,
+		`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM plan_webhook_delivery WHERE project = $1 AND plan_id = $2 AND event_type = 'PIPELINE_FAILED'`,
+		"p1", planA).Scan(&rows))
+	require.Equal(t, 1, rows)
+}

title: perf(tests): share containers and servers across the backend suite
body:
## What

`go test ./backend/...` started **173 Postgres containers and 237 Bytebase servers** per run, nearly all of them rebuilding fixtures no test asserts on. This shares both.

**Containers** all start inside `backend/common/testcontainer` now and are shared per package. One `Container` type and two exported constructors replace six near-identical ones; MongoDB and TiDB join the shared accessors; the Oracle container, unused since #21356, is deleted along with every per-test `GetTest*Container`.

**Servers**: `backend/tests` takes project as the test boundary, which is Bytebase's own tenancy boundary. `startProject` gives a test a project on the package's one server; `startWorkspace` gives it a server of its own when it writes what the workspace shares — a setting, the license, the IAM policy, a workspace-scoped ID, the demo principal's credentials — or asserts on a workspace-wide list.

**Target Postgres** goes the same way, through `Instance.sync_databases`: the syncer imports only the databases an instance's list names, which is how Sample Project Instance already shares one target across workspaces. A test takes a database instead of a server; `createDatabase` keeps the list current. Seventeen provisions stay private — cluster-wide writes (roles), the two tests that need two servers for the same database name, and the one about two instances discovering the same physical `postgres` database.

## Numbers

Measured as a 2×2 rather than in sequence, standalone `backend/tests` on one box:

| | a container per test | one shared target |
|---|---:|---:|
| **a server per test** | 87.9 s | 77.4 s |
| **one shared server** | 76.0 s | **55.3 s** |

Each half is worth ~11 s alone, the pair 32.6 s — the cost is not the container or the boot but the parallel slot a test holds while waiting, so removing only one moves the queue to the other. Full CI command: **1 m 56 s → 1 m 40 s**, 173 containers → 31, 237 boots → 109.

## Two bugs found on the way

- **Nil `*sql.DB` panic on shutdown.** The plan check, task run and review run schedulers spawned per-job goroutines outside the WaitGroup `Server.Shutdown` waits on, so the store closed under them and the process died with a SIGSEGV that surfaced as an unrelated test failing. Each scheduler now waits for its own jobs, and `DBConnectionManager` keeps the handle after `Close` — closed, not nil — so a late caller gets an error; `GetDB` also reads under the mutex it was already racing with `Close` and the PG-URL watcher.
- **`TestCollision_PlanDraftMetadataSync`** snapshotted project B while its own plan check run was still RUNNING and read the advance as a cross-project write. It now uses the `waitPlanCheckRunSettled` helper the package already had for exactly that.

## Also

- CI runs `./action/...`: 48 tests in 4 packages that no workflow ran, while a PR touching only `action/**` ran the whole backend suite. They add 0.15 s.
- One server for twenty parallel tests needs a raised `max_connections`; at the de

## Summary

- Delete `advisor_statement_dml_dry_run_testcontainer_test.go`, the only test in `backend/plugin/advisor/tidb` that needed Docker.
- Add a fake `database/sql` driver test that pins the SQL the advisor sends: plain DML is `EXPLAIN`ed in a transaction, `BATCH` DML dry-runs in autocommit and then `EXPLAIN`s the inner DML, and a failure on either step yields `StatementDMLDryRunFailed` advice. TiDB's own acceptance of the `BATCH ... DRY RUN` grammar is dialect behavior and is no longer exercised here.

## Verification

- `go test ./backend/plugin/advisor/tidb/` passes in about 2s.
- `golangci-lint run` at repo root: 0 issues.

title: test: drop testing.Short() guards and run every test in CI
body:
## What changed

- Removed the five `testing.Short()` guards in the repo: the TiDB dry-run container test, the three MongoDB container tests, and the short-mode branch of `skipUnlessLiveOracle` in the MySQL SDL tests.
- `TestGetListPlanFilter` skipped its creator case as "requires database connection", but `GetListPlanFilter` is a pure function. The case now asserts the generated SQL and args, and the `skipTest` field and skip branch are gone.
- Added one sentence to the root `AGENTS.md` test-placement section: every test runs in CI, so do not check `testing.Short()` or skip a test to park a known gap.

## Why

CI runs `go test ./backend/...` with no `-short`, so none of these guards ever fired there. They only hid the container tests from a local `go test -short`, and they suggested a two-tier test policy we do not have. The `AGENTS.md` line makes the actual policy explicit for future contributors and agents.

## Reviewer notes

- The `MYSQL_SDL_LIVE_ORACLE` gate on the MySQL live-oracle suites stays. Those suites need local MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 servers CI does not have, and the schema package's `AGENTS.md` already says that kind of engine conformance belongs in omni.
- The one remaining skipped table case, "Sequence with ownership" in the PostgreSQL definition test, is left in place on purpose. Un-skipping it fails because the generator renders a column-owned non-serial sequence as a bare `bigserial`, dropping its START, INCREMENT, MINVALUE and CACHE settings. That is a generator gap for a separate PR.

## Verification

- `go test` for `backend/plugin/db/mongodb`, `backend/plugin/advisor/tidb`, and `backend/plugin/schema/mysql`, including the container tests that the removed guards used to skip.
- Full `backend/store` suite and the `TestClaim|TestCollision` suite in `backend/tests`, per the pre-PR checklist.
- gofmt, golangci-lint with `--fix` and then clean without it, and the server build.

title: refactor: load every engine's catalog with omni's LoadMetadata
body:
Every engine built its own catalog from a schema snapshot — PostgreSQL twice, once for query span and once for the SQL review walk-through, written a day apart and patched in parallel since. Each engine's loader now lives in omni next to the catalog it fills, and Bytebase calls it: bytebase/omni#414 (PostgreSQL), #416 (MySQL), #417 (TiDB, Trino, MongoDB, PartiQL), #418 and #420 (Redshift), #419 (MySQL view columns).

This removes about 10,400 lines of loader and loader-test code.

## Changes

- **PostgreSQL** (`parser/pg`, `schema/pg`): `initCatalog` calls `LoadMetadata` and logs the degraded and missing counts at debug level; the walk-through loads with `LoadMetadataOptions{Full: true}`. Deleted `walk_through_loader.go` and `query_span_loader*.go` with their proof-of-concept and integration tests. `query_span_loader_classify.go` is now `query_span_classify.go` with its own test; the integration tests that still apply moved into `query_span_test.go`, `walk_through_test.go`, and `walk_through_apply_test.go`.
- **SQL review for MySQL, MariaDB, and OceanBase** (`schema/mysql`): the walk-through loads its catalog with `LoadMetadata`; `walk_through_loader.go` is removed.
- **TiDB completion:** `LoadMetadata` replaces the DDL text the completer rendered and ran.
- **Trino completion and query span, MongoDB completion, PartiQL completion:** `LoadMetadata` replaces each package's own loader.
- **Redshift:** completion uses `LoadMetadata`; query span uses `UseMetadata`, which replaces the lazy relation resolver, the view-definition qualification, and the function install.
- Bumps omni from 71713ba to 4574e69.

## Behavior changes

All of these come from omni's loaders.

**PostgreSQL**

- **Masking now applies to reads through a partition.** Neither loader installed partitions, so `SELECT ssn FROM orders_2024`, which names a partition directly, got no lineage for `ssn` and masking had nothing to apply to. omni loads partitions, lineage names the partition, and the masker already resolves a partition to its parent table's columns.
- **Query span sees reads in nested lists (BYT-10076).** omni's AST walker now descends into a list inside a list, so query span sees a subquery inside a `FROM`-clause function's arguments or inside a `VALUES` row. The two cases that recorded this gap move to the shapes that must raise the unresolved-columns signal.
- **The walk-through is more faithful:** enum stand-ins, so a broken enum no longer degrades every table that uses it; partitions with their own indexes and constraints; identity sequences with their name and settings; owned serial sequences, so `DROP TABLE t; CREATE TABLE t (id serial)` no longer fails on a leftover sequence. The full list is in bytebase/omni#414.
- **Loading is faster.** For 2,000 tables and 200 views, query span's load drops from 312 ms to 24 ms and the walk-through's (`Full`) from 635 ms to 39 ms. Query span loads a catalog on every query, so every query against a large schema gets this.

title: docs(design): unfold and copy a statement in the task-run log
body:
Design doc for the task-run log viewer: `docs/design/task-run-log-statement-unfold.md`.

The log cuts every executed statement to 80 characters and appends `...`, and it does it inside the model — so by the time a row renders, the statement is no longer in the component tree and nothing downstream can offer to show or copy the rest. For the statements customers actually run (SDL, or a `CREATE TABLE` with a few hundred columns) the row says almost nothing. A failed command is worse: an early return hands back `response.error` before the statement is ever read, so the row that a reader opened the log for shows the driver's complaint and no hint of which SQL produced it — and the error text never names it, because every driver logs a bare `err.Error()`. #21276 finds the truncation and removes it, which is the right diagnosis and a partial fix: the `\s+ → " "` normalization above it stays, so the statement becomes one run-on line, it floods a 200px scroll box, copy is still absent, and the failed row is untouched. The doc lands on one rule: **a row shows one line, and nothing the row is about is destroyed to produce that line.** Frontend-only, inherited by the four surfaces that embed the viewer.

### What the doc decides

- A command row has up to two payloads, and the entry already carries both — the converter hangs `response` on the same entry that holds `Range`/`Statement`. `DisplayItem` gains `statement` and `error` beside `detail`, both verbatim, plus `defaultOpen` — the row the auto-open rule picked. The view cannot derive that one: it sees a section at a time while the pick is made across a whole execution context, and `error` is no substitute, since every transient failed attempt carries one.
- The line is the news: the error when the command failed, the statement when it did not. No length constant survives in the model — the line is clamped by `truncate`, so a wide screen shows more and a narrow sheet shows less, and an error line still wraps whole as it does today.
- Unfolding always reveals the statement, and so does copy — and copy sits beside it, in the row's cluster while the statement is the line and in the unfolded block's corner once it is a block, so position and behavior agree. The error carries no copy button: reaching for an error message in the clipboard is rare next to reaching for the SQL, and it stays selectable text. A row with no recoverable statement gets no copy button rather than one that means something else.
- What unfolds by default says what the row is for. A successful statement starts folded — the reader is scanning. A failed one starts open, with the error as its line and the statement beneath it — but only the failure that explains the outcome: a lock timeout makes the Postgres driver retry the whole command list and re-log every command, so the viewer opens the last failed row and only when nothing after it succeeded — judged across one replica or release file's whole entry sequence rather than within a sectio

title: docs(design): fold retried attempts into one row in the task run log
body: Design doc for the task run log viewer: `docs/design/task-run-log-previous-attempts.md`. Closes BYT-9993. A statement that hits a lock timeout is retried by the driver **inside the same task run**, bounded by the project's Execution retry policy. Every attempt appends to one `task_run_log` stream, separated by a `RETRY_INFO` marker, and the viewer renders any section holding an error as red and auto-expanded. So a run that failed once and passed on the retry keeps a red failure section at the top of an otherwise green, DONE run, `RETRY_INFO` shows up as a green "Retry" section, and three interleaved Transaction rows have nothing marking where one attempt ends and the next begins. The customer's read was that the UI is correct, but the step should not stay red once it passed. This doc lands on one rule: **only the final attempt's failure is state.** An attempt followed by a `RETRY_INFO` marker is superseded — its failure is the reason the retry ran — so it renders as history: gray, collapsed, never auto-expanded, one click from the untouched record. Task-level re-run is not involved and does not change: re-running a FAILED or CANCELED task already creates a new `task_run` row, and `task_run_log` is keyed by `(project, task_run_id)`, so entries never cross runs. The change is frontend-only. ### What the doc decides - All superseded attempts fold into **one** "Previous attempts" row; the final attempt's sections stay flat at top level, in every run state. - The umbrella's note is the **attempt count**, not a failure reason — one reason cannot summarize several attempts. Per-attempt reasons sit on the nested rows. There is no separate run-level retry chip: the umbrella is always visible and already carries the count. - **Gray, and no fill color.** Amber is still a warning hue, and history should not catch the eye. Red survives only on the error entries inside the expanded record — nothing is rewritten. - **Only the retried call is attempt material.** Prior backup and schema sync run once, around `driver.Execute`, so they stay at top level; the doc carries an inventory classifying every entry type by where the executor emits it. A versioned release executes each file separately, so each file that retries gets its own umbrella. - **Colors come from the entries, never from run status.** The two are independent in both directions: a DONE run can hold a red failed schema sync, and a FAILED run can hold an all-green log. - **Expansion clears when a marker regroups the list.** Section ids are positional, so a regrouping would otherwise open an unrelated section. The marker count joins the `datasetKey` the viewer already passes, so the existing reset fires on a marker and never on an ordinary append. - A previous **run** is not a previous **attempt**. title: chore(plan): gate inline comment threads to dev builds
body:
## What

Hides the plan-detail inline comment threads behind `isDev()`, so the feature is available on the Vite dev server and absent from every built bundle.

One gate, `inlineThreadsEnabled()` in `src/utils/featureGates.ts`, read at four sites:

| Site | Effect when off |
|---|---|
| `PlanDetailStatementSection` | no Monaco gutter markers, highlights, or composer |
| `ReviewActivityTimeline` | a thread root renders as an ordinary comment |
| `useUnresolvedThreadCounts` | change-tab and Review-summary counts are zero, so the badges hide |
| `fetchIssueCommentThreads` | the reply pass is skipped |

## Why

The feature has 180 unit tests and no executed browser coverage. There is no e2e workflow in `.github/workflows` at all, and `vitest.config.ts` excludes `tests/e2e/**`, so the 26 journeys in `plan-detail-review.spec.ts` have only ever run locally. #21386 also records the riskiest path as unverified: re-placing a comment onto a newer revision, against a saved sheet.

Rather than ship that to customers while it settles, engineers keep it on the dev server and everyone else does not see it.

## The store split

This is the one non-mechanical part. `useIssueCommentThreadsSync` is the *only* issue-comment fetch on the plan page — it lists the whole timeline, then pages replies for the roots it found. Gating the hook wholesale would blank the plain Review Activity feed along with the threads.

So the timeline load stays unconditional and only the `root in [...]` reply pass is gated. A thread root still reaches the reader when the gate is off; it just renders as a plain comment.

## What this does and does not do

`import.meta.env.DEV` is statically replaced at build time — verified zero literal occurrences in the release bundle — so the gate reliably evaluates `false` and the feature is unreachable.

It is **not** dead-code-eliminated. `bb-thread-card--flash` from `ThreadStack.tsx` is still present in the built output: the gate is a cross-module call feeding a runtime expression, and the thread components are statically imported, so tree-shaking cannot drop them. This is a runtime hide, not a strip. Taking the code out of the bundle would need lazy imports and is deliberately left out of scope.

## Tests

Vitest reports `DEV: true`, so every existing suite keeps exercising the feature exactly as an engineer on the dev server sees it — no coverage is lost. That left the release path untested, so three cases pin it:

- `featureGates.test.ts` — the gate tracks the build flag in both directions.
- `issueComment.test.ts` — with the gate off, one timeline call and no `root in [...]` follow-up; thread roots still reach the cache.
- `ReviewActivityTimeline.test.tsx` — with the gate off, an anchored root renders as a comment row and no thread card.

Four thread describes in `plan-detail-review.spec.ts` are `test.describe.skip`ped in place, not moved: the e2e harness builds without the `release` tag but still serves a `vite build`, so the thread UI is absent t

title: refactor: move the schema metadata proto to omni
body:
`DatabaseSchemaMetadata` and the 35 messages under it moved to omni in bytebase/omni#412. This PR removes them from the store proto and switches bytebase to the omni types. It's the first step toward omni owning the schema snapshot and the conversions between it and omni's catalogs: the walk-through and query-span loaders, `applyDiffToMetadata`, `catalogToProto`, and the completion builders.

## What changed

- **Store proto:** `proto/store/store/database.proto` drops the 36 messages. It keeps `DatabaseMetadata`, `DatabaseConfig` with its catalog messages, and `InstanceRoleMetadata`. Regenerating only touched the store `database` outputs and their docs.
- **Go code:** 188 files now import `metadatapb "github.com/bytebase/omni/metadata"` in place of the `storepb` types. The edit was scripted and only swaps type references and imports; no logic changed.
- **omni bump:** omni moves from `044f516` to `71713ba`. That also brings in bytebase/omni#407 (tests only), bytebase/omni#409 (MSSQL splitting) and bytebase/omni#410 (MySQL Aurora `LOAD DATA FROM S3`).
- **Docs:** ADR-0001 points at the proto's new location, and the SDL guide's snippets use the new type names.

## Compatibility

- **Stored snapshots:** `db_schema.metadata` and `sync_history.metadata` store these messages as protojson, which carries no package name. Field names, numbers, and enum value names are identical: comparing the compiled descriptors found 0 differences across 36 messages and 272 fields. Stored snapshots read back unchanged, with no migration.
- **API:** unchanged. The v1 `DatabaseMetadata` is a separate message.
- **BSR:** the `buf.build/bytebase/store` module no longer has these messages. It's internal, so this isn't labeled breaking.
- **Future changes:** omni's CI rejects renamed fields and enum values (bytebase/omni#413). The frozen-shape rule from ADR-0001 is now enforced there.

## Testing

- `go build` of the server
- `golangci-lint run` — 0 issues, no autofix edits
- `buf format`, `buf lint`, `buf generate` — only the store `database` outputs changed
- `go test -count=1` for `backend/plugin/schema/...`, `backend/store/model/...`, `backend/plugin/parser/...`, `backend/plugin/advisor/...`, `backend/store`, `backend/runner/schemasync`, `backend/api/v1`, and `backend/tests`
  - `TestCollision_PlanDraftMetadataSync` failed once while the other suites ran in parallel. It passed 3 of 3 runs alone, and the full `backend/tests` suite then passed.
  - Cause: the test snapshots project B before B's own plan check finishes. That's a race in the test, unrelated to this change, and it's tracked separately.
- Not run: the per-engine sync tests in `backend/plugin/db/*` (MySQL, Oracle and MSSQL containers). Their packages type-check, and PostgreSQL sync runs end to end in `backend/tests`.

title: chore(infra): restart the devbox from Cloud Scheduler, not a GitHub cron
body:
## Summary

A Cloud Scheduler job, `devbox-start`, now restarts the devbox after a Spot preemption, replacing `.github/workflows/start-runner-vm.yml`. Every minute it calls the Compute API's `instances.start` as the Compute Engine default service account; on a running instance that is a no-op.

- Delete `.github/workflows/start-runner-vm.yml`.
- `scripts/devbox/create.sh`: enable Cloud Scheduler and create the job, in `northamerica-northeast1` since Cloud Scheduler has no Toronto region.
- `docs/design/devbox-and-ci-runner.md` and a comment in `scripts/devbox/startup.sh`: describe the job instead of the workflow.

## Why

GitHub runs scheduled workflows best effort. From 2026-09-03 to 2026-09-11 the `*/15` workflow fired 630 of about 735 slots, a median of 6 minutes late, and each night around 00:00 UTC its runs were up to 49 minutes apart. Of 11 preemptions it restarted 6, a median of 9 minutes later; people restarted the other 5 by hand. GCE's own instance schedules allow at most one start an hour, each up to 15 minutes late.

The job costs nothing: Cloud Scheduler bills per job, not per run, and includes three free jobs per billing account.

## Rollout

The job is already live, so this can merge any time. Since 2026-09-11 07:54 UTC every attempt after the first has returned 200 (the first got a 403 while permissions propagated), and each shows in the audit log as a no-op start. Until this merges, the workflow keeps running alongside it, which is harmless.

## Test plan

- [x] `bash -n` on `create.sh` and `startup.sh`
- [x] `devbox-start` attempts return 200, and the audit log shows its no-op starts
- [ ] After the next preemption, `lastStartTimestamp` lands within about two minutes of `lastStopTimestamp`

@@ -54,3 +54,11 @@ gcloud compute instances create devbox --project=$PROJECT --zone=$ZONE \

body:
Replace the instance form’s “Connection security” and “SSH Connection” labels with “TLS” and “SSH tunnel” across all five locales. Align the TLS help title and shared toggle label, while preserving existing connection behavior.

Includes a source-backed comparison of database-client terminology supporting the wording choice.

--- docs/research/2026-09-11-instance-connection-labels.md (+26/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,26 @@
+# Instance connection labels
+
+Research checked 2026-09-11. Recommendation is editorial judgment, not a claim of a universal industry convention.
+
+## Independent reviews
+
+Three independent reviewers researched DBeaver/DataGrip, TablePlus/pgAdmin, and MySQL Workbench/MongoDB Compass. All recommended TLS and SSH tunnel for Bytebase's section labels.
+
+## Verified first-party labels
+
+- DBeaver documents **SSL** and **SSH** configuration tabs. [SSL configuration](https://dbeaver.com/docs/dbeaver/SSL-Configuration/), [SSH configuration](https://dbeaver.com/docs/dbeaver/SSH-Configuration/)
+- DataGrip uses an **SSH/SSL** tab with **Use SSL** and **Use SSH tunnel** controls. [DataGrip documentation](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/datagrip/configuring-ssh-and-ssl.html)
+- pgAdmin documents an **SSL mode** field, **SSH Tunnel** tab, and **Use SSH tunneling** toggle. [pgAdmin server dialog](https://www.pgadmin.org/docs/pgadmin4/9.17/server_dialog.html)
+- TablePlus documents **SSH Tunneling** and describes its `tLSMode` connection parameter as **TLS mode**; these are documentation terms, not verified current form labels. [TablePlus connection documentation](https://docs.tableplus.com/gui-tools/manage-connections)
+- MySQL Workbench names its encryption tab **SSL** and its selector **Use SSL**. Its documented values include No, If available, Require, and certificate-verification variants. The short protocol name labels the section while the control indicates behavior. [MySQL Workbench manual](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/workbench/en/wb-mysql-connections-methods-standard.html)
+- Workbench calls the SSH connection method **Standard TCP/IP over SSH**. The SSH method still has its own SSL tab: the features compose rather than being alternatives. [MySQL Workbench SSH manual](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/workbench/en/wb-mysql-connections-methods-ssh.html)
+- MongoDB Compass documentation explicitly instructs users to select the **TLS / SSL** tab. It documents Default, On, and Off values. The page title is “TLS / SSL Connection Tab,” but the actual tab label omits “Connection.” [Compass TLS documentation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/compass/connect/advanced-connection-options/tls-ssl-connection/)
+- Compass explicitly names its other tab **Proxy / SSH Tunnel**. It documents SSH with Password and SSH with Identity File as options, and supports using SSH tunnels together with TLS. [Compass SSH documentation](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/compass/connect/advanced-connection-options/ssh-connection/)
+
+## Application to Bytebase
+
+Use **TLS** for the visible section and help title, **TLS mode** as the selector accessible label, and **SSH tunnel** for the SSH section, selector accessible label, and help title. Keep TLS choices Disabled / TLS / Mutual TLS and SSH choices Disabled / Enabled.
+
+“TLS options” adds a generic noun already conveyed by the form. “TLS connection” repeats connection context. “TLS mode” is appropriate for the selector but unnecessarily narrows the heading above certificate and identity fields. “SSH tunnel” adds meaningful specificity over bare SSH: it names the network route to the database. “SSH connection” is less specific about the route. Equal word counts are not needed for sibling sections when the extra word conveys a useful distinction.
+
+This is a small label change; no behavioral or layout changes are needed. Existing help text and link labels should be checked so opening help does not switch back to a different section name.

body: Instance forms currently allow predictable validation failures to reach the backend or disable actions without explaining which field needs attention. Add shared validation for Create, Update, and Test Connection, with localized inline errors on blur that clear as values are corrected. - Validate TLS paths, PEM structure and certificate/key pairs; SaaS IAM credentials; Azure Key Vault fields; and disallowed MySQL connection parameters. - Apply resource-ID and label checks consistently for BigQuery and Spanner creation, and require valid labels and a nonempty title on edit. - Preserve unchanged stored credentials and TLS material when editing other fields. Keep inactive password-source drafts out of validation and IAM requests while preserving them in the form. Full certificate parsing, key matching, and trust verification remain server-side. - Associate field errors with inputs and textareas and add their shared invalid border state. Validation: `pnpm --dir frontend fix` and `pnpm --dir frontend test` passed, including lint, UI/i18n guards, type-checking, production build, and all 4,415 tests across 523 files. title: feat(mcp): show what an access policy mode allows
body:
Implements the design merged in #21397: the MCP Access policy page says what each mode
*allows*, as an ordered list of capability rows of which every mode is a prefix, instead of
three prose descriptions that named no capability.

Pure UI. No API, no schema, no permission logic — the ceiling the gate enforces is unchanged.
The one non-frontend change is a comment on `MCPMethodClass` in `annotation.proto` (and its
generated artifacts), recording that READ/WRITE is disclosed to admins and not only enforced.

## What a user sees

**Workspace → Integration → MCP → Access policy**
- Three icon cards (Disabled / Read-only / Read-write) replace the prose blocks, each with a
  one-line caption and a "Best for" line.
- A collapsible list of 8 capability rows — 3 read, 5 write — shown under every mode, with the
  rows a mode does not serve muted, so an admin can compare two ceilings without leaving the
  page. "Read-only stops here" / "Read-write stops here" dividers mark each prefix. Open state
  and the "Show details" state persist per browser.
- A floor line: what no mode ever allows.
- The edit state renders exactly what the view will show after saving.

**OAuth consent screen**
- "This session may" lists the served row titles — the same strings the admin chose the policy
  by — with one ✕ line for the unserved tier under Read-only, then the bound, masking and audit
  lines. Read-write keeps its caution.
- The three consent panels (ceiling / disabled / undisclosable) now share one card component.

**MCP page**: the "Authentication Required" alert is gone; its one load-bearing clause moved
into the Connect a client description.

## Behavior changes

- **The masking toggle is withheld while Disabled is picked.** It governs what an MCP session
  may unmask, and Disabled admits no session, so a live toggle under "no session can connect"
  would assert two things that cannot both hold. The draft behind it is kept and saved anyway —
  clicking through the modes to read their descriptions must not silently undo an unrelated
  edit — and the footer names the value Save will write, since the control that made it is off
  screen.
- **A save re-reads the policy before closing the editor.** `refreshServerInfo` throws without
  clearing what it holds, so closing first would present the pre-save policy as current.

Neither changes what can be stored or what the API accepts.

## The part worth reviewing closely

Every line on this card must be true under every mode **and** against every engine a workspace
happens to hold, and the card cannot enumerate either. Eight review rounds produced five axes a
claim can be false on, all recorded in `docs/design/mcp-capability-ladder.md`:

| Axis | The failure it catches |
|---|---|
| Mode | the read-only clamp holds only under Read-only |
| Engine | per-engine depth varies; an enumeration goes stale, a universal is false |
| Effect | a refusal is about what a session can *cause* — `CreateIssue`'s webhook posts issue text outwar

title: test(schema): drop testcontainer from the schema plugin
body:
## What

Removes every database container from `backend/plugin/schema`. All five engine packages (pg, mysql, tidb, mssql, oracle) now run entirely in-process against recorded YAML goldens.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| container-backed tests | 14 | 0 |
| images started | postgres:16, mysql:8.0.33, pingcap/tidb:v8.5.0, mssql:2022, oracle-free | none |
| Go test code | — | −12k lines |
| oracle package runtime | container start + tests | 0.05s |

## Why

These tests asserted that generated DDL, applied to a real server and synced back, matched the metadata it came from. That is engine conformance, and it belongs in omni, which runs its own container oracles.

These packages own three conversions — schema text → metadata, metadata → DDL, and a metadata pair → migration DDL. Each test now covers exactly one of them.

## Scope: structural only

This is a test change. **The production code is byte-identical to `main`, with one exception**, and the goldens describe the packages as they behave today.

Recording the fixtures surfaced a number of real defects, and an earlier revision of this branch fixed them. That mixed a behavior change into a test change, so the fixes were reverted and every fixture re-recorded against untouched code. They are listed below so they are not lost, and each is a follow-up.

The exception is the drop path in mysql's `generateMigration`, which walked Go maps and so emitted its statements in a different order on every run. Nothing can be pinned to a byte until it is stable, so those maps are now walked in name order (`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(...))`, 19 lines in `generate_migration.go`). The reordered statements are drops of independent objects within one table, so the DDL's meaning is unchanged. Without this, seven of the 36 mysql migration cases could not have a golden at all.

## Defects the goldens now record

Reachable from production, not test-only. All are recorded as-is, not fixed.

**TiDB parser** (`get_database_metadata.go`) silently drops:

- bare `AUTO_RANDOM(n)` (the `/*T![auto_rand] */` form works)
- `CLUSTERED` / `NONCLUSTERED` → `primary_key_type` never set, so the two render identically
- per-column `CHARACTER SET` / `COLLATE` → a column silently inherits the table default
- `CHECK` constraints, entirely — a diff never sees one added or removed
- `DEFAULT true` on `BOOLEAN`
- column `COMMENT` — table comments survive, column comments do not (mysql's extractor keeps both)

**MySQL and TiDB** emit comments containing an apostrophe unescaped: `COMMENT='It's a table'` is DDL the server rejects. One tidb migration case generates exactly this, so its golden holds invalid SQL; `generate_migration_test.go` names it in `knownInvalidOutput` and skips only that case's re-parse assertion.

**MySQL generator** emits `SET character_set_client = ;` for an empty charset, which is invalid. A guarded helper already exists; two of three call sites do not use it. `CREATE FUNCTION` is also written without the `DELIMITER ;;`

+# Bytebase schema plugin
+
+Additional guidance for `./backend/plugin/schema/`, the per-engine conversions
+between database metadata and DDL. Follow `../../../AGENTS.md` first; this file
+adds to it.
+
+## What these packages test
+
+Each engine package owns three conversions, and a test covers exactly one:
+
+- `GetDatabaseMetadata` — schema text to metadata.
+- `GetDatabaseDefinition` — metadata to DDL.
+- `schema.GetDatabaseSchemaDiff` plus the package's `generateMigration`.
+
+Do not call `driver.SyncDBSchema` here, and never use a live server's answer as
+the expected value: whether our output matches what an engine stores is engine
+conformance, and it belongs in omni. No test in these packages starts a
+container.
+
+A metadata-to-DDL test takes metadata as its input, not a schema text. Deriving
+it by parsing caps the test at whatever the parser extracts, so any generator
+branch nothing feeds goes untested.
+
+## The record process
+
+Fixtures live in `testdata/` as a YAML list of cases, one file per test, named
+after the source file it covers. Each test carries the path and a `record`
+constant:
+
+```go
+const (
+	record   = false
+	filepath = "testdata/get_database_definition.yaml"
+)
+```
+
+To regenerate, set `record` to `true`, run that one test, and set it back:
+
+```bash
+go test ./backend/plugin/schema/tidb/ -run '^TestGetDatabaseDefinition$' -count=1
+```
+
+- Commit the fixture and the restored `record = false` together. A `record = true`
+  left in the tree overwrites the goldens on every run, so the test always passes.
+- Read the fixture diff. A re-record captures current behavior, bugs included.
+- Recording only rewrites the output field. Changing a fixture's input means
+  editing the metadata blob, or re-seeding it.
+
+## Fixture gotchas
+
+- YAML block scalars cannot carry tabs, trailing whitespace, or a leading
+  newline. A value with any of them is stored as one unreadable quoted line.
+  Indent fixture SQL with spaces; trim a leading newline before comparing, as
+  the PostgreSQL definition test does. Trailing whitespace usually arrives from
+  a `definition`/`body` field, not the generator — strip it in the fixture.
+- yaml.v3 escapes astral-plane characters, so a golden containing an emoji is
+  always a quoted line. Two are, deliberately: they cover 4-byte UTF-8.
+- Generated DDL must be byte-stable before it can be pinned. Walk maps in sorted
+  key order in the generators.
+
+## Two deviations
+
+Oracle's migration inputs are `oldMetadata`/`newMetadata`, protojson captured
+from a real Oracle, where every other engine's are `oldSchema`/`newSchema`
+schema text. Converting them would rewrite all 34 cases: a metadata/DDL/metadata
+round trip is lossless for 0 of its 68 blobs.
+
+PostgreSQL registers neither `GenerateMigration` nor `GetDatabaseMetadata`, so it
+has no fixture for either. Its migration generation is covered by
+`metadata_migration_test.go`, whose hand-written assertions carry intent a golden
+cannot. Do not convert those.

title: refactor(plugin): drop the vestigial _omni suffix
body:
## Why

The `_omni` suffix was migration scaffolding. Each engine migration added `X_omni.go` beside the ANTLR-based `X.go`, then a later commit deleted the legacy file without renaming what was left. For mssql, [#20215](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/pull/20215) added the file and [#20547](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/pull/20547) removed the thing it was being distinguished from.

That migration is finished. `github.com/bytebase/parser` is gone from `go.mod` and no parser package imports ANTLR, so outside of TiDB the suffix distinguishes nothing.

## What changed

- **29 files renamed, 10 merged** into the counterpart they were split from. The "pairs" turned out to be a *layer* split — shared state struct and entry point in one file, AST walking in the other — not old-vs-new, so each pair collapses into one file.
- **Three pass-through wrappers collapsed.** They existed only to bridge the two names.
- **Exported surface loses `Omni`:** `ParseTSQL`, `ParseMySQL`, `ParsePLSQL`, `ParseRedshift`, `ParseMariaDB`, `RunRules`, `GetDatabaseMetadata`, `WalkThroughWithContext`.
- Stale comments pointing at deleted files fixed, plus ~18 test names that referenced renamed symbols.

No behavior change — every edit is a rename, a file merge, or a comment.

## For reviewers

**`ParseTiDBOmni` deliberately keeps its name.** TiDB is the one engine still running two parsers: [`dispatcher.go`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/backend/plugin/parser/tidb/dispatcher.go) tries omni and falls back to the pingcap parser, counting fallbacks in `tidbDispatcherOmniFallbackTotal`. There the suffix is load-bearing.

**One test was genuinely broken by the rename, not just stale.** `TestRedshiftQuerySpanEntrypointDoesNotDependOnANTLR` reads its inputs *by filename* at runtime and asserted `ParseRedshift(` was absent from them. The rename both moved the files it reads and made `ParseRedshift` the omni entry point that file is now required to use — so the assertion inverted into a guaranteed failure. Paths updated, inverted assertion removed; the two import assertions it still makes are guaranteed by `go.mod` anyway.

The four large merged extractors (tsql 2,009 lines, pg 1,825, plsql 1,814, mysql 1,826) are concatenations, not rewrites. Each merge was verified line-by-line against the pre-merge file; the only lines that differ are two comment rewrites where the old text referenced ANTLR code that no longer exists.

`docs/plans/*.md` keep their historical file-path references — those are dated migration plans and rewriting them would falsify the record. Only symbol names were updated there, per the checklist's doc-drift step.

## Still says Omni (intentional)

443 identifiers: 155 test functions, 89 `*OmniRule` types, 279 unexported helpers. The only exported non-rule names left are `ParseTiDBOmni` (live) and `GetOmniNode` (names which library's AST it extracts, and `base.AST` has several implementations).

## Verification

title: test(common): drop duplicated doc comments in the relocated UTF-8 tests
body:
Follow-up to #21410, which merged before this fix could be pushed.

Moving the sanitization assertions out of the Oracle driver package left three doc comments written twice, back to back: `countInvalidStringFields`, `TestSanitizeUTF8MessageCoversEveryStringField` and `TestSanitizeUTF8MessageNameFields`. The extraction ran each block up to the next top-level `func`, so it carried the following declaration's comment along as its tail and the next block repeated it.

Caught by Codex on #21410 ([P3](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/pull/21410#discussion_r3977036215)); the fix landed after the squash merge, so it needs its own PR.

Rather than patch the three reported sites, I scanned every `.go` file in the original diff for comment blocks repeated verbatim across only blank lines. That found exactly three, all in this file. Re-scan reports 0; each declaration now has one comment. `go test ./backend/common/` passes, lint clean.

title: refactor(tests): pair every plugin test file with its source file
body:
## What

Test files under `backend/plugin/db` and `backend/plugin/schema` had drifted into suffixed variants (`_testcontainer_test.go`, `_integration_test.go`, `_live_test.go`, `_fixture_test.go`) and topic splits (`sync_column_test.go`, `sync_foreign_table_test.go`), so the tests for one source file lived in up to eleven places. This restores `xxx.go` ↔ `xxx_test.go`, one to one, with `TestMain` in `main_test.go` and shared scaffolding in `testutil_test.go`.

Two commits, deliberately separable — see **Reviewer note** below.

### 1. `refactor(tests): pair every plugin test file with its source file`

- **~60 test files consolidated.** Largest merges: 11 files → `schema/mysql/sdl_migration_omni_test.go`, 9 → `schema/pg/get_database_definition_test.go`, 4 → `schema/oracle/generate_migration_test.go`, 5 → `db/pg/sync_test.go`.
- **Two test files were testing another package's code:**
  - `db/oracle/sync_utf8_test.go` called no Oracle function at all — it tested `common.SanitizeUTF8Message` with Oracle-flavored fixtures. Its generic assertions move to `backend/common/util_test.go`, where they now cover **every** string field of the schema (>100) rather than seven hand-picked `Comment`/`Definition` fields. The two cases that do call `sanitizeOracleDefinition`/`sanitizeOracleMetadataString` stay as `db/oracle/sync_test.go`.
  - `db/mssql/resource_change_integration_testcontainer_test.go` mostly re-asserted tsql parser behavior already covered verbatim in `parser/tsql/resource_change_test.go`. Reduced to what only a live SQL Server can settle — SHOWPLAN_ALL row estimates — and renamed `stats_test.go` to match `stats.go`, where `CountAffectedRows` lives.
- **Dropped the `antlr_dependency_test.go` family (10 files).** They read their own package's source with `os.ReadFile` and asserted `require.NotContains` on import paths, so they passed on broken code and failed on a harmless import-alias rename. The one real unit test buried in the StarRocks file, `TestContainsDelimiterDirective`, moved to `starrocks_test.go`.
- **827 lines of inline SQL → `testdata/sdl/*.sql`** via `//go:embed`, matching the pattern `schema/mysql` already used nine times for its real-world corpus. Each extracted file verified byte-identical to the constant it replaced.

### 2. `test(oracle): run the migration round trip against Oracle by default`

`generate_migration_record_test.go` sat behind `//go:build oracle_record`, so its live round trip — generate the rollback, execute it against a real Oracle, require the schema returns to its starting state across 34 cases — **never ran in CI**. The tag wasn't guarding container availability; the package already runs untagged tests on the same `SharedOracleContainer`. It was guarding a side effect: the `os.WriteFile` that refreshes `testdata/generate_migration/*.json`.

The tag is gone, recording is gated behind the `record` const the package already uses for its `.sql` goldens, and the test is renamed `TestGenerateMigrationAgainstOracle` af

+// fillAllStringFields recursively sets every string field reachable from m
+// (including nested messages, repeated fields, and map keys/values) to the

+func fillAllStringFields(m protoreflect.Message, value string, depth int) {
+	if depth <= 0 {
+		return
+	}
+	fields := m.Descriptor().Fields()
+	for i := 0; i < fields.Len(); i++ {
+		fd := fields.Get(i)
+		switch {
+		case fd.IsMap():
+			mp := m.Mutable(fd).Map()
+			var key protoreflect.MapKey
+			if fd.MapKey().Kind() == protoreflect.StringKind {
+				key = protoreflect.ValueOfString(value).MapKey()
+			} else {
+				key = protoreflect.ValueOfInt64(1).MapKey()
+			}
+			switch fd.MapValue().Kind() {
+			case protoreflect.StringKind:
+				mp.Set(key, protoreflect.ValueOfString(value))
+			case protoreflect.MessageKind:
+				nv := mp.NewValue()
+				fillAllStringFields(nv.Message(), value, depth-1)
+				mp.Set(key, nv)
+			default:
+				mp.Set(key, mp.NewValue())
+			}
+		case fd.IsList():
+			list := m.Mutable(fd).List()
+			switch fd.Kind() {
+			case protoreflect.StringKind:
+				list.Append(protoreflect.ValueOfString(value))
+			case protoreflect.MessageKind:
+				nv := list.NewElement()
+				fillAllStringFields(nv.Message(), value, depth-1)
+				list.Append(nv)
+			default:
+			}
+		case fd.Kind() == protoreflect.StringKind:
+			m.Set(fd, protoreflect.ValueOfString(value))
+		case fd.Kind() == protoreflect.MessageKind:

+
+// countInvalidStringFields walks m and returns how many string values

+func countInvalidStringFields(m protoreflect.Message) int {
+	count := 0
+	m.Range(func(fd protoreflect.FieldDescriptor, v protoreflect.Value) bool {
+		switch {
+		case fd.IsMap():
+			v.Map().Range(func(k protoreflect.MapKey, mv protoreflect.Value) bool {
+				if fd.MapKey().Kind() == protoreflect.StringKind && !utf8.ValidString(k.String()) {
+					count++
+				}
+				switch fd.MapValue().Kind() {
+				case protoreflect.StringKind:
+					if !utf8.ValidString(mv.String()) {
+						count++
+					}
+				case protoreflect.MessageKind:
+					count += countInvalidStringFields(mv.Message())
+				default:
+				}
+				return true
+			})
+		case fd.IsList():
+			list := v.List()
+			for i := 0; i < list.Len(); i++ {
+				switch fd.Kind() {
+				case protoreflect.StringKind:
+					if !utf8.ValidString(list.Get(i).String()) {
+						count++
+					}
+				case protoreflect.MessageKind:
+					count += countInvalidStringFields(list.Get(i).Message())
+				default:
+				}
+			}
+		case fd.Kind() == protoreflect.StringKind:
+			if !utf8.ValidString(v.String()) {
+				count++
+			}
+		case fd.Kind() == protoreflect.MessageKind:

+		default:
+		}

title: fix(wif): backport token binding to 3.22.1
body:
Backport #21309, #21338, and #21350 to `release/3.22.1` so workload identity token exchange requires an allowed audience and a constrained subject. The backfill preserves the shipped audience conventions where they can be derived, and the edit flow preserves configured subject restrictions and audience lists.

The backfill is `migration/3.23.1-backport/0000##workload_identity_audiences.sql`, producing metadata version `3.23.1-backport.0`. Published 3.22.0 images can already record `3.23.0`; the prerelease version runs after that point and before main's original `3.23.1`. Main then applies its existing `.1` comment, `.2` plan, `.3` role, and `.4` WIF migrations normally. No renumbering or repair migration on main is required. #21407 documents and tests the shared convention.

Upgrade go-jose from v4.1.4 to v4.1.5, matching the original #21350 dependency version and including its [JSON nesting, NumericDate, and malformed JWK/JWS hardening](https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/releases/tag/v4.1.5). Add focused WIF regressions for the parsing protections. The WIF production code and backfill SQL remain identical to #21350; release adaptations use the existing test fixtures and preserve the release schema and migration tests.

The complete #21309 prerequisite includes copy-email and checkbox accessibility changes on account pages. These are retained with the upstream commit to preserve the reviewed backport; their inclusion is broader than the audience fix itself.

## Breaking Changes

- Workload identities need a non-blank audience and a valid constrained subject. Create/config-update requests require those binding fields, and invalid existing bindings fail closed.
- The backfill preserves `bytebase` and derivable provider defaults. Custom pipeline audiences and GitHub Enterprise Server defaults may require explicit configuration.
- Complete the replica rollout before creating or editing workload identities, and retain the repaired issuer/audience/subject configuration in Terraform.
- The dependency update rejects malformed JWT/JWK inputs that older go-jose versions could accept.
- Databases that ran superseded renumbering revision `5e1f64fed1` or integer-`.1` backport revision `343cb7c42e` require separate inventory and recovery. Changing a migration filename cannot correct an already-recorded version. Do not rewrite the ledger.

The [operator guide](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/9c52dabc80826e4a9daea073f169e8e6e34d6b58/docs/operations/wif-3.22.1-upgrade.md) explains the supported metadata sequences, image provenance, and rollout checks. This metadata prerelease label does not mark product release 3.22.1 unstable.

## Validation

- `go mod tidy` changed only go-jose and its checksums.
- Full WIF and affected OIDC package tests, migration parser/order tests, real-PostgreSQL backfill/fresh-ledger assertions, API configuration validation, and audit checks passed. The server-backed `TestAuditLogFormat` passed.
- Both new WIF parsing regression

title: fix(mssql): report CREATE UNIQUE INDEX as unique when syncing, and move driver sync tests into their driver packages
body:
## What changed

Two things: a SQL Server sync fix, and the test relocation that surfaced it.

### 1. SQL Server sync dropped `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` uniqueness

`getIndexes` in `backend/plugin/db/mssql/sync.go` reports non-constraint indexes with a query that filters out primary keys and unique constraints (`is_primary_key = 0 AND is_unique_constraint = 0`) and then hardcoded `Unique: false`. It never selected `i.is_unique`. SQL Server sets `is_unique = 1` but `is_unique_constraint = 0` for a standalone `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`, so every such index synced back as **not unique**.

The omni parser disagrees — `get_database_metadata_omni.go:294` sets `Unique: n.Unique` from the parsed DDL — so declared schema and live schema never matched on these indexes. A user who declared a unique index saw it as a pending change on every diff, forever, and `get_database_definition.go:374` emits the `UNIQUE` keyword off that same field, so DDL regenerated from a sync silently dropped it.

The fix selects `i.is_unique` and sets `Unique` from it. Six lines.

### 2. The test relocation that found it

`backend/plugin/schema/mssql/get_database_metadata_testcontainer_test.go` did not call a single function from the `schema` package. It ran `driver.SyncDBSchema()` and asserted on spatial index metadata — driver behavior, tested from the parser's package — and duplicated `backend/plugin/db/mssql/sync_spatial_testcontainer_test.go`, which covered the same ground with different fixtures.

Both are now one test in `backend/plugin/db/mssql`, keeping the union of their coverage:

| From the schema-side file | From the db-side file |
|---|---|
| Configuration bounds (cells 1 and 8192, bbox extremes, fillfactor 50/100) | Index invariants (`Type`, `Unique`, `Primary`, `Expressions`, `Descending`, `Method`) |
| Spatial index on computed columns | `Dimensional` descriptor assertions |
| Columnstore / unique classification | Repeat-sync stability |
| Exact spatial index counts, explicit nil bounding box for `GEOGRAPHY` | |

The db-side version was the weaker of the two, so the merge also removed its per-test container, fixed `time.Sleep` calls, sync retry wrapper, manual `DROP DATABASE` loop, and the `if exists { … }` blocks that passed silently when an index was missing. Tightening one of those loose assertions into an exact count is what exposed the sync bug.

Also in the same spirit:

- The composite-type sync test moved from `schema/pg` to `db/pg` — it asserted only on what `SyncDBSchema` returns.
- `resource_change_integration_testcontainer_test.go` moved onto the shared container, so `db/mssql` starts one SQL Server instead of two.
- Shared sync-test helpers extracted to `sync_testutil_test.go`; new `sync_unique_index_testcontainer_test.go` covers unique/plain/filtered/descending indexes, the `UNIQUE` column constraint, and the primary key.

## Breaking Changes

**MSSQL metadata for non-constraint unique indexes changes value.** An index created with `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` now sy

title: docs: add code comment guidelines for agents
body:
Code comments can bury useful constraints under implementation history and repeated narration. Add guidelines to AGENTS.md that favor short explanations of intent and invariants, keep history in PRs or issues, and require reviewing comments before handoff.

Validation: reviewed the documentation-only diff and ran `git diff --check`. No new links, paths, or shell examples; code tests are not applicable.

 - Follow Google language style guides and AIPs for API/proto design. AIPs take precedence over the proto guide. Enum values use `HELLO`, not `TYPE_HELLO`.
 - Use American English. Avoid collection names ending in `List`.
 
+## Code comments
+
+- Use names and structure to explain what code does. Reserve comments for non-obvious intent, invariants, ordering constraints, external behavior, and public API contracts.
+- Default to one or two sentences. Longer comments must explain a constraint a maintainer needs to change the code safely.
+- Keep implementation history, rejected approaches, review discussions, and follow-up inventories in PRs or issues. For a workaround, keep only the current limitation and a relevant issue reference beside the code.
+- Explain each constraint once, where it is enforced. In tests, let case names and assertions describe behavior; comment only on surprising fixtures or semantics.
+- Before handoff, reread added or modified comments. Remove code narration and repeated rationale, and verify the remaining claims against the implementation.
+
 ## Test placement
 
 Test API and workflow behavior against PostgreSQL. Engine dialect and DDL fidelity tests belong in omni.

title: fix(masking): refuse a query whose table has no synced columns
body:
Closes the masking fail-open WealthNavi reported in BYT-10073.

Replaces #21197. That PR sat in draft while a CTE-scope walker was built to answer one review comment, and then had to be removed. This one is the shape that survived, at 194 production lines instead of 615.

## The problem

Bytebase masks query results column by column, from the stored schema snapshot. A sync that ran while the connecting role lacked privileges leaves a relation listed with **no columns under it**. Masking finds no columns, reads that as "nothing to mask", and returns **raw rows**, with no error, no log and no masking indicator.

`SELECT *` is both the common case and the worst one: the span produces no results, so `doMaskResult` applies no maskers at all. Export uses the same masker, so downloaded files carry raw data too.

The customer changed the role of their Bytebase database user, saw "No Data" for a schema's columns, and got the whole schema back unmasked. Pressing **Sync Database** restored masking with no reconfiguration. Their semantic types were never lost, only unreachable.

## The fix

`QuerySpan` gains `UnresolvedColumnsError`. The PostgreSQL extractor sets it when a relation the query reads is listed in the snapshot with no columns. It reads the snapshot directly rather than analyzer output, so all three lineage paths (analyzed, expression fallback, table-returning function) report the same condition.

Two consumers act on it, through one predicate:

1. `queryRetry` re-syncs the databases the signal names and rebuilds the span. A stale snapshot repairs itself here.
2. `MaskResults` refuses the query if a fresh sync still cannot describe the relation.

Re-sync targets come from the signal rather than from `SourceColumns`: `SourceColumns` names every database the query reads, and only the degraded ones need the sync.

**Only tables are judged.** A view, materialized view or foreign table column can never carry a masking policy: the masker resolves a source column through `SchemaMetadata.GetTable` (`query_result_masker.go` `getColumn`), and `SchemaCatalog`, where semantic types live, holds tables and nothing else. Refusing a column-less one would withhold a result masking never changed, and would break `CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT FROM t` and `CREATE FOREIGN TABLE ft() SERVER s`, both legal PostgreSQL. Partitions resolve through `GetTable` to their parent and inherit its verdict.

## A second fix on the same path

The PR also clears `DetailedError` when it redacts a query error, and that is a separate leak from the one above. `MaskResults` already replaced `Error` with a fixed string when the statement touches masked columns, because PostgreSQL quotes column values in messages like `invalid input syntax for type integer: "111-22-3333"`. It left the structured error alone. `getPgError` fills seventeen fields there, including `InternalQuery`, which carries the failing SQL text, plus `SchemaName`, `TableName` and `ColumnName`, and all of them reach the client v

title: fix(taskrun): roll back leaked test transactions
body:
## What

Five tests in `backend/runner/taskrun` open a transaction and reach `Commit` (or an explicit `Rollback`) **on the happy path only**:

```go
tx, err := s.GetDB().BeginTx(ctx, nil)
require.NoError(t, err)
tasks, err := s.CreateMissingTasksTx(ctx, tx, ...)
require.NoError(t, err)          // <- t.FailNow here skips the Commit below
require.Len(t, tasks, 1)         // <- and here
require.NoError(t, tx.Commit())
```

`require.*` failure calls `t.FailNow`, which runs `runtime.Goexit` and skips both the commit and any rollback. The transaction is never closed.

The connection is not reclaimed afterwards either. `database/sql`'s `beginDC` derives the Tx context with `context.WithCancel` and only cancels it from `Commit`/`Rollback`; with `context.Background()` as the parent, nothing else ever fires `awaitDone`. **The connection stays checked out until the test binary exits.** (Had these used `t.Context()`, the leak would self-heal at test end.)

| site | before |
|---|---|
| `scheduler_test.go:34` | `tx.Rollback()` present but not deferred |
| `scheduler_test.go:119` | no rollback |
| `scheduler_test.go:185` | no rollback |
| `running_scheduler_test.go:168` | no rollback |
| `running_scheduler_test.go:215` | no rollback |

## Why line 34 is the damaging one

That transaction holds `AdvisoryLockKeyPendingScheduler` — the same key [`pending_scheduler.go:75`](backend/runner/taskrun/pending_scheduler.go#L75) acquires in production. A stranded lock makes every later test in the package that runs the pending scheduler take the `"advisory lock held by another replica, skipping"` path. Those tests then **pass without exercising anything**, so one failure quietly turns the rest of the package green-but-meaningless.

## Fix

A deferred `tx.Rollback()` at each site. `Goexit` does run deferred calls, so this closes every path; the rollback after a successful commit returns `sql.ErrTxDone`, which is discarded.

## How they were found

An AST scan pairing every acquisition (`BeginTx`, `Begin`, `Conn`, `Acquire`) with its release across `backend`, `action` and `scripts`, following closure-form defers and ownership transfer.

**All 73 production `BeginTx` sites already defer a rollback** — most via `defer func(){ tx.Rollback() }()`, which a naive grep misses. Connection handling is sound too: `advisory_lock.go` closes on every error path and transfers ownership on success, `AdminExecute` has `defer clean()`, and the `driverConn.(*stdlib.Conn).Conn()` sites are accessors rather than acquisitions. These five tests were the only unpaired acquisitions in the tree.

## Test plan

- [x] `go test -count=1 ./backend/runner/taskrun/ -timeout 15m` — passes
- [x] The five affected tests pass individually
- [x] `gofmt -l` clean; `golangci-lint run -j 8` → `0 issues.`
- [x] Re-ran the AST scan — no unpaired acquisitions remain in `backend/runner/taskrun`
- [x] Verified the load-bearing assumption directly: a `defer` still runs after `t.FailNow()`
- [x] Pre-PR checklist: sect

title: chore(lint): remove dead exclusions, scope the one that works
body:
## What

Seven `text:` exclusion rules, all written as `path: (.+)\.go$` — every linter, every file. I measured what each one actually suppresses by removing the block and diffing the output:

| rule | what it hides today |
|---|---|
| `text: Rollback` | **12 errcheck hits** — deferred `tx.Rollback()`, the standard idiom |
| `text: logger.Sync` | nothing — symbol not in the tree |
| `text: pgInstance.Stop` | nothing — symbol not in the tree |
| `text: fmt.Printf` | nothing |
| `text: Enter(.*)_(.*)` | nothing |
| `text: Exit(.*)_(.*)` | nothing |
| bitbucket `unsecure-url-scheme` | nothing — that line already carries `//nolint:revive` |

Six are dead. The one that works was unscoped, so `text: Rollback` would silently drop **any** issue from **any** linter whose message happened to contain "Rollback". Scoping it to `errcheck` does the same job without that risk.

Also drops `unused` from `enable:` — it is already in golangci-lint's default set (`errcheck govet ineffassign staticcheck unused`), so the line was redundant.

## No change in what gets checked

- Enabled set is identical: 17 linters before and after (`unused` still on, via the default set)
- `golangci-lint run` still reports `0 issues.`
- Removing the one kept rule still surfaces **exactly the same 12** errcheck `Rollback` hits

## Deliberately unchanged: `revive: enable-all-rules` and `govet: enable-all`

`enable-all-rules: true` plus 19 opt-outs looks non-standard, and I initially wanted to move revive to its default rule set. Both configurations report 0 issues on a clean tree, so I probed a scratch package with known violations instead:

| probe | current config | revive defaults |
|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-type-assertion` | caught | missed |
| `waitgroup-by-value` | caught | missed |
| `bare-return` | caught | missed |
| `unreachable-code` (control) | caught | caught |

The first two are real bug classes — a panicking type assertion and a copied `WaitGroup`. Opt-out costs some churn when revive adds rules, but that is a rule to disable, not a bug to ship. Left as is.

`govet: enable-all: true` likewise: that analyzer set is curated by the Go team and stable, so "enable all, subtract the two noisy ones" is low-risk.

## Test plan

- [x] `golangci-lint config verify` clean
- [x] `golangci-lint run -j 8` → `0 issues.`
- [x] Enabled linter list diffed before/after — identical
- [x] Kept rule removed → same 12 errcheck `Rollback` hits, confirming it is still load-bearing and unchanged in scope
- [x] Scratch-package probe confirms revive coverage is untouched
- [x] Pre-PR checklist: sections 3-6 and 8 skip (no `backend/store`, `migrator`, `tests`, proto or code changes); section 2 does not apply — lint config is not user-facing configuration

title: perf(ci): tune golangci-lint GC to cut CPU and cap RSS
body:
## What

Sets `GOGC=off` and `GOMEMLIMIT=10GiB` for the golangci-lint step in CI, and on the documented local command. Follow-up to #21395, which found where the CPU actually goes.

Go's default `GOGC=100` collects every time the heap doubles. golangci-lint holds a **~5 GB live heap** on this repo, so the default spends a large share of its CPU repeatedly scanning it. Collecting only as the heap approaches a ceiling is cheaper — and the ceiling is a real bound on memory, where `-j` only ever influenced it indirectly.

## Measurements

Runner box (20 vCPU / 31 GB), `-j 8`, golangci cache cleared before each run, all runs started at load < 1.5:

| setting | CPU | wall | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`GOGC` default (100)** — today | 491s | 65.6s | 11.05 GB |
| `GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=8GiB` | 449s | 61.1s | 8.22 GB |
| **`GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=10GiB`** ← this PR | **418s** | **57.2s** | **10.22 GB** |
| `GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=12GiB` | 397s | 55.0s | 12.43 GB |
| `GOGC=off GOMEMLIMIT=16GiB` | 375s | 53.1s | 15.99 GB |
| `GOGC=400`, no limit | 388s | 57.6s | **27.25 GB** ⚠️ |

10GiB beats today's default on **all three axes**: 15% less CPU, 13% less wall, 8% less peak RSS. It also lowers the worst-case ceiling, which matters because two runners share the box — `2 x 10GiB` leaves headroom for the frontend and backend-test jobs.

Bare `GOGC=400` reaches similar CPU but peaks at 27 GB on a 31 GB box. The limit is doing the safety work here, not the GOGC value.

Combined with the `-j 8` from #21395, a cold run goes from ~730 CPU-seconds at the stock defaults to ~420 — about 43% less, with no checks dropped.

## Trade-off

With GC effectively deferred, a **warm** run's peak RSS goes from ~0.18 GB to ~1.24 GB (measured, 2 reps each). Wall time is unchanged at ~2.6s. Trivial in absolute terms, but it is a real 7x on the common case, so it is worth knowing.

## What I ruled out

Where the CPU actually is, same conditions:

| variant | CPU | vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | 493s | — |
| drop `staticcheck` + `unused` | 181s | **-63%** |
| drop `exhaustive` | 477s | -3% |
| drop `revive` + `gocritic` | 471s | -4% |

`buildir` — staticcheck's IR builder, feeding `staticcheck` and `unused` — is 46% of analyzer CPU by itself. Those two are the highest-value linters in the config, so this PR does not touch them; trimming anything else is noise.

`--tests=false` looked tempting (407s, -17%) but made `unused` report **50 false positives**, since code used only by tests looks dead. Not viable.

`-j 8` is already near-optimal: j=4 → 595s, j=6 → 476s, j=8 → 493s, j=12 → 654s, j=20 → 732s.

The remaining big lever is cache persistence — a cold run is 2:47 / 2530 CPU-s / 12.9 GB against 2.9s / 20 CPU-s / 0.19 GB warm, because `/scratch` is GCE Local SSD and every Spot preemption wipes it. That lives in the devbox startup script, not this repo.

## Test plan

- [x] YAML parses `GOGC` as the string `"off"`, not a boolean — verified with a parser
- [x] Runtime honors it: `

title: docs(design): show what an MCP access policy mode allows
body:
Design doc for the MCP settings page: `docs/design/mcp-capability-ladder.md`.

Since #21324 removed the per-mode method drawer, the Access policy section describes each mode in one sentence and nothing on the page says what a mode actually serves. This doc lands on one rule: **show capabilities, not methods or permissions.** Eight capability rows in one ordered list, each mode a prefix of it, collapsed by default inside the existing section, following the picked mode while editing. The page also gets shorter: the mode cards shrink to an icon, a label and a caption with the selected mode's "Best for" under them, the disclosure line is the mode's description, and row details sit behind one toggle. The product change is frontend-only; a backend lint binds the row wording to the method classification so the list cannot drift from what the gate serves. A custom policy is out of scope but the list is shaped to become that editor later.

### What the doc decides

- One verb per tier where it is honest: every read row starts with *Read*. The write tier uses *Propose*, *Run*, *Export*, *Manage*, each naming the row's effect on the database; a single write verb was tried three ways and rejected, with the cases in the doc.
- Rows carry plain sub-items ("Schemas · Databases and instances · Projects and database groups…") behind one "Show details" toggle. No method names, no permission names, no counts, no link to a method list.
- The mode cards shrink to a Lucide icon (unplug · eye · pencil-line), the mode name and a three-word caption, in the shape of the instance engine selector, with the selected mode's "Best for" line under them. The card descriptions are gone; they duplicated the ladder.
- The mode chip is the subject of the view and carries the same Lucide icon as its card; the "In force" label, the stripes icon and the mode sentence go. Color stays on the chip only; the cards stay neutral. The disclosure line carries the description and never repeats the mode name. The tightening note shows only while editing and names the change; the audit fact moves into the section description.
- Edit state renders the picked mode exactly as the post-save view: no delta marks, no "adds N".
- ✓ / — marks with a `read` or `write` badge on served rows only. The floor stays as one short line: "Never, in any mode: approve issues, administer the workspace, or handle credentials."
- Approval is stated as the project's policy, never as a promise (review P1 and P2 on this PR).
- Every line says only what the served methods can do (review round 3): both summaries share the same read phrase, since Read-write serves exactly the reads Read-only serves; Read-only says write statements are refused rather than that nothing is written, and row 2 states the depth of that check; "edit" is dropped where no update RPC exists; moving databases between projects is named; the audit claim is narrowed to policy refusals; the masking toggle keeps its engine-coverage limit.
- Recorded as a pr

## Summary
Reorganize instance connection forms into consistent horizontal rows, with dependent TLS, SSH, IAM, external-secret, MongoDB, Redis, and Kerberos settings grouped beneath their controlling options. Authentication and password providers share one dropdown, with configuration labels matching the selected provider. Database sync scope uses a segmented control.
