title: refactor: deprecate PouchDB and refine AI chat UX
body:
## Summary

Replace the SQL Editor AI assistant's PouchDB persistence with bounded `localStorage` and improve the chat history and SQL insertion experience. Close BYT-10154

## Changes

- Remove PouchDB dependencies and the legacy blob, key-value, and extended-tab storage
- Persist AI conversations in workspace- and user-scoped `localStorage`
- Limit history to 20 conversations and 1 MiB, excluding empty conversations to prevent endless growth
- Clean up legacy PouchDB databases without blocking SQL Editor startup
- Build API chat history from stored messages and attach schema context only to the first user request
- Support inline, auto-height conversation title editing
- Replace the delete modal with an anchored confirmation popover
- Improve message wrapping, first-message spacing, and conversation action behavior
- Rename "Insert at caret" to "Insert at cursor"
- Insert generated SQL as a line-aware block with correct newlines and cursor placement

## Migration

Existing PouchDB-backed AI conversation history is not migrated. Legacy databases are removed through best-effort cleanup, and new history is stored in `localStorage`.

## Testing

- `pnpm --dir frontend type-check`
- Focused Vitest coverage for conversation persistence, chat history UI, request construction, message layout, legacy cleanup, and SQL snippet insertion
- Targeted Biome checks

title: fix(api): compare the IAM policy etag under lock (T18b)
body:
Fixes **T18b** from [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md).

## What was wrong

`GetIamPolicy` returns the etag **inside** the policy — `IamPolicy.etag` is the only etag a reader ever receives, and the proto promises that presenting it back triggers `ABORTED`. But both `SetIamPolicy` handlers read only `SetIamPolicyRequest.etag`, the request wrapper. A normal read-modify-write round-trips the etag in `policy.etag` and had it silently discarded, so two admins editing permissions at once lost one edit. If the lost edit was a revoke, access stayed granted.

Tracing it turned up that reading the right field is necessary but not sufficient, and that two more writers had the same defect with no etag at all.

## What changed

**The etag is read wherever the caller presents it.** `requestedIamPolicyEtag` takes `policy.etag` or the request field, and rejects two that disagree.

**The compare happens inside the write transaction, and only there.** New `store.SetIamPolicy` takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock, then `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the full primary key `(workspace, resource_type, resource, type)`, compares, and upserts — one transaction. Comparing in the handler instead would be a check-then-act: two concurrent requests both read the same policy, both pass the comparison, and the later write wins — which is the bug being fixed, one layer up. The advisory lock (before the row lock, per `backend/store/AGENTS.md`) also orders two first writes to a resource whose policy row does not exist yet and so has nothing to lock.

**Checks that compare old to new run under the same lock.** `SetIamPolicyMessage.ValidateReplaced` runs inside the transaction against the policy being replaced. The workspace seat guard uses it: it compared the new user count against a policy read before validation, so for a caller that sends no etag — and therefore gets no compare-and-swap — two concurrent writes could both pass the guard and the later one grow an over-limit workspace.

**Writes evict the cache rather than publishing into it.** The advisory lock is transaction-scoped, so it ends at the commit while the cache write happened after it: two writers could commit in one order and reach the cache in the other, leaving the loser's snapshot cached with no expiry. `policyCache` is what permission checks read, so that meant a process authorizing against a revoked policy indefinitely. Eviction never installs a value, so no interleaving can get it wrong and the next read repopulates from the row. A rejected write evicts too, so a caller's recovery read is not served the etag it just lost with.

**Two more unguarded read-modify-writes on the same policy.** Both present no etag — they are server-side merges, not replacements — so no handler-level fix could reach them. Each read the policy, merged one member in, and wrote the whole thing back, so either could resurrect a member an admin had just

title: fix(api): check the create permission on allow_missing updates (T11)
body:
Closes T11 from [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md).

## What's wrong

`UpdateGroup(allow_missing=true)` creates a group when none exists, and nothing authorized it.

Two mechanisms were each assumed to be the other's job:

- The ACL interceptor's `allow_missing` secondary check routes through `doIAMPermissionCheck`, which returns `true` for every non-IAM auth method. `UpdateGroup` is `auth_method = CUSTOM`, so the block evaluated to nothing.
- The create path calls `s.CreateGroup(...)` **in-process**, which bypasses the interceptor entirely — and `CreateGroup` is IAM-authed, so it has no self-check of its own.

The comment above it claimed both `bb.groups.update` and `bb.groups.create` were verified.

Of the five CUSTOM RPCs that take the flag, the other four were already covered by their own handlers (`UpdatePlan` → `PlansCreate`, `UpdateUser` → `UsersCreate`, `UpdatePolicy` → `createPolicyMessage`'s `checkPolicyPermission`, `UpdateSetting` → the `bb.settings.set` family before the existence lookup). `UpdateGroup` was the only live gap.

**Impact.** Narrower and differently shaped than the audit first recorded. Workspace Member *does* hold `bb.groups.create` — but Workspace DBA and every project role do not. So a DBA-only principal could create a group and name itself OWNER, which `checkPermission` then honors for that group. It stops there: a group confers nothing until someone with IAM-policy rights binds a role to it. Unauthorized resource creation, not privilege escalation.

## What changed

**1. `UpdateGroup` checks `permission.GroupsCreate` itself** before delegating — the shape `UpdatePlan` and `UpdateUser` already had. The group-owner bypass in `checkPermission` doesn't apply, since there is no group yet.

**2. The interceptor stops pretending.** Its `allow_missing` block is now gated on `AuthMethod == common.AuthMethodIAM`. Behavior-preserving — `doIAMPermissionCheck` already returned `true` there — but the code no longer reads as protection where it verifies nothing.

**3. `UpdateDatabaseRequest.allow_missing` removed.** Found while tracing the same mechanism. The `".update"` → `".create"` rewrite is an unvalidated string guess, and this one derived `bb.databases.create`, which is not in `permission.yaml`. `CheckPermission` never matches an unknown string, so setting the flag denied *every* caller including Workspace Admin — on a field `database_service.go` never read and the proto documented as working ("a new database will be created"). Nothing in the backend, frontend, or tests set it. The message now carries a one-line comment saying the flag must never come back, since a database is not independently creatable — it appears when its instance is synced.

**4. `TestAllowMissingCreatePermission`** walks the proto descriptors — the idiom `audit_redact_inventory_test.go` and `mcp_gate_test.go` already use — and turns four silent failure modes into a

title: fix(api): route every CEL filter literal through an escaping helper (T17)
body:
Closes T17 in [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md).

## What was wrong

The frontend built CEL filter strings by interpolating user input straight into a double-quoted string literal. A `"` closes the literal early and the backend rejects the whole filter with `InvalidArgument`:

```
query.contains("SELECT * FROM "public"."users"")
  -> ERROR: <input>:1:32: Syntax error: mismatched input 'public' expecting ')'
```

An escaping helper already existed and was used at 6 of 17 sites. The worst of the other 11 was the access-grant page, whose search box takes SQL — quoted identifiers make the failure routine there.

Not a privilege boundary: authorization is decided by `parent` before the filter is read (`database_service.go:293-331` sets `find.ProjectID` from the parent, not the filter), and every store filter binds its values as SQL parameters.

## What changed

**`celString` / `celStringList` / `celMapField`** (new `frontend/src/utils/v1/celLiteral.ts`) render the whole literal, quotes included, so a call site cannot forget the escape and still look correct. All 17 sites converted — the enum and resource-name ones included, because an absolute rule is the only one a machine can check.

**`frontend/src/architecture/cel-filter-literals.test.ts`** scans `src/**` for the three raw shapes and fails CI on a new one, in the style of the existing `vue-boundary` guards. Test files are excluded: they should spell out expected filter strings literally.

The helpers live in a dependency-free leaf module. Beside the CEL RPC clients they dragged `@/api` into `modules/cel/logic/stringify.ts` and broke that subtree's tests — the full suite caught it.

### Two adjacent defects, neither fixed by escaping

- **A label key with a dash never reached the backend.** Keys validate as `^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,62}$` (`backend/api/v1/common.go:57`), but CEL parses `labels.cost-center` as subtraction, so the store answered `unsupport variable ""`. The frontend now emits `labels["key"]` index syntax and `getVariableAndValueFromExpr` canonicalizes both forms. The key is **bound**, not interpolated into the JSONB path — index syntax admits a quote the dotted form could not, so leaving it interpolated would have opened a real injection.
- **`%` and `_` reached `LIKE` as wildcards**, so a statement search containing either silently over-matched. `escapeLikePattern` (already in-tree for saved queries) plus `ESCAPE '\'` now covers all 13 `contains` translations.

The three copies of the label-filter closure collapse into one `buildLabelFilterSQL`, which also drops an unchecked `raw.(string)` that panicked on `labels.k in [1]`.

## Testing

- New frontend regression tests over every free-text filter builder (`stores/app/filterEscaping.test.ts`) and the label index form.
- New store tests for the wildcard escaping, the index form, and that an injected key stays bound (`backend/store/filter_test.go`).
- G

title: fix: run issue approval filters in SQL, and four edge cases in the issue store queries
body:
## What changed and why

Two things, both in the issue list read path.

### 1. `approval_status` and `current_approver` are matched in SQL (audit finding T13)

Both filters were parsed out of the CEL filter but never reached SQL. The store returned a full page, the page token was minted from that row count, and only then were non-matching issues dropped in Go (`issue_service_converter.go`). So filtering by "waiting for my approval" answered with an **empty list under a live "Load more" button** — the default My Issues view (`MyIssuesPage.tsx` pins `status=OPEN`, `approval=PENDING`, `current-approver=me`, two of which were post-filters). The frontend has no workaround: `usePagedData` derives `hasMore` from the token alone, so the button stays live over an empty table.

Both predicates now run in the store, before `LIMIT`. This is the pattern already in-tree at `backend/store/saved_query.go`, whose comment says exactly why: *"filtering after LIMIT would silently return short pages."*

- **Status** is a `CASE` over `payload->'approval'` mirroring `computeApprovalStatus` branch for branch, including the empty-approvers case that precedes the rejected and approved checks. Payloads are written with a bare `protojson.Marshal`, so the SQL reads an absent key as a zero value.
- **`current_approver`** cannot be resolved in SQL alone — binding conditions and group expansion are evaluated in Go — so the caller resolves which roles the named user holds in each project being searched and passes the `(project, role)` pairs down, the same shape as the saved-query `AccessMembers` predicate. The role a flow is waiting on is `roles ->> jsonb_array_length(approvers)`, which yields NULL once every step has been acted on.

The Go post-filter, `isIssueNextApprover` and `getUserRoleMap` are deleted (`issue_service_converter.go` shrinks by 49 lines), and `next_page_token` becomes truthful for free, since `limit+1` now counts matching rows.

### 2. Four edge cases found auditing every query in `backend/store/issue.go`

All pre-existing, all reproduced against PostgreSQL 16.

- **Search text with no lexeme failed the whole query.** `getTSQuery` fell back to interpolating the raw search text when the segmenter returned no tokens, and `(`, `:`, `'`, `&`, `|`, `!` are tsquery syntax — so `CAST(? AS tsquery)` raised SQLSTATE 42601 and the issue list answered 500. Typing `(` in the issue search box was enough. Fuzzing the segmenter over 20k punctuation-heavy inputs produced 8435 distinct tsqueries, **5043 of them invalid**; every one came from that fallback. It now returns empty, which the call site already handles by searching with ILIKE alone — the same fuzz then produces 170 tsqueries, **0 invalid**. Punctuation is matched better by ILIKE anyway: searching `(` now finds `release (v2)`.
- **The ILIKE fallback interpolated the search text unescaped**, so `%` and `_` were wildcards — searching `%` returned every issue. Now routed through `escapeLikePattern`, which already exist

title: chore: remove config for uninstalled GitHub apps (SonarCloud, Semantic PR)
body:
## What and why

Three GitHub Apps were uninstalled from the `bytebase` org — SonarCloud Code Analysis, Semantic PR, and the CLA bot. This removes the repo-side configuration they consumed, which no longer has a consumer.

### SonarCloud

- **Delete `.sonarcloud.properties`** — this drove the app's *automatic analysis*: source and test paths, exclusions, copy-paste-detection exclusions, and five triaged false-positive suppressions.
- **`frontend/scripts/check-frontend-structure.mjs`** — drop `.sonarcloud.properties` from `agentFiles`. That list asserts each entry exists, so deleting the properties file without this change would have failed the structure check.
- **`docs/pre-pr-checklist.md`** — remove section 9 "SonarCloud Properties" and renumber "Final Verification" from 10 to 9.
- **`AGENTS.md`** — drop SonarCloud from the one-line pre-PR checklist summary.

### Semantic PR

- **Delete `.github/semantic.yml`** — enabled title-only checking and listed the accepted conventional-commit types (`feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `style`, `test`, `chore`, `cherrypick`).

### CLA bot

Nothing to remove. The bot kept no configuration in this repo — it was driven entirely from its own service and only applied the `cla-signed` label.

No GitHub Actions workflow referenced any of the three apps, so the workflows are untouched. CodeQL, Snyk, and Socket Security are unaffected and still reporting.

Historical plan documents under `docs/plans/` and `docs/superpowers/plans/` keep their SonarCloud mentions. Those are point-in-time records of what the process looked like when they were written.

## Knowledge that leaves with these files

Two things were only ever written down in the deleted config, and reviewers may want them preserved elsewhere:

1. **SonarCloud suppression rationale** — why five `go:S2077` (SQL injection) findings in `backend/plugin/db/*/{sync,stats,dump,role}.go` are false positives, and why the issue-detail / plan-detail route pairs are acknowledged clones rather than copy-paste debt. CodeQL still runs and may surface overlapping findings with no suppression to lean on.
2. **The accepted PR title prefixes** — `.github/semantic.yml` was the only place in the repo listing them. The convention is still visible in `main`'s history, but nothing documents or enforces it now.

Happy to capture either in `AGENTS.md` / `backend/plugin/db/AGENTS.md` as a follow-up if that's wanted.

## Testing

- `node frontend/scripts/check-frontend-structure.mjs` → `Frontend structure check passed`
- Repo-wide grep for `sonarcloud|sonarqube|sonar-project|SONAR_|semantic.yml|semantic-prs` returns no hits outside the historical plan docs noted above
- Searched for CLA bot config under every conventional name (`.cla.json`, `.clabot`, `.github/cla.yml`, `CLA.md`, …) — none present
- Config and docs only — no Go or TypeScript source is touched

title: fix(api): make update_mask decide what Update methods write (T15)
body:
Fixes T15 from [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md). Four v1 Update methods let something other than the mask decide what was written, and each failed silently.

## What changed

**`UpdateDataSource` — rotating a leaked cloud credential could silently no-op.** The credential branch dispatched on the request body's `authentication_type`. An AIP-134 client that masks only the credential leaves that field unset, so the write fell through an empty branch: HTTP 200, compromised key still live. The same branch, given a body type that disagreed with the mask, wrote the *other* credential and moved `authentication_type` with it though the mask named neither.

Dispatch is now on the mask path. The effective type is resolved from the mask before the loop, so path order cannot matter, and a mismatched path is `InvalidArgument`.

**`UpdateSetting(APP_IM)` — saving one provider erased the rest.** It validated the masked provider, then assigned the whole request over the stored setting, dropping every provider left out. Now it splices only the masked providers, requires a mask, and treats a masked provider the payload omits as a removal — which is how the console deletes one, so `IMPage` no longer merges the list client-side.

**`UpdateIssue` — unsupported paths were dropped in silence.** `update_mask=["status"]` returned 200 and did nothing. Unsupported paths are now rejected. `status` belongs to `BatchUpdateIssuesStatus` and approvals to `ApproveIssue`/`RejectIssue`, so the supported set was right; only the silence was wrong.

**`UpdateDatabaseCatalog` — full replace, now documented.** A mask cannot express "this one table" while `schemas` is a repeated field, since AIP-161 forbids addressing one element of one. The proto now says the whole catalog is replaced. `allow_missing` is removed and its number reserved: a catalog is not independently creatable, so the flag had nothing to create, and the ACL's derived create-permission check on it denied every caller.

## Breaking Changes

Three RPCs now reject requests they previously answered `200` to, and one request field is removed.

| Change | Previously | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `UpdateDataSource` | credential path disagreeing with the data source's auth type wrote the wrong credential, or nothing | `InvalidArgument` |
| `UpdateSetting(APP_IM)` | a request with no `update_mask` replaced the entire setting | `InvalidArgument` |
| `UpdateIssue` | an unimplemented mask path returned `200` and did nothing | `InvalidArgument` |
| `UpdateDatabaseCatalogRequest.allow_missing` | present, and denied every caller that set it | removed, field number reserved |

No console flow is affected — every frontend call site was checked. `UpdateSetting(APP_IM)`'s new delete semantics do change the console's delete request, which is updated in this PR.

## Testing

Both merges were extracted into pure functions (`applyDataSourceUpdateMask`, `mergeAppIMSetting`), so the behavior is pinned by uni

title: fix: use intent-specific wording for access grant entry points
body:
## What

Completes the wording fix that #21200 started for the export button, under one explicit rule: **"access grant" stays the unified noun** (ACCESS pane CTA, drawer title, gutter tab, settings, feature names), **entry-point buttons carry the user's intent verb**:

| Entry point | Before (#21081) | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Export-blocked result toolbar | Request access grant | Request export (restored by #21200; its broken e2e spec repaired here) |
| Permission-denied query CTA (JIT branch) | Request access grant | **Request query** |
| Masked-column popover | Request access grant | **Request unmask** |
| ACCESS pane CTA / drawer title | Request access grant | unchanged — correct home for the mechanism name |

Two related fixes ride along:

- **Workspace export policy checkbox** (Settings → General → SQL Editor): retitled from a bare "Enable data export" (which had no description) to **"Allow data export without approval"** + a description naming the "Request export" path. Customers read the old title as a hard kill switch and never discovered that disabling direct export is how approval-gated (access-grant) export gets enabled. The project-level "Allow access grants" description now also mentions the export/unmask capabilities so both ends of the flow reference each other.
- **zh-CN terminology**: the unmask grant capability is renamed **取消脱敏** (was 脱敏豁免 — the Masking Exemptions *feature's* name). Those are different mechanisms: an exemption is admin-granted and resource-scoped (evaluated per-column in the masking evaluator), while the grant capability is user-requested and statement-bound (`SkipMasking` on the approved statement only). Reusing the feature name on the CTA sent zh users into the wrong mental model. 取消X follows the zh glossary for "un-X" (取消归档/取消分配).

## Why

After #21081 unified all JIT wording to "access grant", customers reported the export-blocked button was confusing — the label named the mechanism, not what they'd get. #21081's review had accepted the shared label as a documented trade-off; real-world confusion overturned it. All five locales are updated with their existing glossaries.

## Testing

- New tests: a locale-coupling vitest (each locale's data-export description must quote its live "Request export" label — mutation-verified), a 5-locale lock that the unmask capability wording never reuses the Masking Exemptions feature name (mutation-verified with the pre-fix zh value), SQLEditorSection toggle unit tests (title/description keys + `checked={!disableExport}` inversion + dirty tracking), a `bb.sql.info`-only JIT-path unit test, the previously deferred **L7** masked-cell popover e2e (JIT off/on → drawer pre-fill, reusing the export spec's masked-column fixture), and a new `workspace-general-settings` e2e spec (wording + policy→UI + UI→policy round-trip verified via API).
- Gates: Biome, `check-react-i18n.mjs` (key parity across 5 locales, banned-wording), structure guard, `tsc` — all green.
- Unit: 700+ tests across

title: feat(store): add the review_run slot table and store proto for SQL Review V2
body:
## What

First slice of SQL Review V2 (review results become issue comments): the `review_run` status-slot table and its store proto. Store methods, executor wiring, and the v1 API land separately.

- Migration `3.23/0000##review_run.sql` (3.22.0 is cut; this opens the 3.23 directory): one row per (issue, reviewer type), composite PK `(project, issue_id, type)`, composite FK to `issue(project, id)`, an `attempt` fence column (0-based like `task_run.attempt`; the completion transaction is fenced on it so a superseded execution posts zero comments), a four-state `status` CHECK (`AVAILABLE/RUNNING/DONE/FAILED` — no PENDING: review needs no admission control; no CANCELED: runs are side-effect-free until the fenced completion), and partial indexes for the scheduler scan and the heartbeat reaper (cf. `idx_task_run_active_status_id` / `idx_task_run_running_replica`). `type` is deliberately un-CHECKed: the reviewer-id space is open.
- `proto/store/store/review_run.proto`: `ReviewRun.Status` strictly 1:1 with the status CHECK (no unpersisted values), `ReviewRunPayload.error` set only for FAILED.
- Purge and ordering registration: `DeleteProject` deletes `review_run` between `issue_comment` and `issue` (the FK has no ON DELETE, per convention); the store README lock-order chains and the pre-pr-checklist composite-PK table list are updated together, as both documents require.
- `TestCollision_ReviewRunProjectPurge`: seeds colliding `(issue_id, type)` rows in two projects, purges project A, and asserts A's rows are gone while B's are untouched. title: test(e2e): adapt suite to main (plan lifecycle, project-parented DBs, sync allowlist) + fix stopServer race
body:
## What

Brings the Playwright e2e suite back to green on current `main` (test-only diff: `frontend/tests/e2e/**`, 28 files) and fixes one framework race that could take down the disposable server mid-run.

### Adapt tests to product changes on main
- **Plan lifecycle / header (BYT-9722, BYT-9936, BYT-9351):** plan-detail specs drive the consolidated header; `submitDraftForReviewViaUI` follows the 3-tier "Ready for Review" advance (blockers popover / "Submit anyway" override / direct) and treats the button leaving the header as success. Plan creation is UI-driven (`framework/ui-create-plan.ts`: single- and multi-spec creators via `databaseList` + `sqlMap`); the review issue is resolved from `Plan.issue` instead of a `waitForIssue` poll.
- **Project-parented database names:** dashboard DB-detail URLs now carry `?parent=<project-parented instance>` like `autoDatabaseRoute` does — without it `GetDatabase` 404s and `ProjectRouteGate` bounces to `/landing` (BYT-9616 test). `findDatabaseByShortName` takes the project parent.
- **Sample instance sync allowlist:** the selfhost sample registers `sync_databases=[hr_test]`, so hand-created DBs (`hr_prod`) were discovered but never stored. Setup / issue-targets / access-grants now widen the allowlist via `api.updateInstanceSyncDatabases` before `syncInstance`.
- **SQL editor:** batch result tabs are `<instance> / <env> <db>`; the result-pane entry is "Request export" (the ACCESS pane keeps "Request access grant"); the header logo is a plain image; route-ownership refactor (#20942) locators.
- **Schema editor:** `planStatementText()` reads the whole Monaco buffer (scroll-to-end + nbsp normalization) — the "missing ADD PRIMARY KEY" failure was a below-the-fold read, not a product bug.
- **Scroll restoration:** seeds via UI create+submit (draft issues are hidden from the Issues list), dwells on the loaded list before drilling in so the paged snapshot persists, and gives `beforeAll` its own timeout (the file-level `test.setTimeout` does not cover hooks).

### Framework fix
- `stopServer` now waits for the server process to exit before `rmSync(tempDir)`. Killing and deleting concurrently made the embedded metadata Postgres PANIC (`could not fsync pg_xact`) and hung every later test in a back-to-back run.

## Why

After rebasing onto `main` (~330 commits) the full suite was 170 passed / 9 failed; every red traced to a main-side product change the tests hadn't followed, plus the `stopServer` race. No product bugs were found in this round (one suspected schema-editor PK bug was disproved as a test read error).

## Testing

- Full licensed suite (`BYTEBASE_E2E_LICENSE` set), Mode B disposable server, 33 spec files: **180 passed / 0 failed (16.5m)**. The only ✘ line is the `test.fail()` lock for BYT-9481.
- `sql-editor-saved-query.spec.ts` (post worksheet→saved-query rename) run separately: **8 passed** (incl. the Duplicate `test.fail()` lock, still failing as expected).
- Strict ad-hoc `tsc --noEmit` over `tests/e2e/

title: fix(store): make every offset-paginated list sort on a total order (T14)
body:
Closes T14 in [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md), which was filed as "paging through issues across projects skips some and repeats others." It turned out to be a class defect, not one query.

## The bug

Every paginated v1 list reads its pages with `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` — the page token carries `{limit, offset}`, so each page is a separate query. PostgreSQL only guarantees the order the `ORDER BY` specifies, so when the sort key is not unique under the query's scope, tied rows can come back in a different order per page query and cross the page boundary between reads.

This is not a concurrency artifact — it happens on completely static data. Measured on 10,000 issues across 40 projects by issuing the 100 page queries separately, exactly as the API does:

| `ORDER BY` | rows collected | distinct | duplicated | never returned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `issue.id DESC` | 10,000 | 9,764 | 236 | **236** |
| `issue.id DESC, issue.project DESC` | 10,000 | 10,000 | 0 | 0 |

Ties are guaranteed, not incidental. `nextProjectID` allocates `MAX(id)+1` per project floored at 101, so every project has an issue 101. And `created_at` defaults to `now()`, the *transaction* timestamp, so every row written by one batch insert shares it exactly.

A sweep of all 22 offset-paginated call sites found 17 affected (14 of the 17 store functions behind them). Only `ListQueryHistories` and `ListSavedQueries` were sorting on a total order — both from #21203, which was never swept across the other lists — plus `ListPlans`, which is total only because a mandatory `WHERE plan.project = ?` pins its scope column. Those three are left untouched.

## What changed

Each affected list now names tiebreak columns that are unique under its own scope, **written into the SQL**:

```go
// created_at defaults to now() and is not unique; resource_id is the primary key.
q.Space("ORDER BY changelog.created_at DESC, changelog.resource_id DESC")
```

and at the six affected lists that accept an `order_by`, the same columns are appended after the caller's keys — the caller replaces the sort key, never the tiebreak.

An earlier revision of this PR routed all seventeen through a `buildStableOrderBy` helper so an AST test could require it. Review judged that ceremony for the ten lists whose clause is a constant, and both the helper and the guard were removed. The consequence is stated plainly rather than papered over: **nothing enforces this statically**, so a new paginated list added without a tiebreak will not fail CI. Enforcement is step 4 of [`docs/pre-pr-checklist.md`](docs/pre-pr-checklist.md) plus review.

`ListIssueComment` needed a second change. Its `resource_id` tiebreak is a random UUID, so falling back to it would render a multi-field `UpdateIssue` as "labels changed" above "title changed" — stably wrong. `CreateIssueComments` now offsets each row of a batch by its ordinal, keeping `created_at` unique within the batch and in insertion order.

-## Transaction Lock Ordering
-
-Before adding or modifying a transaction that locks multiple rows or tables, follow the canonical [store row-lock ordering](backend/store/README.md#transaction-row-lock-ordering). Lock existing child rows before parents, lock batches in full primary-key order, and treat upserts as existing-row locks. Add the deterministic real-PostgreSQL regression tests required below for new multi-row or multi-table coordination paths.

title: fix: use latest schema snapshot for changelog diff
body:
## Summary

- expose changelog filters for schema snapshots and strict creation-time bounds
- resolve schema diffs against the latest prior schema-bearing changelog
- preserve protobuf timestamp precision and avoid scanning up to 1,000 changelogs
- add backend parser/query and frontend regression coverage

## Root cause

Data-only changes and rollbacks intentionally do not create schema snapshots. The frontend selected the immediately preceding changelog, so the next schema change compared its complete schema against an empty dump.

Fixes [BYT-10146](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10146/schema-diff-broken-after-upgrading-to-3220).

## Testing

- go test ./backend/api/v1 -run ^TestParseChangelogFilter$ -count=1
- go test ./backend/store -run ^TestBuildListChangelogsQuerySchemaSnapshotBefore$ -count=1
- pnpm --dir frontend test: 3,838 tests passed
- pnpm --dir frontend check
- pnpm --dir frontend type-check
- buf format -w proto
- buf lint proto
- buf generate
- go build -ldflags "-w -s" -p=16 -o ./bytebase-build/bytebase ./backend/bin/server/main.go
- git diff --check

title: fix(rollout): scope BatchCancelTaskRuns to the authorized stage (T18a)
body:
## What

`BatchCancelTaskRuns` checked the caller's permission against the stage named in the request, then resolved task runs by project and ID alone.

The stage segment of a task run name is caller-supplied, and the only stage check compared it to the parent's stage — both halves coming from the request body. Those names proved that the caller's strings agreed with each other; they proved nothing about the rows. `ListTaskRuns` then filtered on `Workspace` + `ProjectID` + `UIDs`, with no environment or plan predicate.

So cancel rights in one environment reached any cancelable task run in the project. A caller holding rollout-policy roles in `test` could send `parent = projects/P/plans/1/rollout/stages/test/tasks/-` with a task run name whose stage segment says `test` but whose ID belongs to a running production migration: the name check passes, permission is evaluated against `test`, and the ID resolves by project.

The RPC is `auth_method = CUSTOM`, so the interceptor is not a second gate (`acl.go:252-254` returns early for non-IAM methods) — the handler is the only gate.

This is T18a in `docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`.

## Why it matters

For a PENDING or AVAILABLE row this flips it to CANCELED. For a RUNNING row the store UPDATE does not apply — it covers only PENDING/AVAILABLE — but the handler invokes the executor's `context.CancelFunc` and broadcasts `CANCEL_TASK_RUN` to every replica, aborting an in-flight migration mid-statement.

The gap is wider than the environment axis: with no plan predicate, the IDs could also belong to a different plan or issue in the same project. It does stay project-scoped — both the store UPDATE and the cancel-func key are project-qualified — so it never crossed projects.

## The fix

Confine the lookup to the plan and environment just authorized, and reject an ID that does not resolve within that scope rather than letting it fall through. Rejecting matters: the cancel is driven by the requested IDs, so adding the filter alone would have left a filtered-out ID still being canceled.

`Environment` and `PlanUID` already exist on `FindTaskRunMessage` and ride the `LEFT JOIN task` the query already performs, so this adds no round trips — the handler makes the same number of database calls as before. `task` carries `idx_task_plan_id_environment ON task(project, plan_id, environment)`, an exact prefix match for the two added predicates.

`BatchSkipTasks` derives its environment from the task rows for the same reason, so this brings the sibling in line. I deliberately did not copy its shape of looping the permission check once per distinct environment: the pre-existing name-consistency loop already forces a single stage per batch, so one check provably suffices, and `canUserCancelEnvironmentTaskRun` is the expensive call in this handler.

Also merges the two duplicate parse loops over `request.TaskRuns`, which is where most of the deletion comes from.

## Behavior change

Two request shapes that previously re

title: fix(api): scope DiffSchema and UpdateDatabaseCatalog to the named resource's project
body:
## What

The ACL interceptor authorizes exactly **one** resource name per request, picked by field-name convention: `parent`, else `name`, else `resource`, else `project`, else — for `Create`/`Update`/`Remove`/`Test` — the nested `<snake_case(resource)>.name`. Anything else in the request body is invisible to it. Two v1 methods paid for that, in opposite directions.

**`DiffSchema` (T2)** names both a database and a changelog, and the changelog may belong to another project. Only the database was authorized, so a caller could read schema out of a project they hold no permission on. The handler now confines the changelog target to the source's project before any read.

Naming the database is not enough on its own: changelog ids are globally unique, and both changelog reads fetched by `(instance, id)` without the database, so a foreign id could ride under a database the caller owns and return that project's schema through its sync history. Both lookups are now scoped by `DatabaseName`, matching `ChangelogService.GetChangelog`. (Caught in review by Codex.)

**`UpdateDatabaseCatalog` (T19)** carries its target as `catalog.name`, but the convention derives `database_catalog` from the method suffix, finds no such field, and falls back to workspace scope. `bb.databaseCatalogs.update` was checked against the workspace no matter which database was named — and a Project Owner, whose role carries that permission, was denied. The interceptor now reads `catalog.name`; the route resolver already drops the trailing `/catalog`.

## Why these two

A sweep of all 216 v1 RPCs found 24 whose body names a resource the interceptor never authorizes. The other 22 are already closed downstream — `CreatePlan`/`UpdatePlan`, the three `Release` RPCs, `BatchCreateRevisions`, `CreateAccessGrant`, the `SavedQuery` writes, `CreateIssue`, `UpdateIssueComment`, `TestWebhook` and `GetQueryHistory` compare the second resource's project to the authorized one; `BatchRunTasks`, `BatchSkipTasks` and `CreateRollout` re-derive it from the parent; `UpdateDatabase`/`BatchUpdateDatabases` are special-cased in the interceptor itself.

These fixes are deliberately local rather than a general interceptor change: the resource a caller names must belong to the project they were authorized on, which is also the only thing a cross-project diff could have meant. The class stays latent — see *Follow-ups*.

## Breaking Changes

1. **`DiffSchema` rejects a cross-project changelog target** (`NOT_FOUND`). This is the vulnerability; any caller relying on it was reading another project's schema.
2. **`DiffSchema` rejects a soft-deleted database or an archived instance** (`NOT_FOUND`), where it previously succeeded. The new gate resolves databases with the default `ShowDeleted`, matching every sibling project-ownership check (`validateSpecs`, `validateAccessGrantTargets`, `CheckRelease`). `GetDBSchema` has no deleted filter, so these diffs did work before.
3. **`UpdateDatabaseCatalog` authorization moves f

+	t.Helper()
+	ctx := context.WithValue(context.Background(), common.WorkspaceIDContextKey, "default")
+	container := testcontainer.GetTestPgContainer(ctx, t)
+	t.Cleanup(func() { container.Close(ctx) })
+	db := container.GetDB()
+	require.NoError(t, migrator.MigrateSchema(ctx, db))
+	_, err := db.ExecContext(ctx, `
+		INSERT INTO workspace (resource_id) VALUES ('default');
+		INSERT INTO project (resource_id, workspace, name) VALUES
+			('project-a', 'default', 'Project A'),
+			('project-b', 'default', 'Project B');
+	`)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	pgURL := fmt.Sprintf("host=%s port=%s user=postgres password=root-password database=postgres", container.GetHost(), container.GetPort())
+	stores, err := store.New(ctx, pgURL, false)
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+	t.Cleanup(func() { require.NoError(t, stores.Close()) })
+
+	// A workspace-level instance whose databases sit in different projects: the
+	// shape that lets one name reach across a project boundary.
+	instanceID := "shared-instance"
+	_, err = stores.CreateInstance(ctx, &store.InstanceMessage{
+		ResourceID: instanceID,
+		Workspace:  "default",
+		Metadata: &storepb.Instance{
+			Engine: storepb.Engine_POSTGRES,
+			DataSources: []*storepb.DataSource{{
+				Id:   "admin",
+				Type: storepb.DataSourceType_ADMIN,
+			}},
+		},
+	})
+	require.NoError(t, err)
+
+	for databaseName, projectID := range map[string]string{"app-a": "project-a", "app-b": "project-b"} {
+		_, err = stores.UpsertDatabase(ctx, &store.DatabaseMessage{
+			InstanceID:   instanceID,
+			DatabaseName: databaseName,
+			ProjectID:    projectID,
+			Metadata:     &storepb.DatabaseMetadata{},
+		})
+		require.NoError(t, err)
+		require.NoError(t, stores.UpsertDBSchema(ctx, instanceID, databaseName,
+			&storepb.DatabaseSchemaMetadata{Name: databaseName}, &storepb.DatabaseConfig{}, nil))
+	}
+
+	// The foreign changelog must exist, or the cross-project case would fail
+	// for the wrong reason and still pass.
+	changelogByDatabase := map[string]string{}
+	for _, databaseName := range []string{"app-a", "app-b"} {
+		changelogID, err := stores.CreateChangelog(ctx, &store.ChangelogMessage{
+			InstanceID:   instanceID,
+			DatabaseName: databaseName,
+			Payload:      &storepb.ChangelogPayload{},
+			Status:       store.ChangelogStatusDone,
+		})
+		require.NoError(t, err)
+		changelogByDatabase[databaseName] = changelogID
+	}
+
+	return ctx, stores, instanceID, changelogByDatabase

title: chore: bump omni to the strict doris/starrocks parsers (BYT-10084/10085)
body:
## What

Bumps omni from the #400-era pin to current main (044f516d), bringing in the doris/starrocks trailing-token swallow fix series (bytebase/omni#401–#403, #406) plus the Oracle constraint_state support (bytebase/omni#399 was already included upstream of the old pin's successor).

**Why it matters**: with the old pin, a statement like `SELECT a FROM secret xx yy zz` silently truncated to its valid prefix and *ran*, and malformed statements could yield empty query spans — past masking and table-level ACL checks. Strict `Parse` now reports such input as a syntax error, and `GetQuerySpan` fails closed. The whole enforcement chain (span extractor → `base.GetQuerySpan` → `queryRetry`) propagates the error, so the query is refused before execution.

## bytebase-side adjustments

- **doris**: handle the new `ast.GroupedQuery` wrapper (repeated trailing clause groups, parenthesized WITH scope boundaries) in the read-only validator and the AST query-type classifier — `(SELECT 1 LIMIT 1) LIMIT 2` stays a read-only SELECT.
- **starrocks**: handle top-level `ast.ParenSelect` (statement-level parenthesized queries are newly accepted) in the same two places, and recurse through parenthesized set-op arms in the INTO OUTFILE export gate — `SELECT 1 UNION (SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE "s3://...")` must not pass as read-only (this was a live bypass).
- **starrocks**: flip the LATERAL VIEW smoke test to expect a syntax error — StarRocks 3.4.10 has no Hive-style LATERAL VIEW (container-verified); the old parser only "accepted" it by silently truncating at `LATERAL`. Doris LATERAL VIEW is engine-valid and now actually parsed (bytebase/omni#406) instead of being truncated out of lineage.
- New `query_span_fail_closed_test.go` on both engines pins the contract: trailing junk fails the span extraction, and the newly accepted paren/grouped shapes still report their table reads.

## Verification

- `backend/plugin/parser/doris`, `backend/plugin/parser/starrocks`, `backend/plugin/db/starrocks` suites green.
- `backend/api/v1` MCP read-only clamp tests green.
- Full `./backend/...` build green.
- Every engine-behavior claim above was verified against live Doris 3.1.4 / StarRocks 3.4.10 containers on the omni side.

title: fix(wif): bind workload identity tokens to an audience and a subject
body:
Closes [BYT-10151](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10151). Stacked on #21338; the diff here is this PR alone.

## The problem

`ValidateToken` checks `aud` only when `allowed_audiences` is non-empty, and `matchSubjectPattern` treats an empty pattern as a match. Nothing sets either field for a GitHub or GitLab identity: both create-form presets ship a blank audience, the field sits under Advanced Settings, and the write-time validator added in #21309 returns early for those two providers. The shipped default produces an identity bound to a subject but not to an audience, so any token the issuer signs for that repository is accepted, whatever it was minted for.

Reproduced end to end against a real server before the fix: a token addressed to `https://some-other-saas.example.com` was exchanged for a working Bytebase access token, and the same token was refused once an audience was configured.

`aud` and `sub` do different jobs. `sub` says who minted the token; `aud` says who it was minted **for**. With `aud` unchecked, a token the customer's own workflow minted for AWS, Vault, or npm, and handed to that vendor over the wire, is also a working Bytebase credential.

## What changes

**The exchange fails closed.** The "skip if no audiences" guard is gone: an empty list matches no token, and a blank stored entry no longer binds one. A row holding `[""]` used to authenticate a token whose `aud` claim was the empty string, because the comparison was exact and go-jose reads `"aud": ""` as one empty audience. `matchSubjectPattern` now refuses whatever the write-time subject rule refuses, so a row stored before that rule existed stops admitting every repository behind a broad prefix.

**One validator, extended rather than joined.** #21309 added `validateWorkloadIdentityConfig` with a per-provider switch that validated OIDC and returned early for GitHub and GitLab. Every provider reaches the same token exchange, so every provider now carries the same requirements: an issuer whose keys can be fetched, at least one non-blank audience, and a subject pattern outside the matches-everything class. The subject rule lives in one predicate, `wif.ValidateSubjectPattern`, which both the write path and the matcher call.

A trailing `*` is a prefix test, so `repo:*`, `repo:acme*` and `r*` are the same hole as `*`: in the two subject vocabularies Bytebase models, a wildcard must pin at least the owner segment. A pattern that spells a marker out names its own vocabulary. A prefix that stops inside one, like `r*` or `project*`, needs the row to say which provider it is, and a row that declares none predates that requirement, so it is judged against both markers rather than neither. That is the population the migration repairs, and it is the one a legacy broad pattern would have let through. Outside both vocabularies the wildcard is the operator's call, so a generic OIDC subject like `system:serviceaccount:prod:*` is still accepted.

title: refactor: simplify MCP capability handling
body:
## Summary

- Use `*storepb.MCPSetting` directly throughout MCP policy enforcement.
- Remove custom MCP setting wrappers, raw JSON inspection, unreadable-state fields, and duplicate frontend state models.
- Classify MCP ceilings directly from the stored protocol value.
- Keep enforcement reads uncached so policy changes take effect immediately.
- Use the standard setting update and upsert path for MCP settings.
- Seed newly created workspaces with `READ_ONLY`.

## Compatibility

The MCP capability configuration UX has never been exposed in production. Therefore, this PR does not migrate the legacy workspace-profile capability or backfill MCP setting rows.

Existing workspaces without an MCP setting resolve to `READ_WRITE` during policy enforcement, preserving their previous MCP behavior without persisting a row. Newly created workspaces explicitly persist `READ_ONLY`.

`SettingService.GetSetting` continues to return `NotFound` when the row does not exist. An update with `allow_missing` creates the MCP row, using `READ_WRITE` as the compatibility base for fields omitted by the update mask.

Schema evolution should be handled through explicit migrations when new fields are introduced rather than runtime raw JSON preservation.

## Behavior

| Workspace state | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Existing workspace without an MCP setting | Enforce `READ_WRITE` without persisting a row |
| Newly created workspace | Persist and enforce `READ_ONLY` |
| Missing row updated with `allow_missing` | Create the row using `READ_WRITE` as the update base |
| Recognized stored capability | Enforce the stored capability |
| `CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED` or unsupported capability | Fail closed |
| Malformed MCP setting payload | Return an error and fail closed |
| Legacy workspace-profile capability | Ignore; the production UX never exposed it |

## Implementation

- Remove `MCPSettings`, `RawSettingValue`, and MCP-specific raw JSON helpers.
- Remove `capability_unreadable` and the separate unreadable ceiling verdict.
- Use `storepb.MCPSetting` directly in the MCP, OAuth, and API enforcement paths.
- Simplify the frontend to operate directly on supported MCP capability modes.
- Use the normal `SettingService.UpdateSetting` flow for MCP partial updates.
- Remove the MCP-specific atomic update, row-locking, and audit before-image logic.
- Remove the MCP backfill migration and its migration tests.
- Keep new workspace creation explicitly seeded with `READ_ONLY`.

## Test Plan

- [x] Existing workspaces without an MCP row resolve to `READ_WRITE`.
- [x] Legacy-profile-only workspaces resolve to `READ_WRITE`.
- [x] New workspaces persist `READ_ONLY`.
- [x] Missing-row partial updates with `allow_missing` use the `READ_WRITE` compatibility base.
- [x] Unspecified, unsupported, and malformed stored values fail closed.
- [x] Focused MCP API and OAuth tests pass.
- [x] MCP backend integration tests pass.
- [x] Proto format, lint, and gen

title: feat(api): require re-authentication to change your own credentials
body:
Closes T10 in [`docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md). Design: [`docs/design/reauthenticate-credential-changes.md`](docs/design/reauthenticate-credential-changes.md).

## What and why

A signed-in caller could rewrite their own password, TOTP secret, and recovery codes without proving they still control the credential being replaced. A stolen access token expires within an hour, but nothing stopped it being *spent* on a permanent replacement credential first.

Every self-service mutation of live authentication material now carries a `CredentialProof`:

| Proof | Accepted when |
|---|---|
| `current_password` | always for `ChangePassword`; for factor-touching methods only when no live MFA exists |
| `otp_code` | a live TOTP factor exists |
| `recovery_code` | a live factor exists; single-use |
| `email_code` | Bytebase Cloud, and only when no live factor exists |

Each proof claims a login-attempt slot from the same T9 buckets the login path uses, so no proof channel is an unbounded guessing oracle.

**Factor-touching methods refuse the password while a live factor exists.** `ResetPassword` mints a password from mailbox possession alone, so accepting one at `DisableMFA` would let a stolen session plus a mailbox strip the second factor. `DisableMFA` asks for a proof only when there *is* a live factor, so an abandoned enrollment can still be cancelled; its admin path is unchanged (an admin recovering a locked-out user cannot know the factor being removed — `bb.users.update` and the audit log are the control).

**`email_code` is Cloud-only**, via the new `UserService.RequestReauthCode`. It is bootstrap proof for an account with nothing else to prove, which on Cloud is every account without MFA, since Cloud accounts never have a caller-chosen password. This is scope, not capability: self-hosted keeps an administrator who can reset a password, which is the recovery route there.

**Recovery codes are spent by the verification itself**, with the spend as a predicate on the row (`store.ConsumeRecoveryCode`), rather than edited into the cached user and left for a caller to persist. Two requests racing the same code now resolve to exactly one winner, and `EnableMFA` — which writes nothing of its own — no longer desynchronizes the user cache from the row.

This change needs **no migration**.

## Breaking Changes

Existing API clients of these RPCs will start receiving `InvalidArgument` until they send a proof:

- **`UserService.ChangePassword`** — `credential` is now required.
- **`UserService.ConfirmRecoveryCodes`** — `credential` is now required, and first-time enrollment must also send a fresh `otp_code` (promotion, not verification, is the moment MFA starts gating logins, and the recovery-code download screen routinely outlives one ~30s TOTP window).
- **`UserService.EnableMFA`** — `credential` is required whenever a reusable proof exists: a rotation, or a first-time enrollment on an account that has a password. It mu

title: docs: timestamp display — work queues vs history views
body:
Design doc only — no implementation. D1–D4 and D6 are decided; D5 and D7 (and the doc's "Open items awaiting ruling" section) are marked proposed — reviewer input welcome on those.

Resolves the display question behind [BYT-10140](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10140/issue-history-show-absolute-date-time-by-default-instead-of-x-days-ago) (relative "x days ago" hides exactly the precision an audit reading needs; the shared `HumanizeTs` component renders relative-forever on every surface except the audit log) and the display side of [BYT-10023](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10023/scheduled-rollout-neither-the-ui-nor-the-docs-state-which-timezone-the) (the scheduled-rollout time never states its timezone anywhere visible).

## The principle

**A surface is either a work queue or a history view, and that classification decides its time display.** Future-pointing times are a third kind.

- **Work queues** (issue list, plan list, release list, feeds, sync/meta): GitHub parity — relative under 30 days, then absolute date only ("Jul 12"; year added cross-year), full date-time in the tooltip. The switching logic already exists as dead code (`humanizeTs()` + `RELATIVE_THRESHOLD_MS`); the implementation is wiring it into `HumanizeTs`.
- **History views**: absolute always, in two precision tiers (D7): full seconds + timezone where the time is evidence — the audit log (its export must match the screen) and single-record detail views, which already render this today — and compact date + hh:mm on the scannable embedded lists (changelog, revisions, task-run history). *A history row orients; a history record testifies.*
- **Operational times** (scheduled rollouts, expirations): absolute with an **explicit timezone in the visible string**, minute precision — relative wording ("in 7 hours") hides that a timezone question even exists, which is how BYT-10023 nearly fired a production rollout seven hours early. Time *pickers* (the input side) are explicitly deferred.

Every reduced display — relative, date-only, or compact — carries the full date-time + timezone tooltip (D6).

## Why not the alternatives

- Absolute-always on queues kills the freshness reading a queue exists for.
- A GitLab-style user preference is settings machinery with a wrong default for whoever hasn't toggled it.
- GitHub-style *everywhere* leaves history views hover-per-row for exact times — the original complaint.

The research section surveys 9 products (GitHub and GitLab verified against primary sources; Linear, Jira, Slack, Sentry, Stripe, CloudTrail, Datadog from product knowledge): mature products consistently split by reading mode — queues/feeds relative, records/audit absolute — rather than picking one global convention.

The doc also inventories the three inconsistent absolute-time families already in the product (locale-aware w/ tz, fixed dayjs strings w/o tz, ad-hoc `toLocaleDateString`) and the two dead half-implementations of this exact design, and adds **Work Queue S

title: fix(rollout): show the engine's error on a failed task run
body:
Closes BOT-116. Follow-up to BYT-10132.

## What happened

A BigQuery deploy failed and the reporter could only find out why by reading the server's Docker log. The issue page showed a failed task whose entire content was:

```
Latest · ✗ Failed · 2 hours ago · users/ · 4.8s
  Database Sync   3.3s
  1  16:45:11.591  ✓ Completed
```

Their statement was wrong — the table had no `created_at` column — but nothing in the product said so. Reproduced end to end against a live BigQuery instance.

## Two independent causes

**The BigQuery driver discarded `db.ExecuteOptions`.** It took the parameter as `_`, so it never called `CreateTaskRunLog` and the task run log held only the surrounding sync steps. It now logs one command spanning the whole statement plus a response carrying the engine's error and `NumDMLAffectedRows`, mirroring the snowflake driver, which likewise submits a single job for the whole statement.

**`TaskRun.detail` was rendered nowhere.** It carried the same error for every engine and the API returned it; no component read it. A failed run now shows it.

The second is not redundant with the first. Several drivers — cassandra, databricks, elasticsearch, hive, redis, spanner and starrocks among them — also write no command-response entry, so for them the log can never carry the cause. The alert renders whenever the run failed rather than only when the log lacks an error of its own, because the log loads asynchronously and that condition would flip after first paint.

Both the latest-run panel and the task-run history sheet render it through one `TaskRunErrorAlert`, so they cannot drift. The history sheet's header comment already claimed *"the expanded body shows the full error"* as its reason for hiding the collapsed teaser when expanded; that is now true rather than aspirational.

## Also fixed here

`status.Statistics` is nil whenever the `jobs.get` response carried no statistics block — `Job.setStatistics` returns early on that (`cloud.google.com/go/bigquery@v1.79.0` `job.go:1259`) — and a `, ok` on the `Details` assertion guards the type, not the pointer. All three dereference sites in the file now go through `statisticsOf`, including the two in `QueryConn` and `dryRunQuery` that predate this branch. Without it a migration that actually applied could panic, which the task executor recovers into a failed task with no changelog: the inverse of the bug this fixes.

## Not fixed here

The other seven drivers still take `db.ExecuteOptions` as `_`, so their task run logs keep reading as a clean "Database Sync Completed" for a failed deploy even though the alert now carries the cause. That sweep belongs in its own change; this one closes the reporter's path.

## Testing

Measured against a live BigQuery instance, through the registered driver with an `ExecuteOptions` that captures log entries:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| failing `INSERT` | 0 log entries | `COMMAND_EXECUTE` + `COMMAND_RESPONSE`, error `googleapi: Error 400: Column

title: fix(mcp): withhold Allow unless the consent page holds a served ceiling
body:
## The hole

Every failure of the consent page's policy read landed it on the generic "access
your account" card with **Allow enabled**, and the POST then succeeded. A
transient outage was enough. The page issued an MCP grant without disclosing what
the grant was worth.

Live, on `origin/main`, against a workspace whose real ceiling is `READ_ONLY`,
with only the `GetMCPInfo` request blocked:

> Authorization Request
> This application will be able to: **Access your Bytebase account with your permissions**
> [Deny] [**Allow**]

That sentence is not true of any session this server issues. Every grant is an
MCP grant, and the workspace ceiling decides what one is worth.

The same refusal also killed the workspace MCP settings drawer at exactly the
moment an admin needed it — while repairing an unreadable ceiling.

Both come from one line: `GetMCPInfo` refused whole on
`MCPCeilingUnreadable` / `MCPCeilingUnserved`.

## Why refusing was wrong

The mode contents do not come from the stored row. `modes`, `methods` and
`engines` are resolved from the compiled descriptors and the enforcement code,
and they are the whole reason either surface calls this method. The refusal
withheld the comparison from the one admin who has to repair the row, and left
the consent page with no policy to disclose.

(`capability` and `ignore_masking_exemptions` *do* come from the row — that is
what carries the state to the client. An earlier draft of this comment claimed
the response held nothing from the row at all; pre-review caught it.)

## What changed

**Backend.** The three refusing ceilings are answered. A new `OUTPUT_ONLY`
`MCPInfo.policy_unreadable` carries the one state the number cannot, following
BOT-100's data-not-status-code precedent. It is named for the consequence: a
wrong JSON type on *any* field fails the whole unmarshal, so a malformed
`ignore_masking_exemptions` sets it over a perfectly readable capability. It is
therefore wider than `MCPSetting.capability_unreadable` and not interchangeable
with it — see "One field, two row shapes" below. A ceiling that parsed but no
mode serves needs no field: the number survives on `capability` and `modes` has
no row for it.

A failed read still refuses, with `CodeUnavailable`. It is the one verdict with
no ceiling to describe, and answering with an empty one would read as a stored
value nobody can resolve — which an admin repairs rather than a retry clearing.

**Frontend.** `readConsentCeiling` reads the response into five states, and
Allow renders in exactly one: a ceiling the server serves *and* this bundle can
name. The disclosure is the consent, so approving against an unnamed policy is
agreement to nothing.

| state | when | Allow | way out |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | server serves it, bundle names it | **yes** | — |
| `unknown` | the read failed or timed out | no | Check again |
| `unreadable` | the row resolves to no ceiling | no | repair the policy |
| `unserved` | resolved, no mode serves it | no | admin pi

title: refactor(api): move password and MFA changes onto their own methods
body:
## What

Moves the account credential lifecycle off `UpdateUser`'s field mask and flags onto six methods on `UserService`. **A 1-1 functionality mapping** — no new capabilities, no credential proofs, no re-authentication, no new stored state.

| Old | New |
| --- | --- |
| `UpdateUser` mask `password` (self) | `ChangePassword(name, new_password)` |
| `UpdateUser` mask `password` (admin, cross-user) | unchanged — stays on `UpdateUser` |
| `regenerate_temp_mfa_secret: true` | `StartMFAEnrollment` → `{otp_secret, recovery_codes, expire_time}` |
| `otp_code` (validate only) | `EnableMFA(name, otp_code)` |
| mask `mfa_enabled = true` | `ConfirmRecoveryCodes(name)` |
| mask `mfa_enabled = false` | `DisableMFA(name)` |
| `regenerate_recovery_codes: true` | `RegenerateRecoveryCodes` then `ConfirmRecoveryCodes` |

## Why

`UpdateUser` was one method doing six jobs. Its response meant different things depending on which flag was set — two of the seven code paths answered with enrollment secrets and the rest did not — and it could not state who may call it, because "the caller" and "an administrator" needed different answers per mask. The MCP and audit annotations are per method, so all of it sat behind one classification.

The knock-on was worse: because the enrollment secrets came back on the `User` resource, every read had to remember to drop them, and the client had to carry them across responses that didn't. Both of those disappear here.

## What is preserved exactly

Every check moves across verbatim: end-user-only passwords, the same-password rejection, `validatePassword`, best-effort session revocation on a password change, the `require_2fa` guard with its workspace-admin bypass, the 5-minute enrollment window, and the SaaS cross-user refusal.

The three-step enrollment stays three calls. `EnableMFA` verifies and writes nothing; `ConfirmRecoveryCodes` is what makes the factor live. Collapsing them would show the user recovery codes before their authenticator is known-good, and promote a factor whose codes were never saved — a UX change rather than an API one.

## Breaking

- `UpdateUserRequest.otp_code`, `.regenerate_temp_mfa_secret`, `.regenerate_recovery_codes` — reserved.
- `User.temp_otp_secret`, `.temp_recovery_codes`, `.temp_otp_secret_created_time` — reserved. The secrets now exist only in the responses of the two methods that mint them, which retires `convertToUserMintingMFAEnrollment` and the client-side `keepMfaEnrollment` carry-over.
- `User.mfa_enabled` is now `OUTPUT_ONLY`.
- Self-service password changes through `UpdateUser` are refused with a pointer to `ChangePassword`; the administrator path is untouched.

## Testing

`./backend/api/...`, `./backend/server/` and `./backend/store/` pass; `golangci-lint run` reports 0 issues; 3816 frontend tests pass with `check` and `type-check` clean. The MCP classification inventory is regenerated and the six methods are added to the FORBIDDEN membership list with denial reasons; `auditRecordedFiel

title: feat(store): record when session and grant rows are issued
body:
## What

Adds `created_at` to the three token tables — `web_refresh_token`, `oauth2_authorization_code`, `oauth2_refresh_token` — and reads it back through the store layer. Also indexes the referencing side of the two foreign keys those tables carry.

Migration `3.22/0014##token_row_created_at.sql`.

## Why

**The column.** These tables record when a row *expires* but not when it was *issued*. That is a gap for anyone debugging an account: "when was this session handed out?" is currently unanswerable, and `expires_at` only implies it if you also know the refresh duration in force at issue time, which is per-workspace and can change. It also lets an account-level event be ordered against the rows that existed when it happened. Existing rows default to migration time, the earliest issue time consistent with their still being here.

**The indexes.** PostgreSQL indexes the referenced side of a foreign key, never the referencing side, so both cascades on these tables are sequential scans until they are indexed:

- `user_email` references `principal(email) ON UPDATE CASCADE` — every account email change rewrites the rows keyed on it. `web_refresh_token` already had this index; the two OAuth tables are catching up.
- `client_id` references `oauth2_client(client_id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, and the data cleaner deletes stale clients in bulk on a schedule. It answers no query on its own — every lookup pairs it with the primary key — so this is purely cascade support.

## Testing

`go test ./backend/migrator/` (including `TestLatestVersion`) and `./backend/store/` pass; `golangci-lint run` reports 0 issues. Nothing reads `created_at` for a decision yet, so there is nothing behavioral here to assert beyond the schema itself.

## Note

Split out of the re-authentication work in `docs/design/reauthenticate-credential-changes.md` so the schema can land and be reviewed on its own. The follow-up PR consumes `created_at` as a backstop at token-consume time.

title: fix(frontend): keep session polling from redirecting to 403
body:
## What changed

- Mark the periodic `GetCurrentUser` request from `AuthGate` as silent.
- Forward the silent context through `fetchCurrentUser`.
- Keep login and signup requests non-silent by default.
- Add regression tests for the store and polling path.

## Why

`AuthGate` periodically revalidates the current session. A background
`PermissionDenied` response could reach the global authentication interceptor
and redirect an active SQL Editor to `/403`.

Silent polling still refreshes expired tokens and triggers the in-place
session-expired sign-in flow when refresh fails, but it no longer navigates away
from the current page or emits background error notifications.

Follow-up for [BYT-9972](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-9972/sql-editor-redirects-to-recursive-403-after-session-or-network-change).

title: fix(approval): classify BigQuery statements so sql_type approval rules match (BYT-10131)
body:
Fixes BYT-10131.

## What was wrong

A workspace approval rule that names `statement.sql_type` never matched a BigQuery change. The customer's rule was `!(statement.sql_type in ["INSERT","UPDATE","DELETE"]) && resource.environment_id == "prod"`, and their prod `ALTER TABLE` reported "No approval required".

The chain:

1. BigQuery is outside `common.EngineSupportStatementReport`, so the statement report check returns SUCCESS with no report body (`statement_report_executor.go:73`). That is two of the four green checks the issue showed.
2. `statement.sql_type` was populated only from that report body, so the variable was absent from the CEL activation.
3. `cel.Env.PartialVars` auto-marks every declared-but-absent variable as unknown, so the expression evaluates to `*types.Unknown`, not an error. `matchRulesForSource` then does `out.Equal(True).Value().(bool)`; an unknown fails that type assertion, so the rule is skipped with no error and no log.

The `not in` is not the cause — a positive `statement.sql_type in [...]` rule fails identically. No rule naming `statement.sql_type` could match a BigQuery change, in either direction.

## What this changes

Classify from the parser instead of from the summary report. omni already carries a full GoogleSQL AST, so `googlesql` gains `ParseStatements` and `GetStatementTypes`, registered through `googlesql.Register` so **BigQuery and Spanner both get them**. The approval evaluator falls back to that classification whenever a target has no summary report. Engines with no statement-type handler are unchanged, because `expandCELVars` already no-ops on an empty type list.

`MERGE` gets a `StatementType` value. Without one it mapped to `UNSPECIFIED`, so a rule selecting DML would have silently skipped a statement that writes rows — the same bypass this PR exists to close. It is also added to `base.IsAllDML`, which `computeNeedDump` calls.

Deliberately **not** adding BigQuery to `EngineSupportStatementReport`: that path also requires `ExtractChangedResources` and `CountAffectedRows`, and without them the plan check hard-fails. Decoupling classification from the report is the smaller and safer change.

## Behavior change on upgrade

Not flagged breaking — it starts enforcing what the user configured — but worth knowing: a workspace with a `statement.sql_type` rule and BigQuery or Spanner databases will begin requiring approvals that were previously skipped in silence. Risk level also becomes correct for those engines (an `ALTER TABLE` moves LOW → MODERATE), so `risk.level` rules change too.

## Known gaps, deliberately left

- **The hole is patched in one parser, not at the evaluator.** `statementTypesFromParser` still returns nil — leaving `sql_type` absent and the rule silently dropped — when the engine has no statement-type handler, when the sheet does not parse, or when it is over `common.MaxSheetCheckSize`. Six engines (Snowflake, StarRocks, Doris, CockroachDB, Trino, Cassandra) parse but cannot classify. The s

+		{"dml rule matches INSERT", dmlRule, "INSERT INTO `users` (id) VALUES (1);", true},
+		{"dml rule skips ALTER TABLE", dmlRule, "ALTER TABLE `users` ADD COLUMN status STRING;", false},
+		// MERGE writes rows, so a DML rule that names it must fire and the
+		// DDL rule must not. Only the googlesql engines emit MERGE today.
+		{"dml rule matches MERGE when named", mergeRule, mergeStatement, true},
+		{"ddl rule skips MERGE when named", ddlRuleWithMerge, mergeStatement, false},
+	}
+
+	for _, tt := range tests {
+		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			a := require.New(t)
+			statementTypes := statementTypesFromParser(storepb.Engine_BIGQUERY, tt.statement)
+			a.NotEmpty(statementTypes, "BigQuery must classify the statement without a summary report")
+
+			celVars := expandCELVars(map[string]any{
+				common.CELAttributeResourceEnvironmentID: "prod",
+				common.CELAttributeResourceProjectID:     "project",
+				common.CELAttributeResourceDBEngine:      storepb.Engine_BIGQUERY.String(),
+				common.CELAttributeStatementText:         tt.statement,
+			}, statementTypes, nil)
+
+			template, err := getApprovalTemplate(&storepb.WorkspaceApprovalSetting{
+				Rules: []*storepb.WorkspaceApprovalSetting_Rule{
+					{
+						Source:    storepb.WorkspaceApprovalSetting_Rule_CHANGE_DATABASE,
+						Condition: &expr.Expr{Expression: tt.expression},
+						Template:  &storepb.ApprovalTemplate{Title: "DDL Prod"},
+					},
+				},
+			}, storepb.WorkspaceApprovalSetting_Rule_CHANGE_DATABASE, celVars)
+			a.NoError(err)
+			if tt.wantMatch {
+				a.NotNil(template)
+				a.Equal("DDL Prod", template.Title)
+			} else {
+				a.Nil(template)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+// A sheet of N statements yields N type entries, all identical when the sheet
+// repeats one statement. Every rule is evaluated against every activation, so
+// without deduplication a large sheet costs tens of thousands of pointless
+// evaluations per target, multiplied again by a database group's target count.
+func TestExpandCELVarsDeduplicatesActivations(t *testing.T) {
+	a := require.New(t)
+	base := map[string]any{common.CELAttributeResourceProjectID: "project"}
+
+	repeated := make([]storepb.StatementType, 10000)
+	for i := range repeated {
+		repeated[i] = storepb.StatementType_INSERT
+	}
+	a.Len(expandCELVars(base, repeated, nil), 1)
+
+	// Distinct types survive, in first-seen order.
+	mixed := []storepb.StatementType{
+		storepb.StatementType_INSERT,
+		storepb.StatementType_ALTER_TABLE,
+		storepb.StatementType_INSERT,
+	}
+	got := expandCELVars(base, mixed, nil)
+	a.Len(got, 2)
+	a.Equal("INSERT", got[0][common.CELAttributeStatementSQLType])
+	a.Equal("ALTER_TABLE", got[1][common.CELAttributeStatementSQLType])
+
+	// Deduplication is over the (type, table) pair, not the type alone.
+	pairs := expandCELVars(base, mixed, []string{"users", "users", "orders"})
+	a.Len(pairs, 4)
+
+	// UNSPECIFIED collapses like any other value.
+	unspecified := []storepb.StatementType{
+		storepb.StatementType_STATEMENT_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED,
+		storepb.StatementType_STATEMENT_TYPE_UNSPECIFIED,
+	}
+	a.Len(expandCELVars(base, unspecified, nil), 1)
+}

title: feat: redesign the saved query share popover
body:
## What

Reworks the SQL Editor saved-query share popover (introduced unreleased in #21178) into the standard share-dialog shape, and fixes the level select rendering raw proto enum values ("1"/"2") in its trigger.

- **One row per grantee** with a per-row Viewer/Editor select and a remove button, plus a pinned static **Owner** row (with a "you" badge for the caller), replacing the level-scoped member picker that showed only one level's grantees at a time.
- **Staged adds**: picked accounts sit as chips until **Add** commits them at the invite level in one write — the BigQuery (Save) / Snowsight (Done) / Databricks (Add) confirm-the-add pattern. The level+Add controls exist only while people are staged; the invite level resets to Viewer per compose session. Row-level changes and removal stay per-action, like Docs/Databricks.
- **Picker exclusions**: `AccountMultiSelect` gains `excludeAccounts` (hides the caller, the creator, and current grantees) and `placeholder` props; the fetch over-fetches by the exclusion count so filtering cannot empty the pickable page, and a fully-excluded result shows the no-data state instead of a blank panel.
- **Compact header**: 14px `Share "title"` (title quoting per locale via a `share-title` key — ja uses 「」), "Shared with" demoted to a caption (`people-with-access`), and a separator before the link row.

## Why

The trigger bug came from Base UI's `SelectValue` serializing the raw value when given no render function (unlike Radix, which echoes the item label). The UX rework follows what per-object sharing looks like in BigQuery Studio, Snowsight, and Databricks SQL editor: a flat people list with per-person levels, and an explicit confirm on the add — none of them instant-apply the risky step.

## Hardening

A max-effort review produced 15 findings, all applied, notably:

- A load generation guard plus full state reset when `savedQuery` changes, so a popover instance surviving a switch between saved queries can never write one query's grants onto another (the backend etag is content-only, so two empty policies share an etag).
- Policy rewrites carry bindings at unknown levels through verbatim (forward-compat under version skew).
- Escape closes only the picker dropdown instead of dismissing the popover with the staged chips; focus re-homes after Add/remove; the grantee list carries an accessible name.
- `UserCell` gains real truncation (`min-w-0` + `truncate`); the level selects use `min-w-24` so long locale labels (vi-VN "Người chỉnh sửa") grow the trigger instead of overflowing; a failed policy read shows a message with a Refresh action instead of rendering nothing.
- `GranteeCell` renders through the shared `getMemberBinding` projection (now exported from `lib/memberBindings.ts`), and `getUserByIdentifier` tries the direct `users/{email}` map hit before its linear scan.

## Testing

- New `SavedQueryGrantEditor.test.tsx` (~20 tests: staged-add lifecycle, exclusions, Owner row, unknown-level carry-through, invi

title: feat(metrics): restrict endpoint to loopback by default
body:
## Summary

- restrict `/metrics` to actual IPv4 or IPv6 loopback peers by default
- add `--metrics-remote-access` as an explicit deployment-network escape hatch
- expose the same metrics behavior in SaaS and self-hosted deployments
- reject unauthorized scrapes before Prometheus collection and metadata queries

## Breaking Changes

Remote scrapers that connect directly to the Bytebase application listener now receive `404 Not Found` by default. Run an authenticated reverse proxy on the same host or Pod so it connects to Bytebase over loopback. As a temporary compatibility measure, `--metrics-remote-access` restores remote access but delegates all authorization to the deployment network.

## Testing

- `go test -v -count=1 ./backend/server -run "^(TestMetrics|TestCollisionMetrics)"`
- `go test -v -count=1 ./backend/bin/server/cmd -run "^TestResolveProfileUsesServerDataConfiguration$"`
- `golangci-lint run --allow-parallel-runners --new-from-rev=origin/main`
- `go build -ldflags "-w -s" -p=16 -o ./bytebase-build/bytebase ./backend/bin/server/main.go`

Repository-wide lint also runs but currently reports pre-existing `revive` violations outside this diff.
