title: refactor: unify self-host and SaaS sample instance management
body:
## Summary

Unify self-host and SaaS sample instances behind a shared lifecycle interface while keeping their provisioning details in separate implementations.

- Introduce a shared `sample.Manager` interface and select exactly one implementation at server startup based on deployment mode.
- Move self-host and SaaS behavior into independent `sample/selfhost` and `sample/saas` packages.
- Consolidate lifecycle persistence into `sample_instance_setup` with one row per workspace, relational lifecycle fields, and implementation-owned JSONB payloads.
- Migrate existing SaaS sample lifecycle records from `sample_project_instance`.
- Preserve the existing two-instance self-host experience and legacy static sample compatibility while using random IDs for newly created samples.
- Unify cleanup, metadata registration, seed loading, instance lifecycle handling, and restore validation.
- Expose per-instance expiration information through the actuator API so the frontend can display sample removal warnings.

## Why

The previous self-host and SaaS implementations had separate managers, stores, runners, and lifecycle behavior. This duplicated orchestration and made the two sample flows harder to maintain.

The new design shares only the stable lifecycle contract. Each deployment mode still owns its provisioning payload and implementation details. Because the server selects one manager at startup, the persistence layer does not need a deployment-type discriminator.

## Test Plan

- [x] Run sample manager tests
- [x] Run sample lifecycle store tests
- [x] Run migration tests
- [x] Run relevant actuator and instance service tests
- [x] Run `golangci-lint`
- [x] Build the Bytebase server

title: feat(mcp): show the workspace ceiling on the consent page, and consolidate the connect panel (P1b 1b-6, part 2)
body:
P1b 1b-6, part 2 of two. Part 1 (#21236) is merged, so this now targets `main` and the diff shown is part 2 alone.

**Screenshots:** [the consent states and the connect panel](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/1998569e-bbf1-40d2-b081-cef2b3d628bc). Local copies in `CLAUDE_BB/screenshots/mcp-1b6-consent/`.

## What landed

**The consent page knows the ceiling.** Every grant this server issues is an MCP grant, so the workspace's ceiling already decides the POST that consent produces — `refuseConsentByCeiling` in `backend/api/oauth2/authorize.go`. The page now says the same thing before the person presses Approve: the mode, one line per thing the ceiling decides, the masking line when the workspace ignores exemptions, and what the audit log will hold. The mode-contents drawer from part 1 opens from here too, so someone approving a client can read the actual method list rather than trust five bullets.

**A disabled workspace gets its own state.** No Approve, no Deny — the grant is not on offer. It names the setting, says nothing was connected, and says a workspace admin is who changes it. The 5a backend refusal page stays as the fallback for a POST that arrives anyway.

**One connect panel.** "Option 1: JSON Configuration", "Option 2: CLI Commands" and the first-prompt block were three sections for one job. They collapse into a tabbed "Connect a client" panel, with Claude Desktop and JSON joining the CLI tabs — a client configured by file is no longer a different section from a client configured by command.

**`mcpPolicy` and `MCPModeContentsSheet` move to `components/mcp/`.** Two independent consumers now — the settings route and the auth route — which is the promotion rule in `frontend/AGENTS.md`, not a speculative one.

## The copy bug this caught

The PDF's disabled state says "This attempt was recorded in the audit log." That is true of the *backend* page, which renders after a POST the server refused and recorded. It is false here: this state stops the person before anything is posted, so no row exists yet. The line now reads "Any attempt to connect anyway is recorded in the audit log", and the component carries the constraint so the next edit does not put the claim back.

## RED evidence

Four new cases in `OAuth2ConsentPage.test.tsx`, one per ceiling state plus the fallback. The one worth checking:

| Claim | How it was made to fail | What failed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A disabled ceiling offers nothing to approve | Replaced the `capability === DISABLED` branch condition with `false` | `a disabled ceiling offers nothing to approve`: the page rendered the Approve button |

## Changed since first push

**The masking line no longer promises a restriction where masking does not run.** `MCPConsentCeiling` rendered it from `info.ignoreMaskingExemptions` alone and never read `info.dataMaskingAvailable`, which sits on the same message. title: feat(mcp): the MCP access policy settings surface, and the unreadable-ceiling repair (P1b 1b-6, part 1)
body:
P1b 1b-6, part 1 of two. Moves the MCP capability ceiling off the workspace General page and onto `/integration/mcp`, beside the connect panel it governs. Part 2 (#21237) stacks on this branch.

**The dev gate stays.** `isDev()` wraps the access-policy section exactly as it wrapped the old General-page section. Un-gating is its own flip PR, after BYT-10061.

**Screenshots:** [every state, with what to check in each](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/4a9bc0f1-2cfc-4318-b70c-4c6c09a71f73). Local copies in `CLAUDE_BB/screenshots/mcp-1b6/`.

> **Changed since first push.** The new-workspace `READ_ONLY` default was **removed from this PR** and moves to the un-gate flip. Seeding it here would clamp every new *production* workspace to read-only while the only console control that raises it is still behind `isDev()` — a silent tightening with no UI remedy. The default and the control now ship together. A pre-review pass also found a P1 in the BOT-100 fix itself; details at the bottom.

## What landed

**The access policy surface.** Three mode cards side by side, no Custom card — laid out abreast so the modes compare at a glance, which is the point Peter's mock makes and a vertical radio list does not. The "Ignore masking exemptions" toggle with its education copy. A drawer showing what a mode actually serves: every method it reaches, how deep read-only goes on each engine, and which of the three masking states each engine is in — all resolved live from `WorkspaceService.GetMCPInfo`, never from a list in the frontend. The drawer highlights the WRITE class, so an admin comparing Read-only against Read-write reads the delta directly (57 + 40 = 97, live counts).

**BOT-100.** A stored capability this build cannot read arrived as `CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED`, indistinguishable from "never configured". The page showed **Read-write** over a workspace refusing every MCP connection. Worse: because Read-write was already the displayed value, picking Read-write did not dirty the form, so the row could not be repaired *to* Read-write at all.

The fix is one OUTPUT_ONLY field, `bool MCPSetting.capability_unreadable`. The page says the stored ceiling cannot be read, no card is preselected, and any pick saves. It is true when the row carries a capability key that this build cannot resolve to a ceiling: an enum name a newer release wrote is the legitimate trigger, and a hand-edited `null`, `""` or explicit `CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED` reaches the same state, since all of them parse away to unset without erroring. An absent key gives that same parsed value and means the opposite — never configured, which resolves READ_WRITE.

**The section reads past the store's cache.** The server reads this row uncached because a hand edit or a newer replica changes it out of band; `getOrFetchSettingByName` returns a cached snapshot and never revalidates, which computed the form's dirty state — and therefore the repair — against a value no longer stored.

title: docs: require re-authentication for credential changes (T10)
body:
## Summary

Design proposal closing T10 in [`v1-api-audit-2026-08.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md) — `UpdateUser` currently lets a self-service caller rewrite their own password, TOTP secret, and recovery codes with no proof they still control the credential being replaced, so a stolen session (laptop, shared browser, leaked token) becomes permanent account takeover.

- Traces two more self-service paths beyond the two lines the audit named (`regenerate_recovery_codes`, `mfa_enabled=true`) that do the same damage without touching either audited field.
- Proposes five new `UserService` methods — `ChangePassword`, `StartMfaEnrollment`, `EnableMfa`, `DisableMfa`, `RegenerateRecoveryCodes` — replacing the boolean-flags-on-a-generic-`Update` shape, each requiring a `CredentialProof` (current password, or a live MFA code where the account has one) before touching live credential material.
- Reuses the T9 `login_attempt` lockout for the new checks, so they don't become a fresh password-guessing oracle.
- Covers Cloud vs. self-hosted (Cloud accounts never have a local password; `ChangePassword` rejects when the workspace disallows password sign-in), admin-assisted recovery (untouched, no proof required there by design), and full proto for the new/changed messages.
- Surveys precedent across Okta, Auth0, AWS IAM, WorkOS, Google Identity Platform, Zitadel, Keycloak, GitLab, GitHub, and this repo's own `UpdateEmail`/`login-attempt-lockout` conventions.

## Status

Proposal — no code changes in this PR, docs only. Implementation is a separate follow-up once the design is reviewed.

## Test plan

- [ ] N/A — documentation only

title: feat(auth): bound credential guessing with a per-identity login_attempt table
body:
## What

Implements [`docs/design/login-attempt-lockout.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/main/docs/design/login-attempt-lockout.md) (#21230): one `login_attempt` table gives every guessable credential — password, emailed code, second factor — an attempt limit keyed on the identity under attack, identical on Cloud and self-hosted. Closes v1 API audit **T9** (HIGH).

It replaces the two counters that fail today:
- the **audit-log count**, which reads zero on Cloud (no workspace on the failed-login row), so password and MFA lockouts never fire there;
- the **per-code `attempts` column**, whose delete-on-exhaustion let an attacker reset the resend cooldown — five fresh guesses at a 10⁶-space code per seven requests.

## How

- **Migration `3.22/0012`**: `CREATE TABLE login_attempt (identity, kind, attempts, last_attempt_at, PRIMARY KEY (identity, kind))`; `email_verification_code` drops `attempts` and `workspace`.
- **Store**: exactly three operations — claim (one guarded upsert; `now()` is database time, the row lock serializes concurrent claims), clear, purge — plus a structural backstop refusing unkeyed or >512-byte identities. One shared limit for every kind: **5 attempts / 10 minutes**.
- **Claims** happen before the credential is checked, at five sites: local password (pre-bcrypt), LDAP bind (identity `idpID:username` — `:` is legal in neither IDP resource IDs nor emails, so LDAP buckets can never collide with, lock out, or be cleared by an email account's bucket), MFA on login and on workspace switch (email from the signed temp token), and email-code verify (claimed before the code row is even loaded, shared across LOGIN and PASSWORD_RESET purposes). Success deletes the row. Credential-less MFA submissions are refused before claiming.
- **Size bounds live at the proto edge**: every auth request string carries `buf.validate` limits (emails 254, passwords at bcrypt's 72-byte hard limit, codes 64, tokens 4096/8192, resource names 256), enforced by the validate interceptor before any handler runs; `User.email`/`User.password` are bounded at their source too.
- **Password resets clear the PASSWORD counter** — the API path and the recovery CLI both.
- **Verify no longer trusts send-time context**: `ResetPassword` derives password policy and audit workspace from the user's own memberships; email-code signup gates against the workspace the email would land in (the same resolution provisioning uses, one snapshot).
- **LDAP**: rejected binds surface as `Unauthenticated` instead of `Internal`, so edge rate rules counting 401s see them; the directory's result-49 sub-code (expired/disabled/locked) is logged and kept for the admin test-sign-in response.
- **Cleaner**: hourly purge of rows idle over an hour, coupled to the lockout window by a test.

## Breaking Changes

- `email_verification_code` loses the `attempts` and `workspace` columns (metadata schema).
- **Lockout thresholds unify at 5 attempts / 10 minutes**: password tightens from 10

title: docs: login attempt lockout design (v1 API audit T9)
body:
## What

- New design doc: [`docs/design/login-attempt-lockout.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/login-attempt-lockout-design/docs/design/login-attempt-lockout.md) — one `login_attempt` table gives every credential (password local/LDAP, emailed code, MFA) an attempt limit keyed on the identity under attack, identical on Cloud and self-hosted.
- `docs/design/v1-api-audit-2026-08.md` — T9 trimmed to the finding and pointed at the design doc; severity raised MED → HIGH and moved to #1 in the plan.

## Why

Two guessing counters are broken today:

- The audit-log counter behind the password and MFA lockouts reads zero on Cloud — a failed login's audit row needs a workspace, the only SaaS source is the request's own `workspace` field, and an attacker omits it. One MFA temp token buys five minutes of unmetered TOTP guesses.
- The per-code `attempts` column defeats its own resend cooldown: the cooldown is a predicate on the code row and the row is deleted on exhaustion, so send → 5 guesses → delete → send yields five fresh guesses at a 10⁶ code per seven requests, bounded only by throughput. That is the first factor of every MFA-less Cloud account, which is what raises T9 to HIGH.

The design replaces both with a claim-before-verify counter (N attempts, lock for D, forget after D of quiet, success deletes), folds email-code failures into it so the bound survives code rotation, and drops the caller-supplied `workspace` column from `email_verification_code` in favor of server-side derivation. Every element is precedented (Vault's lockout model, Mattermost's atomic slot claim, Clerk/Stytch/Zitadel/Keycloak's central code lockout); a 29-product survey is summarized in the doc's Reference section.

Docs only — no code changes. Implementation follows in a separate PR once the design is agreed.

## Testing

n/a (design docs).

title: refactor: simplify the sample logic
body: ## Simplifies Sample Instances in few areas ### Target requirements - Support `sslmode=disable`, `require`, and `verify-full`. - Remove validation of unrelated PostgreSQL databases and their PUBLIC privileges. - Validate only connectivity and the control role capabilities needed for provisioning. ### Runtime availability - Remove the stored `targetErr`. - Reject malformed URLs during construction. - Retain temporarily unavailable targets and revalidate them at runtime. - Expose `sample` message in the actuator, also align it with self-host sample. - Cache cloud sample availability checks to avoid repeatedly connecting from `GetActuatorInfo`. - Use a shorter random ID for the sample instance and database ### Environment handling - Use the first environment when available. - Allow sample creation with no environment. - Remove the special preference for the `test` environment. ### Why The previous implementation coupled sample creation to deployment-specific assumptions: dedicated Cloud SQL, mandatory certificate verification, globally hardened PostgreSQL databases, a permanently cached startup failure, and a required workspace environment. None of those are essential to provisioning an isolated sample database. The simplified design validates and secures only resources Bytebase owns, works with local PostgreSQL or an existing Cloud SQL instance, recovers automatically from transient failures, and allows minimally configured workspaces to create samples. ## Frontend Optimization - Add “Enable sample databases” to workspace setup - Redirect project-scoped samples to the project databases page - Make the setup guide larger and more visible - Add a warning alert for the sample instance/database

title: feat(helm-charts): support pod annotations on the Bytebase StatefulSet
body:
## Problem

The chart exposes `annotations` for the ServiceAccount, but there is no way to put annotations on the pod itself. Anything that discovers workloads by pod annotation therefore cannot be configured through values.

The common case is Prometheus-style scraping — `prometheus.io/scrape` and `prometheus.io/port` have to land on the StatefulSet's pod template. Today the only way to get them there is to patch the chart, which we have been carrying locally against `1.1.5` in order to scrape Bytebase with our observability stack.

## Change

Adds `bytebase.podAnnotations`, following the same shape the chart already uses for `serviceAccount.annotations`:

```yaml
{{- with .Values.bytebase.podAnnotations }}
annotations:
  {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
{{- end }}
```

Rendered with `with` rather than an unconditional block, so when it is unset the `annotations` key is omitted entirely — no diff for existing releases.

Also documents the value in `values.yaml` and adds the README row, and bumps the chart to `1.1.6` since `1.1.5` is already published. Happy to drop the version bump if you handle that separately in your release flow.

## Verification

`helm lint` passes. Default render is unchanged:

```yaml
# helm template bb .
metadata:
  labels:
    app: bytebase
```

With the value set:

```yaml
# helm template bb . --set-string 'bytebase.podAnnotations.prometheus\.io/scrape=true' \
#                    --set-string 'bytebase.podAnnotations.prometheus\.io/port=8080'
metadata:
  labels:
    app: bytebase
  annotations:
    prometheus.io/port: "8080"
    prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
```

body:
## What

`TestLintAuditPayloadInventory` walked `storepb.AuditLog` as a root, which put 12 `bytebase.store.*` lines into `auditRecordedFields` — the row's own columns plus every field of `RequestMetadata` and `MCPDelegation`. This re-roots the walk on what `createAuditLog` actually marshals onto the row and drops those lines.

- Roots are now the v1 request/response surface, `google.rpc.Status`, and the registered Any types — not the store row.
- `google.rpc.Status` becomes an explicit root. It was previously reached only because the v1 read API (`v1.AuditLog.status`) happens to echo it; annotating that field OMIT would have silently dropped `Status.message` from the inventory even though the interceptor still writes it via `redactAuditStatus`.
- The 12 `bytebase.store.*` entries are removed; the header comment now states the boundary, and a stale sentence above the list ("every scalar on the row… a new column lands here") is gone.

## Why

The test's remedy for an undecided field is "annotate it with `bytebase.v1.audit_behavior` or list it." For store fields the first branch does not exist: `proto/store` does not import `bytebase.v1`, and `marshalAuditPayload` never runs on the row's own sub-messages anyway. So those 12 lines could only ever record a decision that had one branch. The row's own columns, `RequestMetadata`, and `MCPDelegation` are assigned in Go from headers and verified grant state, and are reviewed there.

## Reviewer notes

- `TestLintAuditAnyFieldsAreRegistered` deliberately still walks the store row. Its remedy — registering packed types in `auditAnyRegistry` — is keyed by field and *is* the live enforcement for `bytebase.store.AuditLog.service_data`, so that guard is real and unchanged.
- `TestAuditRowNeedsNoRedactionBeyondTheAnyPayloads` is unchanged and keeps the note that `caller_supplied_user_agent` is caller-controlled.
- Trade-off: a new string copied onto `MCPDelegation` from grant state no longer trips a test. That is a deliberate edit to `proto/store/store/audit_log.proto` plus `mcpDelegationFromAuthContext`, which is where review belongs.

## Testing

- Applied the re-rooting first and ran the lint alone: it reported exactly the 12 store entries as unreachable and nothing newly undecided, confirming nothing else was reached solely through the row. Then removed the lines.
- `go test ./backend/api/v1/ -run Audit` passes; the three lint tests pass individually.
- `gofmt`, `go vet`, and `golangci-lint --disable=staticcheck` clean; server build OK.
- Full `golangci-lint` panics locally in staticcheck v0.8.0-rc.1's `nilness` analyzer over the third-party `sentry` package — reproduced identically on a clean `main`, so it is a local toolchain issue, not this diff.

title: feat(api): redact audit payloads from proto annotations (BYT-10090)
body:
Replaces the 35 hand-written audit-log redactors with a descriptor-driven walk keyed on the `audit_behavior` annotation declared in #21224. Second and final PR for BYT-10090; design doc at [`docs/design/audit-payload-redaction-from-proto.md`](https://github.com/bytebase/bytebase/blob/byt-10090-audit-redactor-impl/docs/design/audit-payload-redaction-from-proto.md).

## Why

A redactor was a Go function someone had to remember to write, and to extend when a field was added beside a credential. Three leaks came from that gap:

- `Instance.roles[].password` — `INPUT_ONLY` on the field, `OUTPUT_ONLY` only on its container, so clients are meant to send it. `redactInstance` walked `data_sources` and passed roles through.
- `UpdateUserRequest.otp_code` — a failed validation neither consumes the code nor suppresses the audit row, so a still-live OTP was written to `audit_log`.
- `Database.instance_resource.data_sources[]` — not live, and only because `convertDataSources` happened to blank the leaves. The `OUTPUT_ONLY` sat on the container, not the credentials.

The annotation moves the decision to the field it describes, so a new credential is redacted the day it is declared rather than the day someone notices.

## What changed

- **`audit_redact.go`** builds a redaction plan per message type, cached on descriptor identity. Descend arms hold a sub-descriptor rather than a nested plan, so the four cyclic components in the descriptor graph (`TablePartitionMetadata`, `ObjectSchema`/`StructKind`/`ArrayKind`, `google.protobuf.Value`, `google.api.expr.Expr`) are followed lazily to any depth. Subtrees holding nothing annotated are shared by pointer, never copied — a 5 MB sheet in an audited batch used to be cloned only to have its content nulled.
- **`SENSITIVE` with explicit presence blanks rather than drops.** `LoginRequest.otp_code` is the case that matters: a failed login has to stay distinguishable from one where no second factor was presented. Same argument as blanking a oneof arm so the row still records which credential type was supplied.
- **`google.protobuf.Any`** is resolved and redacted at runtime against a registry keyed by destination field, so `Status.details` and `service_data` permit different types. An unresolvable payload is dropped with a logged warning rather than failing the whole row.
- **`getRequestString` and `getResponseString` collapse into `marshalAuditPayload`.** With nothing left to switch on, which side of the call a message arrived on no longer changes what happens to it.
- **`createAuditLog` is not walked as a whole.** `service_data` and `status` are redacted where they are assigned; `request_metadata` and `mcp_delegation` are assigned untouched because nothing under them is annotated, which `TestAuditRowNeedsNoRedactionBeyondTheAnyPayloads` asserts stays true.

Net −856 lines in `audit.go`.

## Breaking Changes

Audit-row **keys** are unchanged and `TestLogAuditToStdoutFormat` still passes. What changes is content inside the opa

title: feat(proto): declare audit_behavior on credential and bulk fields (BYT-10090)
body:
Adds `(bytebase.v1.audit_behavior)`, a `FieldOptions` extension with a three-value enum, and applies it to 78 fields across 17 v1 service protos.

**This PR only declares the annotations. Nothing reads them yet, so it is a no-op at runtime.** The descriptor-driven redactor that consumes them, and the CI lints that keep the set honest, follow in a stacked PR.

## Why

`getRequestString` and `getResponseString` switch on the **top-level** message type and dispatch to one of 35 hand-written redactors, so a secret is protected only on the RPCs someone remembered, and is exposed the moment the same field appears under a new parent. Two live examples:

- `Instance.roles[].password` is `INPUT_ONLY` — only its container `Instance.roles` is `OUTPUT_ONLY` — so clients are meant to send it. `CreateInstance`, `UpdateInstance` and `BatchUpdateInstances` are all audited, and `redactInstance` walks `data_sources` but passes `roles` through untouched.
- `UpdateUserRequest.otp_code` is copied verbatim while the handler validates it as an MFA proof. A failed validation neither consumes the code nor suppresses the audit row, so a still-live OTP reaches `audit_log` and stdout.

Marking the **field** rather than the RPC is what makes "annotate once, redacted everywhere, at any depth" possible.

## The two values

| | must not reach an audit payload | may the API return it |
|---|---|---|
| `SENSITIVE` | yes | only on the response that mints it; never on a read path |
| `OMIT` | yes | yes — returning it is routinely the point of the RPC |

`SENSITIVE` is a credential. `OMIT` is anything else that must not be recorded — unbounded bodies, base64 blobs, bearer capabilities, personal data — and says nothing about the API contract.

Not `audit`, and not number 100000: `bytebase.v1.audit` already exists as a `bool` on `MethodOptions`, and 100000 is `allow_without_credential`. Different extend scopes make reuse legal, but grep is how a reviewer audits this, so the identifier has to be unambiguous.

## What to review

The annotation set is the substance here — each field is a judgment about what an audit row may keep. Worth a second pair of eyes on:

- **`AWSCredential.role_arn` and `external_id`** are annotated `SENSITIVE` though they are not credentials. `redactIAMExtension` rebuilds `AwsCredential` as an empty message today, so leaving them unannotated would *start* recording them. Annotating preserves current behavior rather than taking that widening silently.
- **`User.phone`, `groups` and `profile`** are `OMIT`. `redactUser` returns only `{name, email, title}` today, so these would otherwise start appearing in every audited `Login`, `CreateUser` and `UpdateUser` row.
- **`Webhook.url`** is `SENSITIVE` because it is a bearer credential — whoever holds it posts into the customer's Slack, Feishu, WeCom or Teams as Bytebase.
- **`PurchaseResponse.payment_url`** is `SENSITIVE` for the same reason: a Stripe Checkout URL is a bearer capability, even though no reviewer would ca

title: refactor(api): remove service_key from the User proto
body:
## Summary
This PR refactors the service accounts feature to use the `ServiceAccount` protobuf type directly instead of converting it to the `User` type. This removes the `serviceKey` field from the `User` message and eliminates the `serviceAccountToUser` conversion function, making the codebase clearer about the distinction between users and service accounts.

## Key Changes

- **Removed `serviceKey` field from User protobuf message**: The `service_key` field (field 7) is now reserved in the `User` message definition, as service keys belong exclusively to service accounts
- **Eliminated `serviceAccountToUser` conversion function**: Removed the helper function that was converting `ServiceAccount` objects to `User` objects for display purposes
- **Updated ServiceAccountTable component**: 
  - Changed props from `users: User[]` to `serviceAccounts: ServiceAccount[]`
  - Renamed callback props from `onUserUpdated`/`onUserSelected` to `onUpdated`/`onSelected`
  - Updated all internal references to work directly with `ServiceAccount` type
- **Simplified service account operations**: Removed unnecessary conversions in `handleResetKey`, `handleDeactivate`, and `handleRestore` functions
- **Updated ServiceAccountsPage**: 
  - Changed data type from `User` to `ServiceAccount` in pagination hooks
  - Removed `getServiceAccount` store call in `handleOpenEdit`
  - Updated cache operations to work directly with `ServiceAccount` objects
- **Updated member bindings display**: Inline the User projection creation in `memberBindings.ts` instead of using the removed conversion function

## Implementation Details

- The `ServiceAccount` type now flows through the entire service accounts UI layer without conversion
- Service account display in member bindings still uses the `User` shape for consistency with the UI layer, but this is now created inline as a display-only projection
- All protobuf generated files have been updated to reflect the removal of the `service_key` field from the `User` message

title: feat(mcp): serve what each MCP capability mode contains, resolved live (P1b 1b-5b)
body:
`WorkspaceService.GetMCPInfo` answers "what can be done here": the MCP capability ceiling in force, what each ceiling serves, and the two per-engine facts the ceiling alone does not show.

P1b 1b-5b, stacked on #21221 — **review that first**; this PR's diff is only the delta on top of it. Spec: `plans/2026-08-07-mcp-p1b-spec.md` §1b-5(b) and (d). Closes the option-2 and option-3 halves of BOT-89.

## Everything resolves when the request is served

The method list comes off the compiled descriptors — the same place the gate reads a method's class — and the mode rows read `mcpServingClasses`, the gate's own serving table, rather than a copy of it.

A stored list would pass its tests the day it was written and drift silently after. The first sign would be an admin choosing a mode from a page describing the build before this one.

`TestMCPInfoResolvesMethodsLive` runs the same resolver over two descriptor sets that differ only in one method's `mcp_method_class` annotation, and shows the answer move. It compiles a synthetic `bytebase.v1` file, so the resolver reads a real annotation off a real descriptor, not a stand-in.

## The two engine tables

Both were dropped when 1b-3 removed the per-query `read_only_enforcement` field, for the reason ecmadao gave: no consumer. This is the consumer.

**Read-only depth, three states.** An engine with no read-only classifier refuses a read-only session every statement, including `SELECT 1`. An engine with one gets statement classification. Two drivers always open the database session read-only as well, so the engine refuses most writes the classifier missed — not a proof, since a statement that classifies as a read can still call a function that switches the setting back off (BOT-88), and the enum says so.

The classifier half is *asked* — `parserbase.HasQueryValidator`, the registry the clamp itself consults — so it cannot drift. The driver half is *mirrored*, because a driver reports this by acting on a flag when a connection opens and none exists here. A driver that starts honoring the flag without a row here understates its own depth, which is the safe direction; no unit test can catch that, and the test comment says so rather than claiming otherwise.

Redshift is reported at its floor. Its driver does open the session read-only, but not on a datashare database, and datashare is per *database* while this answer is per *engine*. The engine's note says so, and `STATEMENT` is worded as a floor rather than as a claim about what a driver can do.

**Masking, three states — the BOT-95 shape.** Column masking, where the caller's exemptions are what `ignore_masking_exemptions` suppresses. Document masking, where results are masked but the masker's interface carries neither the user nor their exemptions, so the toggle changes nothing. And no masking at all.

Collapsing the middle state into either neighbour would overclaim: "masked" reads as "the toggle works here", "unmasked" reads as "nothing is masked". Both are wro

title: feat(mcp): audit the two MCP doors that sit outside the API, and filter for them (P1b 1b-5a)
body:
The MCP ceiling refuses in three places. Two of them are echo routes, so neither connect chain sees them and nothing recorded them: the `/mcp` connection gate, and the OAuth2 consent that mints the credential it checks. Both write their own audit row now, and the audit search grows the two filters an operator needs to find them.

P1b 1b-5a. Spec: `plans/2026-08-07-mcp-p1b-spec.md` §1b-5.

## The authorization flow had no ceiling awareness at all

Not a missing page state — a missing refusal. A user in a workspace with MCP turned off approved the consent, was issued a real authorization code, exchanged it for a real access token, and only met the ceiling at `/mcp`. The credential outlived the misunderstanding, and nothing recorded that anyone had tried.

It is refused now at consent, with a page that names what to ask an admin for. `RED`: with the check removed, the test finds an authorization code in the response.

**And at every issuance, not only at consent.** A code outlives the consent by ten minutes and a refresh token by thirty days, so checking once would leave the policy true of `/api/oauth2/authorize` and false of `/api/oauth2/token` — a grant consented while MCP was on would keep minting access tokens for a month after an admin turned it off. `resolveBoundWorkspace` re-checks workspace membership on the same endpoint for exactly this reason, and says so in its own comment.

The check runs **before** the single-use consume, where this file already says refusals belong: "PKCE is verified above so a failed verifier never burns the code". Consuming first would make a reversible policy irreversible — an hour of MCP being off would cost every client its refresh token and force a fresh interactive consent, while the message told them raising the ceiling restores service. Membership stays *after* the consume, deliberately: losing membership is a one-way revocation where killing the grant is the point. Both properties are pinned — a refused refresh and a refused exchange each leave the credential intact and succeed once the ceiling is raised.

## Which refusals write a row

The ones a workspace admin decides:

- a ceiling that serves nothing (`DISABLED`),
- a stored ceiling this build cannot read,
- a stored ceiling this build does not serve.

Not the credential-lifecycle 401s — expired, revoked, wrong signature, malformed claims, audience bound elsewhere. Tokens are replaced constantly by design. A row per expiry would bury the denials this exists to surface under ordinary churn, while telling an operator nothing they can act on.

Not the 503 either. An outage recorded as a policy denial is a decision in the audit log that nobody made — the same split the per-request gate already makes.

Not the token endpoint. It is machine-to-machine, so a retrying client would write a row per attempt; the two doors a person and a session actually meet carry the record. A client that only ever refreshes and never connects therefore leaves no row — it is also
author: vsai12
diff:
--- backend/api/auth/mcp_ceiling.go (+102/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,102 @@
+package auth
+
+import (
+	"github.com/pkg/errors"
+
+	storepb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/store"
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/store"
+)
+
+// MCPCeilingVerdict is what a read of a workspace's MCP capability ceiling
+// means to a caller deciding whether to proceed. Every reader of the setting
+// decides from it and says so with Refusal — the consent, the token endpoint,
+// the /mcp connection gate, the per-request gate, and the mode-contents read —
+// so no two can disagree about a workspace or describe it two ways.
+type MCPCeilingVerdict int
+
+// Each value names what an admin would have to do about it, which is what the
+// doors turn into a sentence.
+const (
+	// The ceiling admits work; which work is decided per method and per statement.
+	MCPCeilingServes MCPCeilingVerdict = iota
+	// An admin turned MCP off. Raising the ceiling fixes it.
+	MCPCeilingDisabled
+	// The stored value is one this build cannot interpret — a mistyped enum
+	// name, a wrong-typed row. An admin has to write the setting again.
+	MCPCeilingUnreadable
+	// The value parsed but no mode this build has serves it: the reserved 2, or
+	// a ceiling a newer release wrote. An admin has to choose a known value.
+	MCPCeilingUnserved
+	// The read itself failed. The only one of these a retry may fix.
+	MCPCeilingUnavailable
+)
+
+// IsPolicy reports whether the verdict is a decision about the workspace, which
+// is what makes a refusal an audited outcome.
+func (v MCPCeilingVerdict) IsPolicy() bool {
+	switch v {
+	case MCPCeilingDisabled, MCPCeilingUnreadable, MCPCeilingUnserved:
+		return true
+	default:
+		return false
+	}
+}
+
+// ClassifyMCPCeiling turns the result of store.GetMCPSettingsUncached into the
+// verdict its caller acts on. Everything this build cannot act on refuses; what
+// the split decides is the message and the audit row. A value nobody can
+// interpret never succeeds on retry; an outage may.
+func ClassifyMCPCeiling(capability storepb.MCPSetting_Capability, err error) MCPCeilingVerdict {
+	if err != nil {
+		if errors.Is(err, store.ErrMCPCapabilityUnreadable) {
+			return MCPCeilingUnreadable
+		}
+		return MCPCeilingUnavailable
+	}
+	if capability == storepb.MCPSetting_DISABLED {
+		return MCPCeilingDisabled
+	}
+	if !MCPCeilingServesAnything(capability) {
+		return MCPCeilingUnserved
+	}
+	return MCPCeilingServes
+}
+
+// Refusal is what a door tells the caller it is refusing: what is wrong with
+// this workspace's ceiling, and what an admin does about it. Empty for
+// MCPCeilingServes, which refuses nothing.
+//
+// Door-neutral on purpose. Each door used to keep its own copy ending in "so
+// the connection fails closed" / "so authorization fails closed", and the
+// copies drifted — the token endpoint borrowed the consent's clause, so a
+// refused refresh told the client that no client could be authorized. Which
+// door refused is already carried by the status, the page, and the audit row's
+// method, so the sentence does not say it again.
+//
+// Lowercase and unterminated: every door but the consent page composes this
+// into a larger error, and that page ends the sentence itself.
+func (v MCPCeilingVerdict) Refusal() string {
+	switch v {
+	case MCPCeilingDisabled:
+		return "a workspace admin has turned MCP access off for this workspace. " +
+			"Ask them to raise the MCP ceiling in the workspace settings"
+	case MCPCeilingUnreadable:
+		return "this workspace's stored MCP capability ceiling is not one this build understands. " +
+			"Ask a workspace admin to set the MCP ceiling again in the workspace settings"
+	case MCPCeilingUnserved:
+		return "this workspace's stored MCP capability ceiling is not one this build serves. " +
+			"Ask a workspace admin to set the MCP ceiling to a supported value in the workspace settings"
+	case MCPCeilingUnavailable:
+		return "this workspace's MCP capability ceiling could not be read. " +
+			"Retry shortly; if it persists, ask a workspace admin to check the workspace settings"
+	default:
+		return ""
+	}
+}
+
+// PolicyMCPCeilingVerdicts is every verdict that is a decision about the
+// workspace rather than an outage, which is what decides whether a refusal is
+// recorded. Refusal covers the outage too; this list does not.
+func PolicyMCPCeilingVerdicts() []MCPCeilingVerdict {
+	return []MCPCeilingVerdict{MCPCeilingDisabled, MCPCeilingUnreadable, MCPCeilingUnserved}
+}
--- backend/api/auth/mcp_ceiling_test.go (+135/-0)
@@ -0,0 +1,135 @@
+package auth
+
+import (
+	"strings"
+	"testing"
+
+	"github.com/pkg/errors"
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+
+	storepb "github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/generated-go/store"
+	"github.com/bytebase/bytebase/backend/store"
+)
+
+// TestClassifyMCPCeiling pins the one split three doors depend on.
+//
+// The line that matters is between a stored value and a failed read. A value
+// nobody can interpret never succeeds on retry, so telling a client to retry is
+// a lie; a read that failed is an outage, so blaming an admin is a lie the
+// other way. Everything this build cannot act on refuses either way, which is
+// what makes the distinction about the message and the audit row rather than
+// about access.
+func TestClassifyMCPCeiling(t *testing.T) {
+	unreadable := errors.Wrapf(store.ErrMCPCapabilityUnreadable, "READ_ONLYY is not a value this build understands")
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name       string
+		capability storepb.MCPSetting_Capability
+		err        error
+		want       MCPCeilingVerdict
+		policy     bool
+	}{
+		{"read-write serves", storepb.MCPSetting_READ_WRITE, nil, MCPCeilingServes, false},
+		{"read-only serves", storepb.MCPSetting_READ_ONLY, nil, MCPCeilingServes, false},
+		{"disabled", storepb.MCPSetting_DISABLED, nil, MCPCeilingDisabled, true},
+		{"the reserved number", storepb.MCPSetting_Capability(2), nil, MCPCeilingUnserved, true},
+		{"a value from a newer build", storepb.MCPSetting_Capability(99), nil, MCPCeilingUnserved, true},
+		// The store resolves an absent setting to READ_WRITE and an explicit
+		// unset to the unreadable error, so a zero value arriving here was
+		// resolved by nobody.
+		{"nobody resolved it", storepb.MCPSetting_CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED, nil, MCPCeilingUnserved, true},
+		{"a stored value nobody can read", storepb.MCPSetting_CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED, unreadable, MCPCeilingUnreadable, true},
+		// The error wins over the value, whatever the value happens to be.
+		{"an unreadable value that parsed to something", storepb.MCPSetting_READ_WRITE, unreadable, MCPCeilingUnreadable, true},
+		{"the read failed", storepb.MCPSetting_CAPABILITY_UNSPECIFIED, errors.New("connection refused"), MCPCeilingUnavailable, false},
+		{"the read failed on a permissive workspace", storepb.MCPSetting_READ_WRITE, errors.New("connection refused"), MCPCeilingUnavailable, false},
+	}
+	for _, tt := range tests {
+		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			got := ClassifyMCPCeiling(tt.capability, tt.err)
+			require.Equal(t, tt.want, got)
+			require.Equal(t, tt.policy, got.IsPolicy())
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+// TestMCPCeilingVerdictAdmissionMatchesTheServesPredicate holds the classifier
+// against the predicate the serving table already pins: exactly one verdict may
+// admit work, and it must be the one MCPCeilingServesAnything agrees with over
+// the whole enum. A mode that starts or stops serving a class cannot leave one
+// of them stale.
+func TestMCPCeilingVerdictAdmissionMatchesTheServesPredicate(t *testing.T) {
+	values := storepb.MCPSetting_Capability(0).Descriptor().Values()
+	for i := range values.Len() {
+		capability := storepb.MCPSetting_Capability(values.Get(i).Number())
+		admits := ClassifyMCPCeiling(capability, nil) == MCPCeilingServes
+		require.Equal(t, MCPCeilingServesAnything(capability), admits,
+			"%v must admit work in exactly one of the two", capability)
+	}
+}
+
+// TestPolicyVerdictsAreExactlyTheAuditedOnes holds the list every door renders
+// wording from against the predicate that decides whether a refusal is
+// recorded. A verdict in one and not the other would either be refused with no
+// sentence or audited as a decision nobody made.
+func TestPolicyVerdictsAreExactlyTheAuditedOnes(t *testing.T) {
+	policy := map[MCPCeilingVerdict]bool{}
+	for _, v := range PolicyMCPCeilingVerdicts() {
+		require.True(t, v.IsPolicy(), "%v is listed as policy but does not report as one", v)
+		policy[v] = true
+	}
+	for _, v := range []MCPCeilingVerdict{
+		MCPCeilingServes, MCPCeilingDisabled, MCPCeilingUnreadable, MCPCeilingUnserved, MCPCeilingUnavailable,
+	} {
+		require.Equal(t, v.IsPolicy(), policy[v], "%v disagrees between the list and the predicate", v)
+	}
+}
+
+// TestEveryVerdictThatRefusesHasWording holds the one wording table against the
+// verdicts that reach a caller. It replaces a per-door version of this check
+// that each door carried: while the sentences were per-door, coverage was all a
+// lint could hold them to — the wording itself was free to drift, and it did.
+//
+// The list spans all five values, not PolicyMCPCeilingVerdicts, because an
+// outage is refused too and its sentence is the one nobody would otherwise
+// exercise. Only Serves is silent.
+func TestEveryVerdictThatRefusesHasWording(t *testing.T) {
+	for _, v := range []MCPCeilingVerdict{
+		MCPCeilingDisabled, MCPCeilingUnreadable, MCPCeilingUnserved, MCPCeilingUnavailable,
+	} {
+		refusal := v.Refusal()
+		require.NotEmpty(t, refusal, "%v reaches a caller and must say what is wrong", v)
+
+		// Composed into a larger error at every door but the consent page, so
+		// it starts lowercase and ends unterminated.
+		require.Equal(t, strings.ToLower(refusal[:1]), refusal[:1],
+			"%v: a door prefixes this, so it must not start a sentence", v)
+		require.NotEqual(t, ".", refusal[len(refusal)-1:],
+			"%v: the consent page terminates it; the others compose it", v)
+
+		// Every refusal names the remedy, not only the fault. A denial an
+		// operator cannot act on is the failure this series exists to fix.
+		require.Contains(t, refusal, "workspace settings", "%v must name where the fix is", v)
+	}
+
+	require.Empty(t, MCPCeilingServes.Refusal(), "serving refuses nothing")
+}
+
+// TestRefusalsDistinguishTheThreeStoredStates pins that the three policy
+// verdicts do not collapse into one message. They have different fixes — turn
+// MCP back on, rewrite a value nobody can read, choose a value this build
+// serves — and a door that said "disabled" for all three would send two of them
+// to the wrong control.
+func TestRefusalsDistinguishTheThreeStoredStates(t *testing.T) {
+	seen := map[string]MCPCeilingVerdict{}
+	for _, v := range PolicyMCPCeilingVerdicts() {
+		refusal := v.Refusal()
+		if other, dup := seen[refusal]; dup {
+			require.Failf(t, "verdicts share wording", "%v and %v say the same thing", other, v)
+		}
+		seen[refusal] = v
+	}
+	require.Contains(t, MCPCeilingDisabled.Refusal(), "turned MCP access off")
+	require.Contains(t, MCPCeilingUnreadable.Refusal(), "not one this build understands")
+	require.Contains(t, MCPCeilingUnserved.Refusal(), "not one this build serves")
+}

title: docs: design audit payload redaction from proto annotations (BYT-10090)
body:
Design doc only — no implementation, no code changes.

## Why

Audited RPCs redact by switching on the **top-level** request or response type and dispatching to one of 35 hand-written redactors (`backend/api/v1/audit.go:564`, `:748`). A secret is protected only on the RPCs someone remembered, and exposed the moment the same field appears under a new parent.

That single mechanism produced all three credentials reported in BYT-10090 (OIDC client secret, service-account key, SCIM directory-sync token — fixed on main by #21110 and #21109). Two more are still unprotected on main, found while verifying the report:

- `database.instance_resource.data_sources[]` on `UpdateDatabase` / `BatchUpdateDatabases` — 22 credential fields echoed into the request payload
- `Instance.roles[].password`

Both are `OUTPUT_ONLY` fields the server ignores and the read path never populates, so neither carries a real credential today. The same mechanism also lets `QueryResult`'s two redactors disagree: `redactQueryResponse` keeps `rows_count`, `redactAdminExecuteResponse` drops it.

## What the doc proposes

Mark the field in the proto, once, and let redaction follow:

```proto
string client_secret = 5 [debug_redact = true];
repeated QueryRow rows = 3 [(bytebase.v1.audit_omit) = true];
```

- `debug_redact` is the upstream `google.protobuf.FieldOptions` field 16 — already in the toolchain, already means "contains sensitive credentials", no new dependency.
- `audit_omit` is one new bool for bulk payloads that the API legitimately returns to clients but the audit row must not carry.
- Redaction runs off a plan built once per message type from the descriptor and cached — nothing ever searches a payload. One copy mechanism: copy along the path to a redacted field, share every other subtree by pointer, never copy an omitted field.
- CI lints fail the build on an unannotated secret.

All 35 hand-written redactors are deleted, including `redactIAMExtension` — a descriptor walk reproduces it byte-for-byte on all oneof arms.

## For reviewers

Claims in the doc were checked against the toolchain rather than assumed:

- `debug_redact` survives into the runtime descriptor (compiled with `buf build`, read back) — it is **inert in Go**, so CI is the only enforcement, not a safety net.
- Go has no filtered clone: `proto.Clone`/`CloneOf`/`Merge` take no options, and field-mask libraries prune after a full clone.
- Performance figures come from prototypes, one run, darwin/arm64, with `INPUT_ONLY` standing in for the annotation set.

Three tradeoffs stated as non-goals rather than buried:

1. It is a **denylist** — a new unannotated field gets logged, where today's allowlist rebuilds fail closed.
2. Goal 5 (credentials never returned on read paths) is **not statically provable**; coverage is the set of converters carrying an assertion.
3. Existing `audit_log` rows are untouched, and there is no purge or sanitization path for that table.

Worth pushing back on if the denylist direction isn

title: fix(schema/mysql): stop duplicating DDL for partitioned tables (BYT-10057)
body:
Fixes [BYT-10057](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10057/fix-sync-schema-duplicate-pkindex-ddl-for-polardb-mysql-table).

## Problem

Sync Schema repeated a table's entire DDL block once per partition. A customer table with 180 partitions produced 181 identical copies; executing the script failed on the second copy with `Error 1061 Duplicate key name 'sindex'` or `Error 1068 Multiple primary key defined`.

The issue was originally filed against PolarDB and suspected to involve a composite primary key overlapping a secondary index. Neither is involved — this reproduces on stock MySQL 8.0.33, and the index overlap diffs correctly. The only thing that matters is that the table is partitioned.

## Root cause

Partitions are registered in `SchemaMetadata.internalTables` under their own key so `GetTable` can resolve a partition name, but they carry the **parent table's** proto (`buildTablesMetadataRecursive`). `ListTableNames` returned `GetProto().GetName()` for every entry, so a table with N partitions yielded the parent's name N+1 times. `GetDatabaseSchemaDiff` walks that list, so each partition contributed another copy of the table to the diff.

Skipping partition entries when listing is unambiguously correct: a partition entry can only ever produce the parent's name, never its own, so nothing could have depended on it. `GetTable("p0")` still resolves.

`ListTableNames` also feeds SQL Editor autocomplete, query span extraction, and backup — a partitioned table was being suggested N+1 times in autocomplete too.

## Second fix: partitioning was dropped on create

The MySQL migration generator never emitted a `PARTITION BY` clause, so a table created by Sync Schema landed on the target unpartitioned. Now emitted through the existing `printPartitionClause`, matching the schema dump.

## Not fixed here

The generator still ignores `PartitionChanges` on an existing table, so partition drift between source and target is silently skipped (the differ reports the ALTER; the generator emits nothing). Closing that gap means generating `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which destroys the partition's rows — unlike PostgreSQL's non-destructive `DETACH PARTITION` — so it needs a product decision rather than a quiet fix. Tracked separately.

## Testing

Each test was verified to fail without its corresponding change.

- `TestListTableNames_ExcludesPartitions` — a table with 3 partitions and 2 subpartitions is listed once (previously 6 times) while every partition lookup still resolves.
- `TestDiffMigrationPartitionedTableEmittedOnce` — the reported table shape (composite PK plus a secondary index over the same ordered columns) at 0/1/3/180 partitions emits exactly one statement set for both the create (1061) and alter (1068) shapes, and stays convergent.
- `TestDiffMigrationPreservesPartitioning` — the created table keeps its partitioning and every partition.
- Two new testcontainer cases against real MySQL 8.0.33. Without the fixes they reproduce the customer'

+
+Bytebase exposes product-health metrics from the server's `/metrics` endpoint.

+
+Installation-state metrics are read from shared metadata on every scrape so all
+replicas report equivalent values. If the metadata or configured license cannot
+be read and verified, the scrape fails instead of returning a partial state.
+
+| Metric | Type | Description |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `bytebase_license_expiry_timestamp_seconds` | Gauge | License expiry as a Unix timestamp. `+Inf` means the Free plan or a perpetual license. A valid expired license retains its expiry timestamp while using Free-plan limits. |
+| `bytebase_license_seats_used` | Gauge | Distinct end users currently occupying license seats. |
+| `bytebase_license_seats_limit` | Gauge | Effective seat limit. `+Inf` means unlimited. |
+| `bytebase_license_instances_used` | Gauge | Non-deleted registered instances. |
+| `bytebase_license_instances_limit` | Gauge | Effective registered-instance limit. `+Inf` means unlimited. |
+
+## Process-local metrics
+
+Process metrics record work performed by the serving Bytebase process. In a
+multi-replica deployment, query each replica or aggregate across replicas as
+appropriate. Canceled shutdown work is not recorded as a failure.
+
+| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |

+| `bytebase_runner_run_duration_seconds` | Native histogram | `runner`, `result` | Duration of synchronous background runner cycles. |
+
+`result` is `success`, `failure`, or `skipped`. Runner values are

+ASCII letters, digits, and underscores are replaced with underscores, and name
+collisions receive deterministic `_conflictN` suffixes. The label schema is the
+union of labels observed by that process; a resource without a union label emits
+an empty value for it.

+The duration metrics use the Prometheus client library's native histogram
+implementation. Their bucket factor is at most 1.1, populated buckets are capped
+at 100, and bucket state is not reset more often than once per hour.

title: feat(mcp): SQL statement clamp for read-only MCP sessions, and the READ_ONLY cutover (P1b 1b-3)
body:
## What this does

A workspace can now set its MCP ceiling to **Read-only** and have it mean something. Until this PR, `/mcp` refused a read-only ceiling outright, because a read-only session could still write SQL through the query tool.

Three things now hold a read-only session:

1. **The method gate**, which already shipped (#21201): a method the mode does not cover is refused before dispatch.
2. **The SQL clamp**, new here: `SQLService/Query` is classified READ, but what it does is decided by the statement it carries, so every statement in the request must classify as a read or the whole request is refused.
3. **The driver session**, where the engine has one: the connection itself is opened read-only, so an ordinary write is refused by the database as well.

The cutover — `mcpConnectionAllowed` admitting READ_ONLY — is the third commit. Nothing before it admits one, so at no commit in this branch does a read-only ceiling admit a session that can write.

**What this claims is classifier-enforced read-only, reinforced by a read-only session where one exists — not a proof that nothing can write.** A statement that reads structurally can still call a side-effecting function, and Postgres's read-only transaction does not stop `dblink` or an advisory lock. That is the conformance lane's subject.

## The clamp

It never calls `base.ValidateSQLForEditor` bare. That function answers *read-only* for an engine with no registered validator — fine for a caller that only routes or formats with the verdict, wrong for one that must refuse a write. MONGODB, ELASTICSEARCH and DATABRICKS have no validator and now fail closed rather than gain one here. `base.HasQueryValidator` is the whole of the new API; the registry stays unexported.

It classifies **the statements the driver will run**, not the request as one string. `queryRetryStopOnError` splits with the engine's splitter and falls back to the whole request when there is none (Redis) or the split fails; the clamp mirrors that exactly. Classifying a different unit than the executor runs is how a batch slips past a per-statement rule — on the engines whose validator classifies by leading keyword, judging the request whole reads `SELECT 1; DROP TABLE t` as a SELECT.

It also refuses **a statement that rewrites the session it runs on**. That one is worth the detail, because it is the seam between the clamp's own two layers and it took a live database to see.

## The session-rewrite escape

Both halves of this classify as reads:

```sql
SET default_transaction_read_only = off;
SELECT nextval('s');
```

`SET` is not a write. `nextval` writes, but from inside a structural SELECT, which no classifier catches — the read-only session is what normally stops it. Every statement of a request runs on one connection, and Postgres applies a changed default to the *next* transaction, so the two arrive as separate transactions. Probed against Postgres 17 on a live container:

```
SELECT nextval('s');                    -> ER

title: fix(parser/doris): unblock read-only Doris queries in SQL Editor (BYT-10070)
body:
Fixes [BYT-10070](https://linear.app/bytebase/issue/BYT-10070/fix-doris-sql-editor-rejection-of-read-only-extract-queries).

Depends on [bytebase/omni#400](https://github.com/bytebase/omni/pull/400), **merged** as `f107d677`; `go.mod` is pinned to that commit on `main`.

## What changed

CG Tech could not run a valid read-only Doris query in SQL Editor. The omni Doris parser has no production for `EXTRACT(unit FROM expr)`, so `validateQuery` failed the whole statement and the editor blocked it before it reached the database. A differential sweep — every parser rejection re-run through a live Doris — found nine more classes with the same shape.

This PR bumps `github.com/bytebase/omni` to pick up the parser fix and adds regression coverage in the read-only query validator for each form.

## One correction to the issue

The issue reports the customer-facing error as `Support read-only command statements only`. That is **not** what this query produces on any 3.18.1+ build — a parse failure returns a `*base.SyntaxError`, which `validateQueryRequest` surfaces as `[invalid_argument] syntax error at or near EXTRACT`. The read-only message only fires when parsing *succeeds* and the AST is not a read-only shape, e.g. a `SET` or `USE` prefix in the same editor tab:

| statement | result |
|---|---|
| the attached CG Tech query | `syntax error at or near EXTRACT` |
| `SET enable_profile = true;\nSELECT 1;` | **`Support read-only command statements only`** |
| `USE game_dws;\nSELECT 1;` | same |

So the screenshot and the attached SQL are most likely different executions. Worth asking CG Tech for the exact tab contents — if they prepend a `SET`, that is a second, separate bug. The issue's acceptance criterion "parser failures surface a precise syntax error instead of claiming the statement is non-read-only" is already satisfied today.

## Regression window

`3.18.1` and later. The ANTLR parser this replaced accepted the query; I confirmed that by running the customer's SQL through the pre-omni validator at `91cb65600e^`.

## Test plan

New cases in `TestValidateQuery` for both `doris` and `starrocks`, each asserting the form passes read-only validation:

- `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM MONTHS_ADD(NOW(), -1))`, multi-line, and inside a CTE body
- `TRIM(s)`, `LEFT(s,2)`, `RIGHT(s,2)`, `IF(a,1,2)`, `DATABASE()`
- `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3)`
- `@@version_comment`, `@@session.query_timeout`, `@uservar`
- `[1,2,3]`, `{'a':1}`, `x'1f'`, `b'101'`
- `array_map(x -> x + 1, arr)`
- `/*+ SET_VAR(query_timeout = 100) */`
- `GROUP BY CUBE(a)`
- `CONVERT(s USING utf8)`, `CONVERT(s, SIGNED)`, `BINARY s`

title: fix(tidb): sync fails on TiDB Cloud version strings (BYT-10062)
body:
## What broke

TiDB Cloud reports a calendar version carrying no upstream semver:

```
8.0.11-TiDB-CLOUD.202603.4
```

`parseVersion` only matched `v\d+\.\d+\.\d+`. That string contains no lowercase `v` at all, so the parse returned an error — and because `getVersion` is the first call in both `SyncInstance` and `SyncDBSchema`, the error aborted the **entire instance and schema sync** for every TiDB Cloud instance.

## Root cause

The version was parsed on the way to storage, before anything knew whether a caller actually needed it parsed. In fact only one caller did: a single feature gate deciding whether to read `information_schema.CHECK_CONSTRAINTS`. Everything else — `InstanceMetadata.Version`, `EngineVersion` in the v1 API, the instance panel — just displays the string.

So an unparseable version cost the whole sync to protect one boolean.

## The change

**1. `getVersion` returns `VERSION()` verbatim.** Nothing parses on the display path, so an unrecognized format can no longer fail a sync.

**2. Parsing happens only at the gate.** `parseVersion`, `isCloudVersion`, and `tidbVersionAtLeast` collapse into one function answering the caller's actual question:

```go
func supportsCheckConstraintTable(rawVersion string) bool
```

**3. The gate reads two signals.** The TiDB version decides whenever it is readable; otherwise the MySQL compatibility prefix does. These mark the same boundary *by construction*: TiDB moved that prefix from `5.7.25` to `8.0.11` in v7.4.0 — the very release that added the table.

That fallback is what makes this robust rather than a patch. `8.0.11-TiDB-CLOUD.202603.4` now passes on its `8.0.11` prefix, not on a pattern matching this particular calendar format, so a future change to that format cannot reintroduce the same bug. A custom `server-version` that hides the TiDB half is covered by the same path.

### Two thresholds worth reviewing

- The prefix is compared against **8.0.0**, not MySQL's real **8.0.16** where `CHECK_CONSTRAINTS` was added upstream. Every TiDB build reports `8.0.11`, so the stricter threshold would answer `false` for all of them and silently drop every check constraint.
- The TiDB threshold stays **7.4.0**, not 7.2.0. TiDB v7.2.0 added CHECK constraint *support*, but the `information_schema` table itself landed in v7.4.0.

## Breaking Changes

**`EngineVersion` changes format for TiDB instances.** It now reports the full `VERSION()` output rather than a trimmed fragment:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| `v8.5.0` | `8.0.11-TiDB-v8.5.0` |
| (sync failed) | `8.0.11-TiDB-CLOUD.202603.4` |

Existing instances pick this up on their next sync. It is visible in the instance detail panel and in the `EngineVersion` field of the v1 API, so an integration parsing that field for TiDB engines would see a different string.

I verified nothing in this codebase compares it: the frontend's two `allowGhostForDatabase` helpers gate on `Engine.MYSQL`/`Engine.MARIADB` only, and the SDL migration paths that do semver-par

title: fix(api): redact three stored secrets on read paths, free the eight reads they blocked
body:
Three reads returned a stored secret in the response body, and the 1b-1 classification had to keep eight methods out of every MCP ceiling because of it. Since the gate shipped (#21201) that is a live regression: an MCP session cannot list projects or instances, so it cannot name a database and cannot do read-only work at all. The leaks were live for human callers too, whatever MCP did. MCP only made them visible.

This redacts all three on the read path and moves the eight reads to READ. Closes BOT-47.

## The leaks

**Project webhook URL.** An incoming-webhook URL is the whole credential: whoever holds it posts into the customer's Slack, Feishu, WeCom or Teams as Bytebase. `convertToProject` copied it out verbatim, and `ListProjects` pages the whole workspace, so one call took the lot. We already treat it as a credential in audit rows (`redactWebhook`).

`url` is write-only now, in the shape this repo already uses for a secret a client sets but never reads back: `INPUT_ONLY` on the field, an `OUTPUT_ONLY` `url_set` bool beside it. That is what `DataSource.password` and the SSL material do a few files away, and `convertDataSources` is the converter this one is copying. Reads leave `url` empty and set `url_set`, so a client can still say a webhook is configured. `REQUIRED` came off the field, since an empty `url` is a meaningful input to `TestWebhook` now.

**Instance role attribute.** On MariaDB the attribute is raw `SHOW GRANTS` text, and the server writes the account's credential into it inline. Verified on a MariaDB 11.4.12 container, three forms:

```
GRANT SELECT ON *.* TO `leaky`@`%` IDENTIFIED BY PASSWORD '*05A6C9A5...'
GRANT USAGE  ON *.* TO `edguy`@`%` IDENTIFIED VIA ed25519 USING 'ZIgUREUg...'
GRANT USAGE  ON *.* TO `multi`@`%` IDENTIFIED VIA ed25519 USING 'GvRmi9un...' OR mysql_native_password USING '*F33AE6DD...'
```

MySQL 8.0.46 and 5.7.44 emit none of these, so the mask is a no-op there, and the other engines store role keywords or role names rather than grant text. This is the one field the write-only shape does not fit: the text around the credential is the grant list a DBA reads, so the field stays and the credential is masked inside it.

One thing worth flagging on the regex: the quoted run is matched greedily, to the last quote on the line. MariaDB does not escape a quote inside the stored auth string. An auth string of `ab'cd` comes back as `USING 'ab'cd'`, which is not re-parseable SQL, so a lazy match would stop at the inner quote and return the rest of the secret. Greedy can only take too much (a `REQUIRE SUBJECT '<dn>'` after the credential goes into the mask with it), and `REQUIRE SSL` and `WITH GRANT OPTION` carry no quotes and survive.

**MFA enrollment.** `convertToUser` exposed `temp_otp_secret` and `temp_recovery_codes` to any read whose subject was the caller, so reading your own profile captured the TOTP seed. That was true of `GetUser` as well as `GetCurrentUser`, which is why the fix is in the converter and not

title: feat: add AIP-132 order_by to ListSavedQueries and a recency index
body:
## What

- `ListSavedQueries` takes an AIP-132 `order_by` (`update_time`, `create_time`, `title`, each with an optional `" desc"`). The default stays **title ascending** — the same stable order as Search, so a row does not jump the list because somebody edited it; recency is an explicit ask (`order_by=update_time desc`).
- Parsing goes through a new strict shared helper (`store.getOrderByKeys`): `-field`, bad directions, and duplicate fields are rejected with clear `InvalidArgument` errors instead of being silently reinterpreted by the lax regex.
- A `resource_id` tiebreak (in the last key's direction) makes every order a total order, so offset pagination is deterministic. `ListQueryHistories` gains the same tiebreak for its already-documented newest-first order.
- Migration `3.22/0010` adds `idx_saved_query_creator_updated_at_resource_id (creator, updated_at DESC, resource_id DESC)` — the per-user recency pull runs as one ordered index scan, no sort node — and **drops** the now-redundant `idx_saved_query_creator_project`, keeping per-update index writes flat.
- `PatchSavedQuery` stamps `updated_at` with the DB clock (`now()`) instead of the app clock, since it is now a sort key; the `order_by` doc defines what counts as a modification (sharing-policy writes and stars do not).

## Why

A customer pulls a given user's saved queries and query history across all projects with a service account (`parent: "projects/-"` + `creator` filter) and needs latest entries first. Query history has been newest-first since 3.21.0; saved queries had only title order with no way to ask for recency. See BYT-10078 for the decision record (default choice, index economics, review findings).

## Testing

- Full migrator package on real PostgreSQL — 0010 applies and drops cleanly on upgrade; `TestLatestVersion` pins 3.22.10.
- e2e `TestListSavedQueriesOrdering`: default title order stays put through an edit (no row-jumping), `update_time desc` / `create_time desc` / explicit `title` orders through the parser, paginated order across fixed pages, and four malformed `order_by` inputs rejected. `TestListQueryHistories` covers the history path.
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a 300k-row seeded schema: the creator-filtered recency pull is an ordered index scan on the new index with no sort; every other live query shape verified served.
- `golangci-lint` and `buf lint` clean; server build OK.

BYT-10078

title: refactor: drop duplicate query data policy fetch in Query()
body:
## What

`SQLService.Query()` called `getEffectiveQueryDataPolicy` twice against the same workspace and project. This collapses them into one call.

- The first call (`limit=0`) was added by #20390 and only ever read `.AllowAdminDataSource`, to decide whether an auto-resolved DML query may use the admin data source.
- The second call (`limit=request.Limit`) fed `MaximumResultRows` / `MaximumResultSize` / `MaxQueryTimeoutInSeconds` into `db.QueryContext`.

## Why it's safe

The `limit` argument only clamps `MaximumResultRows` — it never touches `AllowAdminDataSource`, which comes straight off the workspace policy. So both calls already returned the same value for the only field the first call site read.

Verified before collapsing:

1. `resolveDataSourceID` takes the flag as a `bool` by value, so it cannot observe the clamped row limit later.
2. Nothing between the two old call sites mutates the policy or `request.Limit` — only `resolveDataSourceID`, `checkAndGetDataSourceQueriable`, `GetDataSourceDriver`, and `sqlDB.Conn`, all reads.
3. Full usage audit: `queryDataPolicy` was read exactly once (`.AllowAdminDataSource`); no other consumer depended on either struct.

One intentional behavior change: the fetch now sits above `startTime := time.Now()`, so the policy read is no longer included in the `"query finished"` / `"request finished"` debug durations. The read is policy-cache-backed, so this is microseconds — it makes the logged number marginally more accurate, not less.

No API, proto, schema, or permission-logic change. Not a breaking change.

## Testing

- `golangci-lint run --allow-parallel-runners` — 0 issues
- `go build -ldflags "-w -s" -p=16 -o ./bytebase-build/bytebase ./backend/bin/server/main.go` — OK
- `go test -count=1 ./backend/api/v1/...` — pass

title: feat(mcp): enforce the workspace capability ceiling on every MCP call (P1b 1b-2)
body:
## What this does

Turns 1b-1's 209 recorded classifications into enforcement. The interceptor that denied `FORBIDDEN` now evaluates the whole rule:

**effective = ceiling ∩ RBAC.** The ceiling admits `READ` under a read-only workspace ceiling and above, `READ` and `WRITE` under read-write, and neither `EXCLUDED` nor `FORBIDDEN` under any ceiling. An unclassified method is refused too. ACL still runs after the gate, unchanged — the gate never grants, only refuses.

It does **not** admit `READ_ONLY` sessions. `mcpConnectionAllowed` is untouched: a read-only session could still write SQL through the query tool until 1b-3 lands the statement clamp, so the connection stays refused. `TestMCPCeilingStoredValueFailsClosed/ws-readonly` pins that, and the same test now also asserts the resolver returns `READ_ONLY` as itself rather than as a fail-closed error, so 1b-3 has a green baseline to flip against.

## Breaking Changes

Enforcing `EXCLUDED` removes 93 operations from what an MCP session can call, and the API index stops advertising them, so 13 services drop off `search_api` entirely: AIService, AuditLogService, GroupService, IdentityProviderService, InstanceRoleService, OrgPolicyService, ProjectService, RoleService, ServiceAccountService, SettingService, SubscriptionService, UserService, WorkloadIdentityService. Chiefly workspace administration, plus the project and instance reads that return stored secrets.

- **Every MCP tool keeps working.** `query_database`, `get_schema` and `propose_database_change` call only READ and WRITE methods; a new test pins that a shipped skill may only instruct calls the ceiling serves.
- **`call_api` still resolves a refused operation by ID**, so a call that arrives from memory meets the gate's actionable denial rather than "unknown operation".
- **The `grant-permission` skill is deleted.** All five operations it drove are EXCLUDED, so after this change it was a playbook whose every step returned 403. The in-product frontend agent keeps its own copy — that one runs on the public chain and is unaffected.
- Eight of the exclusions exist only for a leak (BOT-60 webhook URLs, BOT-61 password hashes, the MFA seed in `GetCurrentUser`). Fixing the leak moves each row to READ as a reviewed widening, and discovery follows automatically. **Worth closing BOT-60/61 before 1b-6 un-gates phase 1** — project and instance reads are what an agent misses first.

## Where the gate sits, and why

Same slot 1b-0 took: `validate → auth → audit → GATE → ACL` on the internal chain. Inside audit so a denial is recorded; outside ACL so the ceiling refuses whatever RBAC would have said, before any handler side effect. The ceiling is read live per request through `store.GetMCPCapabilityUncached` — one resolver, shared with the `/mcp` connection gate, so the two can never disagree. `mcp_forbidden.go` is renamed `mcp_gate.go`; it is no longer the forbidden interceptor.

Streaming is refused wholesale at the gate. A streaming handler gets no reques

body:
Bumps [github.com/moby/go-archive](https://github.com/moby/go-archive) from 0.2.0 to 0.3.0.
Release notes

Sourced from github.com/moby/go-archive's releases.

v0.3.0

Security

This release fixes CVE-2026-17106 / GHSA-hfg8-hc9c-6c3h, where a crafted tar archive could use links to cause extraction operations to create or overwrite files outside the intended destination directory.

The issue affected Unpack, UnpackLayer, Untar, UntarUncompressed, and the ApplyLayer helpers. Users should upgrade and avoid extracting untrusted archives with earlier versions.

What's Changed

  • archive: harden tar extraction against path traversal moby/go-archive#45
  • archive: do not follow reparse points in chtimes moby/go-archive#90
  • archive: fix creation time updates on Windows moby/go-archive#79
  • archive: minor cleanups and godoc touch-up moby/go-archive#87
  • archive: RebaseArchiveEntries: fix archive path rebasing moby/go-archive#43

Test and CI changes

  • ci: enable dependabot for actions moby/go-archive#81
  • archive: make breakoutErr unwrap its cause moby/go-archive#91
  • archive: use filepath for filesystem paths in tests moby/go-archive#80
  • archive: use filepath for filesystem paths in tests moby/go-archive#80

Full Changelog: https://github.com/moby/go-archive/compare/v0.2.1...v0.3.0

v0.2.1

What's Changed

  • reject out-of-range device numbers in layer moby/go-archive#36
  • createImpliedDirectories: fix directory detection and path handling moby/go-archive#44
  • createImpliedDirectories: honor NoLchown for implied directories moby/go-archive#70
  • createTarFile: use switch for timestamp updates

title: fix(redis): classify RedisJSON and other module read commands as read-only
body:
## Problem

Kraken cannot run read-only RedisJSON commands in the SQL Editor. `JSON.GET <key>` is rejected with `invalid_argument: Support read-only command statements only` before it reaches Redis.

The read-only gate classifies a Redis statement by looking its first word up in a hand-written map (`backend/plugin/parser/redis/query.go`). The map only ever covered core Redis, so **every** module command was treated as a write, not just RedisJSON.

The container-command fallback could not cover it either. It expects the subcommand as a *second token* (`XINFO STREAM`), while module commands namespace with a dot *inside one token* (`JSON.GET`). That is why `XINFO STREAM` works and `JSON.GET` cannot.

The same `readOnly` bit feeds five consumers, so the misclassification was never only an error message: the Query gate, the Export gate, JIT access-grant matching (`preCheckAccess`, `access_grant_service`), and read-only-vs-admin data-source routing (`requiresAdminDataSource`). Fixing the map corrects all five.

## Changes

- **`moduleReadCommands`** — 54 read commands across RedisJSON, RedisTimeSeries, RedisBloom and RediSearch.
- **4 core read commands** the map had drifted past: `HTTL`, `HPTTL`, `HEXPIRETIME`, `HPEXPIRETIME` (Redis 7.4).
- **`SELECT` removed.** The driver pins the connection to the DB index from the request, then pipelines every line onto that one connection, so `select 3` followed by a read escaped the database the request was authorized against. Verified: `CLIENT INFO` reports `db=3`, and a probe write lands in db3.
- **`TestReadCommandsMatchServerFlags`** — diffs the core map against `testdata/core_readonly_commands.txt`, a snapshot of the server's own `COMMAND INFO` `readonly` flags, pinned by image digest. A Redis upgrade that ships new read commands now fails in CI instead of reaching a customer.

## The list is curated, not generated — on purpose

The server's `readonly` flag means "does not write the keyspace", not "has no side effects". Confirmed on the live server: `FT.ALIASADD`, `FT.DICTADD`, `FT.DICTDEL`, `FT.CONFIG`, `FT.CURSOR`, `CF.COMPACT` and `BF.SCANDUMP` are all flagged `readonly` while mutating index, dictionary, config or filter state. They stay out, as do the modules' internal cluster commands.

## Security finding caught while pre-reviewing this branch

An earlier revision of this PR also added `EVAL_RO`, `EVALSHA_RO` and `FCALL_RO`, because the server flags them `readonly`. That was wrong, and it would have reopened the hole the `SELECT` removal closes.

Read-only script mode rejects only commands flagged `write`. Lua still reaches `SELECT` and every readonly-flagged module command that mutates state. Verified on redis-stack-server 7.4.7, run against database 0:

```
EVAL_RO "redis.call('SELECT',1); return redis.call('GET','marker')" 0
  -> db1-secret          (database 0 holds db0-secret)

EVAL_RO "return redis.call('FT.DICTADD','d1','term')" 0
  -> 1                   FT.DICTDUMP d1 -> term
EVAL_RO "return r
